item.title: [a16z] Building the Cloud for AI Agents | AWS CEO Matt Garman
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：AWS 的"过度工程"正在成为 Agent 时代的新摩擦

Matt Garman 承认了一件行业里几乎没人公开讲的事：AWS 的核心服务对 agent 来说"过度工程"了。一个 agent 要创建数据库、跑一会儿、就扔掉——但 Aurora 默认给你 5 个 9 的持久性。这是人类工程师二十年来视为圣杯的东西，现在变成了 agent 的"负担"。

更深一层的洞察是：整个云计算的价值主张正在悄悄反转。过去二十年云的叙事是"你享受不到的高可用性，我们帮你享受到"；而 agent 时代的叙事变成"你并不需要的高可用性，能不能便宜一点、快一点消失？"。AWS 的护城河——那些花了十年打磨的 durability、availability、consistency——第一次成了被 agent workflow 挑剔的对象。这是基础设施行业罕见的"价值降级"信号：不是技术变弱了，而是客户的时间尺度从"系统寿命"坍缩到了"任务寿命"。

二、跨领域连接：Firecracker 的"意外复用"是技术史上一个被低估的模式

Garman 轻描淡写地提到：十年前为 Lambda 发明的 Firecracker microVM，现在"意外地"成了所有 agent sandbox 公司的底层。这个故事可以和两个完全不同领域的历史并置：

  • GPS 原本是军用导航，三十年后养活了 Uber、Pokémon Go 和整个外卖经济；
  • mRNA 技术原本是治癌症的失败路线，十年后扛住了全球疫情。

共同的模式是：一项技术的"真正市场"几乎总在它被发明的用例之外。Firecracker 的设计目标是"函数级多租户隔离"，而 agent 需要的恰好是"快速启停 + 安全边界 + 低虚拟化开销"——这是同一组技术属性的不同叙事包装。

隐藏的系统性真相是：AWS 真正的复合优势不是任何单一服务，而是"组件库的组合熵"。它拥有的不是 200 个产品，而是 200 个可以被未来十年尚未出现的 workload 重新排列的乐高块。Nitro 卡→Graviton→Tranium 这条链就是同一张"隔离卡"的三次重投胎。

三、被忽略的权力转移：当"IAM 配置"从创业门槛变成创业死刑

Garman 几乎是不经意地说：现在新建 AWS 账户不用信用卡、不用 VPC、不用 IAM，用 Gmail 30 秒搞定。听起来是小改进，但背后是一次深刻的权力转移。

二十年来，云厂商的"复杂配置"是一道隐形的筛子——它让专业工程师比业余玩家更有价值，让大企业的技术团队有存在的理由。而当 agent 替用户填配置时，AWS 发现：这道筛子正在从"护城河"变成"流失漏斗"。创业者的第一个 prompt 是"帮我部署一个 app"，agent 会选择阻力最小的那条路——Vercel、Railway、Cloudflare——而不是让它去啃 IAM 文档。

这里的"啊哈时刻"是：AI 不只是在替代开发者，更在重新定价"复杂度"。过去复杂度=专业壁垒=高毛利；现在复杂度=agent 摩擦=默认流失。AWS 正在做的，是把二十年积累的"深度"藏到一个"看起来像 Heroku"的入口后面——这是一种罕见的、自我降维的战略勇气。

四、补充的隐藏信号：资本支出已经进入"物理学定价"阶段

$220B 的 2026 capex 不是财务数字，而是物理学数字。Garman 列出的瓶颈序列——电力→变压器→HBM→TSMC→施工工人→连接器——其形态和二战时期美国的战时物资调度惊人相似。当瓶颈从"钱"下沉到"原子"，云计算就不再是软件行业，而是一门与化工、电网、造船并列的重工业。VC 们还在用 SaaS 的毛利模型估值 AI infra，但 AWS 内部已经在用"核电站规划周期"做 2028 的决策——这个认知错位，可能是未来三年最大的套利窗口。

📝 转录文本

Building the Cloud for AI Agents | AWS CEO Matt Garman

开场金句

Agentic workflows tend to perform better on AWS than anywhere else. Compute sandboxes, gateways, agent permissions versus people — a lot of those are things that we have built and are building and thinking actively about.

The top frontier labs gobble up every available GPUs. At the same time, you want to promote newer companies that are going to become the enterprises of tomorrow. How are you thinking about balancing?

From the very beginning of when we launched AWS, startups have been the lifeblood of the core of what we do. These are the innovators that are at the edge of technology understanding what's possible. We're very intentional about keeping capacity available for the startups. We recently announced we're going to be buying 2 million NVIDIA GPUs over the next couple of years.

Your capex is what 200 or — $220 billion for '26, and we don't anticipate slowing down anytime soon because the demand is just massive.

With all the debate around AI extension risk and the Hugging Face attack, what are CEOs asking you about all these things?

一、AWS 的起点与规模

Welcome to the podmat. What a time we're living in. So I have a lot of topics to talk to you about.

Awesome. Thanks for having me. I'm excited. Yeah. Absolutely.

So let's start actually right from the beginning, right? So you are the first GM for EC2 — and that was 2006, right? And today you guys are what, 160, 170 billion in revenue?

Yeah. About 169, 170 billion. Yep.

Growing 37%. That's 37% at 169. Yeah, it's — it's crazy.

There's a ton of — and it's — yeah, it's interesting to think about it from, you know, we're there in day day day one when we had the first dollar of revenue. And the interesting thing is we're still at the early stages of what the business can be and what the opportunity is for customers. Most workloads still — there's a huge amount of workloads still that live on-prem today, and the amount of compute that people are doing every single day is more than it was the day before. So you see the tailwind from AI, you see the tailwind from migration into the cloud, and the business has grown really fast. It's been a super fun thing to be a part of.

Yeah, it is. They'll be writing history books and business books about this for a long time to come. I want to touch on the on-prem thing — that sort of boggles my mind. I obviously did my best to keep them there for a long time. You built a lot of stuff on-prem back in the day; now trying to get all of that to move into AWS. So we can talk about that later.

二、从第一天起，创业公司就是 AWS 的"命脉"

So if you think about EC2 in the early days — you got your start selling to startups — and today the AWS cloud service, as you reflect on the evolution, what stands out? Then part two: how has the nature of how you serve startups changed?

Sure. Well, like you said, actually it's funny — I actually interned for AWS in 2005 when it was first kind of an internal project. It was my business school internship, and my project was to come up with an analysis of who we thought AWS would be most interesting to. And the answer was: startups. Probably not surprisingly.

So from the very beginning of when we launched AWS, startups have been the lifeblood of the core of what we do, for a number of reasons. One is: the value proposition is just so attractive — what AWS provides to startups. We spend a lot of time and effort making sure that we're great partners to the startups, helping them not just provide infrastructure but also advice on how to get your company up and running, how to think about your architecture so it'll scale eventually — a whole bunch of things that we do for the startups.

But we also think that for us, it's just good business — because the startups today are the enterprises of tomorrow. It's an imprecise number, but today we estimate that maybe 30–40% of AWS revenue comes from companies that were at one time startups in AWS's lifetime. So it's fun for us to see the companies grow over time and become enterprises effectively.

That's why we invest so much in startups and why we pay so much attention to the brand-new, two-people-in-a-garage type startups — not just because of the business outcomes, but also because that's who we learn from. These are the innovators at the edge of technology, understanding what's possible, pushing our services to say what they'd want more of, what could help them go faster. A lot of times they're pushing more than the banks or the healthcare companies or the governments. The startups are the ones pushing that envelope. And it really helps us to be ahead of the wave — where the banks are going to want some capability five years down the road that startups want today.

三、创业公司的变与不变

Yeah. Compared from then to now, how have startups changed in what they want from you? Obviously they all want a lot of GPUs — we can talk about that — but besides that?

A couple of things have changed. One: startups used to start at a much smaller size. They might have gotten $10 million of funding and had an app idea they were slowly iterating on. Now, from day one, they're valued at a billion dollars, they have $200 million of funding — it's a team and an idea, and all of a sudden they're worth a billion dollars. They just go from our offices to your offices. That's right.

The size and scale and ambition of the ideas requires more capital. They're bigger to start with. They're obviously more expensive too — to go after training a model or doing something a lot of the folks are doing today.

But some things haven't changed. They still think about: once I scale, how do I think about architecture? Security? Performance? Having all the capabilities I need? Setting up my IAM so that when I have more than three employees, this thing is going to work and scale. Which is a lot of times why they like AWS as opposed to going to a neocloud — they actually need all those security and capabilities that come around.

Increasingly, we're seeing teams that want a cloud that is great to work with agents, not just with people. We've spent a lot of time on: how do you think about broad scale? Performance? A well-defined API interface that agents can easily traverse and work across? We were naturally set up to do this well, but we've actually doubled down — things like, how can you start a database in 3 seconds and really get to capabilities that agents are excited about?

四、为 agent 优化：从 S3 Context 到尾延迟

Have you introduced any specific new services explicitly targeted at agents?

What we've done is optimize some existing services so they can work for both people and agents. We definitely have some services designed for building agents — like AgentCore and Bedrock. But when we look at an underlying component like S3, where the vast majority of companies store their data and have their data lakes, it turns out a lot of the use cases for people and agents are similar.

One of the things we have in preview right now, in beta, is called AWS Context — it allows you to build a context layer so that agents can more easily find all the data they want across your various data lakes. Whether you have your data stored in Aurora, S3, or somewhere else in AWS, you can build this context layer. People aren't necessarily going to access data that way, but agents are happy to go across lots of those different things.

For the most part, you also care about latency, throughput, how to make sure the underlying engine is fast and scalable. Agents care a lot about tail latencies — which is interesting. People don't always care about P99.9 S3 latency, but agents do care and get blocked by it. That's a thing we've cared about for a long time, and from a performance perspective it's one of the things that really popped — that's why agentic workflows tend to perform better on AWS than anywhere else.

五、Agent 写代码时代，"legacy 服务"要重新架构吗？

Obviously we see a lot of companies starting out and the very common refrain is that agents are writing all the code for them, agents are selecting the databases and email servers. Has there been a lot of thinking at AWS on how to re-architect your "quote-unquote legacy" services that have been around for a decade?

I think there are some things we've thought about. The core underlying building blocks are in really good shape. There's a usability layer we're thinking about — how to make it easier for the simplest use case, where somebody is coding up an app really quickly and asks it to deploy.

We find the vast majority of our customers will tell their coding agent — whether it's Kiro, Claude, or Codex — "I want to build on AWS, here's my credentials, here's my stuff, this is how I want to deploy it." And the agents go do it.

There are use cases where you're not on a cloud yet, you're just trying something. You say "deploy." Frankly, a lot of times that'll go to some of our partners that have an easier-to-use layer on top. Which we love — we love our partners on those fronts.

But if you're brand new, you don't already have an AWS account, you haven't set up your IAM — a couple of months ago, it was much harder to start up an account. You had to define your VPCs, your IAM roles, all these kinds of things, which are super important things once you get to be large. What we hear from customers is that it was a hard trade-off — they know they'll want those n months or years down the line, but for now they just want to use the services.

So we've launched this: if you go create a new AWS account today — we're slowly rolling it out — you don't have to do those things. You don't have to give it a credit card. You can sign up with your Gmail account. All of those things are handled in default behind the scenes. Within less than 30 seconds, you're up and running and operating in a full AWS account.

And the great part is: it's not a simplistic account where you have to migrate. If you say, "okay, now I actually do want to scale into the organization, I want to fine-tune some things" — you're already in a real AWS account, you can go do all those things later when you need them. There's no migration or move later. That's part of the hard work: how do we make it not a choice for the customer, but an easy on-ramp into the depth of features we know startups will want when they start scaling.

六、"过度工程"的 agent 困境与新原语

What has been some of the hardest things to accommodate as agents have taken over?

Much of our infrastructure was pretty well set up to handle the scale. But there have been interesting paradigm shifts where you could argue some of our systems are — I wouldn't say over-engineered — but:

As an example, many agents want to create a database, do a little bit of work, and then have the database go away. You really need that database to have five 9's of durability? Exactly. When you're creating an Aurora database as your production database, you do want five 9's — durability, availability. For the agent use case, that's arguably over-engineered.

We don't really want to have a non-durable option that's going to cause problems — because you never quite know if the database that's created wants to stay around for a long time or a short amount of time. So we're trying to do the hard work to think about how do you accomplish both: create it quickly and throw it away without wasting resources, but if you do want it durable and long-lived, it can grow into a big production database.

Scale, speed, and latency of creation of durable resources is another one that's interesting.

The other thing we actively think about: are there new building blocks that agents want that we just didn't need before? Compute sandboxes, gateways, agent permissions versus people or service role permissions — a lot of those are brand-new building blocks. You want different permissions for agents. You don't just want to give it Ragu's permissions and let it go do whatever you can do. You actually want time-boxed, short-term permissions to just go do a task. You may not want to give it permissions to a whole tool at all. You may want very fine-grained permissions.

Firecracker 的意外复用

From a sandbox perspective — virtualization is having its act too. That's right. Similar idea, but how do you have it lightweight?

Fortunately, we've done a lot of work with Firecracker, our microVMs. In fact, a lot of the sandbox company startups use Firecracker. They all use Firecracker — which we invented 10 years ago, maybe. It's really purpose-built for — I mean, it wasn't purpose-built for agents, but it's actually quite good for agents because you can spin them up really rapidly. They have a great security boundary, and you don't have a lot of the virtualization overhead you have from a traditional large VM.

七、GPU 的分配艺术：$220B capex 与"60% 的 yes"

Every startup asks us: how can we get GPUs? The top frontier labs gobble up every available GPU. How are you balancing capacity needs with smaller companies that don't have a lot of credit?

A couple of things make it more challenging. One: the capex expense needed to deploy the compute everyone needs right now is massive. $220 billion for '26. At one point, I saw that it's a larger expense than we've ever had — maybe any company has ever had — in a single year. We don't anticipate slowing down anytime soon because the demand is massive.

At some point you're limited by: how fast can you build data centers, deploy capital, get memory and chips? Power, data centers, capital, memory, chips — they're all constraints at various times. Construction people are at a premium today.

With the capacity we are able to deploy — which is still a huge amount, and not enough — we think intentionally about the allocation strategy. We're great partners with the large frontier labs: the Anthropics, OpenAIs, Metas. Those folks are really good customers of ours. We have large enterprise customers — Salesforces, JPMCs — that have demand for fewer GPUs, or accelerators (sometimes Trainium, sometimes NVIDIA).

We could sell every single GPU or AI accelerator we have to probably just the big frontier labs and call it a day. We choose not to do that because we actually want to keep growing the full ecosystem. They get a large number, but we want to keep supporting a broader set of customers — the whole ecosystem will be more healthy, there's diversification, and we know these are going to be big companies over time.

I saw recently that we say "yes" in some way, shape, or form to something like 60% of the requests we eventually get. Sometimes it's a little bit later, sometimes it's in a different region, sometimes a slightly different configuration than the customer was looking for. But we really try to lean in and allocate as much as we can.

We recently announced we're going to be buying 2 million NVIDIA GPUs over the next couple of years. It's a lot — and who knows if that's enough. We're limited by other components as well. But we're very intentional about keeping capacity available for startups.

八、Capex 的历史曲线与"泡沫"问题

When did AWS capex cross — let's say 1 billion or 10 billion a year?

Oh, I don't know. I'd have to go back and look. But it's definitely scaled up over the last couple of years. The AI buildout has ramped our capex spending. Over the last 3 or 4 years, our capex has accelerated pretty meaningfully. Given we're 220 now, we've been spending capex for a while, and the company has been really good about funding that. Obviously the AWS business is one we like to invest in.

For the longest time, we were investing ahead of where the demand was. One of the most painful things is that with the real ramp of GPUs, a lot of the elasticity has unfortunately gone away. Hopefully we'll get back to that in our core compute and storage.

对"AI 泡沫"的回应

I get lots of questions about how I feel about that spend — are you nervous about a bubble?

Because of the position we have: we take this diversified approach. Not all our capacity is bundled up in one customer. If you go to some neoclouds or other providers, you'll see concentrations of 30, 40, 50, 60% with one or two customers. We're nowhere near that — we're in single-digit percentages at the highest, usually less than that for one. We have a lot less risk on one particular customer.

Also, because of our rich set of services, AWS is where people really come to launch their production workloads. The majority of our usage today is core compute, storage, and inference. Those workloads aren't going to go away. You go talk to the customers and say: at the capability today and the cost today, are you seeing positive returns to your business? Almost to a person, they say "oh yeah." That's not going to go away.

Is every billion-dollar startup going to make it? No, they won't. But that's the game — it's been true for 50 years. The numbers have changed, but the principles are the same: you bet on 10, and one makes it and pays for the other 10. You saw that with the internet — a bubble, a bunch of companies didn't make it, and the internet's still a thing. The Googles, Amazons, and others with durable businesses did pretty well.

九、规划 2028：从兆瓦到核电厂

As the scale of these numbers goes larger and larger, has your planning process dramatically changed?

Yes and no. There are things that have completely changed. How do you even estimate 2028 demand?

If you go back 15 years, if we needed more power, we asked the power company for another couple of megawatts. They'd just give it to us because 10 megawatts wasn't that much. That was plenty for us to keep growing. Now, we bring our own power. We pay for power projects. We pay for renewable projects. We're one of the biggest renewable power purchasers each year for the last 10 years. We're regularly bringing on new solar projects, new nuclear projects.

Behind the meter, or working with the operator? We'll do both. Often with these power projects, we'll pay the capital and pay for the project, then it goes into the grid and we get credit. Sometimes we'll do behind the meter too. At the scale we're doing, you have to think about all of those things.

But that's planning where you're thinking 20 years out — power, transmission, capital. That's stuff we never had to think about before.

The other thing: when we used to think about server demand, we'd have multiple-quarter demand plans and talk with our suppliers. Now we work multiple years out, because the size is so much — what do we need for '26, '27, '28?

That's one of the real values we bring to customers: they're not going to do power, they're not going to plan their memory footprint in 2028. They can't do that. That's a whole set of things you don't have to worry about, and that we spend a huge amount of time thinking about.

十、"永远有新瓶颈"：从《The Goal》到供应链韧性

Where do you see constraints being most severe in '27, '28?

I'll answer this in a roundabout way. In undergrad we read "The Goal" — I never thought this would be a useful book, but it turns out: there's never one constraint, there's always just the latest constraint. You have to think about all of them. As soon as you hit one, there's another one.

Every month for us: do you have enough power? As soon as power is no longer the constraint, it might be memory, TSMC capacity, HBM, networking components. There's a blip somewhere in the supply chain — connectors, whatever. At some point you have to think about all those pieces.

Where they happen matters too. We may have a ton of power in Indonesia, but not enough in Germany. Not everything is totally fungible. Some is, some's not. Might be disc drives, SSDs — we think about every single component. We have tens, hundreds of thousands of components we track.

We saw this problem coming probably a decade ago and started thinking all the way through the supply chain — four tiers, five tiers down — what's the component that could cause an issue? Making sure we had guaranteed supply. Remember when there were the floods in Thailand and no one had disc drives anymore? Disc drive crises, memory crises. We think about diversification in manufacturing. We're never going to be perfect, but there's always a different supply constraint.

十一、数据中心的"沉默税收": $5,000 的隐形红利

There's a lot of wide-ranging debate about data centers. Do you think as an industry we have not done a good job of explaining why data centers are good for America and the world?

I think we need to be more vocal and more upfront. We actually do a ton that's really beneficial — both for the communities we operate in and more broadly. We think about renewable energy, being water positive. Our data centers use a really small amount of water; we mostly use free air cooling. We think about being great participants in the communities where we operate — bringing high-paying jobs.

Not all data center operators do that. There are some well-chronicled examples of others that are not great — they don't pay attention to regulations, think the rules don't apply, launch quickly without thinking about those. That causes problems for the whole industry because everybody gets lumped into that.

We need to be more clear about the benefits we bring. I recently saw a report where in one of the communities we operate in, everybody in that county pays $5,000 a year less in taxes because of the taxes we bring to that community. And we don't tell them. They don't even know it. It's invisible.

If you told the communities "by the way, your tax bill is $5,000 less than it would otherwise be if we weren't here," they might have a different thought about the building that's over there.

Much of the data center community, not just us, is actually pretty good actors. There are just a few that aren't, and that's caused some of the angst recently. We need to do a better job of highlighting who's being good citizens and who's not.

十二、自研芯片史：从 Nitro 到 Graviton 到 Trainium

I want to touch on silicon. We were one of your first partners using Nitro a long time ago. Since then, Graviton — tremendous progress. What was the thinking that led to doing your own thing?

It's a fascinating story and a great example of where AWS will innovate, iterate, and continue to think bigger — but prove our way there.

Nitro 的起源

About 13–14 years ago, we were seeing a pretty significant virtualization tax on the overall number of resources. Customers were telling us: I want bare-metal performance. So the first thing we did: we took a network offload card and virtualized all of our network virtualization off onto that card. So network virtualization got closer to bare-metal performance.

We got excited and said: what if we could move storage virtualization off as well? None of the network offload cards could do that. Then we found this one company who had some ARM cores on an offload card — they were doing it for other reasons, I can't remember their original purpose — but we said: could you use those to do storage virtualization and some other functions? They said: maybe. We iterated with them. This was the product. This was the team. We just loved that team — really innovative, really mission-driven. So we acquired them.

We said: could you build us a slightly bigger card that could take all the network virtualization off and basically give us a bare-metal server with no virtualization on it, no VM virtualization — everything through APIs on the card? We had this view that performance would be much better, resource utilization would be better, security isolation would be much better. We could legitimately tell people: we have no access to any of your VMs running there.

This has been a huge benefit for us for the last decade. Frankly, we've been leading, and others have been slow to do this — because this isn't a generalized thing that people can do.

Graviton: ARM 的下赌注

There were a bunch of ARM cores on this offload card. We said: what if we turn that into a server? We did that first with Graviton. It was a very underpowered, very small server that we launched. Customers were excited — "I'd love to have an ARM server, this is super interesting."

Part of what we did: we looked at the slope — ARM cores were getting faster, and the graph showed power utilization. You knew the intercept was going to happen where this architecture would be really good. They just needed somebody to drive the ecosystem and get the pieces in place.

Graviton has been a runaway hit. We land more Graviton ships every year than any other type. It's very popular. They're 20% cheaper at 20% better performance — and have been like that for the last five, six years. That's an easy value proposition. The vast majority — something like 90-plus percent — of our top 100 customers all use Graviton in some way, shape, or form.

For customers, it's the single easiest way to lower their bill: move to Graviton. We've had examples where people moved their whole fleets and cut the number of servers they had in half. The performance is so much better. Half the number of servers, each server costs less — it's a big win.

Trainium: 从训练到推理之王

Five, six years ago, we saw the rise of AI compute happening — not expecting what it was today, but still saw it was going to be a big material mover. We built our first chip, Trainium. We're now in market with the third generation, Trainium 3, and have seen fantastic results. We're sold out on capacity through probably towards the end of next year. We're trying to figure out how we can save some capacity for startups.

The majority of traffic on Bedrock runs on Trainium. We have great deals with both Anthropic and OpenAI to build on top of Trainium, as well as a set of smaller startups — half a dozen to a dozen building on Trainium now.

The name suggests it's a training chip, but everybody's using it for inference. We're vocally self-critical: we're terrible at naming. Originally we had a chip called Inferentia for inference and Trainium for training. As the models got bigger, it turns out you actually want to run the inference on these really large systems — and Trainium is actually maybe the best inference chip on the market right now from an absolute performance and cost-performance point of view.

It's just that the architecture is a little different, and it's much cheaper. We use it a ton for inference — it drives much of the Bedrock inference today. But it's also a good training chip. A lot of our broad set of customers' usage is not in training models but in using it — that's where a lot of people get to use it under the covers. The big customers are interested in it for training clusters too. Particularly as you get to Trainium 3 and 4 — we've announced but haven't launched Trainium 4 — folks have looked at that architecture and said "yeah, that's the future of where I want my training clusters to be as well."

十三、企业采用 Agent 的现状与两道瓶颈

Where are enterprises in their adoption of agents? What benefits are they reaping?

Enterprises are getting a lot of value out of what they've done today. But the agents most enterprises have built are relatively simple, straightforward, and mostly non-autonomous — still kind of people-in-the-loop. Customers are still getting lots of value.

They're thinking about: how do I have these be autonomous, but in a safe way? I think there are two things holding customers back:

瓶颈一：别照搬人类工作流

Originally, enterprises had a workflow and said: great, I'd have an agent do the same workflow. What we encourage them to do is not just replicate. "Bob does steps 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, so the agent is going to do steps 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and then Bob's going to check it at the end" — that's not really the model you want.

Step back and ask: if I want to accomplish something, how can an agent do it differently? It can do it in a massively parallelized way. It can try 50 different things. Rethink how a computer would solve a problem versus a human solving a problem.

That's where you really get value — not just replicating what you're doing today, but thinking from a greenfield approach. I'm sure that's how many of your startups are thinking about this: how do you help customers greenfield-solve a problem, not replicate the thing that happens today?

瓶颈二：信任与自主性

How do you turn those into fully autonomous workflows? How do you actually trust the agents?

We're spending a lot of time building services to help enterprises feel like their systems are secure and that they can trust an agent to make a decision — that they have the right guardrails, the right permissions on their data, that it's not going to delete production systems, that it's not going to make tragic mistakes. That nervousness is probably holding people back — maybe appropriately — from just saying "okay, go nuts." You don't want an agent to just go crazy and accidentally delete a production database. That's going to be pretty bad.

Evals 的新前沿

Are enterprises learning how to do eval systems? They need help, honestly. Both evals — how do you have a constant loop of testing? How do you think about goal-seeking in a reasonable way? How do you have your data labeled so the eval can approximate what you'll be doing in production? How do you measure in production and back-test so you're not seeing drift?

All of those things are problems enterprises don't know how to solve today. I don't think anyone really is great at solving these today. That's why you've seen so many FDE (forward-deployed engineer) teams spin up. AWS and our partners are really leaning into the FDE motion. This is the single biggest area where customers need help.

My view: we want to train our customers to be able to do this themselves. This is not the traditional notion where I want a people-driven business that goes on forever where you just keep paying consultants. Our view on how FDE should work: we go into a customer who's ready to accept owning this when we're done — and in 45 days we do work where we teach them how to make an eval, how to get their data labeled, do work alongside them. At the end of 45 days, you leave, and that customer is good and ready to go and trained up.

十四、数据主权与开源模型：Bedrock 的押注

Some of your industry peers have said: you can't have all your data going into a big frontier model. Enterprises should take an open-source model and post-train on their own data. Where do you stand?

I wholeheartedly agree on the first point. Enterprise data is their most valuable asset. That's why we built Bedrock the way we did. We guarantee that your data never leaves your VPC. If you're running inside Bedrock, your data doesn't go back to the model provider. They never see your prompts. That stays inside your own trusted environment.

Enterprises prefer to run on top of Bedrock. That's why you see that business growing massively — hundreds and hundreds. Every week we see that business exploding. It's why you see OpenAI workloads migrating to Bedrock. It's why you see Anthropic really growing rapidly.

Whether you're using open models or closed frontier models, Bedrock is a great solution. Three years ago I got a lot of heat — speaking of bad names, Bedrock is actually a good one — we got a lot of heat for being slow to the AI world. We built the foundations where we said: we're not just going to rush out a service. We want to think about how we make sure we protect our customers' data and build a service that's going to be durable. Now as people move from proof-of-concepts to production, the vast majority are landing in AWS on Bedrock — because of this, and because of the set of services we have.

We offer open models, proprietary models, a whole set of capabilities around AgentCore. We build these building blocks so it's easier to build agents with any of the models you want — whether they're in Bedrock or out of Bedrock (you can use Gemini or other things). But having that data go back into the model provider is a dangerous thing.

开源权重与 SageMaker 的新生

On open-weights models — it's an area I'm excited about. We're really ramping up our support of open-weights models. A lot of customers believe they have meaningful proprietary data that, if they could mix in — do some post-training, do some fine-tuning on an open-weights model, distill it down — they could actually get a better-performing model at a lower price.

A bunch of pieces have to work out well. They actually have to have a good eval to prove that's true. Most people are doing that in SageMaker today. I think there's more we can do to make that easier. But if you go look at where people are doing that, they do it in SageMaker on AWS today, and they host the inference via SageMaker.

SageMaker is getting a new lease on life — it was always kind of a model-building platform, and now, if you think about what enterprises are doing in this world, they're basically building their own custom models. SageMaker is a great place for doing that. There are things we need to keep building on to make it easier — testing across different open-weights models and so on. It's an evolving space.

十五、AI 时代的安全：从威胁到武器

With all the debate around AI extension risk, security vulnerabilities, the Hugging Face attack — what are CEOs asking you about?

A lot — and they mostly want to say: when I launch agents, how can I trust that they'll do what I want them to do? We're heavily investing in capabilities that allow people to deploy agents safely into their environment. How do you make sure the agents have the right permissions? Right sandboxing? Right guardrails? Is there a human in the loop or not?

The other angle people worry about: are some of these really powerful models going to be attack vectors? That is a real risk — but it's also a real opportunity.

We recently launched a service called Continuum that uses these powerful models to help customers secure their environment. We'll look across their environment, look for vulnerabilities, use some of these powerful models to help customers find vulnerabilities they haven't found before — and most importantly, prioritize which ones, because we know context about their environment, how it's set up, where their permissions are, where they may have compensating controls that make it harder or easier to exploit.

Continuum is incredibly popular with customers. We're bullish about what's possible from AI-powered security. At some point, customers are going to need security at machine speed, not human speed — not at "an alarm goes off and someone goes to look at it."

十六、AWS 内部的 Agent 实践

What's the state of adoption/usage of agents inside AWS itself?

Continuum is basically us trying to expose what we do internally. We use AI extensively for our own security, our own software development, and we use agents across our entire business.

We rolled out Amazon Q to every single Amazon employee. Now I see HR teams building agents to drive what used to take teams of people weeks to do — that a single person can now do in a couple of hours — thinking about team planning and resource management. I have finance teams building agents to pull tax rules from everywhere and ensure compliance across different pieces.

Super cool to see: things that used to be blocked by software developers — actually the line-of-business folks are able to unblock themselves and innovate more quickly. Q has been an enormous — it's grown like wildfire. Small startups all the way to the largest enterprises in the world are rolling it out to their entire employee base.

最大的收益：软件开发

Where have you seen the biggest gains?

Obviously, the answer is software development. The speed of software development — and really product development as a whole, not just coding — the cadence at which we're deploying new products is massively different than in the past.

AWS has always been known for rolling out features really quickly. We've seen a turbo boost on that in the last year or so as we — we call them "frontier teams" — think about agentic development as opposed to traditional development. It's not code completion; it really is agent-first. The agents write all of the code; you're just managing a team of agents and driving that.

The pace at which innovations for customers come out has been massive. And it has to be — our customers have an almost insatiable appetite for new capabilities.

十七、组织形态的实验：从团队到 Pod

Organizationally, are you noticing how organizations should change — agents managing people, people managing agents?

There are going to be lots of people for a long period of time. I do think organizations will change. I don't know the magic answer yet, but we're actively thinking.

We're trying experiments. We're thinking about pods. One example: in a product organization, you used to have a team that owned a particular capability for a long time — you might have 10 people working on that thing. Today, you can innovate so rapidly that it doesn't have to be 10 people. It can be three to four people. They build something so fast that you actually want to move them to different projects and problems.

How do you both operate and maintain the things you've built while being agile and flexible to move around? In an organization as big as AWS, these are active things we're experimenting with. It's fun and enabling for our employees — they love it because they can build faster and do more. But there's real work there.

收尾

It's a fascinating time, and thank you very much for your time. We could be talking about this for hours — but thanks for all your insights.

Thank you for having me. We love having all your companies as customers, and we love learning from them. I appreciate having me here.

We'll keep sending them your way.

Excellent. Thank you.

Thanks.

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：AWS 的"过度工程"正在成为 Agent 时代的新摩擦
Matt Garman 承认了一件行业里几乎没人公开讲的事：**AWS 的核心服务对 agent 来说"过度工程"了**。一个 agent 要创建数据库、跑一会儿、就扔掉——但 Aurora 默认给你 5 个 9 的持久性。这是人类工程师二十年来视为圣杯的东西，现在变成了 agent 的"负担"。
更深一层的洞察是：**整个云计算的价值主张正在悄悄反转**。过去二十年云的叙事是"你享受不到的高可用性，我们帮你享受到"；而 agent 时代的叙事变成"你并不需要的高可用性，能不能便宜一点、快一点消失？"。AWS 的护城河——那些花了十年打磨的 durability、availability、consistency——第一次成了被 agent workflow 挑剔的对象。这是基础设施行业罕见的"价值降级"信号：不是技术变弱了，而是客户的时间尺度从"系统寿命"坍缩到了"任务寿命"。
## 二、跨领域连接：Firecracker 的"意外复用"是技术史上一个被低估的模式
Garman 轻描淡写地提到：十

item.title: [Odds on Open] Ex-Goldman MD: "Credit Markets Move in Step Functions"
item.dc:creator: Odds on Open
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、信贷市场的"阶跃函数"：被忽视的物理学直觉

Jeff 作为哥伦比亚物理系出身的人，用"step function"（阶跃函数）形容信贷市场的运行方式——这不是随口的比喻，而是一种相变思维。信贷市场平时像临界态的沙堆，看起来稳定，但压力积累到某个阈值时会瞬间崩塌、重新组织。这与自组织临界性（Self-Organized Criticality）惊人地吻合：地震、森林火灾、神经元雪崩、心脏骤停，背后都是同一种数学。

令人意外的观察：Jeff 的整个职业生涯其实是在"反物理直觉"中前行——物理学家接受训练去寻找平滑的微分方程，但他真正发家的洞见却是识别"不连续点"。2007 年 Valentine's Day 的 ABX 从 8bp 到 12bp 看似渐进，但他回看时意识到那只是雪崩前最后一粒沙。真正的信贷 PM 不是在预测价格，而是在识别系统已经进入"自组织临界态"的信号。他现在反复提到美国财政赤字、民粹主义时的焦虑，就是同一种直觉：系统已经临界，只是不知道哪粒沙是最后一粒。

二、"末期分布"：CMBS 的衰老生物学

Jeff 对商业地产贷款的描述里，藏着一个被所有人低估的洞见：一笔 10 年期 CMBS 贷款的 50%–75% 的生命里"相当无聊"，但最后 25% 决定一切。这不就是人类寿命的"压缩发病率"（compressed morbidity）吗？——Gompertz 曲线告诉我们，死亡率在生命末期指数级攀升。老年病学家 James Fries 发现，大多数人一生的医疗费用集中在最后两年；而 Jeff 的整个基金策略，本质上就是做"CMBS 的老年病医生"：别人想在壮年时赚利差，他专门在债券的"临终阶段"进场提供流动性。

跨领域连接：这个"末期集中"模式还出现在：企业并购（估值溢价集中在 earn-out 期）、政治任期（跛脚鸭现象）、恒星演化（主序星平稳 90 亿年，然后在最后几百万年里把所有有趣的事都干完）。他真正的 edge 不是信贷专业知识，而是选择了一个"末期回报极度非对称"的生态位——而大型 PE 基金的组织结构根本无法在印第安纳波利斯的 3000 万美元贷款上部署高带宽注意力。这是一个被大基金的"规模诅咒"系统性让出的生态位。

三、"不要搞砸"文化 vs. "100 个 no 里有 1 个 yes"：两套截然不同的效用函数

Jeff 对高盛经验最诚实的描述是："the mentality is don't screw up"（心态就是别搞砸）。然后他离开后发现，LP 融资的世界是"99 个 no 中找 1 个 yes"。这不是风格差异，而是两套根本不同的效用函数：高盛是左偏（避免负尾），创业是右偏（追求正尾）。

让你意外的观察：Jeff 没意识到他自己身上这两种 DNA 的冲突，正好塑造了他基金的奇怪定位——他想用"右偏创业者"的身份，运行一个"左偏高盛人"的产品。他反复强调"低方差 + 高均值"、"80–90% 把握才下注"、"仓位不超过 50–100 bp"——这些都是左偏思维。他的基金本质上是用创业者的勇气去兜售机构投资者需要的低方差回报。这个张力既是他的护城河（大机构没有创业勇气，小基金没有机构级风控），也是他的天花板（Brad Gerstner 那种"幂律思维"的回报，他结构上永远拿不到）。

四、被所有人忽略的 AI 盲点：带宽，不是智力

当所有人在讨论 AI 如何颠覆投资时，Jeff 讲了一句极度非共识的话："Put all relevant information in front of me, then upload into my brain"——LLM 对他而言是带宽放大器，不是决策者。他的论点隐含着一个被忽视的真相：AI 让分析变便宜，但没让"责任承担"变便宜。他基金的护城河正是基于"没人愿意把一个 3000 万美元印第安纳波利斯贷款的决策权，放进一个千亿美元 PE 的决策链里"——这是组织学问题，不是技术问题。

跨领域连接：这与医疗 AI 的困境高度相似。影像 AI 已经比放射科医生准，但谁敢让 AI 签字负责？Jeff 的生意本质上是在"决策不可外包"的裂缝中套利——AI 让分析平民化，反而让"愿意亲自看那栋楼"的人更稀缺、更值钱。

五、他没明说的最大赌注：政治是慢速阶跃函数

Jeff 在访谈末尾吐露的真正焦虑不是信贷技术，而是"没有稳定剂的政治系统"——左右两极都在走极端，没有温和派。他把这当成最大的隐性宏观风险，但没明说的是：这与他 2007 年亲历的 AAA 系统崩塌是完全同构的现象。当年的 CDO 系统也没有稳定剂——所有参与方都在同一方向下注，没有真正的空头提供负反馈。生态学里，没有顶级捕食者的系统会周期性崩溃；今天的美国政治，就是一个"去除了温和派捕食者"的生态系统。

他真正在做的事：买"末日保险"（rates optionality），但方式极其高盛式——"如果保险太贵，说明我漏了风险因子"。这是我在整段访谈里看到最具物理学家气质的句子：价格异常本身就是信息。他把 Fama 的有效市场假说倒过来用：不是"价格反映信息"，而是"价格的反常反映我的无知"。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open

"Every company and every investment bank was just too levered. Tens of billions of protection were sold on that for about 1/10th of 1% per year. You took something that was never ever supposed to take a loss — and then there was uncertainty, and then that lack of trust spread. And I still remember a senior person walking around and just saying: check all of the cash that you have in your PA and where it's sitting and otherwise.

And credit markets move in step functions. If you look at most charts of credit, they tend to blow out for a little while and there's no trust and everyone's like, 'What the hell is going to happen?'"

Opening

Host: Jeff, thank you so much for coming on the pod.

Jeff: Thanks for having me.

Host: You were at Goldman in 2008. Walk me through the worst day.

2008 at Goldman: The Worst Days

Well, that was 18 years ago, so you know, I was thinking a little bit about this — and memories, you know, I have bits and pieces. Some of the most vivid memories I have is, you know, I had the benefit of being in the mortgage department throughout 2008. I moved into trading in 2005 when things were going really crazy.

I remember at one point — I mean, obviously with Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers — that was a crazy situation because that seemed to snowball from an area that we were involved in, in trading the product. So we had, you know, specific knowledge in terms of what was going on, and they had, you know, not great endings.

And then even at Goldman though, the stock was just totally crashing. And at the time I was a couple years out of college, so in hindsight my whole life was ahead of me, but at the time it was like, "Oh my god, I have this great job. I'm working in the mortgage department." And yeah, I mean I think we were a little bit concerned about what would happen to the company — not because we were having losses or otherwise, but I think every company and every investment bank was just too levered. And then there was uncertainty, and then that lack of trust spread.

The Berkshire Moment and Money Market Risk

So I remember one moment when we found out about the Berkshire investment — that helped. That was a preferred equity and a call option, or sorry, warrants, excuse me — as a bit of a stabilizing force. And then on top of that the Fed came in a little bit later, but it was still that moment of uncertainty in terms of "what's the outcome, could we be next" and otherwise.

Other moments, just in terms of the contagion: I still remember a senior person on the desk just walking around — there were so many issues with vehicles that had asset-liability mismatch. So all of a sudden money market funds were becoming a risk, and I still remember a senior person walking around and just saying: check all of the cash that you have in your PA and where it's sitting and otherwise.

And so those are things that you go from — out of college, "I'm working with neat products," to "wow, I'm in an interesting place and a lot's going on, I'm learning a lot, it's exciting." But I mean, obviously there's a lot of people losing money and making money, so the weight of that wasn't lost on me. But all of a sudden it's like, okay, it's here, and these things became very real.

Anyway, those were the memories I could think of in terms of worst moments, but overall it was a rewarding time. It was obviously a very challenging time for many people. I learned a ton. There were some very scary moments. But I guess that's a career in markets.

What Jeff Traded at Goldman

Host: Oh yeah. What sort of stuff were you trading at Goldman?

I had the benefit of being in a number of different roles. Initially out of college I was in a proprietary trading area that looked at CLOs and double-ATCs. So CLOs are securitizations of corporate levered loans. Double-ATCs are aircraft lease securitizations.

Then I moved into asset-backed finance where I was working on larger projects — we were setting up a monoline. I remember I went off and worked on something called a volumetric production payment, which was a securitization of natural gas cash flows, to credit card securitizations.

Mortgage Trading (2005)

But then in 2005 I moved into the mortgage trading business, and that was an interesting area because you had the housing boom. You had a lot of different products that were getting created, both in corporates — so credit derivatives, which were derivatives traded on credit, had been a hugely growing market in corporates — and with the growth in structured finance and mortgage-backed securities and otherwise. So that's securitizations backed by residential mortgages, commercial mortgages, student loan ABS, credit cards, and things like that. We had these new products and there are credit derivatives referencing those products.

So you had a market that was growing. There was more and more origination. There were more and more derivative products. And with my background — I mean, I was a physics major at Columbia. I may have been the only one that didn't get his PhD. For me, it was attractive because I could use the math side of my brain and maybe understand these funky products a little bit better than other people. I released it well enough to get a job and look at it.

The Valentine's Day Massacre and ABX

So I was there and I worked on structuring and trading synthetic structured products, CDOs. And then, as the market started to unravel, I was fortunate enough to be put in charge of a book that was trading tranches on ABX — which is a product called TABX. A lot of people still like to make fun of me because it launched on Valentine's Day of 2014 — sorry, not 2014, 2007 — which people call the Valentine's Day Massacre, because that was a period of tremendous... I'll come back to it a second.

So I was fortunate enough to trade that book for a while, and then I was trading asset-backeds — or sorry, ABS CDOs — as everything was unraveling. Then I moved over to CMBS trading, where I was for a number of years and co-ran that business before I left.

The AAA Illusion: How Insatiable Demand Fueled the Crisis

But in terms of the most interesting times, just stepping back: the period from 2005 to 2006 in hindsight was totally strange, in that you had all these products that were rated AAA, and there was insatiable demand coming from many different sources — some in Europe, some in the US and otherwise.

Because I still remember sayings like, "the loss rate on a structured finance AAA is almost..." — I mean, maybe it was one basis point or 10 basis points, but it was a very low historic number. And so, because of that, you had the products and said, "these products are great and these products have great ratings." And you had many different pools of capital.

The Super Senior Trade

And again, not to say that this is a holistic experience, but anecdotally, you had many different US and European banks that would take tens of billions of exposure to what was called "super senior" on ABS CDOs. Because not only was it a AAA, there was a AAA below it, right? That was there. So this had to be totally remote. And tens of billions of protection were sold on that for about one-tenth of 1% per year — so 10 basis points.

Why? Because that actually looked like a great return on historical losses. There's more to it than that, but that was the basic business model. And maybe that was quite smart. But as it continued to unfold and grow, the fact that that was there allowed so much origination — which put more and more money into the housing market. And there were a lot of bad incentives.

Again, I'm not trying to do everything, but ultimately you took something that was never ever supposed to take a loss, and that helped contribute to prices going up in housing markets and a lot of bad origination through the creation of credit. There wasn't as much alignment as you'd like.

When It Broke

But at the time, everything felt really good. It's like, "I don't know if this will ever move, because it feels like there's insatiable demand for this product. And what do I know? I'm, you know, three or four years out." I mean, I had some thoughts in terms of relative value and what looked rich or cheap, and we were market makers in the products we were doing — so we were trying to make money no matter what happened.

But it was a very stable environment with a lot getting done, and then all of a sudden it starts to break. And all of a sudden housing prices aren't going up and a lot of the mal-origination of the prior couple of years all of a sudden unravels.

So you go from those tranches — super senior off of ABS CDOs trading at 10 basis points — to, I remember in 2007, it's like, "Okay, this had been at eight basis points, now it's going out to 12 basis points." And remember, if you're talking about $50 billion on a book, an extra four bips is a lot of carry and a lot of mark-to-market. But then it's like, "Oh, but all the derivatives are trading off, so maybe this is like 35 basis points — and that's kind of like a crazy level, you're getting paid three times what it was." And then all of a sudden you go a little bit further and it's like, "Oh well, that's trading at five points up front" — so 5% upfront, 500 basis points.

And I think when you actually look back, the TABX product I was talking about as one example — not that this is a great product, but it was still a bellwether of the price discovery — I want to say that started trading when it launched in February of '07. Maybe it was five or 10 points up front, and then ultimately the recovery I think ended up being something between 10 and 30 on that tranche. And why? Because it was senior exposure, but it was senior exposure relative to a lot of very levered underlying bonds that wouldn't perform very well if there was something different than expected.

A Period of Regime Change

Anyway, that is a very long-winded answer, but I just go back to it: it was a period of tremendous shift from one regime and one sort of scenario of the world to something that's totally different. And so it was interesting along the way being in the middle, and "what is the price discovery? Who thinks what? What is right? What is wrong?"

By the way, as these things are moving in price, it's like, "are the products supposed to work if this all happens? Do the documents work? How do you price things at the losses or multiples of what would be expected? How do you compare a 2005 vintage from 2006 or 2007? What do the models look like?" And all that is against a backdrop where people are like, "I think this is rated now, it's been downgraded." How do we tear all this out and make markets along the way?

I look back, I learned a ton. It was a fascinating period. It was a challenging period. But again, back to my original comment: it was almost 20 years ago now.
