David 抛出一个几乎没人敢在 AI 圈大声说的判断：**整个 "alignm

item.title: [a16z Deep Dives] How Valon Is Rebuilding Mortgage Servicing for the AI Era
item.dc:creator: a16z Deep Dives
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞察一：他们建造的不是软件，而是"法律的编译器"——监管本身成了IP

Andrew提到他在COVID期间"每天18小时读监管条文，持续6个月"，做的事情他自己命名为 "refactoring the entire legal code base"。这句话值得停下来品味：他们不是在"合规"，他们是在把法典本身编译成架构。

这里有一个被忽视的护城河逻辑反转：传统认知里监管=成本=摩擦。但在Valon手里，监管复杂度被转化成架构抽象，于是——监管越复杂、变化越频繁，他们的相对优势越大。Linda半开玩笑说"痛苦和折磨是我们最伟大的护城河"，这不是鸡汤，这是精确的商业描述。

与Stripe（支付合规）、Palantir（国防数据分类）相似，但Valon走得更极端：他们没有绕过监管或封装监管，他们把法典本身重写成了可执行的数据模型。这其实揭示了一个更大的模式——在GenAI时代，所有"把非结构化规则结构化"的工作都会成为新一代垄断性资产。谁先把一个行业的"隐性知识"编译成schema，谁就拥有了那个行业的操作系统。

洞察二：1960年代的数据建模错误，是埋在系统里的"延时炸弹"

Linda说的一句话很多人会一掠而过，但它其实非常可怕：

"问题不会那周就发生，问题会在五年后发生——当有人试图付托管款时。"

这揭示了一个被严重低估的系统性真相：技术债不是线性累积的利息，而是时间引爆的地雷。1960年代建模时，房产保险概念简单、继承模式清晰。那些"硬塞进去"的字段，静静躺着，直到2026年某个母亲去世、孩子要查遗产税时才瞬间爆炸——而这时根本没人记得当年谁做出了那个建模决定。

跨领域连接：这与演化生物学里的"evolutionary mismatch"（演化失配）惊人相似。人类基因还在狩猎采集模式，但活在高糖城市里——疾病不会立刻来，而是几十年后以慢性病形式爆发。同样的逻辑贯穿城市下水道（罗马管道）、电网（二战前变压器）、代码库（COBOL）、公共卫生（抗生素滥用）。

真正的基础设施型公司，赌的其实是"抗时间炸弹能力"。Valon在为未来50年设计一个具备演化弹性的数据本体——这才是它和"现代化的旧服务商"的本质区别。

洞察三：AI的意外效应——不是让服务同质化，而是让它"重新有口味"

主流叙事：AI会让所有服务commoditize（同质化、商品化）。 Valon观察到的现实：完全相反。

Linda的原话："It really turns the world from one that is really commoditized to one that is much more specialized and really flavor-driven."

这是对"规模经济"底层逻辑的根本颠覆。 - 过去：规模=通过标准化降低单位成本=cookie-cutter脚本=所有servicer长得一样 - 未来：规模=可以负担的差异化越多=每家servicer可以成为"自己最好的版本"

这个模式会扩散到所有"因为人类带宽有限而被迫同质化"的领域：客服、HR、法务、医疗分诊、金融顾问。AI不是让这些行业更像流水线，是让它们重新具备手工艺时代的"风味"——但以工业规模运行。

这里有个让人意外的推论：AI实际上是在恢复经济学里一个被遗忘的变量——context（语境）。亚当·斯密的分工理论之所以成立，是因为context信息传递成本太高，于是只能用标准化流程压缩context。AI把这个成本降为零，于是"语境即竞争力"重新成为可能。Valon的"flavor-driven servicing"是这个大转折在金融基础设施上的第一个商业化证据。

洞察四（送你一个额外的意外观察）：Valon真正卖的不是软件，是"寡头的解剖学"

注意Linda两句话的组合： 1. "everything is servicing" 2. "revenue cycle management is just servicing for hospitals"

表面：他们在做抵押贷款服务软件。 实际：他们积累的是"高度监管行业中寡头依赖症"的拆解方法论。

$13万亿市场跑在一个1960年代的单一厂商上——这不是bug，这是一种制度性病理。你观察一下：医疗HIS系统（Epic垄断）、保险理赔、公用事业计费、政府福利发放、学生贷款——每一个都是"寡头+legacy+监管"的同构模式。

Valon建的不是mortgage软件，是一把专门用来拆解"寡头基础设施"的手术刀。这就是为什么Linda敢说"it gets easier from here"——mortgage被业界公认是最难的那一关（最监管、最高stakes、最老旧），一旦被破开，后面的垂直领域都是同一套手术刀的变奏。

真正的商业预言：十年后你回头看Valon，它可能根本不是一家mortgage公司，而是一家"寡头继承战略"公司——专门承接那些跑在恐龙系统上的万亿级市场。这个剧本的真正竞争对手不是其他mortgage软件，而是其他敢于把"又慢又痛又监管"当成特性而非bug的infrastructure玩家。

📝 转录文本

开场：被忽视的万亿机会

Mortgage is top three in terms of undisrupted industries that exist. This is an industry that hasn't even caught up to 2000s technology yet. That's sort of the size of the opportunity in front of us.

The way that we are going about it as an industry is creating the infrastructure so that it's a continual learning process. Building a system that allows you to continuously run the evals, make sure you're actually continuously improving the model in a direction that is aligned, not just with the way that servicing should be done generally, but customer specific.

It's 13 trillion dollars of consumer debt that basically runs on a single incumbent that built their legacy system before the internet was invented. It turns out revenue cycle management is just servicing for hospitals. Everything is servicing. It's the underlying critical infrastructure that supports basically anything that has money movements, some sort of regulation, and then an operational component.

We started the company before Generative AI was really working.

Q: What is possible today that would have been in your series A pitch deck? What is possible today is...

Andrew的起点：从数学到系统，再到痛苦

Q: So Andrew, I think a great place to start would be from your time at Soros and how you decided that mortgage servicing was going to be a really interesting problem to work on.

So a fun story is that when I got into the world of finance, I actually had zero background in finance. I never took a course in economics. I barely understood what the time value of money was. And so my general interest in finance was actually just in math.

And what people don't really know about mortgages—which is just like a very random esoteric fact—is that it's actually a place where there's a lot of stochastic calculus. Prepayment models have stochastic calculus. And so when I started the job, I got very interested in making sure I mastered stochastic calculus. I'm taking a course in college, I was going to do all that—and it turns out it's all finger in the air, just guess your way through math. So that wasn't really...

Yes, yes, you just need to guess some number. You're like, "yeah, I think it's going to prepay at X speed."

Anyways, so that was my initial reason to get into mortgages. What happened thereafter was you end up realizing, working with many of the mortgage servicers, that it's a big systems engineering problem—because there's a ton of data, a lot of money moving around, a lot of entries, they have to constantly be reconciled.

And so I spent a lot of time at Soros when I was making these investments, really making sure I understood exactly what was going on and building my own reconciliation systems to make sure the money tied. Turns out it never tied. And so I spent a lot of time trying to fix that problem internally.

And that got me really interested in figuring out: hey, how can I actually build better infrastructure? How can I invest maybe in a company, do it with a company, and actually ultimately build better systems so that none of this would be a problem.

So it really started originally off of systems in my own pain. Maybe I would say: it started off with math, math became systems, systems became pain, and here we are today.

行业现状：Top 3 未被颠覆的巨头产业

Q: Excellent. Discovering a market has a lot of technical problems to solve is one piece of it. Maybe Linda, from a market perspective, describe the state of the world as a mortgage servicing industry before Valon came in.

Yeah, the way that I think about it is: mortgage is probably top three in terms of undisrupted industries that exist. And so it's 13 trillion dollars of consumer debt that basically runs on, for the most part, a single incumbent that built their legacy system before the internet was invented.

And so we're not talking about—you know, for most industries you are fighting with modern incumbents and new startups for the last 20 percent—we're talking about the entirety. This is an industry that hasn't even caught up to 2000s technology yet. And so that's sort of the size of the opportunity in front of us.

And from a deployment standpoint, these are the biggest, baddest enterprise deployments to exist. You have to train thousands of employees. You have to basically rip and replace the core operating system. You're actually deploying AI into the real world in a very heavily, heavily regulated industry.

And what we always tell the team is that the skillset that people will be hiring for in the next decade is the ability to apply AI, and our team's learning that by doing it in the hardest industry possible. So I think: big technical problems, very old industry.

消费者视角：破损的基础设施如何伤害真实的人

Q: One of the other interesting things about this industry, and one of the reasons I love investing in infrastructure, is if you unpack crappy consumer or business experiences, it usually often comes down to the plumbing. So maybe if I'm a homeowner and my home is being serviced by one of the incumbents versus Valon, what might I notice from just a human perspective?

Yeah, it's a classic problem where the average person who pays on time probably doesn't have to notice that much. I mean, this is a very classic thing where—you know, I think whenever people realize that most Americans actually are barely maybe one paycheck away from being able to make their payments, it's a little bit of an astonishing fact. But it's a similar dynamic where in mortgages, most people pay on time, but there are people who have certain events that happen to them that are unfortunate, not predictable, and really cause a lot of stress and anxiety.

一个真实案例：继承悲剧

So here's an example of this. One of the key problems with some of the legacy systems is that they don't really model and really capture all of the context associated with the life of the mortgage. Meaning: you originate the mortgage, they have a snapshot of what's going on right now, but the history isn't fully captured with enough fidelity.

And so a good example of this is when someone passes away. The borrower might end up changing because maybe they were the borrower on the loan before, and then thereafter there's a new borrower on the loan. Now, that is a normal thing. The systems today do not actually capture all of the changes along the way.

And so if you want to look at what happened before that, it's actually very challenging for the servicers because they put it in an ad hoc database on the side. They only have what is going on at any given point in time. And so you might have a situation as an example where a homeowner passes away, their kids are trying to take over, but they no longer have access to the records before. And that might be important because they're trying to file estate taxes, they're trying to figure out what happened before.

And because of how again the systems work, they'll say, "well, you weren't that borrower, you don't have access to that history, we're cutting it off at this point in time."

And so that causes a lot of anxiety and stress—because you have to keep in mind, right, these are real people at a moment in time where they're trying to figure out something really, really tough. And you have to over and over again tell them, "my mom passed away. This is why this happened. Please give me the information."

And so it percolates in that form and fashion. AI obviously helps a lot of this because you can get that context, but it doesn't change the fact that the information must be represented in the right way so that the systems can perform as expected. And so really, the more information represented in the better way possible, the better the experience ends up being.

Escrow、保险爆涨与分摊困境

Q: Some of—you guys used to do this every week, sharing a different story of a customer—if you helped even the more common simpler case of "I can't make my payment this month," or if it's multiple times in a row, you might need a loan modification. How is that different in Valon?

Yeah, there's all sorts of variations of this. Again, one of them is: there is this concept of the escrow when it comes to mortgages. It basically contains both taxes and insurance that need to be paid over time. They generally happen on an annual basis to make sure that homeowners are reserving for the right amounts. You sort of pay it on a monthly basis and accrue a reserve to pay for it when the time comes.

One of the problems right now that everyone faces is actually insurance costs and taxes are actually exploding. And so many homeowners aren't able to make that large payment or change a payment in such a quick fashion. That requires usually a pretty annoying process because one, most systems are designed so that they take the amount and they basically just calculate how much it costs over the course of a year—even though the regulation and many of the right investor standards allow you to amortize it over 36 months.

And so that becomes an ad hoc approval process that has to go to a supervisor, as opposed to having really great systems where you pretty much can immediately determine, should they be approved, should they not be approved, and being able to configure these things along the way—really on the fly—because again, regulations change, there might be some big fire that happened and so many of the insurance companies are raising prices. Being able to offer that right experience really automated, and really give comfort to the homeowners in their time of need—that is really important for a servicer, and that ultimately builds best customer relationship.

1960年代的建模，今天的爆炸

And I think it's hard for people to conceptualize how old the existing software is. Because you have to think about it: when these technology systems were architected, this was the 1960s. And so even something as basic as property insurance—property insurance, mortgage insurance keeps evolving over time—and so the data models fundamentally just don't model the world the way that it behaves today.

And so you end up with sort of over a decade something that someone forced into a system that didn't actually model it correctly. And it's not like the problem is going to happen that week; it's like the problem will happen five years later when someone's trying to make their escrow payment and it compounds.

And so that's the part where it's like: you can have the world's best customer experience team and the most empathetic call center agent in the world, but if fundamentally you were charged the wrong amount of money because the system of record was flawed, then you can't fix that homeowner experience without fixing the infrastructure.

Valon的起点：为什么选择最痛苦的路径

Q: Which is actually a perfect segue. I want to talk a little bit about how Valon got started. The flip side of these technologically-behind, incumbent-driven large industries is they can be very hard to break into. So you had three options: (1) build the software and sell it into the incumbents (like Harvey in law); (2) do some kind of rollup, buy a few incumbents and inject them; (3) build the entire thing from scratch. Why that option to get started?

Yeah, so we went through all three options. And just to be clear, the path that we went down was the last one because it is the most painful and it takes the longest.

Option 1 — Sell software to incumbents: It doesn't work for mortgage because it's so heavily regulated that no servicer is going to use a de novo system. And then even from an R&D perspective, if we managed to get one big marquee customer to sign up, we would basically be beholden to how they want to do things, which will look an awful lot like how they do things today. And so you just run the risk that you wake up 10 years from now and you've rebuilt the legacy system with a really pretty UI. So that crosses out number one.

Option 2 — Rollup / acquisition: The problem is IP. So if you buy an existing servicer that's using an existing legacy platform, the nice thing about being able to build software—sorry, I should say convenient; it actually I think is not long-term correct—is you can basically swap things out module by module. But one, I think that actually forces you into platform design decisions that probably aren't right. And then two, you have this IP issue.

Option 3 — Build from scratch: And so really that left us with the choice of—we got the privilege of starting our own servicer and then just building the software from scratch, not looking at anything. And the software got to evolve as the servicer was growing as well. So it's like we started with one loan, which is really nice, and then ended up with close to a million.

三大起步挑战：牌照、监管入码、客户信任

Q: Well, I think that strategy has proven very prescient now. But to get it started, sort of think of it in three buckets: (1) you needed to get licensed; (2) you needed to turn decades of regulation into code; (3) you needed to convince asset managers / lenders to give this highly regulated asset over to a new company.

1) 牌照：鸡生蛋、蛋生鸡的死循环

Q: Starting with licensing—it's easy to think, I fill out some long forms, I throw them over a wall, eventually I get a license. Maybe talk us through what was that process.

Yeah, I would like to say we were so thoughtful that we already knew all these things going in. There was kind of—looking back—some slight improvements we could make in terms of the licensing process. But for the most part, mortgage servicing and many of these licenses have pretty much chicken-and-egg problems.

One of the key requirements is: they tell you, you actually need to be profitable before you get a license. This is true for the state of New York and a couple of other regulatory approvals like Fannie and Freddie. They'll make some exceptions and you can get around it, but it's quite challenging.

And so when you look at it from the get-go, you end up in a situation where you first notice: holy crap, this is going to take a long, long time. And two, then you end up in a situation where you have to really be methodical in plotting out what licenses you get in what order.

So for us, what we did was we said: okay, we're going to start out with this type of customer. Because we can't get the major government licenses, we needed to look for a specific type of loan that we can get licensed for. It's called at the time—they're still pretty prevalent today, and they're actually, I think, growing—non-QM loans. They only require you to have state licenses.

Here's the problem though. With state licenses, you need to pick the states where people actually make non-QM loans. One of the biggest ones is the state of California. State of California actually has pretty stringent requirements. It actually requires you to have a government application or government loan approval in order to service California loans. There is one exclusion for the Department of Real Estate if you're in the brokering business and a real estate brokering business. So now you need to find someone who is in the department or is a real estate broker to actually help you get that license.

Simultaneously, you also need to show them that you have five years plus of experience across every part of servicing—that's collections, that's customer service, that's payment processing, that's delinquency, that's foreclosure. So you need to do all these different things just to get going.

Most people forecast this type of endeavor taking three to five years at the minimum—and that's if you take the most literal optimal steps—three to five years to get all of the different approvals, because they all stack on top of each other. You can't do one without the other, and by the very end, you end up having to really aggregate not just business but really expertise across a very, very large wide set of domains.

纽约邮件室的朝圣

Q: There's many years of stories, including you going to visit mail rooms of—

Exactly. I'll give you the classic one, which by the way is a funny one. We actually got the approval for New York in a record time of—I want to say—three years. So it was a record time of three years. And we actually never ended up getting approved to license or to originate mortgages in New York. That just tells you how challenging and how difficult it is.

And they have this funny thing where apparently they will review your application, but if they either miss it or deny it, whatever else, they'll reset the clock like three to six months back. And this was right before COVID happened. And so I knew I wasn't going to be in New York for the moment, and so I didn't want to wait another six months before I came back to New York.

And so what I made sure I did was: I went to the mail room and I identified where the package was, because they told me my application was missing. And I was like, "I have tracking on this. I know it's there. Well, let me go visit your offices to actually track this down."

2) 把监管编译进代码：法典重构

Q: So we've made it through that full process. And then maybe talking about taking the regulation and putting it into a platform. It's really easy to knock on the incumbents, but they've had decades to harden state-by-state regulations that changed over time. How did we approach that from scratch?

Honestly, I think the unfortunate reality—which is again, like you've mentioned before, a little bit of a note of how we make ourselves feel better about all the pain and suffering—

(Greatest moat of all time: pain and suffering.)

Yeah. But what we ended up doing was reading every single regulation. So there's a whole bunch of federal regulations—there's RESPA, there's TILA, there's FDCPA, there's GLBA, there's TCPA, there's all these different regulations on the federal level. There's also 50 states where you basically have to cover their mortgage regulations, you have to cover their debt collection practices, you have to cover their real estate foreclosure practices, you have to cover their privacy practices, their escrow practices. So you have to cover every one of these.

And you basically go through—I'm going to say it just as a fun exercise of—refactoring the entire legal code base, if you can put it that way. It turns out many legal statutes are derived off of different states. And so you sit there basically figuring out how to create an abstract framework that handles all of it. And then you put it into your architecture and then you start to test it.

But what really worked for us, quite honestly, was the fact that COVID happened. And when COVID happened, I spent 18 hours a day for six months straight, just every day sitting there reading regulation and annotating and basically coming up with the schematics. And that's what got us through it. It was pure grit, effort, pain, suffering, all these different things.

And then obviously you have the five to six years thereafter of testing and making sure it works exactly as you sort of intended.

(There was a point at which you could cite almost every single state's regulation and I can tell you what code number it was. — Fun at the dinner party.)

3) 赢得第一批客户：靠自己运营servicer当样板

Q: Amazing. And then, okay, so you've got it built—which is a huge challenge—but then convincing customers that probably were not leaning into new technology to start off with. How did you get your first loans on the system?

So the framework that we use internally for software is a little different than how we started with the loan servicer. With the servicer, the nice thing is that unit economics and efficiency kind of largely was the product—meaning that the better we made the technology, the more margin we had. And honestly, we just passed that margin through to the end customer.

And all of these asset managers who own these mortgage assets, they are economic animals. And so at the end of the day, when you lower price, you can get the market to capitulate. And that just requires the technology being good.

From a software perspective, we think about it internally as: you always have to balance safety and urgency.

  • Safety: we built a servicer that actually used the technology and proved for the last six, seven years that it's gone through every state exam, every Fannie Mae audit, Freddie, Ginnie—all of the different compliance hoops that you have to get through. And so it's safe because we actually took the operating risk of running our own servicer on the system.

  • Urgency: honestly, starting to compound something is always the hardest part. It's creating and generating momentum. And so for us, the first thing that we did is we took our servicer and we competed in the market. That's one way of creating urgency, because now you're actually directly competing with your future software customers and hoping that they'll forgive you down the line.

It's like Jensen's quote of: it's not AI that's your competition, it's your competition using AI faster.

经济模型的变革：从微利到高利润

Q: From a traditionally very low-margin business, Valon turned into a high-margin business. What was the economic difference that everyone kind of perked up in the industry?

Yeah, so we are about three times as efficient. And so you take this breakeven business and you turn it into sort of a 70, 80 % operating margin business. And that margin is what we used initially to create that urgency to make things better.

And then it compounds, right? So once you get your first big customer to sign up, then the other five big guys call you and say, "hey, were you actually serious that you wanted to sell software?" and you started the flywheel effect. But without our own servicer in the beginning, it would have been really hard to generate that.

卖掉servicer：拯救世界，不是独享alpha

Q: And so you built Valon Servicing, I think, in the $200 billion. How big exactly? And then you could have kept scaling that—but instead you decided you were going to sell the customers.

Just to be clear, this was the original plan. It was the original plan.

(It was in the deck. We actually share our Series A deck with our new employees—it was like a 60-page PDF of the master takeover plan.)

Q: And then just recently you guys announced the sale of Valon Mortgage over to Carrington, and now you're taking that OS and selling it into the industry.

I think for me and Andrew, we would talk about this every once in a while, as you would expect, where we would sit down and we would say: hey, it is a fully viable path to just build a big servicer. There are $10 billion-plus companies that do this.

But for us, it always came back to—every conversation ended with: we actually want to change the industry. And the thing is, if you keep it as a servicer, you're keeping all of the technology and the alpha for yourself. And at the end of the day, you didn't actually change anything. You didn't fix the core infrastructure problem.

For companies who want to be generational companies, having a clear purpose and mission that's not just "we're going to make more money"—that's great—it's "we want to change the world, we want to fix a rather broken world" is extraordinarily important for the employees and really the direction for the company. Because you want people to not just dream "oh I make enough money now." It's: what can I do that's greater, what can I do that's bigger, what can I do to actually solve the impossible?

"We gotta save the world from mainframes." Q: Wait, that's your mission statement? Yes, exactly. Mainframes, legacy software. And broken critical infrastructure.

AI带来的根本性可能：从确定性到编排

Q: Maybe speaking of the bigger opportunity—you started the company before Generative AI was really working. What is possible today that would have been in your Series A pitch deck?

How beautiful of a problem setup mortgage servicing is for what's about to happen both with AI, but just like overall enterprise and infrastructure and society. Which is to say, what is possible today is you can have these extraordinarily complex cases and you can actually research and basically provide the right set of information to the operators, so that they're more and more in a world where they're effectively operating little mini armies of agents to actually solve whatever set of problems.

一个具体例子：灾害响应

So I'll give you a really simple example. When a disaster happens, you're supposed to make some phone calls, make sure that the homeowner is actually able to continue to pay the mortgage, what their intentions, what their plans are, if they need any assistance—you have to go through all this process.

And that is normal, and that is fine, and people have different scripts to set that up. But changing that on the fly, or handling very, very specific different notifications or tactics or plans per locale, is basically impossible. The only way to do that today as a normal servicer is you basically print out a spreadsheet and you hand a list of loans to one group of people and hand another list of loans to another people, and you say "I want you to do A, I want you to do B, and I want you to go figure it out."

Versus with our systems and really the power of what AI can do today: you could literally in our product suite say, "hey, I want to orchestrate a set of agents to make phone calls, to contact homeowners, to provide them these different plans, run these different workflows." And you can do that in sort of like a fire pilot simulation scenario.

从同质化到"口味驱动"

And that I think provides a lot of both power to the underlying servicers in becoming more efficient, but it actually gives them a lot more customizability. And the latter is actually the really, really cool and important part—because it allows every servicer to be the best versions of themselves. They can really think about how do I want to handle a specific scenario that pops up, versus just saying "look, I need to run this quote-unquote efficiently as much as possible, running zero percent margins. And I thus only have a cookie-cutter way of going about things and I actually can't change it."

It really turns the world from one that is really commoditized to one that is much more specialized and really flavor-driven.

本体论先行：先有结构数据，才能编排agent

Q: So there's one way to think about it: you've now created this very organized data ontology, and then pre-AI, any of the tasks you needed to do on top were definitely more efficient. Whereas now you can spin up—I think you've got dozens of these different agents that can do escrow analysis and sort of any human tasks that you might need to do on top of it.

Yeah, it's a completely different world. Before, you could only automate things that were clearly deterministic, because you could say "hey, I have the right structured data, I have the information, I can automate a very, very small piece of it." You can still generate really great efficiencies, but it's just not the experience that everyone was looking for and desiring—but math still worked out.

What you can do today is completely different. Not only can you automate a much, much higher percentage of tasks—the long tail, the really complex scenarios—but really beyond that, you can orchestrate a very wide variety of scenarios for your agents to handle. And as a result of that, you can actually improve and really do champion-challenger type tactics to really improve the outcomes of your portfolios.

Which just was not possible before, because of—again—the level of training and level of specificity you have to give your human agents to do the work. Now you can just say, "hey, 100 loans. I want to try these different strategies. I want to improve these different outcomes. I want to give these different notifications. Let's see what happens." Just completely different world.

消费者界面：从UI到对话

Q: It makes your job as a servicer a lot more fun. You've got some interesting things on the consumer side too—voice agents and other things you've been experimenting with.

Yeah. So I would say the really fun thing that we get to do now—and everyone gets to do now—is you get to also just rethink how humans interact with systems. Whereas before we were laser-focused on building the right system of record, and the way that humans interact with that system of record is through defined UIs, and then you actually end up hiring human operators whose skill set is knowing how to navigate the UIs.

Now, we get to do things like: we just build our own harness on top of the system of record, and actually you just have that classic chat interface. And you get to do this on the back office side. And then when you think about how our homeowners interact with Valon OS, you can do it through a voice AI, you can do it through a chat AI—there are just so many different form factors now. And it's really cool to think about what it could be.

技术路线图：持续学习的基础设施

Q: And then maybe, Andrew—you Moonlight is one of the most productive engineers as well as being CEO. What are some of the interesting technical challenges on the roadmap or things you're thinking about solving?

So there's the classic set of problems when it comes to, as you're building more and more of an enterprise, really industry-specific harness. Like decide: do you want to do fine-tuning? Do you want to improve your model efficiencies? Where do you want to invest in terms of a harness?

So we've done the classic stuff when it comes to making sure you have vector databases, when you're trying to make sure you're pulling the right context, what is the sequence of context you want to put in. And then there's slight variations of this which are very industry-specific. So in mortgages, as an example, you care a lot more about correctness. And so you would probably want to align the models as much as possible, and really the overall harness outcomes, so that if you don't know the answer it generally says "I don't know" versus "let me give you some hallucinated answer." And so there's small things here and there that really can change how the experience is for the user.

But I think the thing I find most fun—and really the thing that I think is so amazing about the way that we are going about it as an industry or really as a product suite—is creating the infrastructure so that it's a continual learning process.

When you think about a lot of the infrastructure that people build, they're using quite a bit of data from the user input and whatever else—that makes sense when you're doing coding, that makes sense when you have a pretty contained environment. But these are really complex ecosystems where there's so many different components. When you think about servicing, there's the accounting entries, there's the money movements, there's the customer interactions, there's the regulatory aspects, the different vendors that you're interacting with.

And so these things change quite dynamically. And that's a very challenging problem because you can't say "well, here's the bounded problem, this is how we're going to solve it, and we're going to optimize over a very, very clear function."

Building a system that allows you to continuously run the evals, pull the data out, make sure you're actually continuously improving the model in the direction that is aligned—not just with the way that servicing should be done generally, but customer-specific—that is, I think, the part that's super interesting: building an overall set of infrastructure that can handle it at that capacity.

扩展野心：Everything is Servicing

Q: Which segues well—I know even from the beginning, you both had ambitions broader than mortgage servicing. How does the architecture and how you've set up the Valon platform set up Valon to expand into other sectors?

Maybe I'll start off with a little-known fact, which is: servicing is like the nexus of all these different highly regulated enterprises.

The fun fact I always like to go through with people is that people think servicing must be residential, or maybe loan servicing. And you're like, "okay, we're talking about Resi, and Resi is really great because it's regulated, it's the space that we started out in. It's very impactful because of the size of the market. And it's really near and dear to everybody's hearts—it's a home, American homeownership, it's really important."

But you can always take one step left or right, whichever direction you want.

  • Commercial: there's all the data and all the information associated with the real estate, the tenants. People don't realize this, but as a commercial mortgage servicer you actually get the information about the tenants' financials and all the data associated with that. So you could—you know how Toast and a bunch of people used their platforms to figure out how to do small business financing? You could kind of do the same thing if you decide to go through commercial.

  • Healthcare: if you take another step and think about this even more broadly, then you even have things like healthcare, where there's revenue cycle management companies. People get very excited about those type of companies—and it turns out revenue cycle management is just servicing for hospitals and their claims and handling their patients. And the data that you get from that is effectively all electronic medical records.

And so it's a very exciting thing to do servicing first because it is a very, very, very challenging and difficult problem. It's very high breadth. But when you get into it, you're effectively in a position where you have tentacles across the entirety of the business and every element of what they work with and what they end up doing. And so it just gives you that really expansionary opportunity.

重新定义Resi服务

Let me just go back to Resi for a second. People again think of Resi servicing as "oh, I'm going to help you collect the payments and interact with the homeowners." Well, whatever—we turned it into: "I'm going to figure out a way to use this relationship that you guys have with all of your homeowners, and I'm going to call them every single month. I'm going to build a relationship with them. I'm going to make sure I have a pulse on what's going on with them every single month."

And that's never been done before. And that's not how people think of servicing. But with a mixture of the technology that we've built and really where AI is headed, you can do those things. And I think that's what I find so, so exciting about this.

"Everything is servicing." Yes. Everything.

It is the underlying critical infrastructure that supports basically anything that has money movements, some sort of regulation, and then an operational component. And then we just picked mortgages to be first because it's the stickiest, it's actually the hardest and most complicated as well. And so we thought: why not do that one first, and then we'll go conquer the rest.

"It gets easier from here." Exactly.

Rhythm 的400万贷款转移

Q: So I want to tell you a little bit about where Valon is today. You built a servicer, recently announced, sold the servicer to sell the software platform. And then just recently, Rhythm confirmed that they're going to transfer 4 million loans over to Valon, which I think is the largest servicing transfer. It's almost 10% of the market. They baked you off across all the incumbents. What gave them conviction to make such a big move?

So what I would say is that in general, as we were—there's always a timing component to anything. And I would say, actually, in some ways, Andrew and I didn't decide that we hit product-market fit. The market decided that we hit product-market fit.

And so just to give you a sense of just the pent-up demand in the industry: within six months of us officially going to market as a software company, we signed over $200 million of deals. And that just tells you how much the industry has been wanting change.

And so from New Res's perspective, they've partnered with us really closely from the beginning. Valon Mortgage sub-serviced New Res loans; they could see the performance in a very clear, almost like demo-room, basically, of "this is exactly the performance that you get if you run on the software"—actually, I would argue that's the lower bound of the performance that you get if you run on the software.

And then the way that we structure all of our customer engagements is: we want to make sure that we're incentive-aligned with the customer. I think the second that you lose that alignment, that's when you're kind of going downhill as a company. And so for us, we structure everything as outcomes-oriented. For every dollar that our customer earns, or for every dollar that our customer saves, that's when we earn as well. And I think that core alignment was the thing that made it just a no-brainer for all of our customers.

Valon的文化：高agency + 高模糊性 + 高同理心

Q: Maybe I want to end on—anyone who's in New York, highly encouraged them to visit the Valon office, it's got a ton of energy—but how would you describe what it's like to work at Valon, or what might people find surprising?

Yeah, I think—look, plenty of people have really great talent at their companies. There's really smart people obviously working at a variety of different companies. But I think what's really unique about the people at Valon is they're all the type of people where they want to take matters into their own hands.

And I've had this conversation with so many of the people who've joined. These people, if you look at the people who've joined Valon, they have previously worked at or they had offers to go to work at obviously the standard thing—OpenAI, Anthropic, all those type of things.

And what makes the difference for them is the fact that they realize: look, there's a lot of smart people working on these other problems. Those will get solved. Like clearly, at the compute and the underlying model improvements, it's happening, it's working. Are you going to be the person who actually solves this problem?—this really, really important problem.

And finding the desire and finding joy in the fact that you're personally driving that impact in a way that you can so clearly handle or deal with—that is, I think, what really, really gets the people excited.

And then they realize they stay for the people. Because they end up realizing: okay, besides the fact that I love doing this type of work and being very hardcore and making sure we're fixing these really, really challenging impossible problems, you're surrounded by other people doing just the same.

The people make people stay very long. When we look at the way that our company has been built and formed, I want to say like 75–80% of our management team is filled with people who've been here for five-plus years. It's really a demonstration of the type of company you have to build, the type of culture you have to build, and really the type of people who thrive.

部署端：从技术问题到变革管理问题

Q: What would you say on the deployment side?

I would say—and we're kind of going through this learning curve live, obviously—but doing enterprise, especially large, complicated, regulated enterprise, it is unlike what you would imagine if you were just sitting there thinking about it in the abstract.

Because at the end of the day, what we're talking about is really large organizations of thousands and thousands of people. Every single individual has a slightly different objective function. You have layers of the organization that you need to move through.

If you had asked me six years ago, I would have told you: this is a technology problem. What I know today is that this is a change management problem. And so what we've spent the last six to 12 months building is really that change management muscle of: how do you navigate organizations, how do you make change happen? And it turns out change is really, really hard at scale.

But it is, I think, for this moment that we're in with AI, the number one biggest value driver for the next decade.

Q: And you've done a couple of successful deployments. What is the type of person that tends to really thrive in that kind of role?

Yeah, I would say: high agency, high ambiguity, high empathy for the customer. And then the ability to really think from different points of view on what the objective function is and then figure out what is the global thing that everyone's trying to do, bridge that, and then actually come up with a solution.

Usually there are people who are really, really great problem solvers, and then there are also people who are really, really good with dealing with people—and you need both.

"Everything is servicing. Andrew, Linda, thank you for joining the podcast." "Thanks for having us. Thanks, Angela."

## 洞察一：他们建造的不是软件，而是"法律的编译器"——监管本身成了IP
Andrew提到他在COVID期间"每天18小时读监管条文，持续6个月"，做的事情他自己命名为 "refactoring the entire legal code base"。这句话值得停下来品味：**他们不是在"合规"，他们是在把法典本身编译成架构**。
这里有一个被忽视的护城河逻辑反转：传统认知里监管=成本=摩擦。但在Valon手里，监管复杂度被转化成架构抽象，于是——**监管越复杂、变化越频繁，他们的相对优势越大**。Linda半开玩笑说"痛苦和折磨是我们最伟大的护城河"，这不是鸡汤，这是精确的商业描述。
与Stripe（支付合规）、Palantir（国防数据分类）相似，但Valon走得更极端：他们没有绕过监管或封装监管，他们把法典本身重写成了可执行的数据模型。这其实揭示了一个更大的模式——**在GenAI时代，所有"把非结构化规则结构化"的工作都会成为新一代垄断性资产**。谁先把一个行业的"隐性知识"编译成schema，谁就拥有了那个行业的操作系统。
