The Triad: Technique, Physical, Psychological

But if that's how you felt, right, and golf — I mean, that's where it is, right? It's upstairs. If that's how you felt, then there was probably just something in there, which was: your head had the clarity.

Yeah. It wasn't tormented the way it is now. I disagree slightly with you. I don't think golf is all in the head. I think it's still by and large a technical sport. It's a sport that rewards skill first and foremost. So in my view, the biggest component to skill is technique. So if you can master your technique, then I think — and then of course there's a physical element and the psychological element. I find the psychological element most fascinating cuz to me it's the most transient in the sport, and it can fluctuate massively. But yeah, I think that's what makes golf a particularly challenging sport — it's the triad of those three things where you don't often see that maybe as broadly in other sports. You know, you can think of tennis where it's quite physical, or football or rugby where you have huge physical elements and there may be less of the mental, but I think in golf there really is a — you get pulled in all directions on different on those three different key fronts.

Repeatability > Textbook

Drill — can we drill into that? Because I do think — I've just made a lazy assumption or comment that people can make when trying to differentiate the top players, why some people win a lot more than others. And it is an easier thing that we do say. It's like, what's the difference in talent between the top 50 players in the world or, you know, should we say, fine, maybe the top 10 — people make a lazy assumption of those guys are great, but then you could go 20 to 100 — the difference between what can make those ones very good is up here.

I think it's easy when you talk about technique to think of what's textbook. So you could look at an Adam Scott for example and say there's textbook technique, and yet he doesn't win nearly as many golf tournaments as Scottie Scheffler. But the difference is: within golf, too, there is a really important component to technique that you could call repeatability. And so in my view a Scottie Scheffler is more akin to a Jim Furyk. You can see funky movements, but their ability to repeat that movement is second to none. And so once you get that good at repeating a move that is good enough, then you can start to see confidence blossom. I think of confidence as being like the icing and the cherry on top of the cake, but it isn't the cake. To bake a really nice fluffy cake, there's an awful lot that goes into it. And invariably, in my experience, a lot of that derives from good coaching, good technical work, and good physical work in conjunction with that. And then you can start to grow.

Okay. So you have had massively successful moments in your career. You've had very successful years in your career. How happy — if we take away the mental side of the game — how happy would you say you are in the swing you've created, the repeatability that you've created in your golf from, let's just say, the physical perspective?

I don't think I've done a good job at that at all in the last few years. I think, ironically, I've probably done the worst job than I've ever done, even in spite of spending possibly even more time. It's not the time spent practicing. It's obviously the time spent practicing a specific thing that really matters. And that thing has to be the right thing, too. And that's what makes golf even tougher. You can think you're working on the right thing for an extended period of time, go out and play in competition, and soon realize, oh, I'm not nearly good enough. So then you have to go back to the drawing board and try and get better that way. So there's that constant evolution feedback loop that makes it harder for you to get it right.

And things change. You know, injuries — I think in retrospect, looking back at my own career, injuries have had a bigger impact on my ability to swing the club the way I want to swing the club than I maybe would realize. I think Tiger Woods is also a really good example of that. The importance of having the physical ability to do something really matters in golf, too. So yeah, I mean it's a very complex thing. You know, I also think that's the word I would use to describe golf above and beyond maybe any other word. It's the word complex, because there are always emerging things going on week to week, day to day — travel, lack of sleep. You know, I mean, I go back even a week ago to me in Ireland, having had this injury. It's off the back really of being over-practiced, under-slept, over-stressed, just trying to think and figure things out. And you get an injury. And so if you draw every thread back, you realize there's kind of a dozen things there that's gone on. And not to mention there could be personal things as well going on in one's life that we simply don't know. So it's just the most complex sport, I think, in terms of the set of circumstances that you have to put in place to get things right.

2018: Chaos and Peak Performance

But then there's a broad theme as well. So I kind of touched on it earlier — when you go back to me in 2018, which was the best year I ever had, there were pockets and weeks within that where I didn't play cuz I felt depressed. For example, I didn't turn up to the French Open in July of that year, cuz I couldn't get out of bed. I just didn't want to get out of bed. And then 3 weeks later, I nearly won the Scottish Open and nearly won at Carnoustie in the Open Championship. So squaring that is a real challenge from a psychological standpoint. But zooming out and looking in at what actually was happening within my game at that time, there was an awful lot of good stuff. If that makes any sense. I recognize I've rambled on a little bit there.

No, you're not rambling. I love it. Please keep going. When that happens, do you try and understand why it's happening, or do you accept that it's happening and let yourself feel that and wait for it to pass?

I didn't wait for that to pass. I wanted to understand why. In hindsight — and this might sound a bit odd, but when I go back to that period, I was drinking a lot of alcohol and I was eating a lot of sugar. And I actually had a blood test two weeks after the Scottish Open because I felt so out of sorts, and I was pre-diabetic. So the Scottish Open — the week that I came second at Gullane in 2018, two weeks after waking up at the French (the week of the French Open) and just not feeling like I wanted to get out of bed — I discovered I'm pre-diabetic. And so it was a lifestyle — it was just a series of lifestyle habits that I was clearly getting wrong. Now, from that point, I actually made a diet and lifestyle change and went on a keto diet for 6 weeks. And then I won the British Masters 2 months after.

So there's all of this quite unusual stuff happening beneath the surface, let's just say, in my mind and in my body and biology and chemistry. But at the same time, when you go back and look at my golf swing on camera, it looked great. There were some great impact positions and it was leading to the ball going pretty consistently in the right direction. So you can have an awful lot of chaos going on in the background, as Tiger did back in the mid-2000s clearly, and still perform at an extremely high level in a sport like golf. Because — and I think that proves the point I'm trying to make — because golf fundamentally rewards for the most part your skill set, which Tiger Woods had in such abundance in the mid-2000s, irrespective of all of the crazy stuff that was happening off the course, which would have been causing some sort of chaos even in his mind, irrespective of the level of psychopathy that he may or may not have.

Is Golf the Escape — Or the Cause?

Yeah. But do you think then also, is golf is the escape from that rather than the focus?

Well, I think golfers are as psychopathic as sports people as you are probably going to find. And interestingly, it's a sport that — I think it's a sport that you kind of end up a bit that way. You have to become a bit more of a — you know, dare I say it — psychopath to succeed in sport. And you kind of do see — anybody that spent time in and around successful golfers, not every, not all of them, but many of them, you'll see very different personalities on the course, in and around competition, to the ones you might meet on a Tuesday morning having a coffee with. Very, very different people. And it goes to show what the sport can do to an individual, and the directions it can pull that person's mind.

I ask this question from an average amateur golfer. Average is probably being kind. The pressures of golf — if you're playing for fun, just against a mate and you're trying to win and you're standing over putts, or you're standing on a tee box, and if you start thinking about what could go wrong, the likelihood is it does go wrong. When it's your job — and let's pull it away from the Scottie Schefflers and the ones winning PGA Tours — when we're talking about I need my tour card for the European tour, at the end of the day, this is your job, right? So this isn't just a nice to have because you want to play golf. It's an essential to have, because you need to support your life and your family and all of this. What I'm really trying to ask, I guess, is: when it becomes the career, the pressure of life coming into that and making it, that's probably why it may have — that you say — psychopathic tendency, because the cost of not having that is huge.

Yeah. And I think, in my experience and in my case anyway, it leads to apathy, because if you have enough of these experiences, at some point you stop feeling. Why? Because to feel in that moment is to recognize too much of the enormity of the situation, and it's a coping mechanism fundamentally that we would all, I think, escape to.

So yeah, I think that's right. Because if I reflect — even though I go back to I lost my card in 2016 and I just moved house and took a fairly big mortgage at the start of 2017. I had to find a few grand a month to pay for the house, and midway through that year, I hadn't made a cut for ages. Was down to not many thousands at all in the bank account when you're having to fund playing golf. And there's a lot of pressure that then comes in. And that was back in 2017. Now, I responded really well to that and went and had a great year in the end and went off on a great three-year run.

But I think it was easier for me last year, and it's probably easier for me sat here now to approach these moments because I've been through them. You know, I've had two or three versions of that in the past. When I just turned pro, I had no money. You know, it's quite a common thing for a lot of professional sportsmen when they start out in golf to have no money, and then you have to do it. So I don't find that that daunting. It kind of is what it is. It's a part of the sport that I love. I think it was one of the reasons why I was a bit pushy-backy at the start on LIV as well with LIV golf — and I know we don't need to get there just yet — but giving too many people too much at a young age is, in my experience, not the right thing to do from a motivation standpoint.

The Finances of Tour Life

Can you talk about, like, in rough numbers, the financial difference then for you playing on the Challenge Tour versus a European tour for a season? Obviously appreciating you could go and win every tournament, but just in general.

Well, the difference in expenditure actually won't be that great, to be honest. You know, to spend a year playing on the HotelPlanner Tour is going to cost you — if you play 25 times — I'm struggling to see how you're going to do it on less than 75, 100 grand, frankly. And you're going to do well to earn that much. If you do earn 100 grand plus, you're going to get your DP World Tour card. So to play on the HotelPlanner Tour is, I think, effectively to say I'm not making money here. It's a stepping stone.

Yeah.

Which is part of why you could make the argument that tour shouldn't be a place where people can make money, because you should incentivize people to move forward and get better. And that's part of the reason why we don't play for — you don't want people to play for a million pounds a week on the HotelPlanner. But then on the DP World Tour, obviously the prize money is — I'm going to say — 10, 15 times higher. But your expenditure will not be 10 or 15 times higher. You know, you could play on the DP World Tour across a 12-month period and it's still going to cost you a minimum of 150 grand, I would say. But you're going to earn that. And in fact, now the DP World Tour give you a stipend where they ensure that effectively you're not going to be out of pocket come year end if you missed every cut.

Interesting. So a fixed —

Yeah, I think it's £120,000 which they will basically say, look, this is your — if you missed every cut, we're going to pay you this. A minimum salary as a — exactly.

The Stipend and LIV's Hidden Positive

But that's a new thing, and I've come around to accepting that that's probably a good thing. Because that wasn't in place pre-LIV. So when we talk about the things that LIV has — the alternative impacts or the ulterior impacts that LIV has had on the game — that's one of them. And I would say that's a positive, to be fair.

You said you've come around to it. Did you not originally think?

No, I didn't. I didn't originally, because I was okay with the fact that a player could miss 25 cuts and lose 100 grand in a year. As difficult as that might be, there's an awful lot that would be learned during that process. And so my kind of view was, from a character development standpoint, well, it would be tough financially, but crikey, you're going to — that's an unusual position to be in and that's going to teach you some pretty interesting lessons. So I wasn't automatically of the view. And in fact, good friend Laurie Canter, who's played on LIV, we butted heads on this argument because he was of the view, no, that you should be paid to play. And I've come around to his way of thinking on that, I will say.

Burn the Boats

I think you could — and to use Charlie Methven's favorite phrase — two things could be true at the same time. Really successful people will often say — and one, actually, a guy called Matt Higgins wrote a book, Burn the Boats — and his philosophy is literally if you have a backup plan, then the boat that you're sitting in becomes far less important to keep afloat because there is a way out. If you don't — as you said, when you were faced with a challenge to meet a mortgage repayment and all of this — you make sure you do the work that you need to to give it your absolute best shot.

Yeah, I totally subscribe to that way of thinking. And I think that's something that actually at the moment, to bring it to the very present, I maybe am finding a little different because for me now there is a bit of a plan B emerging cuz I'm doing the podcast and there's revenue there, and you can start to see maybe I could start to envisage a future a bit more in the media. And so, for the first time in my life, there is what looks like it could be a plan B. And I won't lie — there are weeks now on the golf course where if it doesn't go my way, you kind of resign yourself a little bit earlier to a potential fate. So I subscribed to — it was Matt Higgins you said? Burn the Boats. Yeah, I think that makes a lot of sense. And that was why when I grew up, to me, I was a golfer. I was always only ever going to be a golfer, and the idea of failure never even entered my mind. And when I heard people talk of plan Bs at the age of 16 or 18, I always thought, that makes no sense to me. You know, why are you not all guns blazing in on becoming a golfer, or doing what you want to do? And I've always taken the approach that if you are engaged and present along the journey, particularly in a sport like golf, even if you fail — when you fail — you're going to be highly employable because of the lessons that you've learned, and the general wisdom that I think you will have acquired in that journey.

Where the Money Goes

Yeah. 150 grand, of course — let's just say, right? What is it: accommodation, travel, like —

The bulk of that will be made up of accommodation, travel, caddy costs, and there'll be one other in there. I actually wrote a recent Substack on this and I tried to dive into a bit more detail. But yeah, there are fixed costs like that that generally don't move a huge amount. And then there are some not-fixed costs like a caddy percentage or a coaching percentage. And people would probably be fascinated to appreciate and realize the extent of the outgoings of a professional golfer, and particularly on coaching staff. You know, if you pay a coach — well, you start with a caddy, they get 8%. You then add a coach, swing coach 5%, putting coach probably 4%, physio 2–3%, psychologist — you're soon up in the region of 20%. So if you earn a million quid in a year, well, 200 grand is just gone on percentage expenditure. And then you've got all your fixed costs on top.

That's on tax.

And then of course you get tax. So a rule of thumb, as it was explained to me when I first turned pro by my accountant, and he was spot on, was: you will see about a third of what you receive. And I think that's right. When all said and done, it is about 33% that you end up net profiting — which of course is still an awful lot of money during a good year as a professional golfer.

Major Championship Logistics

I'm going on from an intelligence level here — I'm going right onto the baseline just cuz I'm fascinated by it. You choose, I guess, what hotels you stay in, what quality, so you can make a call if you go in a really nice one or not, right? Let's run it into like an Open. You're running into an Open and there's obviously huge demand. Do they, like, reserve rooms for players, because you've got what, 200,000 people for a week coming in here? You guys need to make sure that you've got somewhere to stay.

They generally do. The difficult — I mean, I've had Opens — like for example Carnoustie, when I did well in 2018, I only got in because of my performance the week before at the Scottish Open. I had nowhere to stay. There was nowhere on site. So I jumped in with Jordan Smith who had a house booked with all his coaching team, and I shared a room that week with his physio Rob Hopkinson, who actually ended up becoming my physio for a period of time. And I was in this crappy little bed in Forfar — far, as I called it — 40 minutes away from Carnoustie, driving in every — and I ended up making the cut. I ended up then staying at Carnoustie for the weekend. Took Ian Poulter's room cuz he missed the cut. He had a lovely room with the balcony overlooking — naturally. But he missed the cut, so I took his room for the weekend and had a good finish.

So yeah, those weeks — major weeks are incredibly, incredibly expensive. You know, when I went to the Masters, the house alone was $20,000. So you're spending 30, $40,000 one week alone to play a major championship, I would say at a minimum, particularly Augusta. Which is why invariably you end up selling a lot of your ticket allocation just to help pay for the week.

Augusta: Expectation Meets Reality

Yeah. Okay. Let's go there. Come on. Everyone wants to know — what is it like, you walk out into the Masters as a player? You don't seem to me like someone that would ever let themselves get too carried away, but I'd imagine there are moments — whether it's the Open Championship at a very special venue like a St. Andrews, or Augusta — that must sweep you away a little bit.

A little bit. I'm not that kind of person. I think it's probably fair to say that is the one tournament, though, that's come closest to doing that. Maybe the par-3 tournament more than anything. The par-3 course there is really cool. The thing is, the irony with the Masters is that it's — I found it a stressful week, because there's lots to think about. Access is limited. I mean, there was a rain delay one day, and obviously you don't have mobile phones, and I was there with my family and a couple of friends, and everyone's evacuated, and I have no means of contact with the two friends who are being ushered out of the grounds, and we've got no contingency plan as to where to meet them. So I'm then running over to the security guy, "Can I bring my friends in?" just so that they can come in the car with me. Lots of little things like that that make it a bit more of a stressful week than you might imagine.

That being said, once you're playing the golf course — particularly once you step foot on the 11th and the 12th and you start to play the back nine, it is one of those places that meets your expectations. And that's such a rare thing because, obviously, in life generally, what you imagine to be the case is very different to the reality. But the back nine at Augusta is truly special. And it's also one of those experiences I had where you reflect more fondly on it across time, which suggests it was a meaningful experience for me.

Do you find much water in Amen Corner?

I hit it in the water, I think, every day on 13 — second shot from the fairway, I think — three of the four rounds. There was an incredible symmetry to it. I think it was a five iron nearly every time off that slope. Just didn't quite draw it enough. Each day today will be different. I couldn't lay up with a five iron, but I kept hitting the water.

15 and 16

But no, my favorite little pocket of that corner of that course is from the 15th fairway, when you've got that approach down, and there's something so special about that shot into 15. You can see the 16th, the crowd's everywhere. That was my favorite little —

To you — special. I mean, sorry again, nerding it out here, but to anyone that doesn't know, you basically on that hole — it's a par five, right? You drive up and then it kind of goes left down a hill.

15 is a fairly straight hole. 13 goes left, but 15's fairly straight. You're right. It's up and over, but it's a fairly straight hole.

Okay. So you're at top there and then it goes down, and then you have the water, then you have the green — but it's kind of — it's not a deep green, is it? It's wide, but it doesn't have the depth. And then if you go long, you're dropping off into the lake of the 16th. So from — again, let's pull it back to the amateur — I look at that every time and I've, like, how on earth could you ever hit that shot?

Oh — I hate to say it. We've seen Sergio make, I think, a 13 on that hole. We've seen Tiger. Most guys at some point in their career, if they spend — if they go there 10 times, they're going to screw that 15th hole up at least once.

And I think that's what I love even more. So, just to dive in a little more into the details of 15 and 16: say you're hitting a five iron — from memory, I was hitting a long iron into 15, and the only thing that really mattered was the strike, because it was wide but, as you say, fairly shallow. But as long as you struck it well, you were going to be dry. Whereas then you get to the 16th tee, and it's the complete opposite challenge. The strike is less important because it's such a long green, but the direction is super important because it's very narrow. So you've got those two iron shots completely juxtaposed with one another at a really important time of the round, but yet both — if you get them right, you can go eagle-birdie in a heartbeat. You get them wrong, you can go bogey-bogey or double bogey. So there's so much volatility there. It's just a brilliant, brilliant design.

Draws Across the Week

You played well, didn't you? I mean, you were tied 50th.

I made the cut on the number. Which, in and of itself, actually added a lot of excitement to the week, because then I got drawn out with the amateur scorer who was called Jeff Knox — the famous Jeff Knox, infamous — speak Rory. I think at some point in his past didn't quite manage to beat me when I played him. But I kind of was lucky when I played it. It was fairly soft, quite benign. I played the Sunday with Bernhard Langer, and he actually said that it's the slowest Augusta he's ever encountered. So I kind of guess I got lucky. But at the same time, would have loved to have — I think it was this year, the first day this year where it was so so challenging. So it's really nice now when I watch Augusta — I can understand what the players are confronted with to some degree.

Yeah. I mean, that must be pretty cool when you go out with someone like a Bernhard Langer, and, you know, they've won it. And, I mean, okay, that's the other — do you talk?

It will depend on the players, I'm sure. But yeah, I would have chatted a little bit to Bernhard. I remember him being very nice. Not particularly chatty, but he's German, after all. So — but no, nice guy.

Love you all tuning in from Germany. Don't worry, guys.

Many countries I've offended on our own podcast. So —

Don't worry, we do all the time.

It was yeah — I had good draws throughout the week. I think I was with Charles Howell III and Charl Schwartzel on the first two days, and Jeff Knox on the Saturday, and then Bernhard Langer and Rafa Cabrera on Sunday. So I had a good draw across the week.

When It Goes Right

Yeah. From the positive side of this — and that year in particular, and you look at you playing your best golf, which led to wins — you played really well at the Open, right? You came to sixth at Carnoustie. You've already said that you had the challenges, but when it is going right for you, and it's not just you feeling good, but it actually starts to equate to results — does it change anything when you start winning? And I mean around your life, around how people view you commercially maybe. How quickly do those things start to take effect?

I think they can. It's probably — it's going to be dependent on the individual. I would have changed somewhat during that period, but I don't think my values changed or anything like that. I don't think there was too much significant change for me. I always struggled with the notion of earning the sort of money that I earned in 2018. I remember writing about this at the time when I used to blog. You know, I've always struggled a little bit to fully comprehend what that means — to earn 500 grand in a week — because it's such a departure from the life that I grew up as a part of, and that most people do grow up as a part of. So there are things like that that I've tried to explore a little bit — what it means. But no, the only time in my career that I've really actively tried to tell myself to act a certain way or the right way was actually when I've been struggling the most. Because I think when you're struggling, as long as you can still walk past people at a golf tournament, say hello, be good company, then I think you're — I just think it's the right thing to do. It's always felt like the right thing to do for me. I don't think it's that difficult to act up well when you're doing well.

The Players: Confidence as a Lagging Indicator

I just wanted — you finished third in The Players as well, right?

Yeah. So that was in 2019, the start of the year. And that was a good example of a result born out of confidence. You know, we talk about this journey of confidence because I didn't really play that well, but I had had a series of good results, wins, high finishes, and so my confidence was very, very high. My short game was good, and my confidence was high. And that third place just kind of came from nowhere. It came to me. Whereas a year previous, I could have been playing better, but I wouldn't have finished third because I wouldn't have quite had that level of confidence yet. And so, that's the point I try to make with confidence — it's a journey that can lag, and it can kind of lead a bit. But yeah, that was a good result for me, for sure, at the time.

17 and 18 on that course looked like an absolute nightmare as well.

Well, that week's interesting. I played the 17th in three under. So that's a good hole for me. The 17 — and on the Sunday, I holed a really long putt. Played with Justin Rose. It was a great final day, and the crowd were going wild, chanting my name. And I didn't really know what to do or say. An Englishman in — not New York — but Sawgrass.

But that's really, I guess, an additional part of what I meant. Even if you manage to keep yourself grounded and don't let things affect you, we know what it's like in sport, especially outside — it doesn't take much for everyone to start changing their perceptions. And suddenly they're going, "Oh yeah, Eddie Pepperell finished sixth major championship. He's now qualifying for major tournaments. He's finished third in The Players, the fifth major, if you want to call it that." So amongst all of that internal stuff, it's the pressures that can get exerted outside of it. It is the fact — let's be realistic — you said that it's half a million, $700,000. You know, you get these checks, and suddenly there's this different side to sport that comes in that you may not have had to deal with previously.

Yeah, I think that's right. And I think, you know, other people will see you differently. That's for sure. I think as I reflect now, people want to know you when you're doing well, and they may not want to know you when you're not doing so well. But fundamentally for me — my wife Jen, we've only been married a couple of years, but I've been with her since I was 16. My family — there's really not been any sort of, I think thankfully for me, and I'm most grateful for it — there's been so much, I've had such a solid home life. And with my Twitter as well, which I was doing a lot of at that time — I always found humor as my little kind of outlet, and would happily take the piss out of myself irrespective of the good or the bad. So, and other players too. So I think there were things that were in my life that kind of just kept me tethered to the ground. Thankfully, I hope.

The Team

And your team — how consistent have you been with the people around you?

Yeah. Well, I haven't — I mean, I have had quite a few coaches over the years, although really I wouldn't say I have at the same time. I mean, I've had conversations with many coaches, but I've really only ever spent extended periods of time with two coaches. I think the coach is the most important person for a golfer. That would probably be my view. I think when you look at guys like Rory, Scottie Scheffler, and I often use Jordan Smith as an example of this — a really good young English player too — when there is that consistency in terms of your background staff, particularly with your technical coach or swing coach, I think in the long run that is most beneficial. You tend not to get lost. You have somebody that could just be your guard rail. You know, that's something that I haven't had. I've gone off on too many tangents. And though it's entertaining and it's interesting, it fundamentally doesn't really work as it pertains to performance, which obviously is the thing that matters most in all sports. So yeah, coaches are very important people.

And alongside that, do you have the kind of physio locked in? Is it a physio as and when? Are they different ones that you will pick out and use? How does that —

You can have your own physio, and there's been short periods in my career where I have, but the DP Tour offer a physio service every week. So there's a team of probably half a dozen or so, maybe eight or 10 people even, that rotate and travel year in year out. So you can get to have relationships with them, they can understand your body — of course it is an integrated system — so they can take notes and whatnot. They invest a lot of money, the tour, in providing that for the players. So we're really covered well on that basis. And I would say in general, the DP World Tour — as the same will be with the PGA Tour — they do a remarkably good job of covering a lot of those basics for us guys.

LIV Golf: The Initial Ripple

Okay, let's get to it. Everyone thinks I have an unhealthy obsession, and maybe they're right. LIV Golf. Let's start from the beginning. No — being completely serious, one of the most disruptive things that a sport has seen, well, may maybe ever. We're now speaking with the benefit of hindsight, looking back on a number of years rather than the impact that I remember it having right at the beginning, when this news broke that there was going to be something that looked like it was going to disrupt a sport that had operated in a pretty singular way for quite a long time. And I want to understand, you know, from someone that is actually inside it rather than me sitting outside it having a load of perspectives on what it appeared to be. So if we're just looking at when it's kind of announced, what's the ripple effect? What were the original thoughts floating around the players' community?

I honestly struggle to remember. I don't remember feeling that much about it until players started kind of playing on it, and then it hit me — the disruption that this was going to cause. I didn't have too many views ahead of time with LIV, from memory. And then, as I say, once it was clear that, oh, Phil Mickelson's going, and then Cam Smith, and then Dustin Johnson, and all these guys, you start to realize the ramifications and how significant they could potentially be, and indeed were, for our sport. And then I think, depending on how viscerally you feel that — and for me, it was pretty significant. I felt strongly that, though this was going to be a real negative for our sport, of which I'm a very very small constituent part of, but a part nonetheless — and I don't have too many values generally, I don't live by too many ethics, but one I think I would say of is that I do think you owe a responsibility to your industry if you spend enough time in it to leave it in a better place than you found it. And that's certainly how I feel about golf and the European tour. And what I saw were people going to play LIV golf simply for money at the potential cost of the tour that provided them with an awful lot in the years gone by. I found that very very conflicting and difficult, frankly, to accept.

Would You Have Gone?

Did you find it conflicting? Because while it's easy for us again to sit here and have an opinion on it — if an offer was presented to you, like some of them were presented an offer with — this is always my side. It's like, well, it's easy to sit here and say it when it's laid down in front of you. Whether it is the players that went to LIV, whether it's Jordan Henderson, who left Liverpool to go to Saudi and play in the league for 700,000 a week — you know, it happens in sport, and it's life-changing. And there's a couple of occasions where I remember in football, there was a transfer in 2014 from a guy called Oscar, who left Chelsea to go and play in China, and he came out in an interview afterwards and he said, "Look, that 20 million net a year, I look after 31 people. That changes life pretty much forever for us." So, how do you balance, I guess, the reality of an offer like that being presented to someone, while also, as you said, trying to grapple with the ethics of what you think is the right thing to do or the right thing people should do?

Yeah. I don't agree with the idea that everybody will always make a decision for money. You know, I fundamentally don't agree with that. I still think there are a lot of people in this world that have principles that exceed and supersede money. I think I'm one of those people, frankly, and I say that with some degree of confidence. And I would go back to Covid for me — and we don't need to explore too much — but I was somebody that never got vaccinated during Covid, and so my life in 2021 and 2022 as a consequence of that was made much more difficult, frankly. But I still maintained my position. And so I only in the recent past, pre-LIV, recognized that I am capable of making a decision that, though might inconvenience me, nonetheless is one out of principle, and I stuck to it. And so, irrespective of the details of that, it was an example nonetheless of a principled act.

And so I think there are still many people that would have turned down offers for LIV golf. There are still people that would have turned down expensive contracts in China or Saudi, whatever. And so yeah, I've always pushed back a bit on that notion. And I would maintain there was no amount of money that could ever have enticed me to go and play LIV golf, cuz I fundamentally thought that it was so bad for professional golf — arguably more so than it turned out to even be. But nonetheless, I thought it was going to be bad.

Why?

Primarily because of the effects that it was having on formatting. Whether it be shorter events, shorter fields, lack of cuts, the disregard for a meritocratic entry system — which I think is integral to a game like golf, as we touched on at the very beginning with my journey through Q School. Primarily those things. And not to mention as well, the characters initially that were involved with LIV, I thought, were quite flawed individuals. I think time may have borne that out to be true. I'm not trying to be overly pious when I say that — I just think if you go back and look at Greg Norman and Phil Mickelson, you know, greed kind of rules the day with those guys. They had a vengeance against other parties. And to me, I saw a lot of good people still on the side of the DP World Tour and the PGA Tour, and I kind of saw some people going over there who had question marks over, maybe as it pertained to, as I say, character and personality.

But at the same time, I don't want that to take anything away from the admiration and respect I have for them as golfers, because I know as well as anyone just how difficult it is to have had the career that Lee Westwood has had. Lee Westwood I admire as much as any golfer. His longevity and consistency is second to none. But I disagree fundamentally with, obviously, his decision to go and play on LIV, just to use one example.

The Fallouts

Has it been hard as players to have to kind of sit on this different divide, when you still have the respect, the friendships — you mentioned Laurie Canter. Fundamentally, there is a huge difference in beliefs and opinions for those that sit on the side. But you can have your friends, the people you've been around for years, someone that you've idolized maybe like a Lee Westwood or a Phil Mickelson, to then reconcile that kind of in a — we have these differences. But or you know, you go into a Ryder Cup, and you have Rory on one side who's been obviously the advocate, and then you have Jon Rahm who's gone and been the big name. That struck me as the hardest, what must have been the hardest thing of this whole situation.

Yes. I mean, you'd have to say, thankfully, there hasn't been that many occasions where actually you've had to walk past one another in a locker room over the last four years, such as been the divisions that have been in place. That's of course beginning to change. And I think it's fine now because tensions are not high. It's not felt the way it — I recall in 2022 sitting in on a players' meeting the Tuesday or the Wednesday of Wentworth week, this very week, three or four years ago. And it was an extraordinary meeting really because Keith Pelley was having to lay out his stall, and in the room was Ian Poulter, Sergio Garcia, Westwood, every LIV player, and it was acrimonious to say the very least. And I was kind of sat there and I was sandwiched between some of these players and it felt awful. And that's one of the biggest tournaments of our year, and that's the environment on a Tuesday. So it was, you know, when you reflect now, a very strange environment to be trying to compete as a golfer in. It's not nearly that bad now.

So yeah, my relationship with Laurie was certainly challenged and tested, and we had massive, massive disagreements and I would say a fallout on LIV as well. I mean, we've — we get on great now. There's no issue with it. But we're also two characters that probably would butt heads with a number of different things. So there's that natural inclination for that to occur anyway.

"Family" as Cultural Diagnosis

But yeah, it certainly was strange. The only other thing I would say that I found a little maybe interesting — I don't know what you think on this — I think it points to something a bit more into our culture: is how they use the term "family" to explain away an awful lot of their decision. And to me, that doesn't go far away enough from the self for it to actually make the impact I think they thought it would. And I think that's a reflection of just how individualistic as a culture we've become, and we've gotten used to becoming. There are people in the past, obviously, figures that we remember and admire — Martin Luther King, just to think of one. We remember and admire them because they stood up for something that made an impact for millions of different people. To just use the family as an argument — it's too close. It's too small a unit, if you get the point I'm trying to make. But I think it's become acceptable because of the individualistic nature of our society at large and culture. And that's something that I maybe think of.

Do you think they consciously dialed in on that? Because they were effectively saying, golf as a sport has never been a family. It hasn't had that feeling. And it's actually something that could benefit from it. So if we can start presenting this as something that we think the players would resonate with by collective values, we're going to have a more powerful proposition.

Well, I think that did happen too — the us-against-them mentality from the big picture level. But I was talking more on the individual level, for an individual explaining away their decision to go on LIV: I can go on to LIV and I can earn this amount of money and it looks after my family. Great. I get the point. I get it. It becomes accepted in enough people's minds because, to a lot of people now, the family unit is deemed large enough for that to be an ethical and moral point. And in my view it isn't. It's not. I don't blame the players for doing that — it's a reflection, I think, of the culture, and how, again, individualistic we've become. That's the point I was trying to make there.

And that makes even more sense. Well, I was actually just linking it into there. And it's funny you said that because every time I hear people or heard people referencing it, particularly from the inside — or a lot of the players on it — it was the LIV family, and this almost idea that we've kind of broken away to create this collective culture, rather than we're gonna go out every single week trying to beat you, my opponent. And again, that's a perception that's very subjective rather than anything else.

No, I think that happened too. And I think, however, that was inevitable when there was that much disdain and disgust, frankly, that was thrown the way of golfers that initially went to LIV, that you are going to — we need to find a home. We're social beings fundamentally. It's very hard to be on your own. So, you know, it really was no surprise, I think, in hindsight, for them to use that us-against-them family-type language.

What LIV Forced Golf to Do

If golf is going to reflect on itself, right — the existing infrastructures that were most disrupted — whether this was the right or wrong thing, a lot of steps have been taken since to try and improve product, prize pool, etc. But there does have to be that self-reflection and go, well, this did happen for a reason. So while the alternative wasn't great, do you see what it forced the golf industry to do, or what it has forced some of the changes the golf industry has to make? Do you see that as a collectively now longer-term benefit?

Yes and no. I think the most interesting person in that story is Yasir Al-Rumayyan, because I think a lot of LIV golf was his pet project. And it could be his pet project because he plays golf and loves golf the same way you do, and there's really no other sport that an influential person like Yasir can do that. And so I think the disruption that he was responsible for was therefore made much larger because of his love for the game of golf. So I think he's an interesting person to look at in that phenomena.

That being said, undeniably there has been some things that have progressed as a consequence of LIV golf. Obviously touched on it a little while ago with the stipends that are now in place, which I think on balance are good. But I do think, interestingly, though, PGA Tour, as they look out into 2028, going back to larger fields, going back to adding cuts into every event — you know, they're doing the full circle. I mean, you look at the way LIV evolved in the last 12 months — 72 holes. Look at — I think their new, from what I've heard, the new format is proposing larger fields with cuts. So they were a disruptor in some respects, but actually in far fewer than you would have certainly thought on, or even imagined, when they first came into being.

And, you know, we have a mutual, I'm sure, acquaintance, Roger Mitchell, who often makes the point that Jay Monahan wasn't paranoid enough. I think that's an interesting concept. I think as a leader, clearly you have to have some degree of paranoia in terms of what could somebody come and do to upend what I've created here. But at the same time — and I think Charlie Senior made this point recently, or you may have done — no one could ever have imagined the extent of the spend that the PIF were going to throw at such a wasteful product. And so, you know, I don't think anybody could have fully foreseen what was coming.

The Road Not Taken

Do you think there was anything — whether feasible or not, as a belief or not — that if this was going to happen, Charlie and I have talked about the better approach: putting money into existing infrastructure, existing tours to try and get it to be more competitive, so that you had a balance within an industry where a European tour could have had the power to retain more of the top talent to compete with the PGA, to prevent a monopoly that essentially is always the downfall of some sports if they become too powerful and they control everything. You know, do you think that is — having talked about it for the last 6 months, I hope the answer is yes — do you think that is something that, you know, could have been a better alternative?

Absolutely. The issue is — and I think this is where there was a lot of misinformation around at the time — was that there was an idea that was proposed to the DP World Tour as an option, and it kind of really wasn't. You know, LIV was always going to be its own thing. And that was always going to be an issue, not just for the PGA Tour but for the DP World Tour too, because if Jon Rahm is playing on LIV Golf 14 weeks a year, he's only got another, you know, 28 — I don't know, it's poor maths, probably 38 weeks — to do something with. And he's only going to play 20 times. So this is where I fundamentally used to disagree with — you know, I think Kevin Pietersen used to often refer to it as being like the IPL of golf. Well, it isn't, because the IPL is a small format. It's a short format, right? It can happen in a condensed window of time, in and of itself, and each match can be over and done with quickly. So it can kind of fit in with an incorporated bigger structure where you can get Test cricket, T20s and one days and whatnot. LIV golf wasn't like that.

If LIV golf had been 10 exhibition events across a weekend in 10 major cities around the world — or even if it had just attempted to replace the World Golf Championships and maybe gone to six instead of four — I'm pretty convinced it would have taken off, and it would have had an awful lot of buy-in from not just Keith Pelley at the DP Tour, but probably Jay Monahan too, because the pressure from the top players would have been such that, no, we can add in these six tournaments. We've just lost our World Golf Championships, which were free money events. But they didn't do that. They went in with this LIV vision, this 14 events, and it was fundamentally too big for it to ever fit into the golfing ecosystem. And so it was never going to work, no matter. And that was on them. You know, that wasn't on — I believe Keith Pelley when he used to say to me, and us as members, I would have taken a deal from the PIF if it was a good deal, but it wasn't. And I believe him when he says that.

Reintegration

Look, actions have consequences, right? Reintegration has become a major topic. You've got players now that may not continue, who are looking at where they go next. But you've also spoken about how competitive the environment is — the qualifying schools, the Challenge Tour, you know, getting your card on the European tour. This must be a very difficult kind of topic to then look at what the right solution is. If you are going to start opening up the tours that were left for very specific set of reasons to a number of players who now have to deal with the fact that the tour they left it for isn't the same property.

I don't actually suspect it's going to be as difficult as we may think it will be. I think all fundamentally the DP Tour and the PGA Tour are going to have to do is just maintain the rules that are currently in place. And it's simple. If you want to come and play on either tour, you're going to have to find your way to it. You're going to have to qualify. There are a number of LIV players who still have some form of exemption to play on the DP World Tour, providing they clear their fines — and I think they've now all cleared their fines that are outstanding. So next year it's likely there'll be an influx of round about 10 golfers potentially who have been playing on LIV who will come and play on the DP Tour. But to their — and I have no issue with that, because they've earned their right through historic performance that gained them exemption criteria onto the DP Tour. So nobody's really giving anybody anything there. They've earned it.

The question is going to be, how many invites are then given out on top of that to players who have no exemptive status. So a Joaquín Niemann might be a good example. Clearly a valuable golfer. When Joaquín Niemann plays the Irish Open, he's a great player. I enjoy watching Joaquín Niemann on the range. So, you know, I can imagine a lot of other players — people will enjoy watching him as well. So how do we integrate those players is the challenge for Guy Kinnings, the CEO, and the executive team. And there are, of course, only so many invites that can be given out. But I do think on balance they will use them wisely, and they will benefit the DP World Tour in 2027, would be my — I do have concerns about 2028 and beyond with the proposed changes coming for the PGA Tour.

2028: Championship Series and Challenger Series

Whether you want to get into it or not, it's up to you. But I think I do think that's going to provide a really big challenge for the DP World Tour with what they've got planned.

Yeah. So from 2028 onwards, my understanding is the PGA Tour is going to go to what they call a championship series and a challenger series. I would also add in as well, they've got the Korn Ferry Tour. So, you know, to think about that for a moment. If you add in the DP World Tour as well — so you've got four tours there that I've just talked about — roughly speaking, there's going to be around 120 players on every tour. And when you look at the prize money that's going to be played for, as predicted and I think is expected, it's going to be in the region cumulatively of half a billion dollars across those four tours. So the PGA Tour across their 15 championship events will be playing for around 300 million if they're at $20 million events, for example, which they will be.

I don't know how that is sustainable. 500 golfers, of which maybe 50 provide genuine value to the outside world. I mean, you couldn't — if you were to meet, probably — you probably would only recognize 10 golfers in the world, frankly. Right? My Jen watches Patrick Cantlay and still doesn't know who Patrick Cantlay is. And I'm like, he's been in the top 10 for many years. So —

No, I'm weird, but yes, I get your point.

Do you know what I mean? I find it unfathomable that that is a sustainable model that's going to continue to finance itself and fund itself.

But if that is indeed the plan and it goes ahead, my big worry really for the DP World Tour is with the Challenger Series Tour, because the Challenger Series Tour, which is going to sit beneath the Championship Series on the PGA Tour — I mean, the Championship Series is going to be incredible. Everybody's going to want to be there because they're going to be playing for $20 million, the best fields in golf. How the PGA Tour controlled — fundamentally they control access into that tour — and it's going to be on them and up to them to decide how much access comes via the Challenger Series and how much comes via the DP World Tour. And as well as that, they also have more and more control over the prize funds on the DP World Tour as per this strategic alliance.

Why are they doing this — the PGA Tour?

Well, I think this is Brian Rolapp's vision of what a future PGA Tour should look like. It has this pyramid scheme, which I think is the right thing to look at. My concern though — and this is where it will be really interesting to see, I think, what happens — and I try and say this wearing no hat and being objective as I can: my view is that if everything was incorporated, every product would improve. I mean, there would really be no DP World Tour, but at the same time there'd be no Challenger Series because that would become one and they would feed into the Championship Series. But that's going to mean certain things, right? That means a complete incorporation of businesses, which is going to be a challenge in and of itself. But I think if there's an integration of the Challenger Series and the DP World Tour for the most part, that gets elevated. And then the Championship Series could even have the Wentworths of the world and the Scottish Opens and the Dubai Desert Classics. And so that, in and of itself, becomes a better product. In my mind, it sells itself a bit more readily and easily globally. But it's going to require Brian Rolapp — and specifically Brian Rolapp — to have that sort of vision, appetite. Or it might even be necessitated just through sheer market forces that could occur in the next 5 years that mean something like that happens. But yeah, I don't know.

The Real Competitor: YouTube

There's concern for the players in the structure. There's also concern for fandom when you have a lot of this, right? You're always relying on people being interested and maintaining that level of interest that allows 500 million in prize money to even be feasible to distribute, and partners to come in and broadcasters to get on board with it. And there's a level of simplicity that often works within that, allowing people to know exactly where they're going, what they're watching, who they're seeing, and where they're going to see them next week. There is also the side of golf at the moment which, maybe, no sport has — I would say — converted and been as effective at managing itself from a content perspective, with non-professional golfers being able to come into the sport now. Whether that's other sportsmen driving interest, because we see now so many players — whether it's Formula 1 drivers or footballers etc. — and that brings some of their audience in. We see golf content creators all over YouTube, right? I mean, it's incredible. All your reels on Instagram, you — I'm constantly seeing people stinging shots into greens that look about 500 yards away. It's a sport that over the last few years has seemed to kind of capture a breadth of that audience with a content strategy that hasn't necessarily had to come from the powers that be. How do you view the whole content side of what we've seen alongside the professional product?

Well, I think it's — and it's good that you brought that up, because I also think that's the other consideration for Brian Rolapp: his biggest challenge and competitor might not be any other DP professional golf tour. It could well be YouTube. And Bryson might well spearhead that. We don't know. Time will tell.

So that goes back to my point of: he therefore needs to make the Championship Series and the Challenger Series as a product even better. And in my view and in my estimation, if everything came together, it would be better. So that would be another way of fighting what YouTube could one day present as a challenge.

For me personally, I don't watch any golf influencers on YouTube. I'm just not interested in it. But I get that the audience is just enormous. And so I kind of don't have too many views on it, if I'm being completely frank with you.

I guess we can say, look, it's good for the game of golf. Absolutely. Because what we're really doing is we're bringing more people to that game. It's some of the numbers — some of the guys from the PGA actually shared some of the numbers with me recently. It was fascinating to see just the total participation outside of the US globally and how that had increased, and the age profiles of some of the people engaged in it. Which of course in sport now, it's one thing having a bucketload of viewers and participants, it's another thing having a bucketload of young viewers and participants.

No, absolutely. And I do think that's a challenge for all of the tours — how do these young lads who get into golf watching Rick Shields or whoever it may be, how do they — do they one day want to become a professional golfer? That's — I would hope, in my mind, they do, because in my mind that was all I ever considered. But I guess we're in a new world, and to me I still find it completely bizarre that someone would want to be an influencer and not instead be brilliant at that particular endeavor. So yeah.

Do you think at the moment — and you know what, we're still, I would say, in what we would call the first gen of, let's say, the golfing influencer. My perception on those that have actually turned out to be, whether it be a Rick Shields or some of the others, is those people set out to be professionals, didn't quite make the cut, and have been creative in how they've maintained golf as a business for them — rather than just go — I say just never — rather than going and being a coach or something. Now, what will be interesting is in 10 years' time, 15 years' time, when you've had children growing up from the first time they pick up a club having a relationship with someone on YouTube, whether that's something that becomes an ambition rather than an outcome of them not achieving a card on a tour.

Yeah. No, I mean, it's completely feasible, isn't it? It's — I find it somewhat sad, but it doesn't really matter how I find it. It's coming our way, I guess. So yeah, it kind of is what it is.

Looking Forward: Eddie at 35

Okay, back to you before we wrap it up. How do you go yourself now? You're 35, right? You've had major successes. You've had big challenges, as you've talked about. What do you look at moving forward?

Yeah, I've never really been good at setting goals, which is probably why I've had the kind of career I've had, to be honest. The problem is, though, that goals — I know I could have set one, and it didn't mean anything, you know. For me, the trouble I have is finding genuine meaning in something, because that's what I would struggle with. That would be my eternal struggle — meaninglessness, really. I kind of battle with that.

So instead, I suppose I flip that and try and focus very much on the micro. And that's why I think I am infatuated with the golf swing, my golf swing, my technique — because if you struggle to set goals and adhere to them in that respect, then you'll kind of end up over here on the opposite, which is where I think I am and have been for a long time. And that comes with its own pitfalls certainly, but at the same time, it comes with its own enjoyment because I still enjoy trying to improve and practicing. If that wasn't in place, I think I would call it a day, because frankly, there's been so little to enjoy of playing it for a few years now as a game professionally. Why would you do it? Why would you go out there and just put yourself continually through what feels like a lot of suffering — which I don't wish to make that sound, I don't look for sympathy, certainly, it's just that's how the game has felt for me. And I think that's how the game feels for a lot of golfers, and probably other sports people too. So you have to enjoy your daily sort of routine of practicing, and I still do. I find that invigorating. So as long as that remains, that's a key thing, cuz that will drive a lot of my own well-being and self-fulfillment.

DP World Tour vs. PGA Tour

But it's not necessarily "I've never done this yet, so until I do that, I want to —" I mean, you've played and interesting tournaments. I just talked about the Championship Series — I have no ambition to go and play on the PGA Tour. And I think that ties in a bit with the LIV stuff. I think there are players too on LIV who played in America, thought of it what I thought of it, which is: this isn't what it's cracked up to be. Much prefer being at home a bit more, traveling in Europe or outside of the US. As wonderful as the US is, it's not maybe as great as everybody thinks it might be.

So for me, I want to be playing well on the DP Tour. If you were to ask me, how do you want to feel about your next three years? That would probably be my blanket answer. I want to be playing well, feel as though I have control over my skill sets and what I'm doing, and have a good degree of organization across that, and be performing at a good level on the DP Tour, because I think that would really make me feel pretty happy on a weekly basis.

So if you had the choice between the two, you would — you'd want to be DP.

Interestingly, if I had the most remarkable end of this season and got one of the 10 cards, I would say with 95% certainty that I would turn that down right now and stick to playing golf on the DP Tour for another year. Because — and I say that as well — I love traveling in Europe. I love Europe personally, and I've grown to appreciate Asia a bit more. Me and Jen have had some wonderful trips down to Africa this year, and you just don't get that on the PGA Tour. And I think that is the side of playing golf on the DP Tour that is just magical.

What do you think people assume the PGA Tour is that it maybe falls short of?

I think just the general glitz and the glam. You are playing for a lot of money. The events themselves on the PGA Tour are second to none. They're fabulous events. But it's very CY — you stay on a pretty average hotel on the side of a motorway. You get your Starbucks at 6 a.m. on the way to the course. You go play. Everybody seems a bit depressed out there to me. When I was there, I often thought, none of these people seem that happy in spite of all the millions they're earning. And it just feels — everything feels a bit more there, you know. Whereas when you play on the DP World Tour, the vibrancy of experience is so much greater. And I think ultimately this is what saddens me when I hear of Scottie Scheffler not wanting to travel as much, and the Americans who don't travel — because to me, all they're doing is limiting their experiences and their future self. And when you can be offered what they are currently being offered to go and play the game globally, to turn that down, I find just remarkable. Because I would have done it for free, let alone the millions that they will be offered to travel to wherever it might be.

Heritage and Naming Rights

And there's huge history in the European tour, isn't there? I mean, that's again — that was kind of a point that we've spoken about when looking at why it's an amazing investment opportunity — because you've had Seve Ballesteros winning multiple trophies, and you could have grown up as a kid looking at that and going, I have that tournament that I could play in and win the trophy of my idol, as much as you do amazing courses and you go to great places. And it's been, you know, it kind of has everything other than maybe being the glitz and the glamour and the massive prize purse that a PGA Tour event has.

Yeah, you're right. It has the history. I actually have a question for you. I'm sorry, I don't know how much time we're going on for here, but — because you talk about the history of the European tour, and it's interesting you use the word European tour. Of course, it's the DP World Tour now, back — but this is my question: because a few years ago when Keith Pelley sold the naming rights to DP World, that brought in a lot of money, which obviously benefited us and him via his, you know, remit set to him by the board. But my view back then was that's a massive risk for the business moving forward in the long run, because you lose an intangible there in terms of the naming rights and the goodwill that's attached to that and associated, that you can really only sell once, in my view. This is your world not mine, but what do — when you now look at the DP World Tour, from your perspective in the world of business, like — it's good that you still find it valuable based on its history, but I would imagine that association has become a bit more challenged because it's the DP World Tour. And so there's that naming — what's your views on —

I think — yeah. We often think changes happen a lot quicker than they do. And so, kind of coming back to the golf influencer point, to me, like the European tour is a thing. And therefore the name change doesn't change that for me in my head. When I'm first thinking of it, I still think of it as the European tour, whether DP will want to hear that or not. But as if that maintains as it currently is right now and you're — and I'm — and I was 10 not 32, then my perception of the European tour is going to be the DP World Tour.

Will be very different in time. Does that make a difference? Yeah, it will do to the history of that tour. For now, you have a huge number of people that the European tour is grounded in — it's I would say more old traditional format. And personally, I don't think that's likely to change, which is why I've never got too worked up about things like naming rights or stadiums — stadiums are another good example. I remember when Mike Ashley changed Newcastle into the sportsdirect.com-like arena, you know, and of course the heritage of that and what it means is horrendous to so many people. But everyone was still calling it St. James's Park. You still have the associations that you've probably grown up with around that. And it's an unfortunate part of sport in this day and age where heritage is often the thing that is most compromised by money.

Yeah. And it's also cynical, isn't it? Because you know that that's what people are going to think. And I come back to Keith. Keith was, I think, in the end, a maligned CEO of the DP World Tour, but actually I think he was quite forward-thinking in many ways. And this is an example — and I think you've just helped me understand how forward-thinking he was in appreciating the lack of relevance or importance in naming rights. Because to me that was a big issue. But as you've just described, and I think rightfully so, it kind of isn't. And so he brought in that money recognizing there's not going to be as much going out as you might think.

Content Fatigue and the Shape of Growth

I think as with everything now, you know, we're so quick to make our minds up and jump on controversy and try and find the problems in some things. I think particularly in sport, when you really just step back from some of it, 80% of the things that we like to complain about probably aren't really worth the brain space, the head space that we give them. And I also find it very hard — and you know, it's amazing doing what we do here and sitting and chatting having the number of conversations across a number of different sports. The thing I find the hardest is trying not to contradict myself in so many different ways, cuz I can speak about one thing in one sport and another in another, and they can potentially be completely opposite. But it's very hard to sit here and say a tour should do things a certain way and should maintain its heritage and history, but then it should also try and find a better balance to compete with something that is selling something that doesn't have the same challenges.

Well, I think that's the problem of growth, isn't it? If you're always trying to grow, a contradiction is inevitable because you can only extract something from so many sources so often, right? And maybe we're at that point. This is the point of the discussion that I do find fascinating with sport more generally. It's media rights. It's big big picture stuff. Where are we at in the landscape of sport? Because I certainly know how I feel about consuming sport. I feel tired. Much in the same way you would feel tired of consuming anything for 20, 30 years. And we have had a — what, call it a 20, 25 year boom — since the turn of the millennium with TV and sport and all this stuff.

I find it particularly acute for me with football. I used to love watching the Premier League, and since Covid I never watch it really. Because I just think back to the days of Thierry Henry and Bergkamp, and that was when I loved watching football. And modern football to me does nothing compared to that. But I often think it's just that I'm tired of it and I'm looking for something new. And as you say, in the modern world, because everything is so readily available, so newly available every day, it's this rewiring of the brain that's occurring to us all, which is making the old world — frankly, it's — well, it is a thing of the past.

Well, you know what it is really — it's — we now have choice.

Yeah. And previously, exactly — which, you know, previously you didn't have the choice. So what was on was watched. Sorry — sorry to interrupt, but I think this is the challenge — to try and bring it back to the golf and the point I was trying to make with the PGA Tour and the DP Tour coming together: at some point, golf, I think like all sports, is going to have to choose to become smaller to become more profitable and to become more appealing to the average person. And that's a really — that's an almost impossible thing to do when growth is the goal, if you know what I mean. You've got to almost do it in reverse.

That's why I asked you why you thought the PGA Tour was doing this. Because the US sporting ecosystem generally, right, has been built on — I mean, this is central because it's PGA Tour — but if you look at the flagship sport in the world from a business perspective, is the NFL, right? That's what everyone holds up. And it is absolutely built on scarcity. Everyone looks at what you can take from it, and they go, "Wow, isn't it amazing? Look at the size of the media deals. Look at the size of the fans. How much money they make from them." And football will then go and say, "Oh, great. Well, here's another tournament, or we've got another governing body that's going to go and put another thing on, or — as there could be another golf tournament or another." The real learnings now is that I think you have to make people value what you're putting on from a sporting perspective. And just by human nature, the more often you can access something, the easier it is to access it, the less valuable that can often become. And so, from a golfing perspective, I agree — there are going to be moments in golf that people who aren't necessarily die-hard fans will probably always want to tune in. It's the beauty of having four majors and some of the history around some of those, which just almost goes beyond anything in the majority of other sports. It's how do you always — how do you work around that? Because your moments in sport are easily sellable, packaged, and everyone gets behind that. A good World Cup campaign, a Masters win, whatever. Are we turning up for the weekly events that are going on? Are you following that athlete beyond the front line that you see them on? Like, that to me is the bigger question of sport moving forward. But it's interesting, because what you hope happens is the ones that do it best, the ones that are acclimatized best, the ones that deserve to still be around — and in theory, all these things we sit and criticize, it may take a tiny bit of time, but it's very unlikely that something that is hugely unpopular, causes a lot of issues, survives. You just hope that it doesn't go and mess anything up too big time in the middle before that happens.

Where tal go.

Closing

Exactly. But look, honestly, I so appreciate you coming in and chatting through that. It's great. And also, I don't mean it patronizingly at all, but it's amazing to have an athlete feel confident to have conversations and have, you know, an opinion about things that are so important to the sport that you participate in. So, it's great to see that. I love everything that you do on The Chipping Forecast. And I'm so pleased that you enjoy the show as well, cuz it means a lot when something that we were really set up to do actually does part of the job that it's there for. So, thank you for coming in. I've absolutely loved it.

Thanks for having me. Pleasure to be here, as I said at the start, and I shall continue being a fan of the show.

Brilliant.

item.description:
### 一、最反直觉的坦白：安全网正在侵蚀他的主业
Eddie 做了一个几乎没有运动员敢公开说的坦白：当他的播客开始产生收入、Plan B 开始浮现时，他发现自己"更早地认命了"——打得不顺时，内心放弃的阈值前移了。这与硅谷创业圣经《Burn the Boats》所鼓吹的"背水一战"是同一现象的两面，但更深层对应的是行为经济学里的**损失厌恶结构变化**：当"失败"的边际代价从"失去全部"降到"失去一半"，大脑在亚秒级决策（例如一个 30 英尺推杆的收杆节奏）里会悄悄把攻击性调低。换句话说，他的职业生涯正在被他的职业保险所温柔地杀死——而这件事发生在肌肉记忆里，意识根本来不及参与。真正令人意外的不是 Plan B 有副作用，而是副作用的作用点不在意志层而在**微秒级运动控制层**。
### 二、2018 年那个"糖尿病前期的身体"是如何打出职业生涯最好一年的
这是整段访谈里最被低估的一句话：2018 年他身体血糖紊乱、酗酒、抑郁到起不了床，三周后在 Gullane 的苏格兰公开赛打出亚军，又在卡诺斯蒂公开赛拿到第六。常识会说"身体是基础"，但 Eddie 不自觉地揭示了一个更冷酷

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Google's AI Infrastructure Chief, Amin Vahdat, on the Physics & Economics of Frontier AI
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：这不是"芯片战争"，而是"同步性危机"

真正令人意外的洞察藏在Vahdat对"goodput"的定义里。表面上，所有人都在谈论FLOPS、TPU vs GPU、谁的芯片更强。但Vahdat透露了一个被所有人忽略的真相——在10万颗加速器规模下，每小时都会有东西坏掉，而真正的瓶颈不是"算得多快"，而是"如何在不可避免的局部故障中维持全局同步"。

这与我们对AI基础设施的直觉完全相反。我们以为AI数据中心是"更多更快的芯片"，但它实际上是一座被迫以微秒精度跳集体芭蕾的失败管理系统。一颗芯片打喷嚏，10万颗兄弟姐妹就得集体回滚检查点——这意味着"算力"的真正敌人不是物理学，而是概率论。规模越大，恰好所有组件同时正常工作的概率越趋近于零。

一个让我震撼的跨领域连接：这与同步大型管弦乐团的失败模式完全同构。一个首席小提琴手走神，整支乐队必须停下来。所以Google真正在做的不是"造超算"，而是发明一种可以让一万人同时演奏贝多芬第九、而且其中任意一人随时倒下都不影响演出的新型指挥学。TPU不是乐器，是让这种演出成为可能的新型乐理。

二、隐藏模式：Google正在复刻互联网协议战争的胜利公式——但很少有人意识到

Vahdat顺口提到了IP协议为什么打败竞争对手——"因为它是沙漏的窄腰"。这句话被埋在采访中段，但它是整个Google AI战略的罗塞塔石碑。

注意他的动作组合： - 开源JAX，但也支持PyTorch - 卖GPU，也卖TPU
- 推动光开关标准，但不锁死硬件 - 甚至愿意把本地发电"回馈电网"

这不是"做好人"，这是精心计算的协议级战争。Google看懂了一件竞争对手还没完全领会的事：在一个即将经历爆炸性扩张的生态里，占据"窄腰"位置的收益远超占据"顶端"位置。IP协议的发明者没赚到钱，但建立了整个互联网。谁定义了AI基础设施的"沙漏窄腰"——是模型框架、是加速器接口、还是数据中心互联协议——谁就是下一个二十年的隐形税收者。

出人意料的推论：Google开源JAX、支持PyTorch不是防守，是攻击。因为一旦JAX在协议层固化为"标准之一"，TPU的生态位就自动合法化了。这是用标准化武器对抗CUDA垄断——不是打破它，是让它变得不再必要。

三、最被低估的洞察：电力正在改写"公司"的定义本身

Vahdat承认power是"唯一的根本约束"。但真正惊人的是他顺口描述的解决方案——Google开始像电力公司一样思考，并在"最热的两周"把电卖回电网。

这里发生了一件没人注意到的事：超大规模AI公司正在悄悄异变成准公用事业实体。Google不再是"从PG&E买电的客户"，而是电网的协同调度伙伴。他们规划自己的发电、承担输电线路升级成本、在高峰时成为电网的供应商。

跨领域连接：这与19世纪末钢铁巨头为了保证煤炭供应而买下整个铁路系统的历史模式惊人相似——卡内基不是想做铁路生意，但煤炭成了瓶颈，所以铁路成了"外部化失败的内部化解决方案"。

但有个更深的扭曲：芯片6年折旧 vs 数据中心25-30年寿命 vs 电网基础设施50年寿命——这三个时间尺度被硬塞进同一个资本决策里。Vahdat轻描淡写地说"我们规划未来5代芯片"，但真正的意思是：Google正在被迫成为一家需要同时在月度、年度、十年、半世纪四个时间尺度上做协调决策的实体。这种时间尺度的叠加，在人类商业史上只有极少数组织承担过——罗马教廷、英国东印度公司、以及现在的超大规模AI公司。

一个让人脊背发凉的推论：如果电力真的是根本约束，而电力规划的时间常数是20年+，那么今天的TPU v8决策实际上已经锁定了2040年代的AI能力分布。这不是技术决策，这是地缘-能源-算力三位一体的提前宣誓。

📝 转录文本

开场：芯片特化的艺术

In hardware, as you know, there is this opportunity where the more you specialize to a particular workload, the less flexible it is — the faster, the more power efficient the hardware is going to be. So it is this art, and it's this projection of what are you designing to and how persistent is that workload. In other words, if it's going to go away after a month or two months or three months, even if it's big for those three months, you got a really narrow window to intercept it. So it has to be somewhat durable, and you have to be able to project exactly what win you can get for specializing to it.

什么是AI数据中心？

Host: Before we get into it, maybe just a crash course for the audience. What is an AI data center and how is it different from a non-AI data center?

Amin: It's a very good question, in that AI data center and a non-AI data center do have a lot of similarities actually, and they're not radically different. It consists of concrete, an enclosure, electrical yards, mechanical yards, cooling. You have row after row of power being distributed. There's a huge amount of network infrastructure there — in other words, we connect large amounts of computes to one another. A fair amount of storage infrastructure goes in there.

I think the big difference that we're seeing with AI infrastructure is specialization. In the past, when we're building a data center, it really is a 20, 25, 30-year building investment, and we're thinking about how it's going to be evolving over that period. You might have servers go into it, networking, storage, some accelerators — GPUs, TPUs, whatever they might be — but it's a 25, 30-year planning horizon. The lifetime of the hardware might be six years, so many generations that we have to plan for.

An AI data center oftentimes is going to be more purpose-built. We are oftentimes co-designing the building with the hardware that might go into it. We might be saying, you know what, actually we're not going to put a lot of storage into this building. Why? Because a storage rack might have 10, 20, 30, 40 kilowatts of power. You put that next to a TPU rack or a GPU rack that easily is hitting hundreds of kilowatts today — people are talking about megawatts in the next few years.

Designing a building that might take 30 storage racks in a row versus one or two AI racks in that same row — very very different design. Just think of it in terms of the size, in terms of the power and how that would be distributed across the building, etc. Networking would be the same. The amount of networking that you would need for a storage rack is tiny — especially if it's hard drives — compared to an AI rack. So if you're trying to make it fully fungible, you'll probably make it too big and too overbuilt — fungible over certainly a 30-year period.

An AI data center likely is going to be much more purpose-built, co-designed with the hardware, even to the point of cooling and power distribution. A lot more co-optimization.
