The concept of alignment has problems at many levels, put it that way.

But to your point, David — Muse is a direct repudiation of that. And it's interesting that Meta, along with Microsoft, actually has been increasingly loud about this, just straight up saying: these things are software. Stop overcomplicating it. These things are just software. Standard infosec security practices really matter here. And unsurprisingly, to the best of my knowledge, we have not seen Meta models running around on the internet hacking everybody. If anybody can tell me where they did, let me know. And before anybody makes the joke about "that's because they can't" — Muse is now close to the top of the benchmarks for most of these things. So it's totally got the capability and is far above some of the other models.

十七、Ram 的 AI 替身：代理式财富管理的 demo

So I actually — I want to drill into this, Ram, with something that you've been up to, which is that part of why it's getting increasingly important for the infosec framework around these things to work properly, and why I by the way think the AGs are totally justified to be looking into this given the pattern of behavior, is that what you can do with models is getting increasingly complex and powerful, and it's in the hands of people who are not themselves spending 24/7 coding or needing teams of thousands of coders like at the big tech labs to do these things. So you were telling us, in fact, during the break, that you had created your own artificial version of yourself.

Yeah, this inflicted some trauma on my family when I showed them this weekend. We got one — two might be too much to handle. Let me share this with you. It's kind of creepy looking at it.

But anyway — this is in our virtual data room. So Lumida is going to do a venture raise soon. It's premised on agentic wealth management. I strongly believe that agents are going to replace advisors. And this AI is trained on our knowledge base. You can ask it a question. You can start a question. I'll show you right here. And it's got my voice and likeness.

Would you say it's an uncanny Alawalia?

Can you guys hear that?

Yes.

What do you guys think?

That is unsettling.

Yeah, that is deeply… It's almost —

I'm out of a job. Done. Right. I mean, it's almost beyond the uncanny valley, Ram. Right. Coming out the other side.

Yeah. I mean, you can see how — look, there's room to be improved.

No, I mean I think it looks great. Really? I like, in six months though, that's going to be amazing.

Three months ago, we — we've been testing this regularly. It's at a level where it's crossed the tipping point of good enough. That's the standard. The standard isn't perfection. The standard is: is it good enough to be deployed? And it is. Put in our data room. It's powered by a 90-page document, and it saves everybody time.

十八、推理成本崩塌：中国模型 90-95% 的能力，10% 的价格

One of the interesting parts to me about this whole thing is exactly what you just said — which is, it is good enough to be deployed. Because the story of the frontier labs so far — so take Anthropic in particular and OpenAI — has been: you always have to be at the exact cutting edge of this, and we're going to be at that cutting edge and that's where all the value is.

But like, conversely, if I go look on OpenRouter right now, the models getting the most usage are the Chinese models — the DeepSeeks, the Qwens, the GLMs, the MiniMaxes of the world — that are not 100% as capable as the biggest models from the frontier labs, but are 90 to 95% as capable and much faster and much cheaper.

So if we're talking about a business like your RIA deploying an AI avatar version of Ram, the "nuclear bomb" of using the biggest frontier model from Anthropic or OpenAI is now excessive for your needs. You can get there with a much faster, much more efficient to run model, because they've gotten so good. This is the classic — the early adopters pay for all the development, and following behind it are the people who actually get the benefits at scale.

Yeah. They just rolled out price cuts — OpenAI, Anthropic. The inference costs are down 90% for the models that we used to pay for last year. So it's great if you're a builder. This is why we're entering the phase of the application layer, and the frontier labs are entering a world of perfect competition with low switching costs thanks to OpenRouter.

The China models are very impressive now. They keep closing the gap. You know, there are security concerns on using these China models, but nevertheless, they are impressive. So it's an incredible time. If you're a builder in AI, you're in a good spot. Everyone should be refactoring their human capital investment capital around AI. You can't understate — we're all underestimating the impact. And I do think we're now entering a fast takeoff mode for AI. When GPT came out, I said we're in slow takeoff for several years. But things are changing now. These tipping-point moments are happening in several areas.

We're going from chat — which isn't productive — to Claude Enterprise, which produces deliverables now, to agents that can do work. Now you're going to have supervision of agents and orchestration of agents to deliver you organizations. You're seeing these startups at Y Combinator act like small enterprises. And in six months' time, it's going to be very obvious and even more compelling.

十九、数据中心会不会过剩？GPU 使用率的真实信号

But Ram, can I jump in and ask you a question based on what you just laid out, right? So you said inference costs for models that were part of the subscription models one year ago are down 90%. And the Chinese models — obviously you still need compute for that, and all of these are going to need compute. So like, Nvidia, fine, they're doing good. But when we talk about the buildout for data centers in the United States, can you give me numbers that convince me we're not overbuilding?

Oh, we're definitely not —

That is the big question. So yeah, but that's where my one of my questions has lingered for a while about all of this: are we going to wind up with capacity that is currently being kind of underactive?

That's the exact right question to ask. Because one day there will be overcapacity and the party's over. We're not there yet. You can measure that by spot rental prices for GPUs. We have Nvidia H100 series models that came out years and years ago, that are well beyond their fully depreciated accounting life, that still are generating significant economic value.

But that's spot. I mean, what does that say about three years from now?

So fair enough. Fair enough. So let's look at it this way. There's 10,000 data centers out there, most of which are CPU-based. The vast majority of them need to be GPU-based. We're about a thousand to 1,400 of the way into that process. We don't need CPUs where we're going. We need GPUs.

If you look at the value from these agents, you are starting to see glimmers of labor displacement. We're still in the labor-productivity part of the curve, by the way, which means that people are far more productive. It's creating more work for everybody. But you see glimmers of labor displacement. Like I mentioned with agentic wealth management, you're starting to see agents that can do discovery better than an advisor — interactive discovery.

How much are you willing to pay for that? A lot, because it allows you to focus your people on higher-value-added activities and upskilling. Why wouldn't you spend $5,000 on an agent that can do SDR work — sales development representative work — that would otherwise cost 60, 80, or $120,000? Your willingness to pay would be 5,000, 10,000, 20, 25. So long as it adds value versus the opportunity cost. So that demand will be —

二十、数据主权与"本地部署"（on-prem）的回归

I have to — I'm sorry. Sorry, I don't mean to go at you too hard here, but I have to — one other aspect of the story that you just told about yourselves, which is — I don't know if I heard correctly, but you said that it is in your data room, right? You're on-prem.

Yes.

And that's the — it's on the cloud. It's on the cloud. So it's not — we need to find on-prem. It's in the data room, but the data —

So maybe it doesn't apply in this case. Nevertheless, I will just float the point that data security is an issue here. And whatever you say about the technical capacity for tunneling or virtual machines or whatever, there are going to be applications where nobody is going to want their stuff in a warehouse 20 meters away, much less 100 miles away.

Yeah. This is an easier issue than people think, because the AIs communicate with applications using API keys, and you can turn on and turn off an API key. It's actually the same security architecture as we've had.

What's different is this: the action space of an AI is broader when it can utilize your browser to perform actions. That's the novel new action space that could be at risk — when it can represent as you and perform actions. It's not about the API keys. That's not it. It's not about provisioning a resource. That's how you can control AI today. You can just stop the API key access very easily.

二十一、"把 prompt 交给中国"：隐私的管辖权套利

So on that note, as I look at some of my thoughts in the data-security space in general, I also think soon we're going to be in for a reckoning going back to what these AGs are looking at — at how these model companies are using the prompts and using the data that they get from users.

My favorite example of where this went horribly wrong was: I believe Anthropic had turned over data from somebody who was a fiction writer writing a novel with terrorist elements to the FBI, that led to somebody somewhere in the world getting a door knock on this exact topic, and it raised some interesting questions of privacy.

So I've got a friend who's an OG privacy person, so I'm not going to dox him on here with the name. But he was talking to me over the weekend and saying, "This will sound strange, but as somebody living in the West, in some ways I feel more comfortable giving my prompts to the Chinese model companies." And I'm like, "Why is that?" And he's like, "Because they don't really particularly care about me in any way, and they're sure as hell not going to turn my stuff over to the authorities I care about where I live," right?

Without naming the Western government, let's just say if they sent an MLAT treaty request to the PRC, the response would probably be hilarious laughter for about five minutes. And so he was making the point that the whole privacy framework is starting to mutate because of the surface of where prompts are going and who cares. To give an example that was raised, he's like, "If I'm talking about aggressively tax-optimizing for my business, I might care if my local government gets a hold of that because they're going to be very upset about this. But do I care if the PRC sees that? This is so far below their level of relevance that —"

This goes back to David's point on on-prem. Yes, people will want on-prem solutions. That's why Nvidia has built a GPU box that you can purchase, deploy on-prem. So we'll see more of that. But if you're a technology company, you're not going to want to develop your valuable IP on China models because of IP theft. It's a very real thing. You go to China, they will find a way to work out your business model, IP, and replicate. This is a known thing.

二十二、"所有数据湖都是蜜罐"：Brave 的架构启示

Yeah. The interesting part of this to me — you're both right about the on-prem part — but also there are going to be models of this coming forward that, as we have a data breach or two or disclosures like this, people are going to care about.

So one of the most interesting AI implementations to me that virtually nobody talks about right now — and guys, I love you, but it's because you market like engineers — is Brave, right? Where Leo in the browser has an AI implementation with many of the different models loaded in there. And they need to update a few of them, but there are a couple of the more modern ones in there like GLM. And they essentially take your prompt, run it through their models in a sandboxed AWS instance, immediately shred everything after returning the thing to you. So you've got it encrypted in your browser and nobody else has a hold of it.

I think even for consumers, because — ironically, of AI — those solutions are going to start getting more powerful. Because one of the things I think we're about to learn, and to bring it all the way back around that the Hugging Face incident has started to reveal, is that large piles of data that are just left sitting there with access to the internet are all honeypots now. Every single one of these has become a target.

And I would tell everybody: you should assume 100% of what you're putting into one of those will be compromised on some long-enough time frame. Now, you may not care about that. If it's your credit card number and it gets compromised — great, just cancel it and get another one. But there are probably a lot of private communications that you're not going to want being spilled out into the world. Ram, like you, business IP is a great example, right? That's one that clearly people have a privacy interest in and there's nothing malicious about it. But I don't want my internal deliberations of some great new technology suddenly showing up on the internet on Wednesday.

二十三、"律师-当事人特权"能否延伸到 LLM？第四修正案的新战场

Well, yeah. I mean, you got to wonder: when do we see attorney-client privilege show up in LLM? Like, how do I get my lawyer in all the chats? That's going to be a nice unique value proposition to add out there. Because people share their most intimate thoughts with AI. Or medical privacy is another kind of related one, right? The most —

Yeah, it's a huge one. Like the most — boy, all this stuff really — it makes it sound like it would be a great time for somebody to put some legislation together that we might actually be able to pass. But speaking of being in the land of fantasy —

How about we live in the real world, David? Right? Like —

For example — let's not go crazy.

Like in the common law, you can't deposition or force testimony from the spouse to divulge information. Does that extend to AI, arguably, who has a deeper context than your spouse?

I would also suggest there was a recent ruling in a federal district court about Flock where they basically said: no, this is a search. The whole "hey, observing people in public is not a search" thing was predicated around those being individual and discrete observations. Like, the police saw you walk into the donut shop — that's fine. But Flock cameras creating a comprehensive visual record of all public spaces at all times is the equivalent of following that person around. That is a very different sort of search than "oh, we were incidentally there and saw them."

Ram, to your point, I feel like AI is posing a similar problem for the way the world is currently structured — which is, nobody really thought about: what if there's a device with all these connectors that has all of your context about all things? That is obviously much closer to somebody's papers and personal effects in like Fourth or Fifth Amendment terms in the United States.

Yeah. Well, it's the classic trade-off between security and liberty. And people historically have traded away liberty for convenience and security. And one of the remedies is you make that as local as possible. You make that — you attach it to the individual. And if you can't do that, you attach it to the municipality where there's more accountability on local elected leaders who are accessible — as opposed to say the federal government. So that's probably the right approach and balance to strike.

二十四、尾声：Chat Control 2.0、监控资本主义与节目结束

I would jump in there and just say a couple of things. One is that on this subject, I didn't know — I hadn't heard about the Flock ruling, Austin — but that sounds very positive to me from a civil liberties perspective. There had to be some reason this was not just normal. At the same time, we also saw — I think it was maybe either yesterday or early today — the European Parliament has rejected what people have called Chat Control 2.0, which was legislation at that level to get enforcement of back doors for encryption on electronic applications.

But on a more systematically, I would say, pessimistic analysis of this question — the other thing to keep in mind is that none of these entities are going to willingly give up their ability to gather and surveil all of your data, because that is a possible business model. And so from that perspective, I think we do need to look for outside pressure. I won't — I'm a fan of federal power, but on a situational basis.

You're a fan of federal power. Really?

I mean, I'm a — I think there sometimes needs to be some decisions made, and in this one —

That's true.

We're also seeing stuff around gambling where maybe I could see some federal — anyway, for debate. But the point being: I don't think these entities — I think there is some commercial pressure for entities like Brave to offer a more private option, and there will be an audience for those, no doubt. But at a macro level, you talked about convenience, Ram — I think that the business models feeding into the convenience factor…

I mean, one of the reasons Muse is such a big deal is because Meta is really good at designing interfaces. And those people who are really good at designing interfaces also work at companies that want to find every possible way to get money out of their users. So that dynamic, I think, demands some real scrutiny and perhaps enforcement.

Well, on that note, I will say we are past the 5:30 mark. So, rather than subject people to even ever creepier versions of AI avatars of myself and David that Ram has been building during this podcast, we will go ahead and call this one here.

So, as always, thank you everybody for joining us. Remember, we have our new channels. Go ahead and subscribe. We will be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding. David, thank you for joining us.

Great. David, that was fun.

Enjoy, everybody.

That was cool.

Thank you for watching, and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice. And please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

item.description:
## 一、"去美元化交易"的伪装：比特币其实在和软件股共舞
最反直觉的发现藏在数据的分裂里——如果真是债务货币化(debasement)主导的宏观叙事，黄金应该同步创新高，但黄金却徘徊在52周低点附近。Ram一句话点破：**比特币真正的"同类"不是黄金，而是软件股**。两者都是被做空、被厌恶、靠轧空反弹的"久期资产"。这意味着市场偷偷重新给比特币归类了：它不再是"数字黄金"，而是一只"流动性最充沛、估值最有想象力的科技股"。
这里有个被所有人忽视的跨领域连接：**当利率上升，政府债务利息支付反而成为对投资者阶层的隐性财政转移**。10万亿美元国债+5%利率=每年5000亿美元定向流入已经持有金融资产的人手中。所以利率越高，不是"紧缩"，而是对资产持有者的隐性QE。Austin说得克制，但真相更锋利——鲍威尔每一次按兵不动，都在给65岁的母亲加杠杆，给25岁的学生贷款者加税。这解释了为什么消费者信心史上最差、消费数据史上最强：**这不是一个经济体，这是两个经济体通过代际债券持仓发生虹吸**。
## 二、AI"对齐"思维的隐秘代价：它让安全工程师忘了怎么装门锁

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正被颠覆的不是帝国，而是"征服"这个概念本身

读完这段材料最让人震动的，不是科尔特斯多英勇，而是特拉斯卡拉州长官邸墙上的那组壁画——科尔特斯和西班牙人被画成与印第安盟友同等大小、平视对谈的伙伴，而不是教科书里居高临下的征服者。这意味着：五百年来我们熟悉的"西班牙征服阿兹特克"叙事，其实是胜者书写的单线剪辑。从特拉斯卡拉人自己的视角看，这是他们利用科尔特斯完成了一场迟来已久的区域清算，西班牙人只是外包的雇佣兵。更冷峻的数据佐证：最终围攻特诺奇蒂特兰的联军里，西班牙人只占 1/2 of 1%（0.5%）。按任何合理的会计口径，这都不是一次"外来征服"，而是一场由外来触发器引爆的美索美洲内战。

二、科尔特斯其实在同时打两场战争——而第二场更像现代商战

这段叙事里最被忽视的戏剧性时刻，是他把总督派来抓捕自己的那支更大规模远征军，用一场谈判外加小规模冲突，整建制转化为自己的增援。这几乎是人类历史上最早、最成功的"敌意收购反杀"案例：被派来并购你的对手，离开时反而带着你的股票期权。放在现代语境里，这就像一家创始人被董事会派来接管的"职业经理人团队"，用一次会议说服对方倒戈，把罢免行动改写成B轮融资。更深一层的意外之处是：他之所以能这么做，恰恰因为他自己是叛变者——没有总督合法授权的科尔特斯，比总督派出的"合法代表"更有资格许诺财富与土地，因为他的位置不受西班牙王室预算的约束。合法性反而是谈判筹码的减分项，这是一个在今天的政治学、创业学里都很少被讲清楚的反直觉结构。

三、火山硫磺与预制双桅船——这其实是一堂供应链管理课，不是军事史

真正让科尔特斯赢下第二回合的，不是火药，不是马，也不是钢铁，而是一个跨领域的工程—物流综合体： - 士兵用绳索吊入 波波卡特佩特火山口采集硫磺（原料的垂直整合）； - 船只被拆解成预制模块，由不计其数的印第安脚夫翻山越岭运到湖边（分布式制造 + 外包人力）； - 在特斯科科湖畔现场组装成双桅战船，完成湖面制海权（最后一公里本地化总装）。

这组操作放到今天几乎就是宜家 + SpaceX + 集装箱航运 的 1521 年版本：原料开采、模块化设计、分布式制造、本地化总装、形成系统能力。换句话说，阿兹特克人不是输给了枪炮，而是输给了一种更先进的"组织复杂性"。他们能动员的仍是朝贡体系下的人力与粮食，而科尔特斯能动员的是供应链——这在今天的中美科技竞争、乌俄战争里仍然是关键分界线。

一个额外的意外观察（跨领域连接）

奥通巴战役的那一刻特别有意思：阿兹特克人本来已经赢了，是科尔特斯识别出敌方主帅位置、集中骑兵冲阵斩首，才让战局整个翻转。阿兹特克军队在失去指挥节点后立刻崩溃——这是高度中心化指挥系统的典型脆性。有趣的是，用户在片尾用俄乌战争做类比，但更深的类比其实在系统论：阿兹特克帝国是一个单点故障密度极高的网络，它的朝贡体系、宗教中心、军事指挥、神—王一体的"ueytlatoani"全都压在同一个节点上。一旦这个节点出错——先是蒙特苏马被石头砸死、再是奥通巴主帅被斩——整张网瞬间塌陷。这与今天我们讨论的AWS 单区故障、SWIFT 制裁、半导体光刻机、乌克兰电网都是同一个结构问题：显得庞大，但只要你知道往哪里打，它比看起来脆得多。

科尔特斯真正的天才，不在于勇敢，而在于他本能地理解了网络拓扑。

📝 转录文本

开场：被忽略的事实——西班牙人内斗

What people might not appreciate about what happened here, in both the Pizarro story of the Inca Empire (which we'll talk about later) and in the Aztec story, is that in both cases the Spanish were themselves divided — and in fact fighting each other.

So, um, maybe you should tell the story: how Velasquez sends another expedition to go capture and arrest Cortez for going beyond the prerogative of his mission.

委拉斯开兹派兵抓捕科尔特斯

Absolutely. We left the governor on Cuba, of course, fuming. Um, he rallies another expeditionary force, because Cortez is stealing his thunder, right? And he sends this under Pomayz — a larger force than the one Cortez brought with him originally. This lands on the coast.

Cortez appreciates he has to move. So he leaves one of his subordinates, the hotblooded Alvarado, behind in charge in Tenochtitlan. He takes as many men as he can to the coast, confronts Denias, defeats him in a minor battle. And again, the diplomacy wins over the entire expeditionary force that the governor had dispatched. He tells them, "Uh, my friends, why are we fighting? We have the empire at my disposal. Join with me and we can share in the riches." So he wins over the vast majority of this new force. It becomes, effectively, reinforcements.

阿尔瓦拉多的屠杀与"悲伤之夜"

He marches back to the capital. Uh, he finds the mood has turned against him. The problem with not being in charge is you can't be everywhere. His subordinate, assuming that the Aztecs were mobilizing against him, decided on a preemptive strike. There was a festival — the aristocracy, particularly the warrior caste, were celebrating — and Alvarado just descended on them, massacred everybody.

Um, the survivors rally the population, and when Cortez returns, he finds himself effectively under siege. The people are so appalled now with the failure of their Hueytlatoani; when he tries to pacify them, they throw stones at him, mortally wounding him. He either dies, or the Spanish finish him off because he's of no longer any use to them.

So now Cortez is trapped in the city, in Tenochtitlan. He determines to break out — and that is to say, La Noche Triste, the tragic night, because so many of his men are left behind. They're either killed as they try to escape the city across the causeways, or forced to retreat back to the palaces, and they're taken alive and sacrificed subsequently.

奥通巴战役：斩首战术扭转败局

Cortez gets away with a minority of the troops still at his disposal, um, and makes it back to Tlaxcalan territory.

That was the critical aspect — the two features of the entire campaign. One: he has enough strike power, with enough horses, to defeat the Aztecs when they try to finish him off. The Battle of Otumba — they feel he's on the run, they have the numbers, the conquistadors are dragging their tails between their legs as they flee, Cortez himself is grievously wounded. "Uh, we can finish them off." And they had the numbers. They were winning. But again, Cortez identifies where the Aztec general is. He rallies enough horsemen to blast through the Aztec ranks and take out their command and control. The Aztec army disintegrates, and the Spanish were able to flee.

So, the battlefield advantages — they had their horses, their steel, critical — but just as critical was the diplomacy. If the Tlaxcalans had turned on Cortez at that point, he would have been finished. Not one Spaniard would have survived; none of them would have made it back to the coast.

特拉斯卡拉人的视角：壁画里的"平等"

But the Tlaxcalans see — for their own reasons, not out of any generosity or humanitarian impulse to welcome back the conquistadors — they still see, "We are committed to these people and to our alliance." So they give Cortez shelter. He recovers physically, begins to rebuild his strength, and is determined to go back to Tenochtitlan for round two. And this time, "We're not going to be indulging diplomatic niceties."

The Tlaxcalans — their own perspective on this: if you go to Tlaxcala, the territory today, the governor's mansion there has murals on the wall, and these depict Cortez and the conquistadors from the Tlaxcalan point of view. And it's fascinating to look at how the relationship is not between a superior and an inferior — it's between equals. You see them depicted in the same scale, engaged in diplomacy between partners, not between subordinates and dominant figures.

The Tlaxcalans drove a hard bargain: "We want territory carved out of the Aztecs. We want our own fortress in Tenochtitlan after this is over." Uh, they saw this as them using the conquistadors — not the other way around — which is very important to bear in mind.

阿兹特克"帝国"的脆弱内核

That the Aztec Empire, from a distance, if you look at a map, seemed impressive — but this was an imperial construct, and not just the remaining independent entities like the Tlaxcalans, like the Tarascans (who we can discuss later), were hostile to the Aztecs. So were so many of their subordinated peoples: the Totonac coast, the Chalco states on the shores of Lake Texcoco. Um, they chafed under Aztec hegemony and authority, and they too saw the conquistadors as an opportunity to finally shrug off the authority, the demands, uh, of the Aztecs, and get revenge, in a lot of ways.

最终远征：0.5% 的西班牙人

So as Cortez builds up for the final campaign against uh Tenochtitlan — against the new Hueytlatoani Cuitlahuac, um, and then, after he died, his brother, the last of the Hueytlatoanis, Cuauhtemoc — um, he has indigenous people flocking to his banner from all over Mesoamerica, right? He's emphasized that he's still in the fight, he still has those advantages. More reinforcements are arriving at the coast, and they're being integrated into the conquistador army. But the force that marches on Tenochtitlan — the total numbers — the conquistadors were maybe one half of one percent in raw numbers of that force. The overwhelming majority were other Mesoamerican peoples, who see this as their final reckoning with the Aztecs.

技术与外交的整合：火山硫磺与预制战船

And this is the integration again of the technology with the diplomacy. Cortez knows: to take the city, he has to control the lake. And again, the innovations:

  • They need sulfur for their gunpowder — they have guns, useless without gunpowder — so an expedition goes into the mountains, to the volcano Popocatépetl, and they dangle with ropes inside the caldera of the volcano, scooping out the sulfur they need as the critical ingredient for their gunpowder.
  • Another one builds prefabricated brigantines — boats in their different sections — and then has untold numbers of porters, human load-bearers, bring these prefabricated pieces over the mountains to the lake. They're assembled, and then they're let loose in the lake, and now they have control over the lake, right?

So, bringing together the technology, the innovations, with the local manpower — and this is the force directed against Tenochtitlan in the final battle.

俄乌类比：敌人的敌人

I actually didn't know those stories. That's crazy. One of the ways in which — to the extent people are even aware of the story — they might not understand what actually happened, is they have this model of the Aztecs or the Incas as this cohesive single nation.

And I think a better model might be something like: imagine if Russia and Ukraine have been doing trench warfare for a hundred years, and imagine the animosity, and then also the Russians are, like, taking tens of thousands of Ukrainians and, like, doing human sacrifices with them. Um, and then, if some foreign force comes in and says to the Ukrainians, "We can help you march into Moscow" — right? I think they'd have pretty decent odds of getting some agreement there.

Absolutely. The old phrase is: "The enemy of my enemy is my friend." And diplomacy, war — that's always very bad.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

读完这段材料最让人震动的，不是科尔特斯多英勇，而是**特拉斯卡拉州长官邸墙上的那组壁画**——科尔特斯和西班牙人被画成与印第安盟友**同等大小、平视对谈的伙伴**，而不是教科书里居高临下的征服者。这意味着：五百年来我们熟悉的"西班牙征服阿兹特克"叙事，其实是**胜者书写的单线剪辑**。从特拉斯卡拉人自己的视角看，这是**他们利用科尔特斯**完成了一场迟来已久的区域清算，西班牙人只是外包的雇佣兵。更冷峻的数据佐证：最终围攻特诺奇蒂特兰的联军里，西班牙人只占 **1/2 of 1%（0.5%）**。按任何合理的会计口径，这都不是一次"外来征服"，而是**一场由外来触发器引爆的美索美洲内战**。
## 二、科尔特斯其实在同时打两场战争——而第二场更像现代商战
这段叙事里最被忽视的戏剧性时刻，是他把总督派来**抓捕自己**的那支更大规模远征军，用一场谈判外加小规模冲突，**整建制转化为自己的增援**。这几乎是人类历史上最早、最成功的**"敌意收购反杀"案例**：被派来并购你的对手，离开时反而带着你的股票期权。放在现代语境里，这就像

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] 經濟數據危險，但為什麼股市還是創新高？Mark Yusko【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被动投资是"认知殖民"：市场的思考器官被切除了

Mark讲了一个表层故事：被动指数基金按市值加权无脑买入，让"思考者"被挤出。但真正令人毛骨悚然的是——这是一种格雷欣法则在"思考"层面的翻版。坏钱驱逐好钱，而被动资金正在驱逐"主动思考的资金"。

这意味着市场正在失去它最重要的器官：定价发现机制。当60%的美股由被动资金持有，股票的价格已经和"这家公司值多少钱"无关，只和"有多少钱必须买它"有关。SpaceX亏损60亿还能估值2万亿，不是因为有人相信它值这么多，而是因为没有人在被允许说它不值——做空会被挤爆，被动资金则必须按规则买入。

这里有个让我震撼的意外推论：AI泡沫的刺破点可能不在AI。真正的触发器藏在人口统计表里——婴儿潮一代到71.5岁必须从401k强制取款。这把一个科技故事瞬间翻译成了一个人口结构故事：被动买入的虹吸管快要掉转方向，而没有人在定价这件事。

二、"真相替代信任"与哥德尔不完备定理的奇异同构

Mark引用Scottetta和Haber对blockchain的原始定义时说了一句关键话："你需要一个裁判来监督裁判，然后再需要一个裁判来监督那个裁判……"

这不是金融问题——这是数学哲学问题。它是哥德尔1931年不完备定理的翻版：任何自指的形式系统都会撞上"元层级无限回归"的墙。传统金融系统（银行→央行→国际清算银行→……）本质上就陷在这个递归里，每一层信任都需要上一层来背书。

区块链的创新不在技术，在哲学：它用"分布式真相"打破了元层级回归，就像图灵机用"可计算性"绕开了希尔伯特纲领的死胡同。从这个角度看，Bitcoin的意义不是"更好的货币"，而是人类第一次在金融层面逃离了元逻辑陷阱。

跨领域的意外连接：这个结构也出现在物理学中（观察者问题）、神经科学中（谁在观察意识）、以及法律系统中（宪法谁来解释）——所有依赖"信任"的系统，终究会撞上这堵墙。Mark没说出来的是：clarity Act投票失败，不是政治问题，是数学问题——银行必须保卫自己在信任链条中的"中间商税收权"，否则整个元层级会坍塌。

三、"创新周期14年"藏着一个生物钟密码

Mark随口说了一句被人忽略的话："创新周期每14年发生一次，因为那是半代人（half a generation）"。

这个数字惊人地精确：1954大型机 → 1968微芯片 → 1982 PC → 1996互联网 → 2010移动网 → 2024区块链/AI。但为什么是半代？

这里藏着一个生物钟与科技钟的共振：14年刚好是一个孩子从出生到青春期的时间。换句话说，每一次创新浪潮的时间点，刚好让"上一代还在挣扎适应时，下一代已经在本能地掌握新范式"。父亲还在学微信时，儿子已经在玩Discord。父亲还在学ChatGPT时，儿子已经把它当水龙头用。

这意味着创新接受度不是教育问题，是生理问题——人类的神经可塑性窗口和技术迭代节奏之间存在隐秘的共振。而这又揭示了另一个令人不安的事实：老龄化社会的创新接受周期会被拉长。日本不是因为"保守"才接不住技术，是因为人口中枢的神经可塑性已经过了窗口期。Mark说日本"领先走向货币危机"——他看到了表象（entitlements），但没看到更深的病根：一个失去神经可塑性的社会，必然会用印钞代替创新。

四、一个你可能没注意到的黑色幽默

Mark提到：OpenAI + Anthropic + SpaceX 三家公司的估值 > 过去45年美国3365家IPO公司的总和。

但更黑色的点是：这三家公司都是Elon Musk和Sam Altman的朋友圈产物。换句话说，整个"数字时代的未来"目前被定价在约10个人的饭局估值上。这不是科技故事，这是宫廷经济——我们回到了美第奇时代，只不过把佛罗伦萨换成了旧金山湾区。

当"价值"由饭局决定、由被动基金执行、由媒体放大，我们已经不是在投资，而是在参与一场集体性的宗教仪式。Mark没有明说，但这是他真正的恐惧：泡沫会破，但破的方式会非常非常像一场宗教改革——痛苦、血腥、重塑所有人的认知坐标。

📝 转录文本

經濟數據危險，但為什麼股市還是創新高？

Mark Yusko 專訪｜邦妮區塊鏈

開場：三個泡沫、一個謎題

It will end badly. Those three companies — OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX — total value... there used to be a tethering of valuation to production of things called profits. Back in the '90s, we had an untethering for the first time and we had the tech bubble. Like, wait, isn't that the same thing that's going on now?

Bonnie：It is a little confusing. The Fed raised rates for the first time in three years. The Clarity Act failed to advance in Senate. And yet, Bitcoin has rallied and the NASDAQ just hit a record high. What is happening now?

Mark：There's a few stocks that are just going to numbers that just don't make sense to a lot of people. And part of it is — China's playing a really interesting game. They're buying up gold. We have a banking crisis. Nobody wants to talk about it. Scott Bessent the other day said, "We're the house. Bring it all." Who was going to buy our bonds? Every empire in history has fallen the same way.

Over the years, we moved increasing amounts of money into passive strategies, which are based on a simple rule called capitalization weighting. Now the problem is — all great wealth, all of it, came from concentrated positions. You really have three buckets that you need to manage.

嘉賓介紹

And so, pleasure to have Mark Yusko join us today. He is the founder and CIO of Morgan Creek Capital and managing partner of Morgan Creek Digital. And he spent more than 30 years investing across public markets, venture capital, technology, and digital assets.

So good to have you here, Mark.

Mark：Ah, thanks for having me. And I wish we could have done this in person in Hong Kong, but my travel plans got messed up, but it is great to do it virtually and thanks for having me on the show.

Bonnie：I'm sure I'm going to see you in person someday.

Mark：Very soon. Very soon.

一、Fed 加息、股市創高：到底在發生什麼？

Bonnie：Yeah. Let's talk about what's happening now because it is a little confusing. The Fed raised rates for the first time in three years. The Clarity Act failed to advance in Senate, and yet Bitcoin has rallied and the NASDAQ just hit a record high. What is happening now?

Mark：You know, that is the $64 trillion question really. And it's quite common for these types of things to happen where everyone focuses on one thing — let's say the Fed. And so everyone's like, well, if the Fed cuts rates, then everything will be great. And then not only do they not cut rates, they raise rates. And yet everything seems to be great.

I say stocks are new all-time highs. Now, if you peel back the onion just a little bit, it's not quite as great as it appears. There's a record number of stocks below their 52-week high moving average. The market has bad breath, shall we say. And yet there's a few stocks that are just going to numbers that just don't make sense to a lot of people.

全球流動性，不是美國利率

And part of it is a phenomenon related to actual liquidity in the global marketplace, as opposed — everyone focuses on the US, right? I find it funny. I live in the US and there's this American exceptionalism — like all the smart people live here and all the good businesses. I'm like, there's some really really smart people in other places and some really good businesses in other places and really good markets in other places.

But that American exceptionalism — well, if the Fed raised rates, then liquidity must be down. Well, if you actually look at M2 globally, it's actually rising. Well, why? China. And it usually comes back to China.

In most cases, if you look like in 2016 when the world looked like it was going into recession — oil prices were down to like $26 and people were freaking out, commodity prices were collapsing — suddenly we had this big rally. China printed $4 trillion of new capital and injected it, and it finds its way into the capital market.

中國在玩長線遊戲

So part of it is China stimulating. And China's playing a really interesting game. It's the long game. The long answer to your question — what's happening? Well, what's happening is China is stimulating to promote their technological evolution to be more of a consumer-based society rather than just the industrial powerhouse.

That's kind of what happened in America, right? We're the manufacturing warehouse and we had lots of pollution, and then we exported all that to China and China became the manufacturing powerhouse. And now they cleaned up a lot of the pollution — there's still some, but they're moving towards this consumption-based and more of a world dominance.

And the thing that they're doing that's really interesting — they're buying up gold. So they're bringing gold in to back their currency with a hard currency, while the rest of the world issues debt like it's going out of style in all the Western countries. Started with Japan, then Europe, now the US.

二、美國的銀行業危機沒人想談

So what's really happening in the US is we have a banking crisis. Nobody wants to talk about it. But when we had the industrial revolution part two going on in China, China bought a lot of our debt. They used it as a risk-free rate and they bought it, and Japan bought it, and everybody was happy to buy US debt.

Well, then they stopped needing as much debt in Japan and China because they became more self-reliant and more focused again on consumption rather than manufacturing and export. Long story short — who's going to buy our bonds? Because we have this big deficit because we can't control our spending.

回到 1930 年代：量化寬鬆的輪迴

Well, if you go back to the 1930s, we did this before. We were a little emerging market run by a gang, right? And no one would buy our debt. So we bought it ourselves and we invented something called QE — quantitative easing. Japan did it 15 years ago, they called it QQE — quantitative and qualitative easing. And now we're doing it again.

And then Scott Bessent the other day said, "We're the house. Bring it all." Yep.

銀行的套利遊戲與崩潰

And so, you think about it: when no one will buy the bonds, they said to the banks, "Banks, you're going to buy the bonds, but we're going to make it worth your while. We're going to cut short-term interest rates to zero." Okay? So you're going to borrow from us. You're going to borrow from the Fed at zero. Pretty good deal. I don't get to borrow at zero, but they were borrowing at zero. And you can buy bonds at three or four. Awesome. Risk-free. Oh, and you can lever it up 10, 11 times. They were cranking it.

But then what happened? Interest rates went up. Losses on those bonds. And you've seen the chart — TLT and all the bond indices just crashing. So now the banks have these massive unrealized losses. And like, "Oh jeez, we got to fix that. Okay, let's raise short-term rates so now they can earn interest on their deposits."

Clarity Act 為什麼過不了？

And that's why the Clarity Act didn't pass, right? You talk about the Clarity Act and the lack of clarity. The Clarity Act didn't pass because everybody likes not paying depositors interest.

Bonnie：No, no, no. Coinbase and those, they wanted to pay interest.

Mark：No, they didn't. They started saying that, and then they're like, well, if the banks are against it, okay, we'll give on that point. Well, yeah, because if I deposit my stable coin at Coinbase and they don't have to pay me interest and they can stake it and make 5%, that's good for their bottom line. That's what banks do. They take your deposits, pay you half a percent, they lend it out at four or 5%, and they make a lot of money.

So we're trying to reliquify our banks, but we have this debt addiction. So we got a $2 trillion deficit, and when interest rates were zero, the interest cost was pretty low. At 5%, the interest cost is really high.

帝國隕落的統一模式

And so we're stumbling down this path. And the sad thing is it's the same path that the UK followed. How did the UK fall? The UK invaded Mesopotamia in 1913. They incurred a bunch of debt. The pound sterling collapsed. The dollar ascended. Now, it took 30 years from 1913 to 1944 for Bretton Woods to happen, but eventually every empire in history has fallen the same way. They get massively in debt. But it's the same thing every time.

And yet, quietly, China just keeps putting out 96% of the AI citations, all the innovation. They just got that big chip IPO — chip company where they can now manufacture chips without the EUV machines where ASML has had the dominant monopoly.

So that might be the longest answer you've ever had. That didn't exactly answer your question, but —

Bonnie：I think that answered the question perfectly.

三、區塊鏈：從"信任"到"真相"

Bonnie：But to your point, we were talking about Coinbase. I asked the head of institution, John — isn't it better for Coinbase and Circle that this Clarity Act does not pass?

Mark：Good for you.

Bonnie：But the answer I keep on getting is that they want a bigger pie. Do you think it makes sense?

Mark：Absolutely. Look, here's the thing. Digital technology, blockchain technology, stable coins — it's better.

比特幣白皮書背後的哲學

If you read the Bitcoin white paper, which many people have, in the back there are footnotes. And in the footnotes, three of them list Scott Stornetta and Stuart Haber, who were professors out at Stanford. And Scott and Stuart coined the term blockchain because he said: in any transaction where there has to be trust, you need a referee. But you then need a referee to referee the referee. Well, then you need a referee to referee the referee who's refereeing the referee. And that's just a chain of blocks in a system.

And so blockchain — trust is fine and it's worked for 800 and something years. But truth is better.

If I have a Bitcoin on-chain and I want to send it to you, I don't have to have a bank account. You don't have to have a bank account. I don't have to pay the bank a fee. I don't have to go into the branch to send you the wire. I can send it to you — the network, which establishes truth. One, Mark has a Bitcoin. Two, Mark sent the Bitcoin to Bonnie. Three, Bonnie received it and now it's hers. I can't claim it.

Taking a world from trust to truth is far superior.

為什麼銀行恨穩定幣

Well, now we go to — oh, that's why the banks hate this. Brian Moynihan from Bank of America said, "We can't pass Clarity because $10 trillion would leave the banking system." Yep, it would. Because you don't pay your depositors any money to use their money. The banks make a lot of money. JP Morgan is the 11th largest company in the world based on market cap. That seems insane to me — because we should make money on our money, not them.

So if you think about it, Jamie Dimon says it's a scam or it's a fraud. Well, of course he does.

So in the beginning, if you remember when Senator Lummis started the bill — and I don't know if she wrote it, but when she was the big proponent of it, and Brian was all for it, and everybody was all for it — and the banks were really against it. They're like, "No, you cannot pay interest on stablecoins — with all that money, we'll flee the banking system and we'll have a problem." Like, yeah, you will have a problem, but we will collectively be better off because we'll get paid for our capital.

"無需許可"世界的美好

The first time you sit in your pajamas on a Sunday and buy something with stablecoin because the banks aren't open — right? The market's not open. It's glorious. It's so cool, right? You're sitting there and just you just do it because it's your money and you don't need permission.

And look, for people who really want to understand this permissionless — watch Erik Voorhees, right? Just watch Erik Voorhees. He gives this 13-minute speech on what living in a permissionless world is all about, and that's why we all Bitcoin, and that's why this system is so superior to the ones replacing.

比特幣的"下一個區塊"哲學

Well then, Mark, why are they so against Clarity, or why didn't Clarity pass? We have this bipartisanship problem — there was no bipartisan combination. But I think also, unfortunately, we got to the point where the way the act was written from its original writing became so antithetical to what it's supposed to be about.

And so to answer your question — why did Bitcoin go up? There was a great post, and I wish I could give credit to who did it, but he said: "Remember, we didn't have clarity in 2009, or in 2013, or in 2017, or in 2022. We don't have clarity now. So Bitcoin just — tick tock, next block."

四、黃金、法幣與"貨幣的碎裂"

Also, the way the world is set up right now — when you don't like something and you fear that thing, you put it in a part of the financial system that you think you can control. Gold, for example.

So gold is an amazing asset. For 5,000 years, right? When China was ruling the world, when Cleopatra was ruling the world — I mean, 5,000 years. If creating wealth was as simple as printing paper money, wouldn't everyone just do that? Sure. But it's not that simple. And gold is — until Bitcoin — the only money in the world.

貨幣與通貨的區別

Well, Mark, what are you talking about? We have all the currency.

No, those are currencies. Yen is a currency. Dollars are currency. Euros are currency. And money is an asset that exists in the absence of a liability. JP Morgan, who I'm not a really big fan of, but he said it, right? "Gold is money. Everything else is just credit."

So there's this monetary fracturing that's going on around the world. I call it the fiat fiasco. And those who are the least well-off — Japan's in the lead. They have the highest number of elderly. And turns out, as you age, you become less productive. This doesn't mean you're not a nice person, but you're just less productive, and you become ultimately a cost of society, and you have to incur big deficits and ultimately devalue your currency, which is what Japan's going through.

為什麼福利制度崩塌？

Bonnie：Can you explain why?

Mark：Well — entitlements. Entitlements are promises you make that you don't fund and you ask your kids to pay for. Like, who wouldn't vote for that, right? Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, free stuff. Now we're talking about universal basic income.

So think about Social Security. Social Security is a great idea, right? Let's take care of the people who don't make it. But it should operate like insurance. Like, I pay my insurance for my house, but if my house doesn't burn down, I don't ask for all my money back. That's not how insurance works. The problem is an entitlement system that isn't funded doesn't work.

五、重新設計貨幣系統：從黃金到數字黃金

Bonnie：If you were to redesign this whole system, what would you change?

Mark：So the first thing I would do is what we're migrating toward. So I would re-establish the gold base for the monetary system. We went off the gold standard in the United States in 1971, and since 1971, the inflation problem has been ridiculous.

So I would kind of re-solidify the base. But then I would transition over time from gold to digital gold. So it's more divisible and it's more portable. It's a better form of gold. So I would slowly move to a Bitcoin-based monetary system, and that would turn the bad money into good money.

Jimmy Song 的"奴隸論"

And the person who does this the best — I don't know if you ever talked to him — but Jimmy Song, I love Jimmy, you know, cowboy hat, handsome guy. He says it best. He says, "Look, if you work and get paid, you're a slave." And everybody's like, "Oh, you can't say that word." He's like, "No, stop. Just hear me out. You're a slave. You are a slave to the fiat system." Because every day they will steal back from you a portion of that wealth through this thing called inflation.

So he said: imagine a world — that's an inflationary currency — imagine a deflationary currency like Bitcoin, where every day, right, one Bitcoin, like an ounce of gold, is one Bitcoin. So in the whole 17 years of Bitcoin, Bitcoin's never changed, but it went from 0.003 cents to $86,000 for one Bitcoin.

No, no, no. Something must have happened. It must have got better. It must have got faster. Nope. Didn't change at all. What changed is the number of pieces of paper that we have to exchange for that thing.

And so imagine a world where you get paid in Bitcoin, and now your time is free to do the most powerful thing in the world, which is human creativity. Because instead of having to work harder because your money is going away from you, your money is going to appreciate over time.

投資創新：被嘲笑的少數派

Every technology scares the incumbents. And that's why adoption is hard, and it's my pinned tweet on Twitter: "The greatest wealth comes from investing in innovation. To do that, you have to invest in something that you believe in before others even understand it. You'll be mocked and ridiculed for your non-consensus action, but it's totally worth it."

So what the internet did to media and commerce, blockchain was going to do to financial services, and it is doing to financial services. And so our first funds were all about everything financial services — exchanges, software tools, anything that touched financial services. Then in our third fund in 2020, we said, "You know, this AI thing..."

六、AI 是"71 年的隔夜成功"

Now, the funny thing about AI — AI is a 71-year overnight success story. The term was coined in 1955. I'm old enough to remember 1980. Time magazine picture of a rocket — "The year of AI." In 2000, Intel stock over the previous 10 years had gone up 20-fold. Looked just like Nvidia, because their chip was gonna revolutionize AI, and we got Clippy, you know, the little paperclip. Didn't, and it was dead.

In 2020, there started to be some talk about: could we make blockchains intelligent? We actually coined a term called "blockchain intelligence" and we started investing at the intersection of blockchain and AI. And then in our fourth fund that we raised last year, we crystallized what we call the foundation of the digital age.

The digital age is very different in so many ways. And it will have so much more in terms of innovation, and it will create so much opportunity both for investing but also for quality of life.

AI 是不是泡沫？

Bonnie：I think we can all agree that technology is going to change a lot of things, and people do generally believe that AI is good at least in this part of the world. But you said earlier this year that you think AI is in this bubble that is forming. Do you still hold that same thought?

Mark：It's not that AI is the bubble. It's the companies at the top of the food chain that I believe are. And it's true not just of AI like OpenAI and Anthropic and XAI, but also companies like Nvidia and the memory companies.

1990 年代的影子

What I mean by that is: there used to be a tethering of valuation to production of things called profits. And back in the '90s, we had an untethering for the first time, and we had the tech bubble. And we got to a point where Cisco and Microsoft and Intel and all these companies were super overvalued, and eventually they crashed.

Well, why did they crash? It turned out there's a lot of accounting chicanery. Turned out Cisco was kind of cooking the books a little bit, and maybe there was a little bit of circular financing with companies like JDS Uniphase. And like — wait, isn't that the same thing that's going on now? And so we had lots of debt, and Enron was doing some bad stuff, and WorldCom was doing some bad stuff.

And so for a couple years we had to unwind all of the badness. And then we went 20 years to kind of work our way through to the next wave of innovation.

創新浪潮的 14 年週期

And innovation waves happen about every 14 years. Now, why is it 14 years? That's half a generation.

  • 1954 — the mainframe computer
  • 1968 — the microchip
  • 1982 — the PC (up where I live in Seattle)
  • 1996 — this thing called the internet
  • 2010 — the mobile net — suddenly we all carried little supercomputers around in our hand

When Apple released this in 2007, their stock went down 40%. People are like, "I'm not paying $1,000 for a phone." You're right. You won't. You'll pay two, and you'll be happy about it, because it's not a phone, it's a supercomputer. And the reality is it changed everything. Social, local, mobile changed everything.

And then in 2024, we had this innovation around blockchains. And so we're at the very beginning of this next innovation wave.

LLM 的真相：是工具，不是智慧

AI — I find it funny. AI is not what people think it is. LLMs are good tools. They're excellent tools, but they're computer applications. Everybody's like, "Well, they're this new thing. They're not a tool." Like, what do you mean they're not a tool? You type into them, they calculate probability of the next word in a sentence, and they give you an answer. And if they were trained on good data, they give you a good answer. If they were trained on bad data, they give you a hallucination.

Blitzy 的例子

I'll give you an example. I use it a lot to verify facts or gather information on competitive businesses. And we have a business that we've invested in that has this really cool application of an AI agentic tool. What does it do? They take companies in finance, government, military that have old code bases written in COBOL, this dead programming language. It's been around for 70 years, but they're too afraid to change it because — how do you fly the plane while you're fixing it? You can't just shut down the bank while you bring in the new system.

So this company — these guys from MIT — created this agentic tool that actually operates independently for about 3 weeks writing new code. And then the cool part about code: you can actually test it and see if it works.

So I made this investment in Blitzy, and I asked the LLM, "What's Blitzy's revenue?" They said, "Oh, a billion dollars." I'm like, "I'm 100% certain that's wrong, so try again." It's like, "Oh, you're right. That's the valuation of the last round." On my — I know that, because I did that last round.

So it's not even a perfect tool. A perfect tool is a calculator. You put in 2 × 2 and you get 4, with certainty. Like, a quantum computer can't do that — it gives you 4 most of the time. So these tools are good, but the model companies got everybody to believe that they were something else — that they were intelligent.

LLM 不是智慧：四個標準都不符合

But here's the problem. There are four definitions of intelligence. And an LLM fails all four. So it's not intelligent.

There was a paper just the other day that was released. It says mathematically it's impossible for an LLM to actually create anything. Remember, human creativity, I said, is the most powerful force in the world. And it's because of the way a model works. It can only take data it already has and make a probabilistic estimate of what the next piece of the pie should be based on what you prompt it. So it can't just sit around and think big thoughts.

Now, there's rumors and stuff: "Oh, well, it can do that, and it's going to be sentient. It's gonna nuke us all." 10%, just like the climate.

Well, no — just like the climate was going to nuke us all, and just like the Russians were going to nuke us all. Go back in time and look at the cover of Time magazine for the last hundred years. Every 20 years, something was going to nuke us all. And what comes out of that is a regulatory apparatus that protects the incumbents. I don't want that. I don't need that.

SpaceX 的估值荒謬

And so that's where I think the bubble is. I look at a company like SpaceX. It's a perfectly good company. Starlink, perfectly good product. Launching rockets — not a very good business. Actually loses a lot of money. Things blow up. And maybe their AI business will be good. We don't know yet.

But today, the company has $20 billion of revenue and loses $6 billion. There's no planet, including Mars, that that's worth $2 trillion. It's just not. Because value and price are different.

七、被動投資：價格與價值的脫節

And this goes back to the very first question we started talking about. You said, "What's going on?"

Over the years, we moved increasing amounts of money into passive strategies, which are based on a simple rule called capitalization weighting. And capitalization weighting, I think, is just a dumb idea. So the whole idea of market cap is silly.

But the way market cap works: every time new money goes into an index fund, whatever the market cap is of the company, it has to buy that. It can't ask. It's dumb — meaning it's rules-based. It can't think.

WeWork 的教訓

Perfect example — remember WeWork? WeWork was going to be this new-age real estate company. It was going to be a tech company. What did they do? They take buildings and they subdivide them and they rent them out in smaller units. That's been going on for hundreds of years. That's not new. That's not tech. Okay, you have a nice UI/UX, but it's not tech. It's real estate.

Real estate businesses trade down here. "Oh, we get a tech multiple, so we're up here." A thinking person would go short that. But the problem is the thinking people got displaced. Remember — bad money crowding out good. Bad models, bad passive strategies crowding out good.

So there's now more passive money than active money. And if you try to short stocks, you get squeezed by the big guys who take the other side. And so we're in this funky period where it's a self-perpetuating momentum strategy where success begets success. Now the problem is that works until it doesn't.

艾菲爾鐵塔曲線

If you look at all of the charts that go like this in history — every single one of them, they go like this. None of them go like this and then go flat or go up. They just don't.

Now, how far they go up the left side of the Eiffel Tower remains to be seen. But at some point, that virtuous cycle, which is the market cap weighting, buying more, turns into a vicious cycle where as the market cap goes down, the index is forced to sell.

And as the populations go from savers to consumers — like when you turn 71 and a half, you have to take money out of your 401(k). So we're not quite there yet. Most of the boomers are still under 71 — or maybe not most, it's about 50/50.

八、FOMO 與"活著打下一仗"的智慧

Bonnie：So let's say yes, we see the chart going like this, but then also we don't know if we have a 2x or a 5x left. Right now what people are worried about is — okay, I understand that there's a bubble, whatever, but if I don't participate in this, the world is expensive. If my asset doesn't go up at this speed, then there's no way I can make it. So people — they know it might be risky, but they're still on this ride.

Mark：It's the classic dilemma. Part of it's FOMO. There's a famous cover in 2000, Newsweek magazine, and it showed a guy with his hair on fire, and he's like, "Oh my God, my neighbor's getting rich." Nothing makes you crazier than your neighbor or your friend getting rich. Nothing makes you crazier.

Julian Robertson 的教誨

And this is the best piece of advice I got. I had this mentor, Julian Robertson, famous hedge fund guy. And Julian was famous for saying: "Never double down. Live to fight another day." You're not right. The market's wrong. You're wrong. And maybe you'll be right someday, but right now you're wrong. And just live to fight another day.

And the other thing he would do — this goes a little bit counter to what I was saying — when something's working, he actually would double up and he would ride. And to your point, how far do you ride it? There's some magic there that most people can't do.

So what I would say is: that's fine. You can let your winners run. And Peter Lynch said the same thing — "Water your flowers and pull your weeds." Most people water their weeds and pull their flowers because they're afraid of winning.

But I would argue with some periodicity — quarterly, annually — rebalance. Just rebalance and take a little bit off the pros. There will always be good ideas and there will always be good assets.

九、人生的三個桶：Lifestyle、Get Rich、Stay Rich

I'll leave you with this. So if you think about your life, you really have three buckets that you need to manage. You can think about it side by side. I like to think of it as — this bucket drips into the big bucket in the middle, and then there's this hole on this side and drips into the bucket at the bottom.

Bucket 1：Lifestyle Bucket（10–15%）

So the bottom bucket is your lifestyle. It's your spending. 10 to 15% to live. And the hole in the bottom can be small or big depending on how much you spend.

Bucket 2：Get Rich Bucket（10–15%）

Up in the right hand corner, you got the get-rich bucket. That's the 10 to 15% to do the brother-in-law's condo deal or the friends venture deal or whatever. I would say you're going to lose all that, so keep it small. Now, you're not going to lose it all, but that's the get-rich bit.

Bucket 3：Stay Rich Bucket（70%）

But in the middle, that 70% is your stay rich bucket. So either your get-rich bucket or your income flows into your stay-rich bucket. And your stay-rich bucket should be diversified.

Because the interesting thing about investing — all great wealth, all of it, came from concentrated positions. Concentrated stock position, concentrated real estate position, business ownership. But all small fortunes come from concentration.

How to create a small fortune? Have a large fortune and stay concentrated.

Because there are cycles. Over 30 years, 85% of the companies in the S&P disappear. So over a long period of time, natural selection takes over. So don't ride forever. You got to change. You got to go with innovation.

十、比特幣是不是例外？

Bonnie：So can people ride Bitcoin forever then?

Mark：Oh, Bitcoin is different. Bitcoin and gold are different.

So this is what I was going to say. In that savings bucket, you have three time horizons.

5 年內：流動性

In the next five years, you want to immunize those liabilities. Maybe you got to save up for a car. You got to save up for kids' college. You got a big vacation you want to take. You want to buy a house. In that five years, you need liquid. It could be bonds, it could be Stretch, it could be converts — anything where you're getting an income that's guaranteed by something for those five years. Do that.

5–20 年：股權風險

Then in that 5 to 20 year range, you got to take equity risk. Equity risk can be private equity, common stock equity, real estate equity, any type of equity.

And equity — think about investing, there's four ways you make money. All of them require you to take risk. If you take no risk, you get the risk-free rate, hence the name. That equals about 4% long-term, which roughly equals inflation. So if you leave your money in cash, you basically stay even. Now, lately, you've lost because of currency devaluation, but that's another story.

  • Cash / risk-free rate — you make no money
  • Credit risk — buy a bond, make 2%, 3%, 4%; something like Stretch, maybe you make 8% above risk-free
  • Equity risk — 7% above risk-free, 10–11% long-term — because equities are a contingent claim; you only get paid if the bond holders get paid back

Oracle — great example. Oracle bonds are collapsing, their yields are exploding because people are concerned that they don't have enough money to pay the bonds back. Well, if they can't pay the bonds back, the equity should be worth a lot less, and the stock just keeps going down. So equities have risk, but when they work out, they're fantastic.

20+ 年：黃金與比特幣

For that period over 30 years where your biggest enemy is currency devaluation, you have to own gold and Bitcoin. You have to, because it's the only thing — and collectible cars, art, fine wine, some real estate, anything that's scarce. But I'm going to argue gold and Bitcoin at the core. And if you want to have some Pokémon cards and some cars, fine. But those scarce assets are the only thing that will protect you from the long-term ravages of inflation.

配置比例總結

Bonnie：So can we repeat that again? 70% in equity, you said?

Mark：70% in the stay-rich bucket.

  • Some portion of that in liquidity
  • Call it 40–50% in equities (the younger you are, the higher that number)
  • At least 10 to 20% — and that number should grow over time — in the gold and Bitcoin bucket

十一、中美 AI 估值差距：集體幻覺

Bonnie：You guys have been investing across Asia for more than 20 years. So Anthropic is talking about this $2 trillion valuation. OpenAI $1.2 trillion. Well, Moonshot, the company behind Kimi, is around $50 billion. DeepSeek $60 billion as we speak. But the leading Chinese models are only months behind US Frontier, and in some cases some benchmark says Kimi is already ahead. How do you explain that valuation gap — 20, 30, 40 times?

Mark：Popular delusion and the madness of crowds. Great book by that name. It's simply delusion.

The valuations of Kimi and DeepSeek — spot on. Those are amazing businesses. I use both products. I don't use any of the US models. Open weight models are better. Full stop. And they're cheaper and better. And it's because — again, innovation. The DeepSeek guys and the Moonshot guys couldn't get the GPUs. So they had to think: how do we make software or sampling or other means do what we need to do? And it's extraordinary.

So I love both those companies, and I would argue that their valuations are accurate. The numbers that the OpenAI and the Anthropic guys throw out — they're the same delusional stuff that the SpaceX people — and it will end badly. I'm telling you, it will end badly.

一個驚人的數字

Because here's the thing — those three companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX, total value is higher than the 3,365 companies in the US that went public in the last 45 years. That is insane.

And it just goes to show that we've detached thought from the market because of the passive indexing. And that's why Elon did so much work to get companies to rewrite their rules. Normally a company that loses money is not allowed in the indices. It shouldn't be allowed in the indices, because that's widows and orphans money. But he just got him. And is it politics? Is it some other more dastardly thing? Who knows?

But the OpenAI number, the Anthropic number — they're just wrong. They're just wrong on every level. The SpaceX number — overvalued. Oh my gosh. I mean, so overvalued.

中國模型正在贏

And worse, because Kimi and Qwen and DeepSeek are beating them in every way — in innovation, functionality — and companies are figuring it out, and now 60-plus% of the deployments are in the open-weight models.

I struggle because I've been an investor in China for a very long time, and I've had good periods, and the last year has been tough because the companies are better run, there's more innovation, the products are better, the profits are better, the valuations are better, and yet the stocks go down every day.

David Tepper laments it more than me because he's got a bigger position than I do. But it's just tough. It's politics, it's media. The way the system is set up right now favors the winners.

自定義價格的時代

And look, if you can just set your own price — it used to be the market would set the price. You'd go out to do an IPO and you had to get people to underwrite your company and give you the money. Well, now they don't do that anymore. They just say, "Here's the price."

And Elon said, "My company is worth $1.75 trillion." Like, based on what? And then Anthropic came out and said their TAM was $30 trillion for them. Annual? You realize the GDP of the United States is $31 trillion?

Jensen Huang 的數學問題

So your company — and look, Jensen said something similar. Jensen Huang, smart guy, way more important than me, he's richer than me, great representative of the country you're living in. He said, "Well, one 1-gigawatt data center can generate $600 billion of revenue with my chips."

But wait, Jensen — the total profits of the S&P 500 companies, 500 companies, was $2.1 trillion. So you're saying one data center — and there's like 184 gigawatts trying to get built — one is going to generate $600 billion? That's 30% of the total profits of the S&P. That's just not going to happen.

I mean, I'm not going to spend 30% of my profits on Frontier Models. I'm just not. I spend zero dollars until such time as someone gives me something that I want to spend money on.

十二、下一個大機會：亞洲資本流動

Bonnie：One last question before we end this conversation — it's been great by the way. Would you say the next big opportunity would be in maybe Chinese stocks or Asian markets?

Mark：I think global capital flows matter, and they matter in places like Japan, and they matter in places like China. Everyone's been focused on US — all the money's been flowing into US companies. I think that will shift. Will it shift tomorrow or next quarter or the next quarter? I don't really know.

Howard Marks 的智慧

But the thing about buying value — Howard Marks, everyone loves Howard, and he just wrote his latest letter, and he says: you don't get to buy at the bottom. You have to buy on the way down, because it never stays at the bottom very long. When it finally decides to turn...

You saw this with Bitcoin, right? It was $58-60k for a while. Very few people bought it. And then — bang, it's $86k, and they're like, "How did that happen?" Well, that's entertainment. You had to buy it on the way down, because once it decides to bounce, it's violent.

Mrs. Watanabe 現象

I think what will happen — slowly but surely — you saw this in Japan. There's the infamous Mrs. Watanabe, right? The woman controls the purse strings, and she would eventually become an investor, and she would build.

So I think the same thing will happen in China. They'll eventually have the Charles Schwab-ification, and it's already happened. There's lots of day traders in China, but I think what'll happen is the average middle class family will start to graduate to having things like 401(k)s and savings and retirement plans and savings accounts and equities, as opposed to trading accounts.

結語

Bonnie：Mark, that has been wonderful. I hope you come back soon. I find this very insightful. Thank you for the conversation.

## 一、被动投资是"认知殖民"：市场的思考器官被切除了
Mark讲了一个表层故事：被动指数基金按市值加权无脑买入，让"思考者"被挤出。但真正令人毛骨悚然的是——**这是一种格雷欣法则在"思考"层面的翻版**。坏钱驱逐好钱，而被动资金正在驱逐"主动思考的资金"。
这意味着市场正在失去它最重要的器官：**定价发现机制**。当60%的美股由被动资金持有，股票的价格已经和"这家公司值多少钱"无关，只和"有多少钱必须买它"有关。SpaceX亏损60亿还能估值2万亿，不是因为有人相信它值这么多，而是因为**没有人在被允许说它不值**——做空会被挤爆，被动资金则必须按规则买入。
这里有个让我震撼的意外推论：**AI泡沫的刺破点可能不在AI**。真正的触发器藏在人口统计表里——婴儿潮一代到71.5岁必须从401k强制取款。这把一个科技故事瞬间翻译成了一个**人口结构故事**：被动买入的虹吸管快要掉转方向，而没有人在定价这件事。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：这份榜单的"沉寂"恰恰是爆发的前兆

Olivia 轻描淡写地提到"这次只有 11 个新面孔，是历届最少"——大多数人读到这里会以为市场在固化。但真正的信号恰恰相反：消费者 AI 正处于"品类坍缩"的临界点。

想想看：Perplexity 当年用了多少年才做到 10 亿美金 ARR 广告？而 OpenAI 几个月就到了。当新进入者减少、却伴随顶部玩家指数级膨胀时，这不是行业放缓，而是从"工具竞赛"切换到"注意力沉淀"——就像 2010 年移动互联网的 App 爆发期之后，到了 2013 年新 App 大幅减少，但 Instagram、Snapchat、Uber 的用户量却在那两年真正起飞。AI 的 2013 时刻正在发生。

二、一个藏在数据深处的悖论：越私密的 AI，越难形成网络效应

这是整期最被低估的洞察，但 Olivia 一句带过了：

"这个软件比历史上任何产品都更了解我们……可你真的想把这种亲密性引入和他人的互动中吗？"

把这个问题放到跨领域看，你会发现一个惊人的对称：AI 助手正在变成"数字版的心理治疗师"。心理咨询之所以从不发展成社交网络，恰恰因为其价值建立在单向、私密、无评判之上。治疗师不会把你介绍给另一个来访者，否则治疗关系立刻瓦解。

这意味着：消费 AI 的"社交化"可能根本不是未来，而是一个范畴错误。真正的多人价值不会来自"把 AI 介绍给朋友"，而会来自代理与代理之间的交互——你的 Muse 和我的 Instinct 代表我们各自谈判、协作、交易。这才是 agent 时代真正的"网络效应"：不是人际网络，而是代理人际网络（agent-to-agent network）。这件事还没人系统做出来。

三、"4.5% 用户贡献 85% 订阅收入"揭示的更深结构性真相

数据层面大家都注意到了"头部用户 1% 月花 \$93"——但真正值得警觉的是 Olivia 自己说的一句反直觉主张："我其实不希望这 4.5% 的付费比例继续扩大。"

一个消费 AI 投资人为什么不希望付费用户变多？因为她看到了一个被忽略的历史模式：消费互联网史上，所有真正的巨型公司（Google、Meta、Amazon、Uber）都不是靠订阅起家的。订阅是一个"工具型产品"的收入模式，而巨头都是靠交易费和广告，建立在"用户即产品"的反转之上。

这里有一个跨领域连接非常锋利：AI 行业目前的订阅主导，像极了 1998-2001 年的互联网付费墙时代——那时候 Salon.com、Encyclopedia Britannica Online 都靠订阅，所有人都觉得"内容值得付费"。真正改写格局的是 Google 用 AdWords 把搜索免费化，把成本藏到广告商口袋里。

所以 Eugenia Kuyda 那句"人们不是在寻找节省时间，而是在寻找消磨时间的方式"击中了全局：AI 的下一个巨头，不会出现在"效率榜单"里，而会出现在今天还看不到的"娱乐 / 陪伴 / 发现"榜单里。Suno、AI 微剧的爆发只是序曲。

四、彩蛋级洞察：Anthropic 的"克制"是一种被低估的护城河

Claude 付费订阅超过了 Gemini——尽管 Gemini 有 Google 整个分发引擎在背后。所有人都在归因于产品力。但看看这组数据：Anthropic 7.5% 的订阅者在 \$100+/月的 Max 计划上，Chat GPT 和 Gemini 这个比例只有 1%。

这不是"没有广告的选择"——这是一种阶级化定价的隐秘策略。Anthropic 在悄悄做的事情，是消费 AI 领域的"爱马仕化"：不追规模追密度，不追 DAU 追 ARPU。这在历史上有且只有一个成功模板——Bloomberg 终端。Bloomberg 从不打广告，用户也从不抱怨 \$24,000/年的订阅，因为它卖的不是信息，是身份。

Claude 正在成为"开发者和重度思考者的 Bloomberg Terminal"。如果这个判断正确，那么关于"AI 必须大众化才能赢"的叙事，可能完全错了。

The Current State of Consumer AI — a16z 播客实录

Josh Elman： The most interesting big new trend is in personal agents.

Elena Burger： Welcome to the a16z podcast. I'm Elena Burger, and I'm joined by Olivia Moore, who's the author of our ongoing Top 100 Consumer AI Apps report, and Josh Elman on our consumer team.

Today we're digging into the seventh edition of this report: - 谁在为 AI 付费？ - 为什么各大助手正走向不同方向？ - 以及，个人代理能否把日常琐事变成下一个大型消费业务？

Team, thanks so much for joining.

Olivia & Josh： Thanks so much for having us.

第七版报告的几个关键发现
