4. 结构性衰退信号：阈值与指标组合

Q: Let's take a look at the indicators, because you say that most analysts, watchers, people who just look at the markets do not see this recession coming, or at least most of them. How would you say that the thresholds that you would fix for that in terms of the labor market, the consumption as you mentioned before, or even housing, would make you tell "okay, this is the moment the recession has begun"?

4.1 商业周期模型 vs. 单一指标

Henrik: This is where I have a business cycle model. If you rely on one indicator, you'll be wrong — because one indicator can be wrong, two indicators together could be wrong. But if you have an index where you have a whole list of indicators that all need to actually weaken to a certain degree, and some of them might be a little out of whack, but in general you can see that every time you reach a certain level, you will see that that indicator is now flashing — then you have something different.

So I can point to one thing. I can point to the thing that is the most important for the economy, which is the labor market — which everybody seems to be completely looking away from, or dismissing. I don't know if it's because they don't understand the importance of the labor market for GDP.

So my business cycle model told us in November/December 2024 that we will have a slowdown. And as I said, we saw that slowdown with the revised job numbers that we have seen, also with what we see in terms of GDP growth.

4.2 结构性衰退信号：2026 年 7 月已经触发

Henrik: Now, at some point that will develop into an outright recession signal from a structural level — which means that the economy at that point is structurally weak enough to run backwards. That means the labor market, the housing market, and so on.

That point was reached this year in July on my model. Normally when we have seen that structural recession signal coming in, it has been 1 to 3 months early. So that's a pretty good signal. Never missed — never missed once, eight recessions back. Never one false signal. Not too many, not too few.

So when that came in in July this year, I said, "Okay, this is important." Now, one to three months can also be four months. It's not like I am saying it will be within that time period. And as I said, July — so it means August, September, October. We are getting into October soon. There needs to be a few more things, and especially if you have a special situation this time where we have had — not because of the real economy. If this was only to the real economy, you took out AI tomorrow, you would have seen that the economy would already have been in a recession. That's my claim. The percentage growth that you see from AI would have brought us down to 0% in growth.

What I also say is that at some point the AI boom is going to top out and come down. But maybe that can postpone my one-to-three months by one month or two months — all good and fine. What I'm saying is: I know what to watch out for, because now I have the structural signal in place, and I have the clear deterioration in all of the structural elements to it — the housing market, the labor market.

4.3 要盯着什么：短端利率、信用利差、股/债比

Henrik: The things that will tell us now is the point where it hits the fan — that normally happens when we start to see short-duration bond yields coming down strongly. Now we've seen this, and that's also why I've said to my clients: "Well, we're not there yet. We have structural weakness, but we're not there. And for as long as we can see this, this is actually okay, because that tells us we're still in that phase where things are — the demand is still there for capital. So we haven't seen that break," even though the rest of the economy is weakening.

The moment we see that turn, and we see for instance the ratio of S&P to bonds starting to break down — that's the moment when I'll say we are seeing something that is probably the moment. And that's where I'll say I'll try to see if I can point it out this year in this time and say "well, that's the point, that's when we start."

Because the sequencing of things I have all lined up. I have the indicators in place. So watch out for the short-duration bond yields in these next coming months. If they start to plummet fast, then I'm not saying it's there immediately, but then it's within one or two months after that. And I think we're not far from that.

Then you can also look to the credit spreads. Because normally what happens is the whole financial world — they sit and look to one thing, they sit and look at the liquidity. And they say "liquidity is great, so there's no problem." The problem is: liquidity is getting crushed by the situation in the real economy. So the moment consumers are starting to pull back, credit will start to become worse throughout the system. And we can see that in delinquencies on credit cards. We're not really there yet, but that's also why we still have had time for this whole period.

The moment when we start to see those credit spreads moving up — and you can start, as I said, in the lowest quality — that's the moment you need to be careful. And I guess we're starting to see that in the lowest quality. We're not there yet, but we're starting to see it. So if that spikes up somewhat and we start to see a little more volatility in the bond market, then a market top is close. And if we see a little more of that, then the recession is close.

So I don't think we have much time. I hate to put a timeline on it, but I will say that at least I know what to look out for — and I think we are close and we are getting closer by the day. And it's much worse than what people actually understand.

4.4 反方情景与"162,000 就业"数字的拆解

Q: On that, the counter-argument would be: if payroll growth then remains positive and the unemployment stays relatively stable over the next few months, does then that recession thesis still hold? What would be the counter-arguments to that?

Henrik: We just have to remember: if we look at the non-farm payrolls — we got a number — let's look back in '25. Until August last year, we thought we had created around 1 million jobs. Then came August, and all of a sudden it was down to 100,000. And for the rest of the year it was 180,000. And then came the revision just three/four weeks ago, and all of a sudden we found out it was actually down to 16,000 jobs per month for the whole year.

So you have to tell me what all of a sudden will make the economy go in the opposite direction. Because the economy is like a super tanker. When it has a direction, it doesn't just turn. So first of all, I would need to understand: "Yeah, but there's something great coming out now. We have seen lower yields which will help the consumers. The consumer is actually starting to spend more money. We can see the housing market is improving." I see none of that. I see actually quite the opposite.

So why would I all of a sudden think that an economy that has a run rate in April of around 16,000 jobs per month for the last year — all of a sudden extreme going up to 160,000? By the way, we have to remember the US also had the World Cup, which created an equivalent of around 180–190,000 full-time equivalents which were temporary jobs. So that was also in that summer. They will be closed down again.

The economy is in a standstill. The housing market is really severe. The median consumer in the US right now cannot carry a $2,000 extra bill. $2,000 — that's the car breaking down. If it does that, he's flat-out. If he loses his job, he's really bad. And that's in a house he cannot sell. So I just don't see any proofs of an improving economy. I see the opposite with the yields just spiking up as they do right now — also because that puts even more stress on the system.

So yes, that is my answer. If you all of a sudden tell me that I can get revised numbers that will be 100,000, 150,000, 200,000, which this economy should carry — I mean, going into the financial crisis, the month before, the job creation in the US on an average level was 100,000 jobs per month. It is down to 30,000 right now. Going into the dot-com crisis, this was an economy that was 20 million fewer people — I think it was like 30 million fewer or something — and the job creation was 150,000 jobs per month. We're talking about an economy that creates 16,000 jobs until April of this year, March/April. And then we're told that all of a sudden it explodes higher. I just don't see that.

4.5 44% 的调查回收率——Zeberg 的核心统计攻击

Henrik: We cannot just rely on one job number. That job number that everybody's pointing to — the 162,000 — was based there. It's like this: that's where the revisions come in. First you have a first print. There's a survey response rate. That survey response rate for that number was just 44%. 44% of the businesses, which by the way is only a subset of the entire economy. And the survey doesn't ask for if it's a full-time job or a part-time job.

So you have now a subset of the economy, 44% of that subset responds back. Guess what? That is the lowest response rate we have ever seen on the first print. And it created 162,000 jobs. You know what they did with the remaining 56%? They assume that the job creation in the rest of the businesses are the same as in the 44%. That is a pretty good assumption, I would say — that there's very often you see actually those that do not respond are the ones that actually laying off jobs. And that's what they see. That's why you have revisions lower.

So we cannot trust that 162,000 at all. You cannot even trust what it will become here next on Friday when we get the next number, or when we get the revised number. You do that — it's like flying blind, right? You need look to the 12-month moving average, and it's 30,000, 50,000 (if you believe in the 162), but otherwise 30,000 jobs per month. That is extremely low. That's the lowest we have seen in the last 50 years in an economy before going into a recession — just before, outside, we were already in a recession 50 years back.

So as I say, the only reason the economy has been holding up for now is the AI boom, which has not created jobs to the degree it created a lot of investment, which is good for the GDP. But without that, the economy would already be plummeting — and that's what the real economy is feeling right now. That is why the average Joe, Mrs. Johnson as I always refer to, is not in a good state at this point, and it will become worse for them, unfortunately.

5. 房地产：冻结的市场

Q: And you've mentioned the housing, and I think it's particularly interesting also what's happening there right now. Because rates are extremely high, we've seen an enormous divide spread between buyers and sellers, there's much more sellers than there's buyers, and the whole market is kind of frozen. Yet we don't see — correct me if I'm wrong — a sharp decline in prices either. So there's structurally something that looks like 2008 but hasn't materialized yet. Why is that?

Henrik: Yeah, but that's because people are staying put. If you look at the existing number of houses sold — existing homes sold as a part of a population — you would see that this is actually at a level that is only comparable to the depth, the trough, of when we were in the deepest recessions in '81 and '82 in the housing market. And even at the levels where we were at the bottom of the financial crisis. I mean, so there's no housing — homes are not being sold, simply. So it's standing still.

And you can say "that's okay, because then the prices are not falling." Actually, they're not — the price increase is falling actually, if you look for that. And that means that the housing market is frozen still. Everybody's waiting for that person that comes in and buys it. But this is at a time when the unemployment rate apparently is 4.1% — which is also a number that needs a little double-take too. So a very low unemployment and yet the housing market is a complete standstill. Why is that? Is that a strong economy? That seems to be a very weak economy to me.

So you're right, we're not seeing the waterfall moment, but that's not the same as things are great. That's just saying that things are at a standstill. And if we start to see something of a development where the AI boom is wearing off, and we see the development that I call for, it will become even worse. That's why I say: when the stock market pops, when this bubble pops, you're going to see that becoming the domino that will then start to push into that market, with an economy that is so frozen still, with a consumer that has been underwater for a longer time than we have seen in any modern time.

The average consumer is more underwater for a longer time. And you think that that will going to be solved in a nice and easy way with a dip of 20% in the market? I don't think so.

5.1 若收益率暴跌，房地产会迅速反弹吗？

Q: I mean, also one way to look at it: if the bond yields are about to plummet, this would also have an impact on mortgage rates — it would also fall sharply. But then the question is, could the housing activity then recover from that quickly? Will it be kind of a V-shape, or how do you think this would unfold in the sequence as well?

Henrik: That's where again we need to understand the business cycle. Because that's exactly what happens every time we have a cycle. What happens is you see that the bond yield starts to drop, and then the economy will start to recover slowly. It depends on the psychology of the person behind. That's why I refer to how long they have been underwater.

Because if you are a person and you have seen a dip in your income, you lost your job but you got a new one the next day, you thought "okay, that's fine." What you're seeing right now is: the long-term unemployment in the US is higher than it's been at any point outside of recessions, and it's moving up.

So in that market, do you think that that will go quick or slow? I think it's going to go slow because Mrs. Johnson, who's seen the unemployment and a lot of people have lost their jobs and stayed unemployed for longer, she will not say "you know what, we're going to sell our house and we're going to move somewhere else, let's go buy it." And the banks are not going to allow her to do that either.

So the slowdown here, which has been so long and we've been pushing it with this AI boom, has in my mind created a psychological lack — or at least something that is an energy that's going to be coming out later or not coming out, because people will be holding back for longer. Even though they start to see "oh yeah, now we can save some money on our mortgage loan," guess what, it's going to take a little while before it comes through. It's not going to be there the next day or the next week — it's going to take three months, four months, six months. What I'm saying is: that's efficient of time for things to go a lot south.

And yes, the Fed will eventually step in. But at this point, to talk about the Fed going to step in in a massive way — because that's what is required — I mean, we're sitting here talking about they're going to hike the rate again in October, which is ridiculous. So the thing is that I just think there's a complete mismatch between the real economy, the Fed, and the financial markets.

And this is where I say the one that will decide by the end of it will be the real economy. That is the Mrs. Johnson, because that's consumption. That's where you have the money coming into the system, and the rest will be following along. So it's not going to be as snappy to get this reversed. And the problem will also be that the more they will stimulate this time around, the more it will create inflation. The problem is that inflation very often comes on the expectation of inflation. So if they come in — let's say with a fiscal stimulus check, not just saving some money on monetary cuts on the rate, but actually something like they did in Covid — you'll see inflation jump like that again, which will crush the consumer even more. So they are between a rock and a hard place.

They need to support the consumer at some point, and they will — because they will choose inflation over deflation any day. But the problem will be that it will not be easy for the consumer to gain trust. "I've seen inflation going up, I've seen unemployment, I've been trying to make ends meet for such a long time, and now I save a little money. Am I going out and spending it immediately?" Probably not — probably holding a bit back. That's why the recovery of the economy can take longer.

6. 美联储：400 位博士与"锤子找钉子"

Q: Kevin Walsh, the new Fed president — they increased 0.25% the 12th of September. Why do you think that the Fed increased, made a rate hike, even though in your eyes the economy is weaker? They say it's pretty robust, that the spending is resilient, unemployment is stable, and all these other arguments. What is it then? Is it asset price inflation? Is it inflation in general? Is it financial stability? What exactly do you think they did that with an army of PhDs who monitor the economy on a daily basis?

Henrik: I'm not sure an army of PhDs is a good thing. I think that sometimes that can prevent you actually from thinking and questioning the setup that there's there. And you can see Walsh himself is starting to now speculate and say "hey, we may want to do things differently in here," right? I mean, if you had 400 PhDs and none of them thinking about doing this differently — and these PhDs, by the way, were the ones also expecting inflation not to go above 3–3.5% into the stimulus, it went to 9.1%. So sorry, I don't have a lot of trust in those 400 PhDs.

What I see is: they are completely misreading the situation at this point. They're looking at something which is a number — 4.1% unemployment — which, by the way, the only reason that is correct is because the labor force participation rate is plummeting. 1.7 million people has left the labor force since November last year, 1.7 million people out of a workforce of 170 million. That's a lot. And you can say that's a good thing. No, it's not a good thing. Then you create a nice-looking ratio — which is the unemployment number — because you say the number of unemployed people is now smaller, and hence you get a lower ratio.

The thing is, GDP production, the economy needs people to work. So the more people that leaves the workforce, the worse it is. So they look to probably the wrong numbers. They look to inflation and they say "the inflation is going up." Yeah, but look at how it's lagging. If they don't get that, I don't know what's really up and down here, because it's honestly very simple to see. And they have run this economy over the cliff a few times.

2020 was seen as saving the economy. I think it was not — I think they overdid it. '22, they didn't see the 9.1% that we had in inflation there. So we cannot just look at that and say "yeah, they know better because they got the PhD degrees and they are 400 of them."

6.1 美联储的真正目标：泡沫，而非通胀

Henrik: I think they are right now in the process of looking at the wrong numbers potentially. I can only kind of see what they're doing if they look to the asset inflation and to the bubble that there is — we're in. But the two cases we have with that was in 1929 and in 2000, and the Fed tried to do the same. They did not want to talk about the bubble, they did not want to talk about how they were actually trying to quell the bubbles, not let it explode higher.

And they did that in 1929, with those kinds of consequences we saw there. They were hiking right into that bubble bursting, and then you had those kinds of consequences in an economy — I just want to say this — that is arguably maybe even a bit stronger than what we have today. I just want to say it.

And then we had the 2000 situation, 1999 and 2000, where we also saw the Fed hiking into that bubble trying to quell that bubble. Inflation was not crazy high and they were doing a 50 basis point hike in May of 2000, which was after the bubble actually burst and we had seen the first very major sell-off. So the Fed was doing that there — but they had been hiking into that bubble because they wanted to make sure that the bubble didn't expand any further. And they were successful.

The problem is: when you unleash that energy, especially with the whole credit system we have today — and especially with the credit system that has been developing after 2008, where everybody with a billion dollar on their bank account have been able to come in and try to seek yield somewhere because of the low-yield policy — you have a more opaque system right now of credit providers that we do not know how is actually linked. And that is the big problem.

So I say that the Fed is playing with fire here. They're thinking they're looking at this inflation, which they say is the problem, which is on par with what we saw in 2007/2008. I mean, 2008 inflation reached 5.5%. In 2008, in January when the Fed was cutting rates, inflation was at 4.0%. So what we're talking about here now — and it was even higher back in 2000, it was running higher for longer in 2000 and also into 2001. So the Fed is not out for inflation here. I think they had their eyes on the bubble. And that's where I say: they think they can deflate it nice and easily, but we have never seen an example of that.

If the credit system down beneath is rotten, or you have a lot of overvalued stocks, you can see the consequences of that. And that's where I think the domino is going to hit the whole private equity, private credit sector, which will become what will then set things ablaze.

6.2 与 1929 的异同

Q: So you compare this time, in terms of Fed rates or the setup now, to 1929. What would be then different today than that time, in both ways — in terms of consequences but also in terms of the environment we were in back then? There was no deposit insurance, there was no floating currencies, the banking system was totally different.

Henrik: Yeah, but you're mentioning all the things that is improved today. You can say so. That's also why I'm not saying — I always said that we'll get a situation where it's probably the worst we have seen since the 1930s, right? So I'm not saying 1929 again, because I don't think we're going to make the same mistakes.

There was a period also afterwards, we saw the bubble burst — that they still had the belief that you'll just need to let it bleed through. I think we have a different kind of setup today, and I think that is right. But I don't think it's going to be as bad.

But I think the initial — I mean, the stock market decline could be pretty big. You have to remember there was an initial phase in '29, then we had a bounce, and then I think it was in 1931 or something like that we saw another one. And I think you can see the initial phase becoming quite severe here. And it will be depending on when the Fed steps in. But by the end of the day, it's about how soon will the consumer feel safe enough to step back in and start buying, start daring to take on credit, start risking a bit.

And I think, as I said before, the situation into 1929 was on the consumer side not as bad as it is right now. That is the thing. The longer the consumer has been underwater, the worse it is. In 2000, the consumer hadn't really been underwater, because they were actually doing quite well. Real wage increases into 2000 was quite good. So the consumer was well off, and still you had an 80–85% decline in the NASDAQ, which was small-cap companies and so on. Still it was a pretty severe decline in the stock market.

So the situation is bad on the consumer side, and it's bad on the housing side. And I can't see why this wouldn't just fall out like what we saw. A best case for me would be a 2000 scenario — that would be the best case, because that was a very shallow recession because you didn't really see the balance-sheet effect of things.

Unfortunately, I think the whole credit structure today — which as you mentioned also could be the reason why we will not see 1929 — can be the reason why we can see something that is more like 2008 as the main course. Because there's so much speculation going on, and it's been going on ever since they introduced the zero-interest-rate policies. And then now inflation coming up, and then they started to scramble. But there are so many unrealized or mark-to-market kind of valuation levels out there which could come under severe pressure if credit evaporates, which it will in a crash like what I'm talking about.

7. 滞涨之辩：为什么 Zeberg 认为现在不是 1970s

Q: One of the things that I also try to reconcile is the fact that if we have a weakening growth, for you inflation will plummet. Right?

Henrik: Even in the 1970s — people think that inflation was just going up even though growth was going down. They have to look at it: whenever you saw the recessions there, inflation was plummeting. So that's again where we just need to go back and take a look at that. Because when growth rolls over, inflation comes down strongly.

Q: And if we then look at the energy shock which is persistent until now — there's many measures also around the world, especially when it comes to diesel. Diesel prices affect not just vehicles but transportation, that has a spillover effect on foods and all kinds of other things. There's all kinds of other commodities also linked to the Strait of Hormuz choke, that also have trickle-down effects on agriculture and other sectors. If this persists and does not remain temporary, can we maybe in this world link both a weakening of the consumer that does not eliminate inflation while still having a weak economy and a weak growth? So have this stagflation we said?

7.1 滞涨需要富裕的消费者，而不是贫穷的

Henrik: No, but that's not where stagflation arises. That's where people are mistaken also, because stagflation always comes when you actually have the economy where a consumer starts to actually have money in their hands. And this is where again people compare it to the 1970s, which is completely off — because if you look to the consumer savings rate at this point, it's 3%.

Guess what? In the stagflationary days in the 1970s, the lowest it was down to was 9%, but it was up to 20%. So people had up to 20% of their income that they could save up back those days. That is an environment that can carry inflation — because it means when I stand by the gas pump, I'll say, "Yeah, I'll just put — oh, damn these prices, huh? But I'll just put some extra on it anyway." It's not good, because inflation can keep pumping.

But in a world where the consumer cannot carry a $2,000 extra bill and has a savings rate of 3% and cannot sell his home, inflation is not going to be a problem. You can see a spike inflation shock from supply, because it meets a demand. But at some point, in order to have prices staying up, you need demand. And if demand is plummeting, you'll see prices coming down. That is what we saw in 2008. We saw price going up 150 on oil — I think it was 140-something — and what happened? Vomited.

So you cannot have that situation. And that's where people are again seeing — they have a hammer and now we need to find the nail, and we see inflation and we point to 1970s and we make two charts where we say "these two kind of resemble" — but there is nothing underneath that resembles it. The job creation actually also in the 1970s was rather strong. So if you look again and say the non-farm payrolls back then compared to the labor force size, it was rather high. So people could actually lose their job and get another one. What they also could do is, as I said, they had 9 to 20% of their earnings coming in that they could save. Today it's 3%.

But that is why — what you see right now, the spike in inflation, that is already a taxation. That is the hammer on the consumer as is. And you can beat the consumer up as much as you want, he's not going to buy any — yeah, he will buy less because it's already expensive for him, but it's not going to help inflation. Because as long you have to remember it's a calculation — and right actually tomorrow we're going to get the PCE numbers, and the PCE numbers are going to be changed now. So all of a sudden there will be a correction in the inflation because they changed the composition of it.

And this is again where people need to understand: one thing is a mathematical calculation of what inflation is. The other thing is what are we actually seeing on the ground. And we are seeing a consumer that is completely depressed at this point. And then we want to hammer there with a fist because we think we need to push demand down. It's not demand driving this inflation hike.

So you can have a supply shock that for some time can create this. But at some point it's going to implode. And this is where people are getting it completely wrong — where the oil prices can go up, but why would it stay at $100 (or $200) if people can't afford it? It will drop. That's what we see in recessions, and even as I said in the 1970s, even when people had more savings rate, we saw inflation coming down strongly in recession.

7.2 真正的滞涨是在萧条之后

Henrik: Again, I encourage people: take a CPI inflation chart, look it up, put in the recession areas, and then see what happens in the recession. Inflation comes down strongly. Though if we're heading into a recession now, you're going to get by far what you want to have in terms of deflationary pressures, and we are getting closer to the recession.

So I don't see that scenario. But what I can see on the other side — and this is where stagflation really can develop, and this is what I also said back in South Africa — is that when the Fed comes out after this and we start to see that there'll be pumped money into it, and you have a consumer that is more conservative and does not want to take on too much risk, then that's a problem. Because then you can have a lot of money coming into a financial system which cannot stand idle, and that can start a process where it can start circulating into things that could do well in that kind of environment. And of course it will bounce in risk assets, but it will also find its way into commodities and so on.

That slowish kind of reversal on the consumer can become something where the Fed can overcook the steak once more from the other side. And I think that is why we can see a stagflation in development after the bust. You do not get stagflation in a situation where the economy is plummeting. It's never happened.

I do the study. I sit down, I actually ask these questions that you do, I go back, I put up the charts, and I just say: what is it that we're looking at? And we see clearly that inflation comes down strongly in recessions. And when we have stagflation, it is because the consumer is actually rather well off, and it's when the economy is starting to grow again — because then it's running a bit too fast there. And that's the problem. It's been running too fast and money that's chasing in the system, but the economy cannot really follow suit. And that's why the unemployment rate stays high for longer while inflation starts to push up. That's the stagflation. And that can last for a year, two years, three years — which will be immensely well and good for gold and commodities and so on. And I think we get to that phase, but we see the bust first.

8. 美元：93–94 目标与"主拨盘"

Q: Now talking about also one key component of your framework, which is the dollar. You also wrote in your four-phase playbook that this is kind of the master, the dial, I think you called it — the DXY, the dollar, to fall towards roughly, I think, 93 or 94 before then the crisis of the rally. If that dollar strengthens materially before reaching those levels, does your sequence then start to break down, or how does it then go from there onwards?

Henrik: No, it doesn't. The thing is — I mean, first of all, I feel pretty good about it, that the call where we're going to DXY, because I say that will go hand in hand with what we're going to see in the short-duration bond yields, and I think they're going to come down. So you're going to have a situation where everybody will think that it's okay for the Fed now to become less hawkish. And that's why that will be the excuse. And at the bottom of it, we will see people talk about how the dollar is dying at 93/94 — which again is wrong, but that'll be the next narrative, I think.

But anyway, so yeah — no, it will not. Because even let's say I'm wrong on that assumption and we don't see that kind of development, we actually see the dollar coming up from here. I could see a situation — and there could be a scenario which could be plausible, like working from economical firms — where the dollar actually strengthens, and you'll see it's because of the rotation of capital coming into the US. And that will then bring the dollar higher, and you can see risk assets rally on that. We saw some of that after Trump coming in. We saw the dollar going up and we saw actually also the more riskier assets like crypto rally on that.

I could see that scenario, but it just doesn't really go well. In my model, everything has to be calibrated with hundreds of yards. It's the one that is applicable, but it's not the most likely. So I think we will see that plummet. And I think what we're seeing now is the hype in terms of yields will go higher and the dollar is following that, and then all of a sudden you see that kind of situation.

It could be tomorrow. It could be like PCE numbers tomorrow — which by the way would be impacted in a downward kind of way by the change in the composition of it. So I think if the market is not — well, real market participants will be aware of this, but there could be some that are not, and this can put all of a sudden "oh, the inflation is not that high." And that's the PCE number, which is what the Fed really is looking out for. Say you get a very low number there — I don't even dare to say anything, but it's a low number. Then could you see that developing into like a dollar declining for two or three months? Yeah, I think that could be it. And that would be very bullish for the whole risk-on market, because you have still the risk-on sentiment going. You have the NASDAQ pushing, and I think it's going to push to new all-time highs here soon.

And then you'll see a rotation into other assets as well. It will also be bullish gold and silver, but I don't think it's going to be putting gold and silver into a new all-time high. I think it's going to pop later into this year — a new bounce, but a new lower bounce. And then you have the decline while the dollar then really soars into the inflationary development. That's further out, but that's the kind of path that I see.

9. NASDAQ：37,000–39,000 的目标与扩展

Q: Let's talk about NASDAQ, because I think in March you made a call — target was around 30,000 — and then you went from 30 to 33,000. Now it's up to 40,000, if I —

Henrik: 37, 39. Yeah [laughs].

Q: There's a bit of delay. I was saying: what is then the objective rule that tells you that the structure has an extended from the original target?

Henrik: Yeah, but you see that this is where people always come out. You said this. I mean, yes — correct. When we stood in '22, I said 6,300 on the S&P. At that time, we were 3,500. The 6,300 was a Fibonacci extension. I could see — and I dared to say we get there. It was seen as insane.

When we were talking last year in February, we went down. I can't remember the dip — I think it was down to 16,000 on the NASDAQ or something in April last year, right? And at that point, calling for that kind of level of around 30,000 was again an extension I could see.

What always happens into these phases — which I cannot predict, but I have indications of it based on the Fibonacci extension — say "this is going to go that far." I will always call the most conservative one, and not take this one up here — because then you're really seen as an insane person if you go from 16 and say you can go to 39.

Could have seen it back then that it could go higher potentially, maybe. But I said the 30 and I felt good about that. That was seen as an insane target at that point, I think. And I still say that this is the level that we're probably going to hit, because when we get closer and closer, you can see — look at the chart, and it's kind of spiking up into a vertical kind of move almost if you look on a monthly chart. There are some levels there, and there are some things that are beginning to show that we have a break.

What am I talking about? Let's look at the market breadth. Right now we're seeing fewer and fewer stocks actually carrying this rally. This was not the situation earlier. So now we're starting to see that thing, right? We're starting to see that there are some fatigue in some of the big ones. We have seen some of them actually — we've seen Oracle starting to plummet, there's some problems there and so on.

So as we get higher and you can see the spike there — yes, you can do some Fibonacci levels, and you can say we are getting closer and closer. And at this point I say 37 to 39. If it becomes 41, I'll still say — well, 16 to… and I've been bullish all the way up and I've been long since '22. So it's not like it's been a bad journey for me, that I've been on the wrong side of things. I've been long since '22, when everybody was bearish and we stood down there at 3,500 on the S&P.

And see where we are today, and my call for the S&P is 8,500 to 9,000 or something like that. So it's been a pretty good journey, and things have been developing slower than I expected. Again, hands down, that is what it is. But there's no changes in the path from here. And now it's more about seeing when we start to see the unfolding of the things — the first indicators that things are coming falling a bit apart. There is also something about credit. We really need to see — look to the credit side. Because when that all of a sudden starts to develop, then I think we have a problem.

9.1 关于被批评"反复推迟衰退预测"

Q: It's important also in that sense, because you just mentioned — you also see a lot in the comment section or even online, people who criticize you for always making calls and then being off. I mean, you've been in the right direction for risk-off for sure — that's been proven. But especially for the recession calls, or other calls about giving a number, it's always about also giving a time. And when that doesn't materialize, people get after you. What is for you in your thesis the most important? Is it then reaching the price target, hitting the timing window, or seeing the correct sequence of the market signals?

Henrik: Yeah, see, this is where I need to align with how the market apparently thinks. So when I see a slowdown — you remember also when we sat there in South Africa and I said "yes, there's a recession coming." And the reason I said that back then, which was in February last year, was because when you look at the deceleration of the economy, then it was clear that you were going lower, and we have been going lower.

Could I foresee that we would see levels now that are considerably under what we have seen going into all recessions 50 years back, and been there for quite some time — as I said from April last year to March this year, down to 16,000 non-farm payrolls at this point? Right. Would I foresee that things would have made me have an AI bubble? No, I could not. And that's where we would see that these things can come in and can become externalities that will have an impact. But it's not the same as saying that the direction in terms of that we are seeing a deceleration — and I said that the recession will come, because you will not all of a sudden see spiking it back up again, like the economy is all of a sudden improving. That has been correct, and that is why I said it comes.

But we'll need to see certain things develop. So what I need to do in the future is to say "well, we have a slowdown, and that may develop into an outright recession signal at some point." I need to use the word slowdown instead. I used — I made it more interesting by saying "the recession." There was a slowdown, and the slowdown will develop into something that will become an outward recession later, but for now let's talk about the slowdown. It can go on for some time.

And then I'll need to watch the indicators and not call it before. That's why I've been very strict on that in the latest year or so — "it's not now, it's coming, you're going to see higher levels, but this and this and that." And that's to point out that you can see it already, that the thing is there.

The thing is where people do think that a recession is something that comes like this — it's a black swan and boom, that's there. That is incorrect. And if you think that, I cannot help you. But if you really understand and study, you'll see that these structural developments are quite not simple to follow, but they are quite [strong] in their prediction power. And that is why I need to communicate in a better way, I think. That is it. And that's why I have had this hate coming against me. That's all good and fine. I've been long since '22, and that's proven. So I will not — I need to communicate better. That's simply it.

And then let's see how it goes. But there will always be somebody who tries to misunderstand what I'm saying, and that's all good and fine. But in the future I'll communicate according to what I see in the model. I will also say "now we have a bottom in the economy and we'll see a recovery" — doesn't mean the stock market actually will start to recover the day after, but it means that from now on we'll see that the economy is actually starting to improve. And that is also something that the model can identify.

10. 黄金：短期回调，长期 27,000–29,000

Q: There's also the question of gold, right? We talked with Francis and Matthew back in 2025 February — you were expecting gold to correct in some form or shape. Where would you say that you were right and where are you wrong? I know that you are long-term bullish on gold, you have more of a tactical perspective on gold in terms of the price action now. From what I understood, you still expect gold to correct. We've seen yesterday a 4% correction in the price of gold, which is quite massive. Silver also took a hit. What is your perspective on that, and feel free also if you have any charts to pull them out.

Henrik: So here we have the short-term chart for gold. When I was wrong — I was wrong in terms of how high gold could jump before we saw the correction. So my mistake — if we go out to the longer-term chart here — was to say that when we stood in '25 in mid-February, somewhere around there, that we saw this first before we saw the correction. Because the correction we're in right now is what I saw then.

You can say "yeah, but then the guys were ready, right? Because we actually saw higher, we probably are not going to go below that point." And there is something to that. I was wrong on that — no problem. And that just shows also what I [said] long-term: that gold is something you need to hold. And I've always been holding gold as well.

But the pullback that we could see here, which I think can be quite severe still, is the pullback that will then set us much higher.

This is the long-term chart. Let me just go to the short-term chart. Because this move we saw here into the top in January was clearly driven by an anticipation of inflation and so on, and also there was this talk about the debasement and all these things. And honestly, I don't see that — I think that's very wrong. It was driven more by the euphoria around that than it was driven by real economics. And you can see that the dollar was not all of a sudden the reserve currency of the world and all these things — it was a narrative. But that's fine. I mean, that can drive things a lot higher, and I think the move we saw here was quite fantastic.

I do think now we are in a correctional phase, which makes sense. Because in this phase here, everybody thought it was inflation — that's why you need to be in gold. Now people start to realize that probably inflation is not so much, and then they'll see the dollar coming up strongly. This is the move that I see. But first, as I said, now we see the dollar is going to decline somewhat down to the 93/94. I do think we're going to see gold coming lower. But come, let's say, the correction we had down here — then definitely, I mean, that's absolutely a point where I would be looking at buying gold, and I will be buying gold in this decline we're going to see.

Because I think in the next move, when the Fed steps in and when you see the real stagflationary potentially developing, that is when we move high. We had a real stagflation here. This was real stagflation. This was topped-up stagflation. There's no stagflation here. But this was the real stagflation, and that's where you saw, in a matter of two and a half years, that gold went up seven and a half times. That is fantastic.

We also saw it here during the early 2000s, that we had a fantastic bull market, and then we had the correction into the bottom there in 2015 and so on. So I think it's going to be on the minor scale — but you know, you can say again, like the guys also there in South Africa, "you should buy it and then just hold it," like Matthew would say. And I say yeah, that is true. But there will be some kind of pullback, so we just need to be clear of that.

I do think gold goes a lot higher, and I think this is actually based on some of these Fibs again, and I think 27–29,000 by 2030 would not be controversial to me. Because with all of the debt that we have in the world, gold is simply going to be the one asset — which I also stated back in '25. So it's not something I have changed on. But wrong was on this — that we move this higher. I think we're going to see somewhat more of a correction, 3,100 maybe, and then I think it's takeoff time.

Because the Fed will step in and do everything they can the moment they start to see the deflationary development, which is not what people see right now. But when the dollar starts to push up to the 120, which I see on the Dixie, before we get through the bad times there — and then the Fed will be driving this. That is what I call the real case for gold. But again, I said this was where I was wrong, and this is where you can hold it like Matthew said, and then you'll sleep soundly at night. Because if I did what he said back then, we would still have been up even though we get to this pullback here. So that's a case learned also.

10.1 黄金对冲 S&P 比：Zeberg 的"双重打击"框架

Q: And how would you then pin it against, let's say, the S&P or just stocks in general?

Henrik: I haven't found that chart, but there is a famous chart that I actually developed a long time ago already, and you can see how the S&P in gold — the price of gold — is actually now breaking lower. And we have seen that three times before this time.

We saw that in 1929, when you have a speculative bubble bursting, and we saw how gold was then moving up for several years versus stocks. That happens when a speculative market all of a sudden comes crumbling down. We need to get down back to what is sound money — and that is where gold wins every time.

We saw it after 1971 — this crossover also, in 1971, after Nixon came out and took the dollar off the gold convertibility there temporarily. And then you saw also that decline in the S&P versus gold for some years.

We saw it in 2000 after the dot-com top there, and we saw gold again stepping up when there was a speculative bubble.

I see these as different things here. I see 1929 and 2000 as speculative bubbles. 1971 was more of a "what's wrong with this monetary system here? Can we actually trust it?"

I think we have a double whammy this time. I think we have one of the largest speculative bubbles we have ever seen — that's my take on the risk asset at this point. And we're starting to see some problems also in terms of the trust to the dollar or to the whole monetary system. And I think these two drivers can bring gold up tremendously into the next move.

That's why I say: yeah, I will be buying as we see the dollar getting stronger here, buying some of the gold, silver, whatever, and then ride it higher for that next leg. So we have a double whammy coming, and it's going to be a bad situation — speculative bubble and potentially challenges to the monetary system. That is an environment that gold will absolutely love. But a pullback to 3,100 is still in the cards as I see it.

So I should have taken Matthew's advice back then — but I was right then on the stock market, and it has actually been doing quite well also, I would say.

11. 比特币与山寨币：Zeberg 的转向

Q: And if we look at now Bitcoin — when we spoke in December, you thought that Bitcoin could reach potentially I think $150,000 — yeah, if I'm not mistaken. But more recently, you sounded much less certain about a new Bitcoin high. What did Bitcoin do to change your view on that?

Henrik: What Bitcoin did was that it actually crushed more than I expected. So again, as you said, when we talked — I think it was on the 22nd here, actually around this time in December — I saw that there was a possibility that we could see Bitcoin going higher one more time, that it was part of a topping setup we had here. That was wrong. And we saw when we started to see this move down here, and especially below this level here, that was when I said "something bigger is now happening."

So we are actually now, as I see it, in a — this was the beginning of the bear market on Bitcoin as I see it. I know that's not a very popular story among Bitcoiners, but I think this was the top. We saw a very strong decline, and I think we're now in that fool's rally. I think we're going to go to 115,000, which is where it will outperform gold. And you'll see that it actually starts to do that already together with Ethereum. And we see — I had this talk with Francis also — we see that Ethereum is now starting to outperform gold and silver. And that's because we're not in that debasement phase that we talked about there.

That means — you can say I was right on that — because if that was the case, we would probably not have seen the development we have seen so far. But the situation is now that this risk-on rally I think still goes up to around this level here, and I think we're going to go much lower. And I think Bitcoin needs to prove its worth to actually stay above $10,000 when we see this deflationary bust. Because we know there's one thing Bitcoin does not like, is when we have busts like what they had in 2020 where it fell by 60-some% in a matter of three weeks. It is a risky asset, and that's why it's going to perform very badly in that environment.

Which means that if I'm right that the dollar is going to bottom out and start a rally, which then would bring be at a time when I think Bitcoin is up here, then I think it'll be bad news for Bitcoin for some time. And also for gold. So I think Bitcoin can outperform — that's also what my ratio on it says — but Bitcoin can outperform gold in the coming phase here, but not in the long term. In the long-term setup, I think there will be one king, and that will be gold. And that is actually also what is shown by the charts clearly. So we need to differentiate between what is a temporary kind of boom and what is the general direction of things. And I think gold will prove as the real value foundation at the end of it.

11.1 山寨币季与以太坊 7,200–7,400 目标

Q: What about then altcoins in crypto? You mentioned Ethereum, but how do you see this then? Would you see a decoupling between Bitcoin and altcoins in this phase as well? Do you see altcoins — so not just Ethereum, but just in general like the altcoin market — outperform Bitcoin in that ratio, or how is your view on that?

Henrik: I think altcoins and Ethereum are going to outperform Bitcoin this phase here. And then people say "how is that, why is that?" Actually, that is something we've seen before. People need to go back to '21 and see that you can have a phase where Bitcoin is only doing kind of the bounce, and then you'll see some of the altcoins in the altcoin phase actually outperforming Bitcoin. And you'll see the plummeting of Bitcoin dominance, and so on. And Ethereum will take on a leading role there — which is also what I said back to Francis in December. We're starting to see that we have seen the bottom in April last year — actually we saw the first move. We then saw a consolidation that took, again, longer. But now clearly starting to move up, and we've seen the Ethereum outperforming Bitcoin for the last — I can't remember — since June I think it was of this year.

So we will see that continuing for some time and accelerating. So I think altcoins can go much higher. I think the altcoin market can reach a market value of around 2 trillion, which will be double the size that we saw when it was at this peak. And I think Ethereum can reach a level of 7,200–7,400 in that environment, which is an environment where the dollar is pulling back, and this is this 93/94, right?

So I think that environment should be unfolding soon. And that's where we have this final push in everything. The NASDAQ, everything goes up in that phase. Gold bounces higher. And then all of a sudden we see that there is an end to it, and that's going to come with the pop of the bubble in the stock market, and then it'll be all about dollars.

So I think we'll have a great alt season, and that has actually started already, and I think that is very clear. If you look to SUI and you look to a lot of the — there are a lot of alts that are actually already moving. There's one called… there is one called… you know, others that have been moving quite a lot already, and they're clearly in a bull market at this point. But people have really not seen it just yet. We need to be above this 50% of the pullback before people really start to move in. But that is running right now, and I think you're going to see silver and gold being outperformed by a lot of these.

11.2 加密生态的健康性与"亚马逊式幸存者"

Henrik: Is that a sound development? Or is that healthy and all? No, I don't think so — and that's also not the reason I say it. I do think, and this I want to say every time, I think there will be one, two, three, five, seven candidates amongst all these altcoins that down the road is going to prove that they are the new Amazon or the new something. Which one? I do not know. But I think there will be some of those that can perform really well into the future.

But the whole plethora of these and all these meme coins and so on — we need to have these cleared out. And that is what a good, sound, healthy recession will do. It's going to clear all this mapped-out for all these things. So there will be a lot of pain. But I think the ones that can actually make it and have a sound utility to it — whatever that is, whether it's in the AI world or whatever it can be — can have a fantastic journey from there on.

So I think they will all pull back when the dollar starts to run and we see the pop of the bubble — all of them. But I don't see Bitcoin becoming a reserve currency or anything like that. Actually, I think it's so misunderstood that this has to do with currency or a reserve something. This has to do with the technology down beneath, which will help us in the digital transformation here — where we will start to see tokenization, smart contracts, and all these coming out much more, which will help on trade on a global basis in the future, which will be fantastic. But new currency and talk about how it's going to replace the dollar and all that — no, it's not going to happen.

12. 三个月后：Zeberg 的具体预测与"魔鬼代言人"

Q: To conclude, Henrik — if we sit again in 3 months, we talk to each other in 3 months again, what would you say is, in terms of calls, what we should expect — the things that we will look back on in the last 3 months or 3 months from now?

Henrik: I'll say: plummeting short-duration yields, which will start to lead long-duration yields plummeting. I think you'll see that there will start to see some credit stress, which means that there will be problems in private credit even to a larger degree than we have seen now. And we'll see credit becoming more of a shortage, which will be a problem also for stocks.

And I honestly think that if we do this by New Year's Eve, that we potentially have seen the stock market top. I could see it in January, but I think it is possible that we see it in this quarter here. And I say it because we have a trajectory that shows that it could happen actually already in November. I have December, and we could be in January. But things are deteriorating faster.

Of course they are all interlinked, and in credit we need to see that deteriorating first. But we are seeing the first signs of it, and I think that could be developing here. But I think plummeting short-duration bond yields is one thing. I think the dollar declining and potentially even finding a bottom before we talk on New Year's Eve. Let's say it was that. And then that next phase is beginning at that point, which means the bond yields will continue to move lower, dollar will start to push higher, equities will be under a lot of pressure, crypto will crumble, and so on. Which will be into the first quarter of next year.

12.1 Zeberg 为自己唱反调

Q: Great. And on the other hand, like, now it's about playing your own devil's advocate [laughs]. What would be the economic outcome, or just specific market forces, that would prove that your blow-off top thesis was then wrong, or too early, or delayed?

Henrik: First — okay, if it's a blow-off top, then it needs to have a top. First of all, I think we have seen enough to say at least we have had an aggressive development in the markets, to say at least we have the one side of the Eiffel Tower. Now, we need the other side of the Eiffel Tower for me to be correct.

But if I'm incorrect, then it's because we will see that the housing market starts to pick up again. We'll start to see that all of a sudden, for some whatever reason, we'll see that there are more existing homes sold, housing permits start to rise again. We'll see that the yields are maybe not plummeting, but they're coming down maybe in a more gradual manner. And we will see that we get a healthy correction in the stock market — which I find a little difficult here, but anyway, let's say like that. But it'll be healthy, and it will then start to pick up from there.

But it will start in the real economy, and it needs to start with also that the labor market is also finding — that I'm wrong, that we do not have a run rate that is 30 or 50,000 jobs per month right now, but we have a run rate that is all of a sudden starting to accelerate up to 80, 100, 120,000. Even 100,000 right now would be fantastic. So then we could level out. This would be the soft landing. That would be the soft landing. And then we could see that things could develop from there.

What else? Yeah, these are the major things. So the housing market needs to start to show something, because you cannot have an economy that runs on zero houses sold. I mean, you need a housing market, and you need the labor market to start running. These are the things. So that is what I would be saying when, if I'm wrong, and the whole economy is wrong, and we're not going to get that deep dive that I think we're going to get.

13. 关于 Zeberg 的新书

Q: Great. Thanks a lot, Henrik. Well, it was a long conversation — I think we impacted quite a lot. I hope this was also very insightful for viewers and listeners. I also would like to talk about your book — you released a few months ago. So in between conversations, you also released a book. Maybe you want to say a few words about it.

Henrik: It's actually almost a year since it came out, but yes, I can say something about it. I think the thing has been very clear that for me it's going to end in pain — this, what we see now with AI bubble or whatever. But it's really to try to at least come up with an input on the narrative that is going to be embracing this whole development.

If I get it right — let's say I get it right — then I'm sure everybody would point to Trump. And me being a Dane, I'm not sure I'm a big supporter of Trump. But anyway, it doesn't matter, because I don't think it's Trump's mistake. It's not him. It's not his fault. Of course he's done things that are maybe not good for the economy. But the thing is: the focus of the book is more that this experiment that we have been embarking on in 2008 with money printing — even though they try to call it something else and expanding balance sheet just exponentially almost — will have a wealth effect for some time, but it has a bad ending. It always has.

And it's a misunderstanding from central banks that they can create wealth out of thin air like this. And it's going to come down in a bad manner. And actually, because of their actions, it's going to be even worse than it would have been — if they had been not as arrogant, I don't want to say the word arrogant, but there is a piece there, there's a degree of arrogance when you think that you can push down the inflation rates from 2.4 on the core PCE to 2% using a sledgehammer like the Fed funds rate. There's a bit of arrogance there, because you can easily make it too hard, or there is a lagging effect and so on.

So I think the understanding of that — that it's not going to be the sitting president at any point that will be the reason for this multi-decade bubble that has been developing — and he might be somewhat of the pin, but the reason is more that we have tried to experiment again with money printing. And it's coming down badly, which it also has done every time we try. And gold has been the one that has been benefiting from it, which is also why I think it's a good long-term investment.

14. 结束语

Thanks, Henrik, and also I want to thank the viewers and listeners who until now were actually watching and listening to this episode with Henrik. If you like this episode, give it a like. Of course, we always welcome subscribers, so just click that subscribe button — it means a lot to us.

Henrik is also to be found on X, where he shares regular tweets, but also his Substack. You can also subscribe over there. There's also a paid version where more extensive articles are published from Henrik's research. And do not forget to leave a comment in the section to let us know what you like, what you didn't like, and all kinds of reactions that you have about this team.

Henrik, thanks again for your precious time and knowledge.

Henrik: Thank you so much, Alex.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的核心命题：通胀是滞后指标，而非领先指标
Zeberg 整场访谈最具颠覆性的论断，是把市场、美联储、乃至 Luke Roman 等"债券义勇军"叙事的因果链条**反转**了：所有人都把通胀当作领先信号在定价，Zeberg 却坚持通胀是**跟随劳动力市场的最末端滞后变量**。
这里有一个被几乎所有宏观讨论遗漏的、惊人的"幽灵数据"事实——**2024 年 4 月至 2025 年 3 月期间，美国非农就业的真实月度均值仅为 16,000**。这意味着过去 50 年里，没有任何一个非衰退时期的就业创造率低于这个水平。更尖锐的是：2008 金融危机爆发前最后一个月，美国在人口少 2000–3000 万的情况下，还能每月创造 10 万个岗位——而今天的"繁荣"经济体，仅能挤出当年的 15%。
真正让人脊背发凉的隐藏观察是：**162,000 的"亮眼"就业数字，是基于 44% 的历史最低调查回收率，然后把剩下 56% 没回复的企业"假设成和回复企业一样"**而推出的。这在统计学上近乎二战中那张著名的"幸存者偏差"轰炸机图——我们正在用回音做决策，然后把回音当成信号。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、把征服者看作"回形针最大化器"：历史上第一次国家级的 AI 对齐失败

转录中最锋利的那句话——"他们基本上就是不在乎这块大陆产能的 paperclipper"——其实在无意中把一个 2026 年的 AI 安全术语塞回了 1521 年。征服者是一支目标错对齐的智能体：他们把"白银数量"当成了"国家繁荣"的代理指标，然后以惊人的效率去最大化这个代理。结果整个代理指标被打爆（Potosí 的白银产量超出历史任何想象），而真正要被代理的那个目标（西班牙社会的生产力与人均福祉）在同一条曲线上一路反向下跌——实际工资下降、资本市场缺失、工业化缺席。

这不是比喻的巧合。它揭示了一个几乎没人指出的结构：西班牙帝国是人类历史上第一个因为"proxy goal collapse"而失败的大型组织。它比凯恩斯早四百年遇到了度量劫持（Goodhart's Law），比 Bostrom 早五百年示范了"工具性目标吃掉终极目标"的全过程。

二、潜在的意外观察：西班牙是 16 世纪的 AWS，但它忘了给自己定价

通常的叙事是"西班牙剥削新大陆、剥削中国"。可是把现金流画出来会发现一个让人错愕的结构：

  • 真正的生产者：明代中国（丝绸、瓷器、茶叶——有使用价值的实物）；
  • 真正的终端消费者：欧洲贵族与新兴资产阶级；
  • 中间的协议层 / 清算网络：西班牙帝国（白银开采 + 大帆船航线 + 马尼拉—阿卡普尔科走廊 + 塞维利亚结算）。

西班牙在 16–17 世纪事实上搭建了人类第一个跨太平洋结算基础设施——这是巨大的技术与制度成就。但它犯了一个今天任何风投都会立刻指出的错误：它只收"运输费"，没有在协议层收"租"。它既没有抽真正的交易佣金（没有运作中国货到欧洲的商业资本），也没有在协议之上长出"应用层"（没有金融业、保险业、制造业）。结果荷兰人和英国人在它搭好的全球轨道上，用它开采的白银，把它绕开来做了真正赚钱的生意。

你可以说：西班牙是 16 世纪的 AWS，但它只收电费，不收服务费；它造了协议，没有造应用层。这与 2010 年代以来的协议/应用价值捕获之争几乎是同构的。

三、Potosí 其实是明朝中央银行——货币主权的隐秘输出

这段里有一个一旦看见就无法视而不见的事实：明朝晚期的货币体系实际上由玻利维亚的一座矿山维持。张居正"一条鞭法"之后白银货币化，而这些白银大部分并非产自中国，而是通过马尼拉—月港、再从阿卡普尔科跨太平洋输送而来。换句话说，明朝把它最重要的宏观变量——货币供应——外包给了一个它既不认识也无法影响的外国私营矿业集团。

于是出现了人类史上最诡异的宏观因果链条之一：17 世纪前半叶，西班牙王室财政问题 + 新大陆矿脉含银量下降 + 荷兰海盗劫掠大帆船 → 白银流入骤减 → 明朝军队无饷 → 关外满人入关。清朝入主中原，在某种意义上是波托西矿脉减产的下游事件。

这件事的跨领域含义极其黑暗：全球化的第一个版本就已经包含了"货币主权被远程摧毁"这个漏洞。它不是 1971、不是 2008、不是比特币时代才出现的问题。只要你把结算单位的主权交出去，你就把兵饷、把军阀、把王朝更替一起交出去了。

四、更深层的跨领域连接：资源丰裕让"反馈信号"失灵——从进化生物学到创业公司

南北美洲的对比（西班牙 vs. 英属殖民地）、美国南北战争的对比（棉花奴隶制 vs. 工业资本），其实不是三个独立故事，而是同一个机制在三种时空尺度上的重现：持续的外部补给会压制系统本应收到的痛苦信号，让它无法启动适应性演化。

  • 进化生物学：生活在稳定富营养环境中的物种会丢失基因冗余，变成"特化家"（specialist）；一旦环境波动就灭绝。深海热泉旁的管虫很牛，但你把它搬到两米外它就死了。
  • 成瘾神经科学：持续的多巴胺奖励会下调基线敏感性（tolerance），系统再也无法从正常刺激中获得信号，于是必须加大剂量。西班牙对白银的依赖在生理学上和海洛因依赖同构。
  • 创业公司：拿到巨额早期融资的公司通常会推迟 PMF、推迟盈利模型的进化。约束被解除，意味着学习信号也被解除。
  • 你个人的能力：任何时候当你发现一件事"不费力就有回报"，这其实不是好消息——它说明你此刻正在失去关于这件事的学习反馈。

所以这段视频表面讲的是西班牙帝国，底层讲的却是一个对任何系统都成立的黑暗定律：

你的回报速度决定了你能学到多深。当回报比学习更快到达，你就冻结在了你当时的能力水平上，然后在那里慢慢变脆。

西班牙从 1545 年 Potosí 发现白银到 20 世纪末才真正"追上来"，用了四百五十年才摆脱那座山的诅咒。这是人类历史上最长的一笔宿醉。

📝 转录文本

1. The Conquistadors as "Paperclippers"

It's sort of interesting to think about what this Spanish New World conquest really accomplished. So, they're basically after gold and silver. In a weird way, they're sort of like paperclippers who don't really care about this indigenous culture or even the productive capacity of this new continent. They just care about these metals — which are not in and of themselves productive assets, right? They can't generate wealth. They're basically like crypto, if you think what gold and silver are.

So, they're just obsessed with this. Um, initially — we were talking about this yesterday — this helps them fund the, you know… Europe's in a tough spot at this time because of the Ottomans and other forces, and the reconquest just happened. So the Spanish have been fighting off Arab armies that had control over parts of the Arabian Peninsula, and they use this gold and this silver to, I guess, help pay for the defenses back at home.

2. No Net New Wealth — Just Imported Inflation

But if you think about what's really happening here, there's no new net wealth that has been generated, right? It's just basically redistribution among Europeans: if they're using bullion as currency, now the relative ratio of bullion has changed. So you get inflation plus some redistribution. It's basically like the government printing more money — it doesn't create more stuff. There's no productive… at least initially, the Spanish are not getting any new productive capacity out of the New World.

3. Silver Flows East: The Ming Monetary Vacuum

What does change is that during this period the Ming dynasty is in charge of China, and it has really messed up the circulation of paper currency. Nobody trusts it. Every time there's inflation they just make up a new currency and people's stocks of wealth are totally worthless.

And so now the Spanish set up these silver mines in the New World and they ship that silver off to China. And China is then sending millions of pieces of porcelain and tons and tons of silk and spices and fine goods to Europe — basically hundreds of tons of real goods (I don't know, it might have been thousands of tons) in exchange for basically a medium of exchange, basically to make up for the fact that they don't have a reliable means of exchange at the time in the Ming dynasty.

And I think that is an important, interesting piece of what is a function of the Spanish colonies in the New World. It's not generating any net new wealth in the grand scheme of things. It's basically helping get, I don't know, Chinese stuff for free in some sense.

4. From Conquistadors to Bureaucrats: The Encomienda System

Yeah. The conquistadors really didn't appreciate what they accomplished. Many of them — some of them — died doing what they did.

The ones who were lucky, who were good, lived long enough to settle down on what were called encomiendas: local estates with many of the local peoples to farm the land for them in a kind of peon service / serfdom.

The later iteration was the bureaucrats, right? Once the conquistadors had cleared the ground, the bureaucrats would arrive from Spain and they would begin running and administering what would become Mexico, Peru, South America generally. The conquistadors in South America rebelled against that; had to be put down by force to retain South America within the Spanish Empire. Once that was accomplished, though, the whole process became very integrated into the Spanish imperial orbit — the first empire on which the sun never set.

5. Potosí and the Last Piece of Globalization

Once the Spanish had discovered and exploited a mountain of silver — Potosí, what's now Bolivia — they put the last piece of the puzzle in place for true globalization.

Initially the gold and silver was all going east, as you say, into the coffers of King Charles I — sorry, King Charles I and his son King Philip II — for their wars of evangelical defense and expansion against the Ottomans, to keep the Netherlands under their control, and ideally through the Armada to bring the one true apostolic faith of Catholicism back to England. Most of those ventures, of course, were failures.

6. Spain's Negative Return: Inflation and the Capitalism That Never Came

And as you say, the net impact for Spain was ultimately quite negative. Because by infusing Europe with this enormous expansion and liquidity through the silver that was pouring off the treasure ships every year arriving in Spain, all they were doing was importing inflation and pushing prices up to levels — and real wages in Spain actually fell during this period, because yes there was excess liquidity, but this meant prices for even staple goods were much higher than they had been previously.

And the ultimate negative effect was that the seductive drug, essentially, of having silver on tap meant that Spain never developed towards what we call functional capitalism. It never developed capital markets or independent banking systems the way that were emerging in places like the Netherlands and England during this period. So those powers moved ahead while Spain and Portugal were left behind — didn't really fully industrialize during the 19th century, were left very rural and poor and backward by the 20th century. Still now they're catching up from that.

So the average Spanish gain from this was quite marginal. Yes, we can afford fleets necessary to face off against the Ottomans at Lepanto in 1571 — which is good — but in terms of the development of the society, that really plateaued and stayed that way for hundreds of years.

7. The Other Side of the Equation: Manila, China, and Trans-Global Trade

The other side of the equation, as you mentioned, is China. Once the Spanish had fully become able to exploit the silver mines of South America, they could then take advantage of their developing knowledge of the Pacific Ocean's wind currents to send those great ships west to the Philippines — to Manila, their base in the Orient — and from there meet with merchants coming from Japan, from Siam, and most of all from China, bringing goods with real practical value for exchange for that extracted silver.

So, as you say, the Spanish are buying goods with value with excess liquidity, and the real benefit from that is not something that's structurally to the advantage of the country as a whole.

So, yes: what the conquistadors did was historically put the last pieces of the puzzle in place for true globalization. Trade is no longer trans-Eurasian or even transatlantic — it's trans-global. The networks now affect everybody at some point along the line.

8. 1640s Cash Crisis: How Silver Flows Toppled the Ming

And the Ming found that out in the mid-1640s, when there was a cash crisis. Having fully transferred the basis of exchange in their empire to silver, when access to silver was cut off — or at least minimized — for a number of reasons during the first half of the 17th century, the Ming, at the worst possible time with the Manchus at the gates, could no longer fund their armies. They couldn't pay to put a military in place to hold them off. So the Manchus moved in at a moment of supreme advantage, blew out the Ming, and replaced them as the new hegemons over the Chinese imperial zone.

9. Virginia vs. Mexico: The Extractive-vs-Productive Divide

Yeah. It's interesting to contrast the Spanish, who had immediate and outrageous successes in the New World, with the English around the same time who are setting up the colony in Virginia. And there's so many letters from that time where people are complaining about the Virginia Company — is just literally a waste of English money, and… yeah, exactly, and just like everybody's dying. They're not getting… there's like nothing to farm here. There's nothing to get out of this.

In the long run, of course — I guess the British did lose control of the New World — but for a while they did gain these productive new colonies in the New World.

And I don't know what the right way to think about this. I mean, there is this way of thinking about: maybe the Spanish set up this extractive [model] because they had this very quick initial success. They set up a very extractive settlement which didn't result in net productive capacity in the long run. Whereas the British were forced — because there was no, you know, just crazy bullion floating around — they were forced to build up some productive capacity, build up these kinds of institutions that would allow them to make most use of America, Canada, and so on.

10. The Latecomer's Advantage: Netherlands and England

Yeah. You look at the Netherlands and England — the two latecomers to the game of imperialism, Protestant powers marginalized for that reason in Europe. And the Netherlands especially has nothing — natural resources, absolutely zero.

So in that environment, you're forced to innovate and think about how you can achieve capital gain and true economic expansion.

11. The Lottery Trap: Why "The Quick Fix" Destroys Societies

Everybody wants the quick fix. Understandably — we play the lottery for that exact reason, right? But be careful what you wish for, because you may just actually get it. And those societies that have arrived at the quick fix — whether that's gold or silver, or monocultural crop production of some kind which gives you a monopoly on its provision — they become satisfied with that. They become trapped within an environment that exists solely for that purpose, and they don't develop beyond the essential thresholds that allows for.

12. The American Parallel: North vs. South

Even here in the US, we can look at the difference between the North and the South — that geographic line. Below that line, yes, you can get the quick fix. You can put all your capital into buying slaves and have them work at providing cash crops: tobacco (the original one), indigo and sugar, and of course the big one, cotton.

The North didn't have those advantages. You couldn't just buy land and then extract the resource from it. You had to think about how to make money. And that's why all the investment money in the North was going into things with long-term productivity: into trade and commerce, into advanced capital markets in the banking system, and of course into industrialization — right? And that all happened in the North.

So when the rupture came in the 1860s and the North and South went to war, all those advantages were with the North — not just population, but the industrial base, the capital markets necessary for it to put in place a winning long-term strategy for actually defeating the South in that conflict.

13. The Long-Term Lesson

That again is the long-term lesson: that having life too easy from the beginning leads to a certain — I don't want to call it laziness, but a lack of vision, perhaps — in alternatives that may in the longer term actually be more advantageous.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.
