item.description:
## 一、最大的反直觉：他们卖的不是"自动化"，是"主权"
表面上 Gumloop 是 agent builder，但真正让 Shopify、Instacart 这类公司签单的，是一个被低估的词——**"agentic sovereignty"（代理主权）**。
注意 Max 说的那句被低估的话："当那些实验室带着八位数合同来找我们、而我们已经全部用了他们的方案时，我们**有能力说走就走**。"
这揭示了一个隐秘的商业模式转换：**Gumloop 本质上在卖"对冲工具"**，而不是生产力工具。它的核心价值主张不是"让 AI 替你干活"，而是"**让你永远不被任何单一 AI 实验室绑架**"。这就是为什么他们的定价模仿 OpenRouter——token at cost——因为他们在把自己定位成"**AI 时代的瑞士**"而非"AI 时代的 SaaS"。
这就解释了一个数据之谜：为什么他们的首要买家不是业务负责人，而是 **IT leader**？因为 IT leader 买的从来就不是功能，是**可撤回性（reversibility）**。
## 二、跨领域连接：Gumloo

item.title: [Business of Sport] Manchester City: The Verdict
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个让人意外的角度

1. 曼城的"原罪"不是作弊，而是买错了俱乐部

主流叙事把这个故事讲成"沙漠石油贵族入侵英超、腐蚀公平竞争"。但如果你把时间轴拨回 2008 年 9 月 1 日，会发现一个几乎没人点破的反转：曼苏尔买曼城时，欧洲足坛还没有财政公平法案。换句话说，他是基于"花钱买冠军合法"的旧世界规则买入的一个中游资产。两年之后，游戏规则突然改了——而且是其他俱乐部专门为了压制他而改的。

这就形成了一个商业心理学的经典陷阱：被困住的赢家心态（trapped winner syndrome）。你不是在赌场输了钱，你是赢了钱之后被告知规则改了、钱不许带走。这种时刻，人更容易做出极端决策，因为"沉没成本 + 身份羞辱"的双重压力远超理性。曼城高管在 2011-12 之间做出"系统性撒谎"的选择，并不是贪婪，而是被困住的尊严——一个国家主权层级的身份绝不能接受"重新变回中游球队"。

2. 跨领域连接：这是一场典型的"合规套利 → 合规崩塌"叙事，和加密货币 FTX 的脚本完全一致

把曼城换成 FTX，你会惊讶地发现剧本几乎逐字相同： - 新玩家进入一个监管尚未成形的高增长行业 - 用真金白银 + 虚构账本同时撬动增长 - 利用"规则还在追赶创新"的空窗期建立不可逆的既成事实 - 当监管终于到位，选择"双倍下注否认"而非认罪求情 - 最终由一个事后追溯建立的独立机构（独立委员会 / 独立财务监管官）终结游戏

更惊人的是，萨姆·班克曼-弗里德和曼城主席 Al Mubarak 的辩护逻辑同构："你们看不到的那部分证据才是真相。" 这是所有"后真相式辩护"的共同句式——它不是在反驳证据，而是在否认证据的可知性，让对方陷入认识论的陷阱。Charlie 用了一个精准的词：gaslighting（煤气灯操纵）。这不是法律辩护，这是心理战术。

3. 真正的系统性真相：英超的罚则其实已经"自动执行"了，不需要任何人下判决

这是最反直觉的洞察——曼城的沉没已经在数学上既成事实，剩下的只是时间。看看这个结构：

2026 年 11 月 2 日 - 2027 年 2 月 27 日 独立足球监管官（IFR）法定的"重新申请期"
法律框架 直接移植自金融服务业的"适格人员测试"
对"知悉或鲁莽地提供虚假信息"的处理 强制禁业
曼城 114 项罪名中落入"严重类别"的 68 项

换句话说，议会在 2023 年通过足球治理法案时，就已经不知不觉地把曼城判决了——只是没有人在当时意识到。独立委员会和 IFR 这两条独立的时间线像两艘航船，各自航行了三年，直到 2026 年 10 月才在同一个坐标点交汇。这是一种无主体设计的制度共振（institutional resonance without designer），类似于金融市场里的"闪电崩盘"——没有谁按下按钮，但所有机制同时触发。

斯塔默首相今天早上说"曼城老板走了我会很遗憾"——这句话之所以让 Charlie 气炸，不仅因为政治越界，更因为它暴露了一个更深的事实：连首相都没搞懂自己的政府已经自动把判决执行了。他以为这还是可以讨价还价的政治议题，但其实游戏结束已经写在法条里了。

元层面的洞见：这个案子最终将成为一个研究案例——不是关于足球作弊，而是关于国家主权在跨国规则体系中的"面子不可退缩性"如何成为战略盲点。中东主权基金在未来十年会反复复盘这个样本：当你用一个国家的尊严去持有一个受规制资产时，你就把自己变成了一个不能道歉的玩家。而在现代合规体系里，不能道歉就意味着不能生存。

📝 转录文本

开场寒暄

Good afternoon, Charlie. Hi, Charlie. Um, I am hot off the plane from from Milano. Um, and as you've seen, I've dawned my special sky blue polo shirt for for this moment.

I'm gutted. I didn't say this to you when we were just chatting beforehand. I've clocked something here. I'm not going to say it. I want to see his reaction when he jumps on. I was interesting choice of color today.

Very deliberate choice of color. I'm showing I'm showing solidarity with the wrongans of this world.

If you're not watching, it's got that city blue feel to it. Yeah. Yeah.

I mean, it's it's a little bit more turquoisey, isn't it? Yeah. Yeah. It's a little bit more like sort of, you know, what they call it when the reform party teal. Teal. Yeah. Teal. Teal. And it's like that suit that Farage wears.

Quiet week. Well, quite quiet week.

一、本周事件回顾：114 项罪名成立

So, um, I guess what what what Chaz Jr. is talking about here is that um this time last week um pretty much it uh started to leak out that after 3 years of investigation or or the case you know being pursued for 3 years um that finally Man City had been found guilty on 114 of the 115 charges that have been laid against them by the Premier League by an independent commission.

I think it's very important to say that this is not the Premier League finding one of their members guilty. Is the Premier League making allegations which an independent commission has found Man City guilty of?

Yeah. Which when this first came out, actually it was first revealed in 2018. Yes. Uh if you look back, that was when the Premier League took on the responsibility. They did a lot of their research. UEFA jumped the gun. They tried to punish them for similar stuff. They got Man City overturned it through CAS on technicalities basically through things sitting outside the time frames with which UEFA were allowed to pin them on things which is why they had to jump the gun.

Exactly. But the Premier League kept going. They kept their own um investigation and that point in 2023, February 2023, that was when they passed these findings, which was the 115 charges to that independent commission.

Yeah, we have been waiting a very long time for this. Last Friday when that came out, I mean, Charlie, I don't know about you, I was actually in a recording and I came out of my phone, including one message from you just kind of like blown up from news sites, uh people, you know, positing opinions. It was that moment, I guess, for for the journalists, and you've heard them say it, where they've been, this is what they've been waiting for for so long.

为什么没有立刻做紧急节目

But despite lots of people saying, "Oh, you guys going to do an emergency pod? When are we going to hear? When are we going to hear?" I think it's important to say um, you know, we we didn't want to jump on it immediately for a couple of reasons.

Firstly, we didn't actually know a huge amount more than we had known for the years previous when the guilty verdict was handed down. It was really going to entail — handed down yet. It had been leaked. It had been leaked that this was going to be the decision, but it actually hadn't yet been fully handed down. And what had definitely not happened was that the full um sort of report of what had happened in that case had not been published.

Exactly. Right. So, it wasn't clear.

So, if we were doing it, it would have been more speculation really based on okay, they're guilty, but what about the punishments? Which is really the conversation we've been having for the last three and a half years. In sitting on it, I think we have now a far broader picture, a far more accurate picture of what that information really means.

The Premier League statement has now come out, which it hadn't done last week, which was uh Belgian Football Federation rather than HP. I mean, it was it was pretty pretty un-Premier League, I thought. Um, and hopefully right as of today, as of as of recording, and guys, we are doing this as close as we probably could get to releasing the show and recording it to ensure that nothing goes out of date because this is changing by the hour. I've got my phone on here in front of me with uh Twitter or X, sorry, riding on because you got new information all the time. But we want to give you the most accurate picture. This will release less than 24 hours after we've recorded it. So hopefully we managed to achieve that.

二、115 项指控的分类拆解

Should we start by laying out the charges?

Yes. I mean, effectively the verdict. Yeah. What what have they been found guilty of, Charlie?

So, to remind everyone of the 115 charges, there were a number of things that Man City were accused of doing.

54 项：未提供准确财务信息

Uh 54 of the 115 were a failure to provide accurate financial information. Um, now on that, the Premier League is a member organization that, you know, relies on its members accurately providing that information.

35 项：未配合调查

35 of the charges were a failure to cooperate with the Premier League investigation. If you remember um Chelsea's case earlier this year, which people were bringing up in tandem, the reason they got their punishment was actually highlighted at length around their cooperation.

You mean the reason why they got a relatively less punishment, less lesser punishment. Now, of course, the number of charges that Chelsea were being um accused of were were much much smaller. And also um it was 70 odd though, wasn't it? Um yeah, was it 70 odd? 74, I think.

But they they tended to be um you know of of a slightly lower type, right? So you know related basically to player payments effectively, right? Which was still fundamentally in breach, but they happened under the previous ownership and the new ownership had been thoroughly cooperative. In fact, not as cooperative. They themselves had highlighted these payments to the Premier League and had then cooperated fully with the Premier League in trying to get to the bottom of what had actually gone on.

Yeah. So it's a totally different situation both in type and in scale. And people were last Friday it was one of the first things that people were trying to balance between the two. So it is important to make that difference but the important point here cuz it's going to run through is cooperation.

Yeah. And denial basically.

关键对比：切尔西 vs 曼城

14 of the charges. So we've had 54, 35 — truth and lying. Truth. Well true. Right. So so Chelsea were truthful. Man City as these findings lay out were not. Chelsea were truthful about their lying. Man City are lying about their lying. Chelsea were truthful about the previous ownership's lying. Yeah.

This time it's very clear from the report which is as you say a full-on Belgian Football Federation style um you know firing with both barrels um announcement that they were found thoroughly guilty both not only of not having raised it themselves. Far from that then not only then denying it but also then on top of that not providing the information in a timely and accurate way which then enabled the investigation to be to sort to happen in the right way. So it's it's it's layer upon layer upon layer as opposed to one misdoing. Oh massive.

14 项：球员及经理薪酬造假

And so 14 charges uh accounted for a failure to provide accurate player and manager financials. So if people remember some of the earliest stuff I remember coming out about this was looking at things like Roberto Mancini's contract and trying to figure out how he was paid through the club. So that includes stuff like this Yaya Toure has actually speculated on. And this is the bit which is similar to the Chelsea charges right this is the this is the section of the Man City charges which could be made comparable to the Chelsea issues — players basically. Yeah.

7 项：违反盈利与可持续性规则（PSR）

Um now the next one while only seven of them is very significant because it's breaching the Premier League's profit and sustainability rules. And if we look at how clubs like Everton and Forest have been punished recently, it has been for breaches of profit and sustainability for one breach, right? There were seven of these charges attributed to that.

And if you remember the circumstances of those breaches where they were fundamentally accidental, right? So they were things where they hadn't got their house in order in time. And I think it was in Forest case, if they'd actually sold one player three days before they did sell him, they wouldn't have breached.

It was Brennan Johnson. Yeah. Yeah. But they still got done. Yeah. Right. despite having cooperated fully.

So effectively it's I actually haven't heard much of it Charlie you know the whole well this is sort of like like other cases so therefore they should be treated the same as other cases. I haven't heard too much of it but for those people out there who are trying to make any kind of equivalence between this and anything that has gone before ever, you is is for the birds. This is on a totally new epochal level of cheating.

5 项：未遵守 UEFA 规则

It is. I'll finish it off with five charges being a failure to comply with UEFA rules in the Premier League regulations. There is actually a piece around you must um abide by UEFA rules. Now, as I mentioned before, UEFA had had their own dealings with them. Far less successful. Man City overturned it at CAS. Uh they got a 10 million fine rather than a 2-year suspension from European football, which is what the initial charge was. But interestingly, I think a lot of the reason they got the 10 million fine still from CAS was because of a failure of compliance. Yeah. Sorry. Failure to cooperate. Yeah.

So there there's a there's a theme here.

小结：系统性而非偶然性

So the reason why Charlie's laid all laid that all all out for you is that you'll hear a lot about the 114 um and you'll get get some references to specific instances. What he's done there is segmented the charges into three if not four different pots, right? To make it clear that this is not about one particular type of malfeasance. This is about a systematic regime of wrongdoing across every single area that one possibly could get into. They were into it, these findings report. Okay. And then on top of that, they then failed to comply cooperate when these things started to be investigated as well.

三、曼城的回应：双倍下注否认

Now I think probably before we get into you know what we like to think we do best which is the breakdown um there's one last bit of housekeeping which needs to be done which is after these findings were published by the Premier League in other words the findings of the commission um at that particular point in time Man City had not made an official comment but subsequently their chief executive and indeed chairman have did right.

两种策略：认罪求情 vs 双倍下注

So effectively I've been in situations advising organizations before which have been under intense public scrutiny following you know major issues having happened and you've got sort of two main routes to take.

One of which is hold your hands up, put your put yourself at the mercy of the court of public opinion on the one hand but obviously of the authorities in the other hand and say look we're really really sorry we're basically good citizens please show us some mercy.

The other way to go is to double down. Now the double down is a very risky strategy. I think in whatever it was a couple of decades as an adviser on these types of things, I pretty much never recommended it if I'm being honest with you because fundamentally what you're doing then is you are removing any requirement of anybody ever to show you any mercy whatsoever.

Right? So it's rather like if you imagine in the criminal court system when you've got somebody who's accused of having committed some horrific crime and instead of pleading guilty they plead not guilty. The tariffs are higher then, the the punishments are fiercer right because you haven't he— you haven't shown contrition, you haven't shown remorse, you haven't held your hands up. And that applies here as well ultimately when it comes to sanctions which we'll discuss later on. If you if as an organization you still maintain that despite the findings against you, you have done nothing wrong, then by definition the sanctions have to be far harsher and always will be.

Al Mubarak 与 Soriano 的声明

And to be clear, the two statements from Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano um have been I mean so effusive in preaching their innocence as a as the Premier League statement was in condemning them as you know creating sham contracts and and inflating their revenues. You you've you've got what feels like an impulse at the moment.

Well, I don't think it's an impulse at all. I think that's what Man City want you to think, right? And I've read a couple of um pieces of media from elements reasonably sympathetic to Man City which run along the lines of well, you know, it's all six one, half dozen the other. The Premier League say they've won and Man City say they're totally not guilty.

No. What has happened is Man City have been found guilty by an independent commission. The Premier League, which effectively has won that case because they were the one who brought the charges, have put out a statement welcoming the findings of the independent commission and laying out what those findings are. And Man City have totally ignored the findings of the independent commission in frankly a arrogant, hubristic, and gaslighting way and have basically said, "Well, we're totally ignoring that." Right? I think the phrase was this is only the start of a long process.

Now, this is not the start of a long process. This is the beginning of the end of a long process. The long process, as Charlie Jr. um has noted, started with the original leaks of these breaches back in 2018. Just bear that in mind, viewers and listeners, 8 years of investigation and trial. 8 years.

行业反应：伊利湖畔的集体错愕

So when the senior executives at Man City say this is just the start of the process that shows a fundamental disregard for the justice system as in as as applied within this country and I think that that is something which has profoundly shocked the industry.

I've just come from a industry conference in Italy which had people from the UK had people from other parts of the world all of whom flew in for this sports industry conference in Lake Como and we were all sat there when these statements started coming out and there was a big intake of breath. And I'm talking about from people who run other major European clubs, people who run federations, people who are heavily involved at the top ends of the game saying, "Oh my god, really? They're really going to pretend this hasn't happened at all."

They're going to pretend that there is, as I think the quote was, an irrefutable body of evidence, irrefutable. Right? That's a that is a word which says it simply cannot be questioned. We can now get back to being not the brand front for a Middle Eastern country. We can now get back to actually being a proper football club.

Yeah. Brilliant. Well, worth the wait, Charlie. I enjoyed it a lot. Thank you so much. Look forward to keeping it going. Thanks a lot.

item.description:
## 三个让人意外的角度
### 1. 曼城的"原罪"不是作弊，而是买错了俱乐部
主流叙事把这个故事讲成"沙漠石油贵族入侵英超、腐蚀公平竞争"。但如果你把时间轴拨回 2008 年 9 月 1 日，会发现一个几乎没人点破的反转：**曼苏尔买曼城时，欧洲足坛还没有财政公平法案**。换句话说，他是基于"花钱买冠军合法"的旧世界规则买入的一个中游资产。两年之后，游戏规则突然改了——而且是其他俱乐部**专门为了压制他**而改的。
这就形成了一个商业心理学的经典陷阱：**被困住的赢家心态（trapped winner syndrome）**。你不是在赌场输了钱，你是赢了钱之后被告知规则改了、钱不许带走。这种时刻，人更容易做出极端决策，因为"沉没成本 + 身份羞辱"的双重压力远超理性。曼城高管在 2011-12 之间做出"系统性撒谎"的选择，并不是贪婪，而是**被困住的尊严**——一个国家主权层级的身份绝不能接受"重新变回中游球队"。
### 2. 跨领域连接：这是一场典型的"合规套利 → 合规崩塌"叙事，和加密货币 FTX 的脚本完全一致
把曼城换成 FTX，你会惊讶地发现剧本几乎逐字相

item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这位"比特币多头"其实悄悄投降了——而他自己没意识到

孔剑平最意外的一句话不是"革命刚刚开始"，而是那个比喻："比特币是过去十年的月亮，但太阳升起后月亮就看不见了。"

这是一位在Bitcoin Conference 立下"百万美金是起点"旗帜的人，在一年之后把 BTC 从主角贬成了"背景光源"。更有意思的是他给出的资产配置——50-70% AI 股票 + 30% 数字货币——这不是比特币信仰者的仓位，这是 AI 多头顺便拿点 BTC 当对冲的仓位。他嘴上说长期看好，身体已经转向了。

这揭示了一个比特币叙事中的隐藏裂缝：比特币最大的敌人从来不是监管，而是"更性感的新叙事"。当资本注意力被 AI 虹吸，连核心布道者都开始用"月亮"自我安慰时，这个资产面临的是比熊市更危险的东西——相关性坍塌。

二、"台积电股价提前一年见顶"背后的时间悖论——这是一条可跨到航运、油轮、半导体历史的规律

他说台积电只能满足 70% 的 GPU 需求，产能限制决定了未来三五年持续增长，但股价可能在增长见顶前一年就提前见顶。

这不是技术分析，这是一条周期性产业的通用规律，而且发生过很多次：

  • 1980s 油轮：航运业老兵经历过暴跌 PTSD，拒绝扩张，造成 2003-2008 结构性短缺，但 BDI 指数在实物短缺最严重前就已见顶
  • 2018 芯片周期：三星、台积电的 CapEx 犹豫导致 2020-2022 全球缺芯，但半导体股票早在 2021 年 Q4 就见顶
  • 今天的 GPU 供应链：孔剑平亲口说了关键——"产业链老人经历过太多周期，看过太多尸体，所以保守"

这里有一个被忽视的洞察：产业老兵的"创伤后保守"本身是一种宏观稀缺性制造机。他们活下来的方式正是让下一代继续短缺的方式。这不是产能问题，这是代际记忆的金融化。

三、最反直觉的发现：中国开源模型拯救了软件公司，而不是毁灭它们

这是整场访谈最像"啊哈"时刻的部分，但主持人没追问下去。

常识叙事是："AI 会取代所有软件公司"。孔剑平给出了相反的因果链：

  • 闭源模型价格高 → 软件公司成本结构被挤压 → 真正的死神是闭源，不是 AI
  • 开源模型价格降 10-100 倍 → 节省的差价由云厂、软件商、客户、模型方四方瓜分 → 软件公司重新获得毛利空间

这里有一个跨领域连接非常震撼：这和心理咨询师 vs ChatGPT 的护城河是同一个结构。

心理咨询师的壁垒不是知识——ChatGPT 知道的心理学理论更多。壁垒是情绪价值的分发通道。同理，B 端软件公司的壁垒不是算法——而是对无数细分 B 端用户的 workflow、合同条款、历史数据的占有。大模型公司永远碰不到那层最后一公里。

所以 AI 革命的真正受益者不是"AI 公司"，而是"旧渠道 + 新算力"的结合体——它们像是继承了燃油车经销商网络的电动车公司。

四、隐藏的终极洞察：AI 为什么会选比特币而不是稳定币存钱

他说："AI 雇人挖金子，人把金子搬走了，AI 找不回来；但 AI 存比特币比人更能守住。"

这句话被包装成一个段子，但里面藏着一个产权革命的预言：

  • 稳定币 = 支付中介（人类法律系统的延伸）
  • 比特币 = AI 能独立行使所有权的第一类资产

人类资产体系的所有权本质上依赖人类暴力机器（法院、警察、合同执行）。AI 没有身体、没有法律人格，它无法真正拥有股票、房产、黄金。比特币是迄今为止唯一一种 AI 用密钥就能完整主张所有权的资产。

当 AI 产生 AI、AI 开始需要为自己攒钱时——比特币不是加密货币，它是"非人类主体的第一桶金"。这才是比特币十年后真正的 utility，而不是"数字黄金"。

📝 转录文本

台積電股價恐提前見頂？算力危機全面爆發

嘉賓：Jack Kong 孔劍平（Nano Labs） 節目：邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain

開場：中國芯片依舊是"紙板箱項目"

In China, chips are still a project of cardboards. Because the card can't get in. But China's open source model is growing fast. So it requires a lot of computing power. So in China, chips are the biggest growth space.

一、一年之後，百萬美金起點論還成立嗎？

主持人：大家應該還記得孔博士，Nano Labs 的孔博士去年在 Bitcoin Conference 的時候說比特幣超過100萬美金才是起點。今天，一年後的今天，你還這樣相信嗎？

孔劍平：我覺得過去一年這個挑戰的確比以往更多了。對，但我覺得還是依然非常看好比特幣的一個長期前景。

主持人：但如果說現在一般人想要讓整個家庭是很舒服的，他應該要……

孔劍平：I think in the past 10 years, Bitcoin has been a moon. Um... yes, when the sun rises, the moon and the stars are not visible anymore. So I think in the next three to five years, the development speed of AI will still be very fast. At this time, other assets, including Bitcoin, will definitely be affected by this. As a family configuration...

二、AI 革命該投哪一層？——"運氣 + 熟悉領域"原則

主持人：There are many different levels of technology revolution in AI. For example, there is a hardware-related investment in Nano Labs. AI has electricity and other different levels. How should people decide which one to invest in?

孔劍平：I think investment is mainly based on luck. Most people can't predict what the future will be.

For example, a few months ago, you might think that the capital spending of cloud companies is very high. This is too low and the asset load rate is very high. In the past month, cloud companies have suddenly become good assets. Because its GPU recovery can be extended, and the rent can be increased. Anyway, the more capital you spent in the past, the more cards you bought, the more the credit you got.

So the trend has been changing. But overall, it's about the direction of the technological revolution. At this time, you actually have to be in your familiar position. Continue to do certain things, maybe your success rate will increase. But if you jump differently, keep jumping, in all the areas you are not familiar with, if you keep jumping, it may be difficult for him to enjoy this wealth and prosperity.

主持人：You mean to say that choose one layer to study and then invest in that layer. Don't want to take a little bit of everything, right?

孔劍平：Yes, yes, yes. Although everyone makes money by luck, but on the basis of luck, you may still have to add some understanding of this industry and some judgments of the future trend of this industry.

三、AI 泡沫？孔劍平：革命才剛剛開始

主持人：For example, the stock price fell a while ago. I just want to know what your judgment is.

孔劍平：My judgment is that the revolution has just begun.

主持人：The revolution has just begun, but the value of American AI stocks is very high. 大家在想，OpenAI 會不會是 AI 泡沫的雷曼兄弟，會爆掉，估值太高，你覺得呢？

孔劍平：我覺得這看階段。如果這是一個AI革命的爆發的初期，那這種情況會有一些企業會爆掉，但大部分頭部的企業還是能活下來。

But if this is a late revolution, it's like the last three or five years of China's real estate — many companies will report it, many AI companies will report it, including because of the guarantee of various kinds of credit receipts, it may form a continuous problem. But I personally judge that this is still early. It has enough space to deal with these risks.

主持人：Is it because they have produced enough income?

孔劍平：一是 AI 的使用、AI 的生產力在整個人類社會中仍然非常低。二是我們看到 Anthropic 這類公司的收入已經可以實現利潤。許多雲公司也已經實現了利潤。

Like Amazon's financial report, its entire GPU will be able to return in three years. Like DeepSeek's internal speech by Liang Wenfeng, its GPU will be able to return in ten months. So this is a very healthy investment.

四、中美雙源競爭：閉源 vs 開源的"共生式對撞"

孔劍平：China's AI is also very strong now. I think the Chinese open-source model is developing very fast. The US's B2M model has obvious advantages in all aspects, with a large capital and a lot of experienced technology personnel.

So I think the long term of the future of AI design is a long-term competition between the US B2M model and China's open-air model. But this competition will not consume the other party, but will promote the other party's further growth, because the entire market is growing.

主持人：So you think the US will always be the source of the currency, and China will always be the source of the currency, and these two forces will compete for five years?

孔劍平：Yes, I think in the next three to five years, these two forces will grow together in competition. I'm not saying that because China's model is stronger, the US model will fall. I think it will still develop very quickly.

五、賣鏟子的台積電：產能卡住 70%，但股價會提前見頂

主持人：Can I say that I don't want to guess who will win in the end, so I will invest in people who sell shovels, such as Taiwan's TSMC? Can I?

孔劍平：I think TSMC is a great company. And now, cardboard is actually cardboard TSMC. Because the latest financial report also said that it can only meet 70% of the customer demand because of the production capacity limitation.

這個產能限制來自於台積電和其他上游供應鏈的限制。If TSMC can expand further, it can produce more GPUs for more users. It is clear that TSMC will continue to grow in the next three to five years.

But the stock price may reach the top one year before its growth. Why? This is the second-tier market.

⚡ 廣告插播：MyTrade 交易平台

想要嘗試參與市場，MyTrade 這個投資平台擁有全球四大監管機構的交易牌照，而且商品種類很多——股票、外匯、加密貨幣指數、大宗商品、ETF 都可以交易。

MyTrade 是一個差價合約（CFD）交易平台，用戶不是買賣資產本身，而是在買賣交易價格的變動。它支援信用卡跟 USDT 直接出入金，不用先換成美金再轉帳。交易本身免佣金，點差偏低，槓桿最高可以開到 200 倍。

TradingView 平台裡面還提供很多資訊、新聞跟交易策略可以參考。達成入金和交易條件之後，可以免費得到彭博社一年的新聞網站訂閱。他們也是阿根廷國家足球隊官方贊助商，2025 年獲得了歐洲最可靠經濟商、最佳數字客戶體驗等金融類獎項的肯定。現在有一個頻道專屬的活動……

六、軟件公司為什麼能活下來？——開源模型反而救了他們

主持人：這軟件真的很有趣，因為前一陣子就說 AI 會取代所有軟件，然後現在好像又沒了，這個敘事變得非常快。

孔劍平：對。前段時間是因為這些閉源模型特別強，軟件公司只能採購這些閉源模型為客戶服務，那至少它成本非常高。

而現在中國的開源模型上來以後，開源模型的價格是閉源模型的幾十分之一甚至幾百分之一的價格。The savings of dozens of times the gap was shared by cloud companies, software companies, customers and open source models. At this time, its service price can be lower, and the customer experience can also be lower. 這時候軟件公司有了另一次發展機會。

主持人：But why weren't they threatened before?

孔劍平：They were threatened. Because all their income was taken away by the closed source model. Now the open source model provides software companies 低成本切入大模型服務的機會。

主持人：但作為用戶，我可以直接用 AI 模型，而不去付錢給任何這些軟件公司？

孔劍平：因為 AI 軟件公司更多不是為 C 端用戶直接提供服務，更多是服務 B 端用戶，B 端用戶會有無數的細分需求需要去滿足。

These software companies are originally rooted in these distributed channels and have more data in distributed channels and the needs of distributed channels users. So they know their users better than large model companies.

Just like a psychologist, he can provide emotional value to his users. In fact, you may ask ChatGPT a lot of psychological questions, but when the psychologist tells you, they will give you more emotional value. So more software companies, compared to large model companies, they will also give their users more emotional value.

七、AI 泡沫的警示指標在哪裡？——老兵的保守反而製造結構性短缺

主持人：If the audience is worried about the trend of AI bubbles, what kind of data or what indicators do you think need to be more conservative?

孔劍平：I think...

（關於世代差異）The 90s and 00s were naturally very busy. They didn't care about the price and just wanted to develop. The 50s and 00s went through too many economic cycles and saw too many bodies. So they were relatively conservative. When the market expanded, they didn't care about the price and just went for it.

So at this time, the expansion of these chips, the expansion of the upstream supply chain, 短期內永遠跟不上大模型的發展速度。所以沒有什麼資本支出太多的問題，資本支出很多依然跟不上大模型的增長，以及未來 AI 生產 AI 的增長速度。

現在還是人跟 AI 偶合在生產，未來就是 AI 生產 AI。AI produces AI, but the production power of humans and AI produces humans are different.

主持人：So you are watching the news, CNBC, they are all talking about AI bubbles. You don't feel worried?

孔劍平：No bubbles at all.

主持人：No bubbles at all?

八、AI 芯片的"折舊年齡" vs 真實使用壽命

孔劍平：The age of AI chip recovery is different from the actual age of it. It's like mining back then.

比特幣五年前跌的時候，礦機還能賣；比特幣一年前跌的時候，礦機就必須淘汰。The price of Bitcoin fell 5 years ago, and the mining machines can still be sold. The price of Bitcoin fell 1 year ago, and the mining machines have to be eliminated. Wow.

九、普通投資人如何選到"穿越熊市的公司"？

主持人：How do ordinary investors catch up with these news?

孔劍平：I think it's like having Internet bubble in 2000. But after 2000, cloud computing and Internet applications have seen a rapid growth.

In the past, some traditional companies, such as hardware companies, had problems. But new companies have seen a rapid growth. 它們拿到過上萬倍的回報——but some of them are dead.

主持人：But how do we choose whether this company is able to hold out in the fall?

孔劍平：I think it depends on whether it is in the core position of an industry chain.

In the past, it may be a GPU company, a storage company, a fiber factory. As its growth rate exceeds the high-speed stage, I think it is still in the high-speed growth stage, so don't worry. In the future, it may be the core VAF cloud company.

十、AI 與比特幣：為什麼不是穩定幣？

（關於 AI 自主性與資產安全）AI will be trapped by humans when it creates its own creativity. As an AI, I hired a few people to mine gold, but people moved the gold away. AI can't find it back.

But AI can store Bitcoin better than people. Because it has better encryption methods and better management methods. It can also find better ways to have a loophole. It's definitely better managed than people.

So digital currency is definitely an AI-suitable currency.

主持人：Why not stable currency? Why Bitcoin?

孔劍平：Bitcoin is a wool（原料/本位）. Stable currency is a payment tool. 支付中介。These two are not in conflict.

For example, the daily payment of agents is definitely stable currency. It is not possible to be Bitcoin. But if AI makes money to save money, it can only save Bitcoin.

十一、終極倉位配置：100 萬怎麼分？

主持人：Last question. If the audience has one million now, I don't care what currency it is. How do you distribute it now?

孔劍平： - 50% ~ 70% → AI 相關股票（未來增長空間） - 約 30% → 以比特幣為基礎的數字貨幣

In the future, AI development or digital currency development or AI and digital currency development in common, you can enjoy this red power.

主持人：I really want to hear this. Thank you.

孔劍平：Thank you.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] The Future of Frontier Model Architectures with Walter Goodwin, Founder & CEO of Fractile
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被所有人忽略的"25,000倍剪刀差"

Walter 在访谈中轻描淡写地提到一组数字——过去 20 年 FLOPS 增长了 100 万倍，而内存带宽只增长了 40 倍。这是一个 25,000 倍的结构性剪刀差。整个 AI 硬件行业都在用一只被过度放大的手（算力）去配合一只萎缩的手（带宽）。

真正令人意外的是：这个剪刀差正在反向塑造模型架构本身。MoE 本可以稀疏到 1/256 来节省算力，但没人这么做——不是因为智能不够，而是因为今天的 HBM 带宽承受不了。换句话说，当前所有"前沿模型"的架构选择，都是在带宽牢笼里跳的舞。Walter 的赌注本质上不是造一块更快的芯片，而是通过改变带宽的供给曲线，从硬件层去解锁一类迄今不敢被训练出来的模型。这是一种罕见的"反向因果"——芯片决定模型应该长什么样，而不是反之。

跨领域连接：Amdahl 定律的三次递归

Walter 用 Amdahl 定律解释芯片设计瓶颈时，无意间揭示了一个美妙的递归结构：

  • 芯片内部：能并行的部分极快，不能并行的（place & route 的 NP-hard 求解）成为瓶颈
  • 组织内部：前端设计可以用 AI 加速到几周，但 fab 周转依然是 3–5 个月的物理硬墙
  • AI 研究内部：推理 token 可以无限生成，但实验本身的 wall clock 时间（跑一次训练）成为瓶颈

这三层瓶颈的本质是同一个结构：每当你把"思考"这件事加速了 100 倍，"行动/验证"这件事就从背景变成前景。这解释了为什么 Walter 对"硬问题（hard problems）"下这么大的赌注——他真正押注的是一个元规律：在 AI 时代，所有行业都会收敛到"思考便宜、实验昂贵"的新平衡态。谁掌握加速实验的工具（无论是芯片的实验还是科学的实验），谁就捕获最大价值。连 Dwarkesh 节目里"用一百年人类等价时间去思考每一个实验"的玩笑，都是这个规律的一个脚注。

最反常识的观察：垂直整合的"自杀陷阱"

一般叙事是"大厂终将自己做芯片，第三方芯片商会被挤死"。Walter 给出了一个博弈论上无可反驳的反论证，却几乎没人注意到——

如果 Lab 1 全押自研硅，而 Lab 2 发现了一个只在别人硬件上能跑的算法突破，那么 Lab 1 会在部署追赶的 9 个月里直接死掉。

这意味着前沿实验室之间的竞争结构本身，强制要求硬件多样性。越是接近 AGI 的赛道，越不能单一下注硬件——这是一种被"算法创新速度"反向规训的多样性需求。

更深的连接来自金融学：这是典型的"相关性风险"问题。前沿实验室之间的智能差距会消失（开源 Kimi 已经证明了），所以差异化只能来自部署速度，而部署速度要求你能跑多个异构平台。这就把 Nvidia 当下看似无敌的垄断，变成了一个被博弈论自身限制的垄断——客户必须养活多个供应商，否则他们自己就输了。

彩蛋级观察：Walter 说某些第一方芯片"主要功能是压低 Nvidia 的报价"。这句话翻译过来就是——超大规模厂商在用数十亿美元流片，去做一次价格谈判。这可能是人类商业史上最昂贵的议价工具。

Right now we're trying to build a single chip. If you crack open an Nvidia system, it has anywhere between kind of six and nine custom chips all built by Nvidia to come together to build something that is really, really potent. So there's already a gap there. You know, it'd be great to be productive enough that we could start to build our own responses in that same kind of way.

This idea of being able to have at any given moment a kind of rolling frontier of bets that you hope are deeply aligned — in which you're ready to trigger the ramp of — this is a huge advantage if you can kind of build that machine and build that engine. It's the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a 3 to 6 months of the advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments.

Introduction

Hi listeners, welcome back to No Priors. Today I'm here with Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full-stack AI chip company, Fractile. We talk about what it means to be full stack as a company, the technical bets they're making, why he's so focused on memory bandwidth, his predictions for frontier model architectures in the future, and the structure of the chip market at the frontier today and tomorrow amongst Nvidia, AMD, internal efforts, and this new class of accelerators.

Sarah: Welcome, Walter. Walter, thanks so much for doing this.

Walter: Very good to be here, Sarah.

What Fractile Does

Sarah: You started this incredibly interesting company called Fractile. Can you give us an overview of what you guys do?

Walter: Fractile is a chip company. We build very, very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. This sort of bet on speed is something which we've had right from the outset. Started the company in summer of 2022.

At the time we were starting to see two things. One was obviously the arrival of foundation models trained on the internet and generalizing across everything. The other was a few kind of wise people saying, you know, we need to find a way to pour more compute into these models at test time. We need to find a way to take what we had for kind of AlphaGo — where you have a capable neural network, but then it becomes superhuman as you roll it out at scale — and bring that to kind of language modeling, for example.

Our big pursuit over the past 4 years has been to find a way to build chips that will allow for simultaneously taking these huge models and running them much, much, much faster than the chips of today — but do that in a way that kind of scales. Scales to models beyond the frontier today, scales to extraordinarily long contexts. That's the mission that we've been on.

The Chip Landscape: An "Embarrassment of Riches"?

Sarah: It's become a much more interesting chip landscape in the four years since you started the company. Where would you place yourself in the overall GPU and accelerator landscape for inference?

Walter: Yeah, there's an extraordinary zoo now of options available. If you look across this entire space of kind of AI ASICs, one of the things that is very striking is there's a lot of relatively identikit chips out there.

This is a structural industry property. If you look especially across hyperscaler efforts — Google kind of kicked this off with the TPU more than 10 years ago — you see this paradigm where although there are a number of proprietary internal chips (Google with the TPU, Meta with MTIA, Microsoft with Maia, OpenAI now with Jalapeno), these are chips that are ultimately developed and delivered in partnership with a relatively small number of what we might call ASIC houses — these back-end delivery houses. Broadcom is the largest, at a $2 trillion company, that help people realize these designs.

When you zoom into this seeming embarrassment of riches and the spectrum of what exists today, you see that actually there's a lot of similarity across these platforms. All of these chips: you have HBM, this type of DRAM memory that is common to Nvidia GPUs, AMD GPUs and all of these other ASICs. You have the same kinds of bets on tensor cores to do your matrix multiplications, the same advanced packaging with TSMC.

One of the things that we see in the landscape is there's a relative dearth still of efforts that go all the way up and down the silicon stack and try and build fundamentally new capabilities. There's just not that many teams that have decided we're going to build from what you might call the architecture layer, the front-end design layer — which mostly looks like writing code — but also all the way down to what we call physical design, the process technology, the foundry interactions, the stuff that essentially has you flying back and forth to Taiwan or Korea every week. That's something which actually tends to still be left to a relatively small number of companies.

The Architect / Broadcom Handoff

Sarah: For people who don't work in the chip industry, what is the common abstraction or handoff between what architecture-focused players are doing and a player like Broadcom?

Walter: Let's say you're Google and you're designing the TPU. You have a number of people in your team who have a really strong understanding of the workloads that they're trying to accelerate. Going back over 10 years, this is a world that then sees you conceive of things like the tensor core — which is a designated circuit dreamt up by an architect, that is exceptionally good at matrix multiplications — because you have this insight that matrix multiplications are the overwhelming majority of the flop count in these models that you're running. That's the preserve of the architect: somebody who really understands the way that chips behave, but also ideally has a very strong understanding of the target workloads.

What you'll then see inside those same organizations is a set of very smart people that lower that down into essentially a circuit-level description of how this chip should behave. A lot of this is what we call front-end design. Mechanistically it still looks like writing code on a computer, and it's still code that is then handed off to a player like Broadcom.

That front-end design — which describes the underlying intent of the chip, the underlying logic of the chip — is then transformed ultimately into something that gets shipped to TSMC in the end: literally a kind of bitmap. We have this file type called GDS2, and it's literally where do I put the metal layers, where do I put each individual transistor. It's a full layout.

You go through this process of synthesis of that RTL into a set of circuits that then ultimately get laid out. A lot of the complexity there is around — in Broadcom's case — ownership of analog IP that is used for chip-to-chip connectivity, and this physical placement that is specific to a given process node at TSMC. So we talk about 3 nanometers, 5 nanometers, etc. That piece is still today generally an outsourced activity for all of these projects.

The Fractile Team: Full-Stack and Agile

Sarah: You are describing what feels like a very large project to do end-to-end new chip creation. From a workload perspective you're working with several frontier players to characterize that and make sure that you can serve them. How did you think about what the Fractile team looks like today? How can you do that as a startup?

Walter: There are a lot of industries where there will be a waterfall-style approach to doing things, and then suddenly along comes a new way of thinking, and it's more agile — to borrow from management philosophy.

For us as a very full-stack company — we have a team that does span very deep workload understanding — we actually try to run ahead in many places and look at where would we change a model architecture to be more exceptionally aligned with our bet. What do we think is the scaling-law vector for the particular bets that we are taking? Then we can advocate to our customers and our partners on that, and it also helps us inform a set of bets for a chip that isn't going to necessarily exist in volume for one or two years. That becomes a really important part of the muscle that we have to build.

As we look across this ability to spin a very agile loop, it means that inside Fractile we have front-end designers, we have our own physical design team, we have our own back-end implementation team, we do our own work on advanced packaging. And that's not an enormous headcount — Fractile today is about 150 people. We're sort of skinny in every single one of those sectors, but what it allows us to do is have this much more agile closed loop.

That's becoming increasingly essential as you look at the cadence needs that are set by this industry. The chasing perennially of the tail of the workloads — you have to in the AI chip space, more than any other kind of chip play before, you have to really place your bets correctly. You have to have a lot of skill and a lot of luck, and you also then need to strike very fast. This structural setup where we have the entire story in-house is very, very different to this prior approach where there's almost a handoff point, and to some extent you're at the mercy of how that other partner then behaves.

Fractile's Key Technical Bets

Sarah: What do you think are the single most important technical bets that the company has made?

Walter: For us, one is the direction. Four and a half years ago, you were obviously right in the heart of an inference story, but I still felt that we were educating the world about what inference meant for two years or so following that. Some of the inference chips today — including one that recently went public — was a training chip until about 18 months ago.

There was a real avoidance of this idea that this small final marginal cost — "marginal cost" has two senses: it either sounds like it's a small cost, but what it in fact means is this is the cost that you pay every single time you deploy these models. So firstly, just the sheer bet that we were going to slip into a deployment era, and the bet on speed — that was something that really informed a lot of what we then did as an architectural response.

From SRAM to High-Bandwidth DRAM

On the architectural side, we've been through a journey. For the first 2 years or so of the company's life, we were working — a little like Groq or Cerebras — working on an SRAM-based chip. We'd made the observation that SRAM is this super-high-bandwidth memory. It lives on the same piece of silicon as your logic, so you have this extremely high bandwidth between your compute (where you're running the maths as you run these models) and let's say the weights of your model or the KV cache of this model as you're rolling it out. That's something which can then drive you to thousands of tokens per second on these language models.

One of the things that we started to worry about towards the end of 2023 and certainly in 2024 was the scalability of this approach. There are two things that grow with AI today: one is obviously the parameters of the model, but the other — and this was the one that really got us nervous about that architectural approach — was the growing context length that was becoming more and more part of the story for how we saw these models rolling out.

That has taken us over the past couple of years to what we see as a more exciting bet, which is working more closely with memory vendors as well as our logic foundry partners to find ways to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher-capacity memories. For the past couple of years we've been involved in these skunkworks projects to move away from SRAM, looking at how we can get, for instance, much, much higher bandwidth to DRAM memories.

This has been a very exciting bet for us, because it's allowed us now to put together a platform which will be ramping in the second half of next year — which unites the scalability of these higher-capacity, lower-cost DRAM memories that you have on a GPU, on a TPU, with all of the speed advantages that you get from a Groq chip or a Cerebras chip.

Why Speed Matters: Beyond "Faster Horses"

Where we see this as especially vital is if you look at where it is that speed really moves the dial today. There is a version of this which is a snappier chatbot. But this is like when Henry Ford sort of asked the rhetorical question of what people would have said they wanted — "faster horses" rather than a car. The snappier chatbot is kind of the "faster horses" of fast inference.

The place where the ability to take a multi-trillion-parameter model and run it comfortably at many thousands of tokens per second — in our view, that's a fundamental elevator on capability for AI — is in taking these very long-running agents and making them radically faster.

There's a tantalizing mismatch today between the properties of the fast-inference chips that we have — which have super-high-bandwidth memory but incredibly low capacity. If you look at the technical detail of how they actually get employed and deployed today, they're not running long-context attention. You still flip back to a GPU to do that. There's this tantalizing mismatch where precisely the area where we are almost able to go and take these things and make them much faster, we also don't have that technical capability.

In a sense, like many technical challenges, it boils down to a slightly mundane technical observation, which is: we need chips that have this particular ineffable property, which is incredibly high bandwidth to memory, so we can load the weight, so we can load this state many thousands of times per second — but also have economical memory, because when you look at what it looks like to run inference at data-center scale for thousands of users, the economics actually collapse down to essentially a cost per gigabyte of the memory that you're employing.

That's been the other key focus for us: unlocking this fundamentally new building block, which is finding a path to get aggressively high bandwidth from the world's lower-cost memory — DRAM memory.

Compressing the Chip Design Cycle

Sarah: You've said a few things that are not the conventional wisdom. One, in terms of making a bet yourselves on where the workloads are going. And two, the idea that — you know, traditional chip people might think of delivery of chips in a generation, every year or a little faster than that, and big architectural changes come slower than that tick rate. But you've aspirationally said within Fractile that you think the speed of change in architecture, and change in the technical plays you're making, can be much faster than that. Can you talk a little bit about what would enable that to happen? Because I think people have a better understanding of the physical limits of the supply chain today than they used to. So what is the flexibility that the industry could have?

Walter: There's a nuance on this. What you want at any given moment in time for an AI chip is you wish that you had a chip that was precisely targeting the workload that you care about and in your hand today in volume. But if you had that chip, you're going to want something else again in 6 months' time — these workloads move on very fast.

Sarah: Well, today we have a model coming out about every two weeks.

Walter: That's right. Sanity comes from looking across those models and saying: okay, what's common to all of these? Thankfully there's enough that is common. It's always the case that a new LLM desperately wants to have orders of magnitude more bandwidth to memory in order to run faster. It remains the case today that these LLMs tend to be autoregressive — very low batch as you generate text — with this fundamental trade-off again between throughput efficiency and cost and the speed that you can serve these models at.

There are certain things that these models are unified in crying out for, and memory bandwidth is one of them. But then, as you say, there are these evolutions. Especially if you look at the frontier of open-source Chinese models, the exact nature of an attention mechanism will churn every couple of weeks in terms of what's at the frontier — the sparsity, the sparsity level, the sparsity on the attention itself. We may be in for bigger shocks as well. There may be more fundamental shifts.

Amdahl's Law for Chip Companies

There's this duality around the limits of the physical and financial world, and then these demands of workloads that churn at the pace of essentially software. Although there is this clear desire to be able to ship new platforms aggressively faster, there are also some fundamental brakes on this.

At Fractile, we're extremely excited about being AI-forward in how we do chip design. We've seen this ability to own the entire end-to-end gamut of the problem is really enabling a fundamental rethink of how we do things.

If you think about classic CS law — Amdahl's law — everything I can parallelize becomes very, very fast, and the part that I can't parallelize doesn't. It's similar when you're in a long chain of organizations. There isn't necessarily an overwhelming need to, or return on, radically changing your processes as a front-end-focused chip design startup adopting AI in aggressive ways to shorten your timelines from being maybe 12 months of front-end design work to a tiny fraction of that — if there's then going to be the conventional bottlenecks and the conventional pace on the next piece.

To some extent there will always be those bottlenecks. We all have the same fab cycle times with our foundry partners. From the moment you send the chip to them to getting it back is 3 to 5 months even in a super hot-lot scenario. These are the innate latencies in the industry.

When you get that chip back, it is vital to look at the way that these chips actually become financializable — which is that they have a payoff period. You have to have really a 3-to-5-year amortization window for that chip to make it a sensible financial decision.

There are these two things that are in tension, and which I believe at the same time. One is: there is a huge value in being able to take the overall chip design cycle and compress that. There is also what we don't lose: the need to place really thoughtful and subtle bets architecturally, because the chip you actually end up making does still need to have a three-year-plus useful lifespan.

More Shots on Goal

For me, what it means to be able over time to compress that chip design cycle is essentially that you get to have more shots on goal. You want to be forever ready to take a given flagship platform and say, "Right, that's it. That is actually the flagship, and this is the one we're going to ramp" — but then it's a 12-month, 18-month volume ramp, and you're expecting it to have longevity. You're expecting it to actually continue to drive value to your customers.

The subtlety here is: I'm not a believer in the idea that we will ultimately get to a place where we are shipping a fundamentally new chip every few weeks just because we've shortened that down. Because this is a physical world. There is a certain amount of constraint on data-center power. There are latencies to installing these things, and you need to finance the actual underlying silicon — it needs to have that payoff period.

But what you can get to is a world where the shorter you can make that latency — that gap between an observation and realizing that bet in volume — that is where there's an enormous amount of value to be captured.

Sarah: If only because the decisions that you make about what to ramp are the correct ones.

Walter: That's right. You want to be — and maybe you get to have more irons in the fire as well. One of the things that is so exciting about AI capability rising is: as we do become more productive in doing things, there are these two responses generally across the economy. One is, "Oh no, we're not going to have as much to do — maybe there's jobs loss." The other is: we get to do more things.

Standing here from Fractile, right now we're trying to build a single chip. We know that we're up against competitors that — if you crack open an Nvidia system — it has anywhere between six and nine custom chips, all built by Nvidia, to come together to build something that is really, really potent. There's already a gap there. It'd be great to be productive enough that we could start to build our own responses in that same kind of way.

This idea of being able to have at any given moment a rolling frontier of bets that you hope are deeply aligned, in which you're ready to trigger the ramp — this is a huge advantage if you can build that machine and build that engine. And the six-month gap that that might then perennially give you against your competition — that is the wedge that allows you to drive in. We see this in frontier labs, right? The equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a 3-to-6-month advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments.

Sarah: There's a meme in here somewhere of CEO saying, "Wow, this AI stuff is great, and we structure the organization in a way that can consume it. Instead of one program, we're going to have six guys" — and everybody cheers.

Walter: Yeah, I think there's some truth in that.

From Architect's Intent to GDS2: How Fast?

Sarah: I was talking to one of the top three semi CEOs, and he wouldn't let me put this prediction on air — but I asked him, like, how soon until we can have essentially intent from chief architect into a fully usable GDS2 file? And he's like, "10 years. It's not going to happen." Like, now, what is your view on that? Or where do you see the impact first in your organization?

Walter: A heuristic that has been successful over the past couple of years is to just always question your logical assumption, and then divide it by four on time scale. There is a world in which 10 years seems like a very sensible time frame for that, but I would divide it by four, and I probably subtract a bit from that.

I think that we will have a space where there is a prototyping that goes end-to-end in the next few years. One of the things about chip design that is very interesting is: there are still these loops in the middle of it that are conventional solutions to NP-hard problems. If you really want to output that GDS2 file today, you are still running through a bunch of layout tools that are doing place-and-route with conventional algorithmic approaches which will run for days on end.

The Experiment Bottleneck

This is a really interesting thing that we see — and actually to bring it back somewhat to the workloads that we're excited about as well. A lot of hard problems in the world look a bit like this, where there is a lot of thinking that can now be automated. There's a lot of cerebral work. But then there is also this intrinsic latency to something that you do.

We see this in AI for guiding AI model development today — the RSI work. Yes, we can now have extreme intelligence that is guiding our experiments, but now we're just experiment-bottlenecked. We're compute-time bottlenecked. With chip design it's a little bit like this. To take the architect's-intent-through-to-GDS2 question, it's a little bit like the RSI question in that the things that will prevent us getting there extremely fast is the fact that in that flow there are a number of things that are genuinely computationally expensive in a more conventional way.

Sarah: And they won't be replaced by surrogate models.

Walter: Well, there are definitely these simulation models driving approximations — all of the models that we see today for finite-element analysis and thermal estimation and so on. There is a huge return to that kind of work, precisely because of this Amdahl's law: as we accelerate the intelligence, as we accelerate the period between these experiments, between these trials —

Sarah: They become the bottleneck.

Walter: It becomes much more important to accelerate those trials as well. We are looking internally at: what is actually in the guts of some of those algorithms, and is there a crude approximate way that you could do some of this?

Chip design is not going to change in the final sign-off for quite some time. It's incredibly valuable to have Cadence and Synopsys, who've been working with TSMC and the other foundries for decades, to build the final checkmark that says this thing is what we call DRC- and LVS-clean — it conforms to the rules that that foundry has set. That is actually where that work is immensely valuable. But could you have some kind of fuzzy placement algorithm in the meantime that gets you almost all the way to your final design faster, helps you iterate faster? That is exactly where people should be doing more work, because otherwise that is the bottleneck.

The other part — and this is true of RSI for AI experiments as well — is that as we do become higher and higher in our intelligence levels on the thinking that then drives that experiment, and as that experiment therefore becomes the bottleneck, we do more thinking. This is just generally Fractile's workload bet. It's the reason we're so excited about hard problems, and it's the reason that we see Fractile as the chip that takes us toward accelerating the solution to hard problems in general: it becomes almost a moral compunction to think harder before every single experiment that you fire off.

It was maybe Baron Milage on Dwarkesh recently who said: perhaps you should think for 100 years of human equivalent with these models before you fire off an experiment, and then think for another 100 years about the results of that AI experiment — because the experiment in the middle is pretty expensive and takes a certain amount of wall-clock time. You get there also with things like chip design, where there are these fundamental wall-clock-time bottlenecks for the more conventional algorithms. We're going to be generating a lot of reasoning tokens before we go and place a given circuit.

Workload Bets and the Gravitational Pull on Models

Sarah: You are making workload bets and then collaborating closely with design partners on the model architectural shifts, hopefully a little ahead so you can actually do some planning. What are you seeing?

Walter: The biggest thing that we're doing of course is this kind of speed chasing — maximizing memory bandwidth in order to be able to run these models faster.

One of the dualities you have to span as a chip company is to build something that is both exceptionally good at the gamut of workloads that are coming down the pipe, under this idea of the hardware lottery — where these will be trained on HBM-based GPUs or XPUs. It's great that this is then a chip that's exceptional at taking today's autoregressive transformers and running them much faster and more efficiently.

But what's exciting about building chips with fundamentally new capabilities is you then also get to explore whether there are gravitational pulls that you yourself get to pull the new model landscape in, because of those properties.

Scaling Laws for Bandwidth

For Fractile, this idea of having 25 times more bandwidth per chip than an HBM-based chip — we get to explore, for instance, internally these ideas of scaling laws for bandwidth. Basically, scaling laws traditionally we think of them as flop scaling laws — we get better and better performance the more flops we pour into these models at train time and test time.

If you look at just the known landscape of ideas today, we already see some scaling laws for bandwidth. One is: these mixture-of-expert models — it's pretty well known that actually ideally we would make them sparser and sparser and sparser. For like-iso intelligence, you will save a ton of flops if you go from being 1-in-16 sparse to 1-in-128, 1-in-256. But one of the challenges, one of the headwinds to doing that, is that it becomes incredibly prohibitive on today's HBM-based GPUs and XPUs to serve those models efficiently. You end up often bandwidth-bottlenecked. You end up serving at really, really low MFU — low flops utilization.

There are these areas where even as you build for today's world you get to look at where you can unlock greater capability. With LLMs today it's very similar actually with attention. There are forms of attention that are less bandwidth-hungry. They tend to be more flops-hungry for a certain level of intelligence.

One of the things we're excited about is: as we elevate this other quality, this property of memory bandwidth which hasn't really been scaled so much on chips recently — we've scaled flops a million-fold in the last 20 years; memory bandwidth has gone up about 40x in the same time frame — as you scale that frontier, you get to conserve more of the other thing. We get to reduce the number of flops that we're using on these models to get to a certain level of intelligence. That's a really multiplying factor on global throughput for these models.

Sarah: I will resist asking you if that changes people's ideas about how they should train, for now.

Market Structure: Who Buys What in Five Years?

Sarah: One last question for you, just on market structure. Here it's very unclear to me, 5 years from now, what a large AI player or a hyperscaler buys in terms of chips they consume — between the Nvidias and AMDs of the world, the new accelerator class, and at least four of these players have their own internal efforts. How do you make sense of this?

Walter: Today we see behavior where really everybody who is deploying at scale is trying to deploy as many separate platforms as they can. One thing that will remain the case is that there will be a real need for a diversity of supply as something like compute becomes so existential to these players.

There's a bit of a joke today that the first-party efforts' primary purpose is to reduce the price that people pay Nvidia. There may be some truth to that as well, because those efforts are architecturally quite similar — it's a bet that is not on enabling a fundamental capability that those other chips cannot enable. It is this gamesmanship of: can we build some of this over here? Or can I buy something from AMD so that maybe I then get a better price from Nvidia? And a play also for aggregate capacity and a bit of control.

The Case for Frontier Third-Party Chips

As you then see this move into chips that actually give new capabilities — that's a place where I suddenly see, for what we're doing, a real need for everybody that wants to deploy AI at the frontier. They have to have some solution to running these models orders of magnitude faster.

For the frontier labs, there's this window of premium capability, premium intelligence that is their entire raison d'être — otherwise we'd all be using Kimi models all the time. As you do have this pressure from behind from open source, it becomes clearly even more important for folks that want to deploy at the frontier to have every aspect of what that means. The best model weights, but also the fastest deployment, so you can do the most reasoning in the shortest amount of time. This premium end of the chip space — where you're optimizing for speed over everything else — becomes a very important part of this world.

The Asymmetric-Game Argument

One thing that is notable about the dynamic between a chip vendor and a frontier lab: if you look at Fractile, we try to be as aligned as possible with the needs of the frontier. We try to look a bit like some of those teams as well — we have people that really think deeply about these workloads.

One of the cases that we sometimes need to make is explaining why we believe that over multiple decades the world sustains some kind of frontier third-party chip players. Why does this not just roll up into these labs?

That comes down to the asymmetric game that all of these labs and frontier players have to play. They're exposed to an enormous risk if they go all-in on a hardware bet. Suppose I'm Lab 1, and I've gone all-in on some proprietary silicon, and then Lab 2 discovers some new computational breakthrough that delivers far better computational efficiencies for the same level of intelligence — but it only works on the chip that they've decided to deploy. I could die in the 9 months before I get to deploy enough of that chip that I've also now gained that 5x in computational efficiency.

There is a really urgent need for these companies to deploy the same platforms as one another. They're playing different games, right? They're trying to compete in the middleware. Having deeply differentiated bets and going all-in on those differentiated bets at the chip player is sort of an irrational and a very dangerous move for anybody that is playing at the frontier.

Closing

Sarah: Well, I think that's a great place to end. Thanks so much, Walter.

Walter: Thanks very much, Sarah.

Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen — that way, you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

## 一个被所有人忽略的"25,000倍剪刀差"
Walter 在访谈中轻描淡写地提到一组数字——过去 20 年 FLOPS 增长了 **100 万倍**，而内存带宽只增长了 **40 倍**。这是一个 **25,000 倍的结构性剪刀差**。整个 AI 硬件行业都在用一只被过度放大的手（算力）去配合一只萎缩的手（带宽）。
真正令人意外的是：**这个剪刀差正在反向塑造模型架构本身**。MoE 本可以稀疏到 1/256 来节省算力，但没人这么做——不是因为智能不够，而是因为今天的 HBM 带宽承受不了。换句话说，**当前所有"前沿模型"的架构选择，都是在带宽牢笼里跳的舞**。Walter 的赌注本质上不是造一块更快的芯片，而是通过改变带宽的供给曲线，**从硬件层去解锁一类迄今不敢被训练出来的模型**。这是一种罕见的"反向因果"——芯片决定模型应该长什么样，而不是反之。
