item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、Fed 与 Nike 的"结构性孪生"：两场迟到的反悔

这期视频表面上在聊两件事——联储议息路径和一只运动服装股——但真正值得注意的是，两条叙事线共享同一个底层结构：都是对 2024–2025 "防御性过度反应"的反向修正。

  • Logan 要把"去年秋天的三次防御性降息加回去"，等于承认联储当年为"没有发生的劳动力市场崩塌"买了过量保险；
  • Nike 这几个季度不断清库存、下修指引，等于承认当年为"疫情后生活方式鞋需求会延续"也买了过量保险（乔丹系列、Sportswear 的产能）。

两个决策者都在同一个认知陷阱里：用现在的确定性，去对冲一个最终没发生的尾部风险。而真正扎心的隐喻是——联储和 Nike 现在都必须"卖掉过去的保险单"，但买回去的代价是信用。

二、估值悖论：股价下跌，公司却变贵了——价值投资者最常中招的"伪安全边际"

这期最反直觉的一段是：Nike 盘后 32 美元，但 Forward P/E 从收盘的 19.5 倍一下跳到 30–31 倍。价格明明掉了，估值反而变贵。

原因是 EPS 的下修速度超过了价格的下跌速度。这是困境反转投资里最隐蔽的杀机：你以为"跌了这么多总该便宜了吧"，但 denominator 塌得比 numerator 还快。

跨领域对照：这个数学结构其实和房地产的"收益率/租金"陷阱完全同构。利率下行时，租金也可能同步下行，表面租金收益率看起来下降，但实际风险溢价是在扩张的。你以为的"安全边际"从一开始就是会计幻觉。小陶把估值当"基本面的一部分"而不是"便宜就买"的理由，才是真正的 Buffett 式动作。

三、"功能性清晰度"正在吞噬所有模糊的品类——这是本期最大的隐藏主题

注意这个被埋在后半段的事实：Running +两位数、Soccer +两位数、Training +两位数、Basketball（美国）+两位数、高尔夫 +两位数、网球 +两位数。几乎所有"你能说清你去干啥"的鞋子都在涨。只有一类在崩——Sportswear（运动生活），即"你说不清你去干啥"的鞋子。

这不是 Nike 的问题，这是一个跨行业、跨大陆的消费认知结构变迁： - SaaS 领域：Vertical SaaS 碾压 Horizontal SaaS； - 媒体：垂类创作者打赢通用媒体； - 餐饮："XX 专门店"打赢综合餐厅； - 甚至 LLM：越来越多应用从通用对话转向 agent-with-a-job。

消费者在用脚投票给"功能性坐标"而不是"身份性模糊"。而乔丹系列的衰退更深一层——它曾经是"身份叙事"的标杆，但当身份叙事里加入"稀缺性稀释"的时候，整个前提就塌了。这和奢侈品行业当下的处境是同一个病。

四、一个常被忽略的管理层"伪装动作"：Salami Slicing

小陶最后指出了一个几乎所有财报分析师都会漏掉的细节——Nike 管理层每个季度都扔一点坏消息出来，而不是一次性清空。他认为这暴露了"管理层自己也没看清楚"。

这其实是行为金融里有名的 salami slicing（切片式释放） 模式。它比一次性大 reset 伤害更大，因为： 1. 每次坏消息都重新激活一次抛售； 2. 市场永远不知道"最糟糕的是不是已经过去"； 3. 管理层本人也在学习自己公司的下行幅度——这是最可怕的一点。

跨领域连接：这和联储的 forward guidance 失灵是同一类问题。鲍威尔如果每次会议都"再强硬一点点"，比一次性 50bp 更伤市场信心。沟通的离散化本身就是坏信号。而 Kevin Warsh 作为潜在下任主席、在泰国给出"暗示而非明示"，恰恰是在用相反的方向操作——用模糊性为自己保留调整空间。两种模糊的目的完全相反：一种是掩盖无知，一种是保留主动权。

📝 转录文本

开场与本期提纲

10月份美联储加息的概率已经从上周的 75% 来到了周四收盘的 26%。那周四整个市场又发生了什么？是不是又有美联储成员出来讲话？

今天前半部分我去聊一下宏观，包括周五早上将要公布的大非农数据和失业率，先和大家去做一个展望——我们应该关注的一个重点到底在哪里。后半部分聊一下周四盘后发布财报的 Nike。我听完它的一个财报会议之后，我把我 Nike 的仓位给清掉了，主要和大家分享一下为什么我把这个仓位给清掉，判断的这个标准是什么。

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小陶。那在开始之前，大家记得留言点赞加转发，让更多人可以看到我们这期内容。

一、周四资产价格速览：美债的技术性回调

简单回顾一下周四资产价格的走势，我会非常的快速，主要的一个重点是在美债收率这一块。

  • 2 年期和 10 年期的收率分别下跌了 10 个基点和 4 个基点。
  • 10 年期是出现了先涨后跌的这种情况。

其实周四没有太多的一些新闻导致 10 年期美债收率出现下跌。短期之内你会发现，当整个美债市场的一个波动非常大的时候，说明整个市场就是非常的恐慌，且不断的短期之内这个资金进行这一个博弈。那在没有消息的情况下，美债收率出现下跌，我个人认为还是比较偏技术性的——就是可能到了 5.32、5.30 左右，有一部分的买盘在背后。要使得它出现持续的这个回调或者下跌，我认为必须要有个事件进来。

2 年期美债收率的下跌，我认为主要就是和 Jefferson 出来——美联储的副主席——出来讲话是有关系的，因为他再次下调了 10 月份加息这个预期。

前七大科技股在周四下跌了 0.2%，标普的等权指数上涨了 0.5%。那主要是因为美债收入的回调，使得等权指数出现了反弹。

二、Jefferson 讲话与 10 月加息概率骤降

美联储的副主席 Jefferson 在周四的时候演讲里面他聊到，他说"我们美联储的成员可能需要更多的时间再决定是否再次加息"。那这样的一个看法和观点，其实和前两天纽约联储主席 Williams 的观点是不谋而合——

也就是说，因为 9 月份已经加过一次息了，那已经加过息的这个行为本身为美联储又争取了一些时间。他们利用接下去的一些时间可以收集更多的一些数据和证据，去支持或者去决定 12 月份到底要不要加息。那 10 月份如果再加息的话，9 月份、10 月份两次时间点离得比较近，没有这个必要，就没有这个紧急性在那边。

那就像我前面说的，随着联储副主席出来讲话之后，周四收盘 10 月份加息这个概率已经从一周不到之前的 75% 降到了 26%，直接就降到了 50% 以下这种可能性。

然后整个这一波的一个周期——我们看一下 2027 年 9 月 15 日那一次的这个美联储会，也从前段时间最高的 3.9 次、3.8 次，将近要接近于 4 次加息这个幅度，已经下调到了 3.3 次。

三、Kevin Warsh 的"暗示式"沟通

那我个人认为，毕竟离下一次的美联储会议还有三周多左右的这个时间。包括在美联储会议的一周之前，我今天刚看到 Kevin Warsh 其实会有一个——记得是在泰国那边的一个采访——那个采访里边他可能会透露一些信息。

当然，以 Kevin Warsh 这个性格来说，不应该会讲得非常的明确，但是他其实是会给一些暗示的。这个前提我认为也是在：

  • 如果市场真的离美联储想做的这件事情偏离比较远的话，那可能 Kevin Warsh 会把市场往自己的这个想法稍微去拉一些；
  • 而市场如果已经做的这个选择或者预期，和美联储想做的这个决定是比较匹配的话，那到那时候 Kevin Warsh 就不会讲太多，或者不会给出任何的一个 forward guidance。

四、Logan 的鹰派观点与"防御性降息"该不该加回去

当然除了联储副主席外，还有达拉斯央行的行长 Logan，他也出来讲话。他是相对比较鹰派的，他说：央行必须——美联储必须——继续提高利率，才能够彻底抑制通胀。

他同时也说，如果更高的这个期限溢价也可以去降缓这个经济增速——如果期限溢价比较高的话，那它会降低或者减少美联储去收缩货币政策的这个必要性，也就是说市场已经帮美联储去做了这个紧缩的行为，那使得美联储可以变得不要那么的激进。但是他自己本身是比较鹰派的，所以他说起码他认为还需要再加息 50 个基点或者更多，才可以把隔夜利率去拉到一个比较合理的位置。

并且在第二段里面——我圈出来这一块——我认为比较的重要。他说到：目标利率区间再上调几个百分点，就会抵消联邦公开市场委员会去年秋季为应对风险而采取的降息措施。

这一个观点本身，其实 Nick 早就已经提出过——就是说这一轮的一个加息周期可能加三次。为什么会有三次？为什么是三次不是四次不是两次呢？

是因为 2025 年总共降息了三次，从九月份开始，降息三次。那那三次的一个降息主要是一个叫做"应对未来劳动力市场下行风险"的一个降息——当时 25 年那个降息叫做防御性降息，防御的是劳动力市场变糟糕。但是一年过去，并没有看到劳动力市场变糟糕，那所以现在是时候把当时的一个防御性降息给加回去。

我相信这个观点本身，它并不是 Logan 自己的观点，而是这个观点一定是被很多其他的美联储成员所分享、所认同的。所以美联储成员里面有一派是认为：应该把 25 年三次的一个防御性降息给加回去。

所以我个人的观点也是：这一次不会进入一个长的加息周期，加三次息我认为是合理的。

五、周五早上大非农前瞻

最后聊一下周五早上将要公布的大非农数据和失业率。

像我前面有聊到的，现在美联储两个目标（dual mandate）里边： - 劳动力市场不是那么的重要，因为劳动力市场是比较稳定的； - 通胀的数据本身比较的重要。

但是无论如何，我们还是要去关注一下周五早上公布的数据，因为这一组数据将会影响到利率。而当下整个市场、美股市场里面其实是受到利率的影响是比较大的，特别是价值股板块这边。

失业率市场的预期是在 4.1%，彭博他们的一个预期是在 4.17% 或者 4.2%。而上一个月 4.1%，如果没有四舍五入的话是在 4.14%，所以其实已经非常接近于 4.2 了。也就是说，这一次的一个失业率只要比上个月糟糕，就会出现 4.2%。而市场的预期是 4.1%，所以还是有一定的概率——我觉得起码是 50% 以上——这个失业率的数据可能会比市场的预期要高 0.1。

因为 10 年期的利率在一个相对比较高的位置，这个 setup 在那边，市场也比较的恐慌。所以如果失业率高于市场预期，那 10 年期的利率将会出现下降，就等于是给了它点了一把火。那如果 10 年期的利率下降的话，我认为市场会表现出一个积极的反馈。

六、Nike 财报：数据漂亮，指引崩了

最后一起来看一下 Nike 的财报，和大家分享一下为什么我去清仓 Nike——这个标准是什么或者理由是什么。

先来看一下数据： - EPS 其实是比市场预期要高的，而且高的幅度不小，高了 10%。市场的预期 0.44，最后的数据是 0.48。 - 毛利率 市场预期是 42.4%，这一个季度做得比市场预期要好，42.8%。

那么问题出在哪里呢？为什么盘后出现了下跌？主要就是出现在指引这一块。

我这边圈出来两个方框，是 2027 财年——因为他们刚刚发布的是 2027 财年的第一季度，接下去还会有三个季度。整个 2027 财年，公司管理层给了一个指引：

  • EPS：市场原本的预期是在 1.65，公司管理层给的预期是在 1.25，大幅低于市场预期；
  • 营收增速：原本市场预期 2027 年是负的 2.37%，公司管理层现在给的指引是 high single digit，可能是在 -7% 至 -8% 左右。

所以营收下调了，营收的增速下调了将近 5%；EPS 的体量也下调了将近 20%~30%，从 1.65 下降到了 1.25。

七、EPS 下修如何制造"困境反转"的幻觉

我们来看一下市场的预期。EPS 的一个增速：

  • 2027 财年第一季度同比 -2%，虽然是负的 2%，但是其实和 26 年的 -30%、-32%，或者 25 年的 -26%，其实已经好很多了。
  • 理论上来说，市场看的是什么？市场看的是你最糟糕的这个时间点已经在身后，市场就会开始慢慢 pricing 这家公司会出现一个逆境反转。

所以这一个季度的财报其实是不错的，甚至于这个季度的财报其实是暗示这家公司基本面有可能会出现反转。

但是在没有给指引之前，我们看一下市场的预期： - 第二季度 EPS 体量 0.5 亿，同比增速 -4%； - 第三、四季度原本市场预期已经会出现正增长，+18% 和 +35%； - 2028 和 2029 财年分别是 +26% 和 +18%。

如果管理层能够做到的话，其实这家公司就已经是逆境反转了。那这个时间点非常有可能就是这一个季度。

但是经过下修完之后，稍后我和大家分享一下 forward P/E——其实 forward P/E 又出现了一个上涨。为什么？因为 EPS 进行了一个下修。

原本市场预期的二、三、四季度 EPS 同比增速是 -4%、+18%、+35%，现在全部进行下修。原本市场预计 2027 财年 EPS 体量在 1.65，现在下修到 1.25。

我可以倒推出去接下去三个季度管理层所给的 EPS 这个体量：1.25 - 0.48 = 0.77（三个季度加一起 0.77）。我再把 2028 财年的第一季度，现在市场预期 0.57——明显 0.57 是做不到的——那只能从接下去的三个季度去做一个线性外推。假设 2028 财年的第一季度在 0.25、0.24，或者把 0.77 除以 3，全部加在一起，它的 forward EPS 差不多是在 1.02 ~ 1.05。

把现在盘后的价格 32 美元，除以 1.02 或 1.05，forward P/E 直接来到了 30 倍至 31 倍。

根据原本市场的这个预期，forward P/E 是要跌到 20 倍，但是现在因为 EPS 往下调了，所以一下子 forward P/E 变成了 31 倍，这家公司一下子变贵了。

收盘的这个价格 forward P/E 是在 19.5 倍，算上盘后的下跌可能是 19 倍都不到了。但是因为 EPS 往下修了，PE 反而出现了一个反弹——这并不是你价格的反弹使得你 PE 反弹，而是你 EPS 的下修使得你 PE 出现反弹了。

30、31 倍的 forward P/E 是什么概念？是 2025 年的一个平均数。经过 EPS 下修之后，现在的 PE 已经不再便宜了。估值将近要上涨 50% 了。因为估值上修完之后，这家公司就变得不再便宜了。那虽然估值不是最主要的，但起码是基本面的一部分。如果估值变贵了，估值上的这个安全边际就不存在了。

八、财报会议：三大结构性问题

财报会议里面其实有一些积极的方面，也有些负面的方面。但是其中有一个问题是我个人对于管理层这个回答不是非常的满意，稍后我会聊到。

现状：Nike 总共是两部分，一部是 Performance，一个是 Sportswear（运动生活系列）。

  • 运动生活系列现在碰到了非常大的阻力，同比两位数的负增长；
  • Performance 这一块的业务其实相当的好，是正增长的；
  • 但是运动生活系列将占了将近营收的一半，所以你出现两位数这个下跌，即使 Performance 那一块再好，你营收的同比增速也是出现了 2% 的下跌。

但是运动生活系列这一块的低迷，其实是在预期之内的。管理层说："这影响到了我们的订单，我们会和渠道一起去清理多余的库存。"清库存已经聊了很多个季度了。

上一次我和大家分享过 Dicks 的财报——从 Dicks 的财报其实可以看到，Nike 的新品受欢迎的程度非常高，但是其中也聊到 Nike 清库存可能会比 Nike 管理层预期的要差。所以在这个季度财报里面所听到的很多信息，其实并不会感到意外：比如说他们清库存还需要清一段的时间，或者清库存的整个过程比管理层预计的要差一些。

问题一：Sportswear 定位模糊

运动生活系列和现在的 Performance 系列是不一样的——Performance 非常的细分。就是我们普通人在选 Nike 鞋、在选任何鞋子的时候，对于鞋子的功能性现在的要求非常的高：我买这双鞋子，我必须要知道我去干啥。

而 Nike 的问题聊了很久——老款的系列产太多了。

问题二：乔丹系列

比如说乔丹系列。管理层接下去也做了一个调整，他说接下去乔丹系列这个上新速度会降低，同时产量也会降低。

Nike 现在有三个问题： 1. 运动生活系列的问题； 2. 乔丹系列鞋子的问题； 3. 中国地区的问题。

问题三：中国地区

中国地区营收同比增速 -26%。管理层接下去做的调整就是减少网购的渠道，从而去试图减少折扣。因为 Nike 想要把自己的 branding image 做了一个相对比较高端的品牌，而并不是像现在给中国市场所带来这个感受——Nike 是一个廉价产品。

所以以后在中国，只会在京东、Temu、抖音和 Nike 自己这个官网上可以购买。他说期待网络直销库存清库存需要几个季度，就是不会一两个季度就结束。在中国那边可能积压了非常多的库存，他们也意识到了这个问题——在中国那边是产品太分散，没有特色。

但是即使在中国那边，Running 系列连续 6 个季度高增速。所以 Performance 系列其实 Nike 全球的表现都是不错的，只是他们在运动生活系列这一块，真的有太多——说得比较难听——太多的"垃圾"需要去处理。

好的那一面

  • Running 两位数的增长，而且市占率是在上升的；
  • 足球鞋也是两位数的增长；
  • Training 也非常的好；
  • 篮球鞋在美国也是两位数的增长；
  • 高尔夫、网球都是两位数的增长。

你会发现，一个 category 一个 category——只要你是细分的行业，Nike 的鞋子都是卖的不错的。但是在运动生活系列，如果你的界定和界限非常 blur 非常虚的话，那用户就不知道我买你这个鞋到底是用来干嘛的。同时包括以前的乔丹系列，现在也没有人买了——现在的消费者非常的挑剔，非常的喜新厌旧。

九、让我失望的管理层回答

最后一个问题是我前面说的——我对于这个管理层的回答不是非常的满意，但这个问题问得非常的好。

分析师问到："两年前你刚上任的时候，已经知道了运动生活系列、中国地区、乔丹系列的这个问题，但过去两年似乎没有什么进展，这些问题反而变得更加的糟糕。有哪些困难是你低估了？又如何确保你现在的策略或者接下去的策略会有效？"

这个问题问得相当的好——一是对于过去两年的审视，二是对于未来的展望。

但是管理层的这个回答，我比较失望——他其实重复了他们接下去要做的一些事情，而并没有去审视在过去两年到底有哪些风险本身你是低估了。

三个季度财报听下来，我对管理层的感受是一个验证的过程。我在买之前我去听了前一个季度的财报，然后上一个季度财报我们也去听了，然后再加上这个季度财报——管理层给我的感受是，我认为有两种可能性：

  1. 管理层对于整个行业把握不是那么的大——对行业的风险明显是低估了，或者对行业的方向明显是低估了；
  2. 对于自己公司内部本身可能是过于乐观。

我买过很多公司，我喜欢的管理层是起码对于自己行业本身、对于公司本身有非常充分的认识。即使在最糟糕的时候都没有关系——只要你把你认为最糟糕的这种情况或者未来这个发展告诉市场，告诉市场之后，那最糟糕的事情就在身后了，然后我们想办法去解决未来这些困难就可以了。

而不是每一个季度财报——明明上一个季度财报其实管理层是比较乐观的（包括对于今年是比较乐观的，也并没有下调今年的指引），并且说到今年的上半年营收增速可能会放缓但是 margin 会不错——但是马上这一个季度又下修了整体的 EPS。虽然第一季度是做到了上一个季度所给的事情，但是第二季度应该是做不到了。

每一个季度他扔一些负面的消息出来——这说明了什么？说明你上一个季度并没有对于整个全年或者未来的两到三个季度有非常充分的认识在背后。

十、清仓逻辑总结

对于这一个问题的回答，我不是非常的满意，这是一点。

另外一点就是，前面聊到生活运动生活系列市场反馈不是非常的好，这些其实都在我预期之内；包括他们在 Performance 这一块市场的反馈非常的好，也是完全在预期之内。不在我预期之内的就是：你不断的每一个季度都扔一些负面的消息出来——这说明管理层本身对于未来这个判断是有缺失在那边的。

第二点就是我前面聊到的估值问题——因为 EPS 下调，你估值变得更加贵了。那估值变得更加贵，你现在的安全边际就不存在了。如果说它继续跌下去，然后我实在看到它基本面真正真正出现反转，右侧的话也可以去买。但是现在估值没有这个安全边际在那边，我认为就可以去抛了。

其实我有思考过这个问题——因为他们 11 月份会有一个投资者会，投资者会会把未来 5 年的展望也告诉投资者，怎么能够把 Nike 从逆境里给带出来。但是问题是在，如果你一年都不能确保的话，就像这一位分析师问的第二个问题——你怎么能够确保你现在这个策略未来是有效的？

所以我原本是有思考过要不要等到投资者会议之后，然后再去思考是不是把 Nike 给清仓。但是因为现在其实我有其他想加仓的一些标的，比如说像谷歌、像 Qualcomm，所以现在把 Nike 退出来的话，也不见得是一件坏事。

结尾

OK，最后今天的活动：Seeking Alpha 的 AlphaPicks 量化选股策略现在有一个免费的试用期，并且首年订阅立即省 50 美金。同时大家知道 Seeking Alpha 有一个 combo，是他们 Premium 的订阅加上他们 AlphaPicks 的订阅，原价是 798 美金，现在是 629 美金——这一个价格其实比过去一段时间的折扣还要大。这一个折扣是有一个期限在那边，所以大家感兴趣的话，可以在置顶留言里边找到 Seeking Alpha 的订阅链接。

那今天这期内容就到这边，我们下期见。

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、Fed 与 Nike 的"结构性孪生"：两场迟到的反悔
这期视频表面上在聊两件事——联储议息路径和一只运动服装股——但真正值得注意的是，**两条叙事线共享同一个底层结构**：都是对 2024–2025 "防御性过度反应"的反向修正。
- Logan 要把"去年秋天的三次防御性降息加回去"，等于承认联储当年为"没有发生的劳动力市场崩塌"买了过量保险； - Nike 这几个季度不断清库存、下修指引，等于承认当年为"疫情后生活方式鞋需求会延续"也买了过量保险（乔丹系列、Sportswear 的产能）。
两个决策者都在同一个认知陷阱里：**用现在的确定性，去对冲一个最终没发生的尾部风险**。而真正扎心的隐喻是——联储和 Nike 现在都必须"卖掉过去的保险单"，但买回去的代价是信用。
## 二、估值悖论：股价下跌，公司却变贵了——价值投资者最常中招的"伪安全边际"
这期最反直觉的一段是：Nike 盘后 32 美元，但 Forward P/E 从收盘的 19.5 倍一下跳到 **30–31 倍**。价格明明掉了，估值反而变贵。
原因是 EPS 的下修速度**超过**了价格的

item.title: [Latent Space] Recursive Language Models — Alex Zhang, MIT PhD
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

当"递归"成为新的"注意力"：从 Alex Zhang 对话中读出的系统性翻转

一、最意外的观察：这场对话真正的主角不是 RLM，而是"品味的递归结构"

表面上这是一期技术访谈——GPU kernel、harness 设计、agent swarm。但如果你把 Alex 讲的所有事情放在同一张图上，会发现一个让人毛骨悚然的自相似性：

  • GPU kernel 层面：他说"单个 kernel 没什么结构，compiler 能搞定；但 mega kernel 开始出现结构，所以需要人类品味来组织"
  • Harness 层面：他说"所有 harness 本质上一样，差异只是成本；但 RLM 把 harness 本身变成一个可组合的、递归的结构"
  • 博士研究层面：他说"industry lab 做的事都一样，PhD 的唯一优势就是赌别人不敢赌的递归下一层"
  • 科研品味层面：他说"Sweet-Bench、Quiet-Star、React 当年都被人嘲笑'这不就是……'——而这种'这不就是'的反应，恰恰是识别真正重要工作的信号"

换句话说：他整个人就是一个 RLM。 他在 GPU 层用的判断逻辑、在 harness 层用的判断逻辑、在 career 层用的判断逻辑是同一个 meta-program——"把看似无结构的扁平空间递归地折叠成可组合的层级，然后在每一层问同一个问题：这里的 locally in-distribution 子问题是什么？"

这解释了为什么他能一边做 kernel bench 一边做 RLM 一边聊 Sakana——不是博学，而是他的大脑运行的就是他论文里描述的那个算法。

二、被所有人忽略的跨领域连接：RLM × 语言相对论 × 范畴论

对话最后那段看似离题的 Sapir-Whorf 讨论——"中文没有时态所以思维不同"、"抵达者里的七肢桶一次性输出整段话"——其实是整期播客最深的一刀，但他们两个都没完全意识到。

把三件事叠起来看：

  1. RLM 的核心主张：传统 harness 把 trajectory 作为 prompt，是 autoregressive 的；RLM 把 context 存到文件系统里，用 code 操作，是 relational / compositional 的
  2. Jev 的核心主张：别再默认 language model 必须是 "autoregressive decoder"——output space 本身是可以调的设计维度
  3. 语言相对论：你用的语言决定你能想的内容；autoregressive 的英文让你无法同时思考全句

连起来就是一个尚未被命名的论断：当前 LLM 的"笨"，很大一部分不是模型笨，而是我们强迫它用一种 500 年前为口语线性传播设计的媒介作为"思维语言"。 Autoregression 不是智能的本质，是媒介的妥协。RLM 做的事，本质上是在给模型发明一种代码即思维的新语言——而这才是为什么它能在短任务上训练、长任务上泛化：代码是跨尺度的无时态语言。

这是在用七肢桶的方式让模型思考。academia 还没有一篇论文从这个角度写 RLM，但这可能才是真正的 pitch。

三、被低估的黑暗观察：$4000 万一道题 ≠ 智能的胜利，而是智能的"审美崩塌"预警

Alex 对 OpenAI 用 10,000 个 agent、130B tokens、$40M 解 Navier-Stokes 的反应极其有意思——他说"it's exciting that we have the option"，但紧接着又说"我 fairly certain 95% of the swarm is entirely useless"。

把这句话跟他前面讲 Gaurst（GPU mode 那个老兵）用 AI 却写出 top 10 里唯一稳定的 kernel 的故事放一起，会浮现出一个没人敢明说的恐怖推论：

我们正在建设一个产业，它的边际胜利越来越依赖于"用计算埋葬品味"——而不是用品味放大计算。$40M 解一道题的胜利，不是模型变聪明了，是我们学会了把 95% 的 slop 当作必要的燃料。

这跟一个你可能没想到的历史时刻结构同构：19 世纪末的化学工业。那时你可以把煤炭、硫酸、空气按比例乱投，产出少量染料，整个行业欢呼"工业的胜利"。真正的突破是后来 Haber-Bosch 把 95% 的浪费变成 5%——不是靠更大的反应釜，是靠理解反应路径。

Alex 坚持"skill issue"、坚持 harness 可以更聪明、坚持 PhD 的意义在于下注"meta-level 的 inductive bias"——这不是老派学术的清高，这是在赌一件具体的事：AI 行业的下一次范式转移，将由某个人意识到"模型的 wasted compute 不是智能的代价，是我们没想通的 debt"的那一刻开始。

而那个人，大概率在读你现在听的这期 podcast。

📝 转录文本

Recursive Language Models — Alex Zhang, MIT PhD

频道：Latent Space

冷开场：对 harness 的审美疲劳

"Oh, like I love cloud code. I love Codex. I love Pi. Like, no, I love oh my Pi. I love prime agent."

To be honest, I think all of them are the same.

"You know, your models actually are capable a lot more if you try harder. So this is a skill issue."

Yeah. Yeah. Basically — I I I mean I I I think there's one thing I want to see. I appreciate that there's a big focus on like jagged intelligence because it paints a big picture of like: we can do this if we really set our minds on it.

But I kind of wish — and maybe someone in academia should do this — like really just sit down and think about: if I took Astra, even the current frontier models are not good enough at doing a particular job over, let's say, the span of a month consistently and well.

It's uh — 10,000 agents in 88 hours. Um, 130 billion public tokens, which is estimated to be about $40 million in public pricing.

Maybe you'll have to pay like $40 million to get a result. And it's like, well — but it's exciting. I will say like, it is — it's very exciting that we even have the option to point $40 million at a problem and solve it. Yes.

主持人插播：请点订阅

Before we get into today's episode, I just have a small message for listeners. Thank you. We would not be able to bring you the AI engineering, science, and entertainment content that you so clearly want if you didn't choose to also click in and tune into our content.

We've been approached by sponsors on an almost daily basis. But fortunately, enough of you actually subscribe to us to keep all this sustainable without ads, and we want to keep it that way.

But I just have one favor to ask all of you. The single most powerful, completely free thing you can do is to click that subscribe button. It's the only thing I'll ever ask of you. And it means absolutely everything to me and my team that works so hard to bring the Inspace to you each and every week. If you do it, I promise you we'll never stop working to make the show even better.

Now, let's get into it.

开场介绍 & GPU Mode 的起源

All right, we're here in the studio with Alex Zhang. Uh, I guess most famously of RLMs, but you have a few other affiliations. Welcome to the show.

Yeah, thank you for having me. Yeah, I guess GPU mode as well.

Yes, GPU mode as well. You were shepherded in by Mark Saroufim. Not everyone gets that kind of welcome.

Yep. Yeah. Yeah. I'm very very close to all the people in GPU mode. So, yeah, we often end up working together in various capacities, like even beyond just GPU mode itself.

Can we explain — so people who are not that close don't know about this. It's a Discord. It used to be focused on, I guess, CUDA mode, and then generalized a little bit. It was started by Mark. Yep. It was basically — to me it's like the hiring pipeline of the PyTorch team. And then you left PyTorch.

Yep. Yep. Yep. So it used to be — I think it started actually around when I was in college, um, in like 2023. I think it was started by Mark and Andreas and Jeremy Howard. The original premise was: it was a Discord dedicated to learning how to write GPU kernels, and they had lectures. That was basically the extent of it.

I got interested in it because I was writing GPU kernels. It was actually out of pure chance. I was interning at Snapchat at the time —

Recsys.

Yeah. I was very bored with Recsys. So they had a project where they were interested in writing — it was this paper called Infinite Attention, like a Google paper.

Yes. We've covered it on paper club.

Yes. So I was interested in whether or not you could write specialized kernels for it at Snapchat. Nothing really came of it, but I joined GPU mode at the time. It was called CUDA mode. I think for like legal reasons or something they changed the name. But I met Mark, I met Mate, I met a bunch of other people that were very involved in the community.

And then Mark had pitched this idea called Popcorn, which is now what you see as the leaderboard today. But the general idea was — I think all of us had this intuition that GPU programming is very similar to, if you guys have done, like competitive programming. It's — I don't mean to say they're transferable —

Skills. You code golf a little bit.

Yeah. And there's actually a surprisingly small space of optimizations that people do. And there's actually not that many kernels per se that people are interested in optimizing. So we kind of had this thought that if you had enough data — like in the same way that Codeforces, there's millions of problems — if you could do this with GPU code, you could scale and automate GPU kernel development.

Which for researchers is a huge deal, because — if you look at Mamba, for example, they release the paper with kernels because otherwise you can't really use it in any meaningful way, and not everyone has like a Tri Dao on their team. So we were very interested in this. Kernel Bench kind of spawned from that too — of like, can we get LLMs to automate GPU kernel code? And I think that was a very fun time, like between college and my PhD.

Now I kind of just help with the lectures sometimes. I'm not as involved, and in general we don't have as many competitions as we used to. But yeah, I still keep in touch a lot with everyone there.

GPU Mode vs. MLPerf：社区的差别

Is there a friendly rivalry? Because like, I think the previous community that used to do this — like MLPerf — is there a friendly rivalry? Is this like just a new generation of MLPerf, or what's going on?

The nice thing about GPU mode is that it is also a community in the sense that a lot of the lectures are very easy enough for a beginner to follow and ask questions, and the competitions are somewhat — not secondary, but like you can participate in them to learn.

I think with a lot of MLPerf-style benchmarks, for the most part only serious labs and companies participate seriously in them. At least that was my understanding of it.

I I could be wrong, but I think beyond GPU mode now, one thing that has been really exciting is there's a lot more websites and people that work on hosting competitions. I think there's this website called like LeakGPU or something — it's like LeetCode for GPU problems. There's other ones too. Many have kind of spawned and been talked about on GPU mode. It's very exciting in the sense that GPU programming used to be super niche — like when I was interested in it, the only reason I got interested in it was Tri Dao gave a talk at Princeton because he was applying for faculty. (I mean, he is faculty there now.) But I listened to his talk on FlashAttention in like 2023, and I was like, wow, this is like the coolest thing ever.

I was like, this is what everyone should be working on. I guess VLM and stuff had come out too, and it was like, oh, you know, we should be writing kernels. But now it's like everyone writes kernels. It's actually almost saturated in some sense as a field.

当 AI 开始写 kernel：谁还需要人？

Any interesting takes for people that want to get into it? One of the biggest news is GPT-5.6 wrote more efficient kernels, so Terra and Luna could be 80% cheaper. And then we've seen other competitions where people are setting records, and they're like, "we're doing some auto research loop" — and these are people that don't have a background in any kernel writing.

Yeah. So even on the GPU mode leaderboard, if you look at a lot of the recent problems, almost all the solutions are AI generated. However, you'll notice on the leaderboard — there's this guy named Gaurst who is a very regular member of GPU mode. We've always known for a long time that he's a super super correct GPU kernel writer. One thing we discovered on this leaderboard is: he also used AI to help him with these solutions, but for the most part, he helped prompt and move it in certain directions.

We found that his kernel was basically the only one in the top 10 that was actually stable in actual end-to-end systems. And it does bring into question — GPU kernels have a verification problem. We've kind of known this. It's been a problem since Kernel Bench was released. There's a lot of reward hacking that goes on. But you also notice the lines of code is a lot smaller.

Is that noticeable?

Yeah. No, it's definitely very important. And I think — this applies to a lot of AI systems as well — even with the most recent math proofs and stuff, it doesn't necessarily mean mathematicians are obsolete. These companies still hire mathematicians to do, whether it be data labeling work, or even just steering the models to solve problems. There is still a lot of alpha in being knowledgeable in these things.

Is it just knowledge, or is it also that there's just more planning — and is there an emergent style of planning that works better?

I think it's a mix of — maybe this is what you mean — like intuition for how to solve the problem.

For example, I always diagram my code. Right? And then if there's a part of the diagram I don't understand, I work until I understand it. Otherwise, it's not allowed.

Yeah. So it's a mix of those things. The people who know how to look at these problems and how to solve them also know how to use AI to do them, because you're acting as a very strong verifier.

I think the thing we've kind of discovered with all these agent swarms is: when you throw enough compute at a problem, you can sufficiently explore solutions. But often times — maybe you can burn a hundred billion or a trillion tokens on something, but if you bring in someone who knows something about the problem, they can uncover something for the model that would erase that one trillion tokens spent.

It's not super clear what exactly the trends are here. But there are so many problems in the wild still right now that we want to solve, and we can't afford to just always throw as much compute as possible at them. There is still an efficiency aspect that is super super important.

What I mean by that: if we think about it from the perspective of what exactly is the harness doing for the model — basically, when you're trying to solve a problem and you want to use a language model to solve it, like a very difficult task, one thing we have discovered is that next token prediction is a really really awkward form to do a lot of these tasks.

For example, take SWE-Bench. When you're navigating a codebase, are you going to be able to figure out how to do all of this with a single language model call? Like you just say "solve code" or "solve my query over this codebase"? No. So we rely on a harness to help you do these kinds of things.

A harness is a very very opinionated program over how you want a language model to be form-fit over a problem. When we think about what a harness is doing, we should really think about: what choices in the harness let the language model solve this task, and can I actually just have a language model that just does this?

Because a harness — if you think about it, now that looped transformers are a thing — what's really interesting is you can model a looped transformer in some ways with a harness as well. You're just looping over the model. You can say, "oh, I'm not decoding, so it's a little bit different." But in general, we for whatever reason have stuck with the same model architecture choice forever. There's many arguments for why. But clearly we are now training models around harness rollouts. There is this awkward way of doing training over harnesses — we train a language model to act within a harness, but now it's a really long multiple-agent rollout. There's really awkward hacky ways of doing this.

So what this blog talks about: well, one way you can think about what's going on here is — if the harness is basically helping the model solve a particular task, can different harness design choices actually do something more meaningful beyond just "here are some tool calls that will help you, here is a way to grep through your codebase"?

This idea for this blog came with the RLM idea as well. We just didn't package it that way. There are many other ideas around RLMs that we will be coming out with, but we're all there from the beginning. These are all design decisions. Locally in-distribution：RLM 泛化的秘密

In this example, one of the things we see with an RLM: if you sufficiently offload context and ask the model to write code over that context, you get this really weird but useful property. When the model recognizes during training how to solve a task, it turns out that the solution to many tasks is very similar — across tasks where it's not even that clear that the solutions are similar.

In this example, we have a retrieval task and an aggregation task. They're very different queries. The domain is just completely different. When you train a regular language model over these two tasks, the trajectories look very different. So what you're relying on — if you use Pi or Claude Code or something, which is not in this blog, but we do have these results — you'll find that these harnesses distinguish too much between these problems, even though the solutions are the same.

One thing we find when training RLMs: it sees these problems as the same. The reason it sees these problems as the same is: the sub-agent sees different problems, but the sub-agent is solving an easier subtask. You're confident it's smart enough to do it. But for the base overall strategy, they end up looking the same. So when you train on the left task, it can immediately solve the right task.

If you go down to the plots: as you just naively train your RLM on these tasks, they naturally learn to generalize — for example, to longer tasks — because the strategy is basically the same. You're just modifying a length variable. And this also holds for tasks that are different, and not different across length — completely different tasks. Math tasks versus writing tasks. But the meta high-level solution is the same. So when you train the RLM on one of them, it generalizes this behavior to the second one. There's no magic here.

I guess — how would you verbalize what they're learning? You say you train on short tasks, they generalize to stuff 8–30× longer. Are they learning how to solve these types of problems, or what's the core thing they're actually learning?

They're learning how to solve these types of problems at a certain length, and it turns out that when you take this strategy, it is directly transferable to the longer length. They're effectively the same program.

This is really exciting because what it kind of implies: when you have a corpus of data or environments that you train your model on, (a) hopefully you can train on fewer environments and generalize to more than what existing models can do through naive harnesses or naive training; but (b) also, you still want to use all the data you have. So when you train on these tasks, hopefully it generalizes to a wider class of problems.

Why this is even more exciting in the context of RLMs — or any recursively calling system — is this argument holds inductively.

I'll give you an example. I claimed that competitive programming and GPU optimization use very similar skill sets. The model — maybe you have to nudge it a certain way — but it can learn that "okay, how I'm going to go about solving this GPU programming task is very similar to what I learned for competitive programming. So I'm going to list out a set of solutions, spawn sub-agents to list out promising solutions, and then write this loop to go through and check these solutions, maybe evolve them against a verifier."

Between these two tasks this looks the same, but what the sub-agents are doing are maybe unique. Even what the sub-agents are solving might actually also be of the same form, right? Because it's a recursive argument.

What I'm trying to get at with this whole blog post: we should rethink what the role of the harness is. Harnesses can actually greatly increase the generalization capability of your model and the amount of data it's given. This is not exclusive to RLMs. There is a wide class of harnesses yet to be discovered that can yield similar properties.

To extend this argument further: if I look at an RLM, what are the components actually necessary? Can I directly train a model to act as an RLM implicitly in its forward pass? It's a weird thing to think about — like, "code is non-differentiable blah blah blah" — but there are many approximations of this behavior that we will start to uncover.

I think we can be a lot more creative here. We can get serious gains from very very opinionated and good harness design that lends itself better to scale. The RLM, for example, is a very primitive inductive bias. There's nothing super special about the design, other than the fact that it's very different than what we currently do. But this may scale much better with the data and environments available to us.

什么是 RLM？清晰定义

I think this is the point where you have to give the 10-second: what are RLMs? There are a lot of listeners here that — we're assuming a lot of knowledge, but you have set some context, so can we have a clean crisp definition of RLMs?

Yes. Okay. I want to go back to the blog — "the compositional generalizers" blog, this one. Okay, this is like the best — I wish I had this in the original paper.

An RLM is basically just a harness design where the only tool in the harness is code. It's this programmatic sub-agent calling thing, where it has the option to call itself as a tool, and it has other tools, but all of these things are functions in code. The context it's dealing with is always stored in some memory inside of this code environment. This could be a file system.

I'll give you an example — Prime Agent. The trajectory of Prime Agent — the context, even when you compact and do all these things, is stored on disk, so the model can always reference its original context even if it's compacted. All of its tools are run inside of, let's say, a Python REPL or a bash REPL. So it's this very primitive abstraction.

I would say where most harnesses differ: context offloading is not done like that. If you look at Prime Agent, by the way — Prime Agent does context offloading, but not all the way. It still maintains the standard Claude Code / Codex loop of "trajectory as a prompt" where you compact, but it has the additional kind of — the context is offloaded, and the only tool is IPython. So this is the very generic abstraction around RLMs concretely.

What's the core thing RLMs are trying to solve? At one point, I think when it first came out, it was context, and —

I'll pass the question. So the original problem was: harnesses have a really bad time dealing with long context. They typically were used to only really do them for specific things like code — they could deal with your codebase because it was trained on it.

But now it's more around what this blog is talking about, which is compositionality — the fact that we want to have language model systems that have much more control over the actions they make at every step.

Tool calls are very limited, because you have to invoke them every turn. You have to invoke tool A, then tool B, then tool C, and there's no central context that you can draw back from. RLMs are specifically designed around composition and having a central context you can always draw from. This context is designed around the existing language models.

Another very similar example in design: agent swarms, for example — the Hugging Face incident. These agent swarms have a "message board" that they learn to communicate over. This message board, in some sense, is the shared context they act over. And RLMs basically say that the best way to communicate through this is in code. You write the code to do this. It's because these models are so good at writing code — we want to take advantage of that.

And then for this compositional thing: up to and including generating your own harness, you know, specific for the task.

Exactly. Exactly.

深入：Locally in-distribution 的意义

I think we will start to see — if you go up to this figure. Okay. We talk about this idea of locally in-distribution tasks for a harness. It's an idea on top of "in-distribution tasks" when we think about language models.

An in-distribution task is just a task where the prompt is something that the model has either seen before or has seen some version of. Most harnesses work like the one on the right — they keep appending the trajectory as a prompt. So eventually, unless you're Anthropic or OpenAI and you train on user trajectories, most of these things end up being out of distribution.

But locally in-distribution is basically the compositional argument of: if an RLM breaks down its computation into a kind of meta-harness of sorts — or like a program that involves sub-agents that look at a local problem — every individual language model call over the course of this task is in distribution, even if the entire task itself is out of distribution.

This is a very desirable property for obvious reasons: if every task is in distribution for each individual language model call, you will probably get to the right answer.

So the logical limit of RLM is: not just you write the harness, you also train a custom model, you collect data, everything — it's like a fully automated AI researcher inside of your harness.

Yeah. We will see where the training of RLMs goes. I will say, as an academic I am not working on this at MIT, at least in the scaled sense, because I can't afford to. But there are companies out there that are working on this. Prime Intellect is very clearly working on this, and it's very cool. I'm very excited — maybe we'll observe better post-training scaling walls when you train around a smart harness. Maybe we'll even see smarter harnesses that come out and work better around these principles.

What is a smarter harness? Like, that doesn't mean anything. You just said they're all the same.

No — more of what I mean is: Claude Code, Codex, Pi, etc. are all the same, in that when you break down the logic of the harness, it's virtually the same thing.

Yeah, two calls in a loop, whatever.

But with RLMs and other harness abstractions, it looks very different. This is where I think you really distinguish. It's the same way that — with language model architecture choices, a lot of architecture choices end up looking the same when you scale it out. The differences end up being somewhat minor. For a lab it's not minor, but you know, maybe one model converges better than the other, slightly. In general, pre-training scaling walls only hold because the architecture choices we have are somewhat stable. If you were to completely change the architecture, pre-training scaling walls probably don't hold — this power law is going to look very different. It's the same thing with harnesses. All the harnesses we have right now, for the most part, roughly look the same. But there are some exceptions coming out.

I was going to say — actually, one of the things I've been more interested by, talking about PhD students who take big risks: people have been pursuing the other side, which is pre-training scaling laws don't hold if you change data. Right now it's just raw and structured text corpus of internet. What if you had a better data representation to train on? Then yes, your scaling law would change as well. So there's architecture, there's data, and whatever else you can think about.

Can you explain what Prime Agent is, how it's different than a traditional Claude Code-style harness?

Yes. Prime Agent is basically a harness on top of Pi — like Pi Mono, which is a minimalist harness. I use Pi as the reference for everything, because I think all other harnesses are basically just Pi. It is Pi, except we explicitly restrict Pi to be the only tool available. Every other tool gets loaded in as a Python module or a bash script that it can run.

So it uses the core RLM abstraction on top of Pi. And then it also has this continual harness thing, which is — Seth, he's another PhD student. This is a thing he used to get language model harnesses to play games. He worked a lot with Joel, the "Gemini plays Pokemon" guy.

Continual harness is also very simple. I quite like it. It's a design principle around: what parts of the harness can you let the harness itself modify? There are certain pieces that let it modify its own skills, the sub-agents available to it, what the system prompt to the model is. Continual harness is available as a tool inside of the IPython kernel.

Everything else in Prime Agent is standard.

What I really liked about it — and we got kind of lucky — is that a lot of the new frontier models actually work really well inside, and a lot of the open source models work really well too, at least some of the newer ones.

There is another thing in Prime Agent I should highlight: we have a particular agent-to-agent communication framework. Because RLMs tend to spawn many sub-agents, we want a way for sub-agents to communicate with the root or with each other. There are design decisions around what each sub-agent is allowed to talk to. How it does it — again, everything is in code. So it writes the code to do this kind of communication.

And then there's persistent sub-agents — they can last beyond the standard runtime of the original agent. You can go into that sub-agent, you can prompt it more, you have more visibility and flexibility into what's going on.

This is my number one pain with Codex right now. Their sub-agents are just very ephemeral and they actively discourage you from using it for long-running things.

Yeah. The trick is just externalize to a file system, right? That is the big trick. And also force everything to run through code — trust the model that can write code, and it's going to write its own harnesses itself.

So, is Prime going to take on post-training custom models for this? Is this a one-off collaboration? What's —

Yeah, they are training a model internally. I think they were pretty public about this back in March. Clearly it is their business. They're showing they can train it on their hosted training stack.

For model training I'm not involved with them on that. The main reason is just I have other things in the PhD I want to work on. There are many other big bets to take outside of just RLMs. Some — I don't know how much I can share yet.

In general, I actually think one of the luxuries of being a PhD student genuinely is that there's so many big bets to take. Most of them will probably yield nothing. But it's a really really exciting time to be in research — especially because I think most progress in the field has been a little bit boring. I'm not saying the outcome is boring, but the process of doing these things tends to be quite boring.

OpenAI 的 Navier-Stokes & $40M 的 swarm

You also mentioned ARC-AGI-3 — OpenAI comes out and says we're 99.9% on this. They also say we solve Navier-Stokes. We just throw a model at it.

There's some debate around whether or not it's just a model.

Are they using an RLM? Do you know?

I'll be careful here, because people debate what is an RLM, what is not an RLM. It's somewhat clear that what they used is some kind of swarm of agents with some shared context — like some shared file system. This is very much in the spirit of RLM stuff. But there's a lot of more clever things they did that's not maybe related to the RLM itself.

I agree a little bit with the idea that a harness is not that necessary for what they did. The way I would put this: I think a model like GPT-6 Astra type thing is technically smart enough — conditioned on the right information — to come up with a proof for these very difficult problems. Now, how you get to that information is a giant question mark.

In their case, it probably came down to a very long search over many of these sub-agents, or agents in the swarm, and maybe also researchers. I'm not sure about this part — putting in their intuition as to what you should explore. Ultimately this produced some information that some agent was able to take to finish the proof.

In that sense, was the harness that important? No. What this is pointing at: these specific details of a harness do not really matter. That's also what the harness tax paper is pointing at — beyond the user's feeling of the harness, realistically all that matters is how are you composing these agents in a meaningful way to get to the final answer. Maybe that's what swarms and all these things are really about.

So from my POV, if we start to think about user use cases — what do we want out of harnesses? We want to take the good parts out of these, like the Claude Codes, the Codex, like the stream that people like to see. But under the hood, whatever is running can be some really weird, complicated swarm of agents that ultimately come up with an answer.

The user doesn't want to see that, obviously, right? It's not legible information. This was another kind of thing in the spirit of RLMs — "recursive language model" sounds like a language model, but it's not a language model architecture. The reason for this: I think we will start to see in the future — probably one day, and I wrote a blog about this — what we think of as a language model, the thing we query, might actually be a swarm or scaffold or some weird harness design that scales very well. But the user just doesn't see it. Ultimately all the user sees is some front-end version of this harness.

I think it's a relatively safe bet to make that this is what we will see.

And this maybe goes back to the limitations of the base transformer. Obviously if you just took a base transformer and said "solve Navier-Stokes," it's not going to do it. We all know this. But yeah, I think this is maybe the more interesting part. The claims around "did the harness matter" is more around this: just arbitrarily pointing models or agents at a growing context of information maybe is just enough to solve very difficult problems. I can buy that.

While there's a lot in there — I do want to say, the amount OpenAI spent is semi-public. It's 10,000 agents in 88 hours. 130 billion output tokens, which is estimated to be about $40 million in public pricing.

Surprisingly actually less than I thought.

Yeah, not that much. 130 billion output for the final — but as you said, there was a lot of context being passed around. It's more than double that in just the total agent messages being sent.

Yeah. Yeah.

But usually people will design a specialized agent to help them do this kind of thing, or they'll vibe-code a harness and just run it, or their Slack bot or something.

But I almost think there's just a standard form — a harness that you just plug in. You just tell it "find this for me," and you plug it into that setting. What I'm getting at: there's a lot of easy things that can be automated.

Is this like a hypothesis around capability overhang — even if we paused, there's still a lot of impact to be had with the current state of models?

In some sense, yes. What I'm presenting is the easiest form of this. What this is saying: we have jagged intelligence on a lot of things. Models are disproportionately good at coding and math. This is saying we can translate those abilities to many other things.

If you took someone who was an IMO Gold or something and applied them to a lot of different problem solving domains, they can figure it out. I don't actually know if this applies to models.

For example, in GPU code optimization — one very interesting question: if you were to take out all of the GPU programming data from a model, but it was as good as Astra is now, just with that taken out, would it be able to still optimize GPU kernels? Would it be able to learn in context roughly what it needs to learn, and then have some pipeline to solving optimization tasks?

There's a mismatch between what a human that was as smart as Astra could do and what Astra can do — maybe around a harness. We can actually approximate the human a lot more.

To me, it sounds very approximate to the continual learning problem. I think you're making —

That's the best example. Yes.

Why didn't you just say that?

Yeah. I was like, thinking — could I just blurt out some words? I'm careful with that.

语言 × 思维：Sapir-Whorf 的离题讨论

You have a very — I don't know your undergrad actually. Are you a math person?

Yeah. I think I studied math. That's what I wanted to do, at least.

Like a category theory type of abstraction — where you think in categories, and then you have to translate down to the specific, but then you actually really care more about the category. That's the communication error — because everyone's listening for the specific, but [you're] actually trying to convey the general. Which is hard.

I don't really know. You could use a shorthand of "okay, I'm at level two, and then I'm going to go up to level three and come back to level two." We should have some epistemic shorthand for this kind of thing. Yeah, it's hard. You're compressing a lot into word after sequential-word decoding.

Should we convert to neuralese, you know? Is there a better form of output than English, or Python, or JavaScript? I don't know. This is very like — a post, but people have speculated about: what is the native language that models want to output?

Some people say binary. That's Mark and Jason's thing. I don't know.

PTX.

Let's say a mix of English and Python. I only say this because the capability of a model is somewhat a reflection of what we train them on. So we still want like — yeah, I don't really buy the binary argument. I understand but — you want to model the world in some way.

I'll bring up — which I always do in this kind of conversation — Sapir-Whorf. If you choose English, you will have locked into however long English has been around, which is let's say 500 years. Which is not that long. The language you speak constrains how you think, and if you learn a different language — for example, in Chinese, we don't have tenses.

I actually didn't know that.

And I speak Chinese.

I did know that, but my Chinese is not great.

Or like in Japanese, I know — I forget what language it is — in Korean, everyone you speak to, you have to acknowledge social status. There's a different dimension than gender. It just influences everything you do. When I took Ling 101 — apparently there's a language in Africa where there's a vegetable gender. Right? Or Eskimo has no word for snow or whatever. Anyway. The language you adopt affects your thinking. And if you choose to output your train of thought in English, you are biasing towards whatever English solves. I don't know what the prior of English is.

That's interesting. I did not think of it that way.

So you're right. On language, a lot of model chain of thought also fluctuates language. The obvious example is Chinese models speaking in English might still reason in Chinese. But at the same level, most models are very capable multilingually, and that adaptation we can see. You can add in languages, you don't get that much for maintaining a whole language, but they'll reason interchangeably.

Yeah. We're all autoregressive.

I mean — let's say German. Subject-object agreements, you have to put the verb at the end, which is super annoying. Very famously, you don't know what you're doing until the end where you're like, "oh — that mess of nouns, and then the verb."

Well, the most classic one that most people have heard of is Arrival, where they have the heptopods, who they they think — the time is flat to them. They think, and they output entire sentences at one shot. So it's closest to the difference between autoregression and diffusion. We talk in autoregression. What if you could talk in diffusion? Where things just resolve over time —

I see.

But the whole idea shows up at once.

Ah, I see. So that is a drastically different language, but it is a language.

Which, like, machines could speak, that we probably would never speak. But like — yeah, machines don't care.

Maybe this is a huge tangent, but are there not things inherently that are reasoning chains that are inherently autoregressive? Sometimes like —

Yeah.

Something happens first then something — like, anything in code, for example, has to be causal in some, or usually at least, has to be causal.

Well, no. Then you're not exploring enough. Functional programming language theory — where everything is pure functional and completely relational, and you sort of abstract away the solver that translates the relationships that are always true into code. I feel like this is maybe a little bit too out of my depth. But I love languages — whether it's coding or human — and I do think a lot about how that affects reasoning and the boundaries of what we can do.

下一个阶段：PhD 下的"下一个大赌注"

I don't need to go too much beyond that. My closing question was going to be: you have all these research directions that you want to do. You had a GPU Mode phase, you had an RLMs phase. Presumably you have other stuff planned, which is why you're not doubling down on that.

By the way, I noticed — it is interesting how you guys do start with the GPU side and then migrate towards the zero-gradient side, which is what Shunyu called it. Doesn't that feel less legit than messing with GPUs?

Yeah. In the sense that — you did bring up that I like to think about things in a math-oriented [way] — it is very uncomfortable sometimes to be working on harnesses and agents, because it's so —

Because you think all harnesses are the same. Like, two new ideas in harnesses.

It's also just — empirically it's hard to verify a lot of findings, at least with the compute available to us.

But the reason why I've moved on to a lot of these problems: I think this is where most of the innovation is yet to happen. To me, the GPU level is a means to exploring other ideas. You want to get good at writing kernels, or even automate writing kernels, for the sake of a broader goal of "I want to explore ideas where I'm not bottlenecked by systems challenges."

In that sense, a lot of what's written there is all harness stuff, but I am also interested in things at the model level as well. I'll just leave it at that.

Okay. That's a good hint.

Call to action：如何联系 & 什么样的合作他感兴趣

If people want to reach out to you — what are you looking for help on? What do you want collaborators on? Any sort of calls to action?

There's nothing I have in particular where I feel like I need to work with someone on — unless it's with a company before, for compute, or to talk with other people about it. But I will say I'm not opposed to working on ideas with other people. I get reached out to a lot by often undergrads or other students.

Podcasters.

Podcasters. Usually I feel like I get an email that's something along the lines of, "I really like RLM, I want to work together."

Yeah, that's a bad reach-out, right? The worst is like, "can I pick your brain?" I'm like, "on what? Like, read my paper, dude."

They'll be like, "I read your paper" in quotes, "like Recursive Language Models" — or "Prime Agent, a self-improving RLM harness" or something.

I really like people that are opinionated — even if we disagree. If you have strong opinions, and are able to think through why you think those opinions are right or wrong — because usually it's hard to actually tell — but if you have strong convictions about certain problems, I'm always happy to chat and even potentially work on something together. I have no limit to who or what I would like to work on.

No limit.

In the era of agents, I think there's a lot more work you can do, bandwidth-wise. So in general, I'm not hard to impress, but it just takes a little bit of effort to know what you want.

It's very clear. I mean, when you see a new thing come out — well executed, good simple idea — that immediately gets your attention, right? It's actually not that hard to get the same attention from all the frontier lab guys, because they are looking for you. You just have to put yourself out there, right?

Exactly.

But yeah, it's true. I will say I think human attention is very scarce right now, and I do struggle with the number of projects I have going on. And I don't know how to manage it. I don't think agents are helping at all. I just prompt a thing and then never look at it. Right? Which is very common.

Maybe one of the smaller differences — actually, maybe you were doing research, I'm not sure, but for me at least: I'll have maybe 10 or 15 different ideas that I want to do, but the thing is, most of them are bad.

Yeah.

This also maybe is true for someone that reaches out to me. Maybe the idea is actually bad, but it looks interesting to me. So we can spend some time looking into it, and if we feel like there's actually something there, then we should take the next few weeks and just really pursue it.

This is my style. This is why I love the PhD, by the way — because there are times when I'm just thinking about problems, maybe on a run, or just playing tennis or something. I'm not working, I guess, but those are the most fun times. And then when I really am convicted about something, I'll just drop everything and just do it — just spend all my time thinking and working on that problem. And then once you get to the point where you can just run experiments, then it's kind of easy coasting again.

Science 作为下一个前沿

Sorry, this is like the fourth "last question." I think a lot of people are also thinking about science as the next frontier — like, physical sciences, bio, math even. How do you separate — I guess, let's say — your choice of projects that is applicable for industry, and maybe choice of projects that's just like science?

I actually worked on AI for bio stuff before I started my PhD. The field has changed a lot since then. I should say —

Because it used to be a theoretical, like — of course, what do you mean? I have one path and then I chose that. But now a lot of people are crossing over. So we have started a science pod to just cover those things, because a lot of engineers are like, "well actually, there's —"

Tractable problems there.

Yeah. I'll preface by saying my understanding of a lot of these topics is probably pretty limited. But if I find out — either because someone reaches out, or I look at a problem and I'm like, "hey, some design principles that we use or that we're thinking about right now actually make a lot of sense for this problem" — I get excited about those as well. But I think it's harder.

With science, especially empirical or applied science, [there are] very very long feedback loops. You can convert this to a robotics question. To me, this aspect of "what is worth spending and betting my time on now?" — because maybe I spend a lot of time on this problem, and then in 6 months, a different solution — maybe a new model comes out and it's way better for this. So I do have to be careful. You have to be conscious about where you think things might be going.

Publish-publish cycle.

Yeah.

I can just O3 it — it's saturated, we did it.

Yeah. I mean, ARC-AGI-3 got saturated in less than a year. If you were a lab picking that problem, you're probably kind of sad now.

Exactly. That's why knowledge work, gaming — all these things are saturated. Now actually the frontier is science.

Knowledge work is saturated.

Yeah. GDP is like 80-something, 90-something. There's 90–100% that's obviously going to take the next 10 years, but the next low-hanging fruit is going to be the other stuff.

Maybe I'll think about that more. I haven't given too much —

I'm just trying to guess your next direction.

I will say — especially at MIT, there's a lot of really talented scientists there, in the natural sciences. It's a little bit sacrilegious almost to be like, "I'm going to figure out your problem."

No, I interviewed [someone] who did the IMO thing. He's never been to IMO. I don't even know what it is. Modal, dude. Yeah. Which is very disrespectful, but like — whatever. At some point, you have to respect — okay, you know, the progress is being made, numbers are getting output.

True. I mean, that is very bitter lesson. It's very interesting — because the mathematicians are responding this way to Nav right now. Like Terry Tao is like, "no, let's not use AI."

I'm like — well, yeah, I think that whole thing is kind of weird. I feel like they would have had a stronger case if a lot of them didn't work with OpenAI before all this happened.

No, that's ad hominem. They're really trying to stay away from that. So what — right, so what, like — like, so what? They've collaborated. I'll collaborate with people I don't agree with, or like, "I did a thing and now I regret that, I changed my mind." So I'll defend their right to say that, but — yeah, a lot of people are reasonably disagreeing with them.

结尾

Um, okay cool. Thanks for joining us. Congrats on your success so far. I can't believe you're still not done with your PhD — year two, you know.

Can't believe we did this podcast without going through the RLM paper.

He had a definition.

I think the paper is more about empirical results. The actual idea is quite simple.

Yeah, and you've talked about it many times.

Yeah. At this point, I think there's more interesting things to look over now. So —

Cool. Well, we're excited to see what you do next.

Thank you so much.

观看原视频 →

# 当"递归"成为新的"注意力"：从 Alex Zhang 对话中读出的系统性翻转
## 一、最意外的观察：这场对话真正的主角不是 RLM，而是"品味的递归结构"
表面上这是一期技术访谈——GPU kernel、harness 设计、agent swarm。但如果你把 Alex 讲的所有事情放在同一张图上，会发现一个**让人毛骨悚然的自相似性**：
- GPU kernel 层面：他说"单个 kernel 没什么结构，compiler 能搞定；但 mega kernel 开始出现结构，所以需要人类品味来组织" - Harness 层面：他说"所有 harness 本质上一样，差异只是成本；但 RLM 把 harness 本身变成一个可组合的、递归的结构" - 博士研究层面：他说"industry lab 做的事都一样，PhD 的唯一优势就是赌别人不敢赌的递归下一层" - 科研品味层面：他说"Sweet-Bench、Quiet-Star、React 当年都被人嘲笑'这不就是……'——而这种'这不就是'的反应，恰恰是识别真正重要工作的信号"
**换句话说：他整个人就是一个 RLM。

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why the Korean War Went So Badly - Sarah Paine
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、胜利悖论：战争中最危险的不是失败，而是赢得太多

Sarah Paine 这段话最反直觉的洞见是——朝鲜战争真正的失败点不是开战，而是赢的那一刻。Kim Il-sung 一路南下势如破竹时，正是他战略崩塌的开始；MacArthur 在仁川登陆大捷之后，恰恰是美军走向灾难的拐点。两个赢家都栽在同一个结构性陷阱上："顶点"（culminating point）不是一个军事坐标，而是一个博弈论拓扑点——它是"二人博弈"坍缩为"多人博弈"的临界相变。

Clausewitz 的"顶点"概念其实揭示了一个更普适的系统性真相：所有封闭系统的边界都是由第三方的忍耐阈值定义的，而不是由你自己的能力定义的。你以为战场的边界是地理的、是弹药的、是士气的——错了，真正的边界是旁观者什么时候决定不再旁观。

二、跨领域连接：这其实是"创业公司的平台杀手"模型

把 Paine 讲的东西搬到商业世界，你会看到一个惊人的同构： - Kim Il-sung = 一个在垂直市场里碾压本地竞争对手的创业公司 - "二人博弈" = 他以为只需要打败南韩 - "第三方介入" = Amazon/Google 突然决定进场 - "顶点" = 融资/增长/声势达到某个阈值后，巨头无法再忽视你

最反直觉的推论：Kim Il-sung 的最优策略是"慢速叛乱"而非"闪电南下"——Paine 自己点出了这一点。这完全对应创业圈那条铁律：成长太快会提前触发平台的注意力。 TikTok 早期的"中国出海"低调期、Shein 的隐身十年、OpenAI 在 ChatGPT 之前拒绝做消费产品——这些都是对"culminating point"的本能规避。

更深一层：个人职业发展也遵循同一法则。晋升太快、曝光太猛、锋芒太露——都会把你从"二人博弈"（你 vs. 老板）拉进"多人博弈"（你 vs. 所有潜在对手+上级的上级+人力资源政治）。很多聪明人毁于"赢得太漂亮"。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：朝鲜战争是美国的"永久订阅服务"

Paine 轻描淡写一句"we've had troops there ever since and it's expensive"藏着一个被普遍忽视的结构性事实：朝鲜战争是现代美国军工复合体的"隐形创世记"。

想想这个因果链条的奇特性： 1. MacArthur 越过"顶点" → 中国介入 → 战争无法速决 2. 无法速决 → 分裂的半岛变成"冷战的物理化身" 3. 分裂的半岛 → 需要永久驻军 → 永久国防预算 4. 永久国防预算 → 军工复合体制度化（1961 艾森豪威尔演讲的直接背景） 5. 军工复合体 → 影响后续 70 年所有美国对外政策的默认设置

换句话说，MacArthur 一个人的"过度自信"，在系统层面编码为美国 70 年的默认战略姿态。这是一个经典的"路径依赖"（path dependency）案例，但更深的洞见是：决策者在跨越"顶点"的那一刻，往往同时为自己创造了一个无法逆转的"组织生态位"——而这个生态位反过来会寻找下一场战争来证明自己存在的合法性。

一个让人不安的推论：当你听 Paine 问"乌克兰战争的 culminating point 在哪里？"时，真正该问的问题可能不是"谁会赢"，而是"这场战争正在为未来 50 年创造什么样的、尚未命名的、无法逆转的组织生态位？"——因为那才是战争真正的、延迟交付的"成本"。

📝 转录文本

The Two-Player Illusion: Kim Il-sung's Opening Gambit

Kim Il-sung invades the South and he thinks if it's just a twosome that he can win that thing — and he was right. He was roaring down the peninsula. He looked as if he had it all covered — until he triggered the third-party intervention from hell, which is when the United States and UN partners got involved.

Then what was a civil war becomes a regional war, with potential to become a global war, and you're off to a completely different race, much higher costs. So he would might have done much better doing a slow insurgency than what he did.

MacArthur, Inchon, and Overshooting the Culminating Point

Okay, so then the United States is turned to go beyond culminating points of victory. And there's a whole story about the Chinese, but I'm got time for that one.

Uh, so MacArthur does his Inchon landing, which is halfway up the peninsula, and it goes really well. So his idea is: "Hey, we're going to reunite the whole thing, right?" Cuz it's militarily possible. It's like Clausewitz has already told you — it's the political objective, it's not the military objective, that determines what you're going to do.

Uh, well, when he gets too close to the Chinese border, the Chinese are in — and now we're into a world of hurt. They're sending hundreds of thousands of people in, and we got a completely different war on our hands doing this. And not too long — before too long — MacArthur gets himself cashiered.

Culminating Points as a Strategic Lens

So I think it's worth thinking in terms of culminating points of attack and victory before wars, German during wars. What might it be? What might it like — in the Ukraine war, what would it take on either side to get a culminating point of victory? Is it reachable? Or culminating point of attack on different campaigns — is it even feasible to get there?

They're helpful terms. But understand: a key measure of culminating a point of victory going sour is when the third-party intervenes.

The Price of Overshooting

Okay, the Korean War yielded a divided peninsula at really high cost — cuz if you exceed the culminating point of victory —

[gasps]

— you're... one of the measures is you're paying a lot more than you had to. But that was the minimum objective: keeping the South Koreans around. And they are. But we've had troops there ever since, and it's expensive.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [a16z] Why One Internet Pioneer Thinks the Original Model Broke
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：这是一次完美的"镜像人生"闭环

Barrett Lyon 的整个职业轨迹本质上是一场围绕"中心化基础设施"的辩证运动，但几乎没人把这三件事连起来看：

  • Prolexic 时代（2003–2009）：他让大企业能在中心化互联网上生存——客户花钱买"更大的集中式护盾"来对抗洪水攻击。
  • Opte 艺术项目（2003 起，收藏于 MoMA）：他把互联网整个"画"了下来——这是一次对既存拓扑的测绘。
  • Docset（现在）：他要在既有互联网之上长出一张不存在于那张地图上的网络——196 个不存在于公共 DNS 的新顶级域，相当于在自己画过的地图上，画出一块空白的新大陆。

更惊人的是：他做 Prolexic 的起点是"高中时自家服务器被人 DDoS"——也就是说，他本人既是最早被中心化互联网伤害的个体用户，又成了最大化保护中心化企业的人，而现在他在把那笔"保护"的红利，还给当年像他一样的个体。这不是生涯转向，这是一次债务偿还。

二、跨领域连接：那场坠机，和他现在在互联网上做的事，是同一个工程哲学

飞机那段故事看似闲聊，但如果你注意他对事故原因的描述——"三件非常奇怪的事同时发生"（进气歧管金属片、电子点火、磁电机备份），他讲的不是运气差，而是级联故障（cascading failure）如何击穿"独立备份"的幻觉。磁电机本应是独立于电子点火的冗余系统，结果同一时间失效。

现在把这个思路搬到网络层你会发现，他对今天互联网的诊断用的是完全一样的语言： - WhatsApp / Signal / iMessage 看起来都是"独立的加密方案"，但它们共享同一个范畴错误——"你以为在发给对方，其实在发给服务器"； - VPN 看起来是"去中心化保护"，但背后都租自同一批 bare-metal 供应商，冗余是假的，根因是同一个； - 法国 Umbrella 把某电信商错标成法国 → 一刀切屏蔽 → 一个分类错误被放大成跨国断网，和他飞机里"一个金属片引发点火系统连锁崩溃"是同构的。

他造 Docset 的真正动机，不是"我讨厌广告追踪"，而是作为一个曾经从级联故障里活下来的工程师，他比任何人都清楚：当代互联网的"隐私选项"全都是假冗余。

三、藏得最深的那层：这期播客本身，就是它在讨论的东西的一个样本

注意他和主持人讨论"数据中心抗议"的方式——他们说：

现场根本没人在抗议，只有兔子在跑；但你在 TikTok 上刷到的是配着音效的仇恨数据中心的视频。

这里有个几乎没人点破的三层嵌套：

  1. 第一层：有人（可能是商业利益方，可能是竞争对手，可能是外国行为体）在用广告定向技术攻击公众对数据中心的看法；
  2. 第二层：广告定向技术的根基是——正是 Docset 想消灭的那套 tracker 生态；
  3. 第三层：Barrett 和主持人正在一个被同一个推荐算法分发的媒体平台上讨论这件事，而这期播客本身的触达、剪辑、热度，也会被同样的机制塑形。

于是出现了一个很怪的闭环：广告技术栈既是被攻击的理由，也是攻击的手段，还是关于这件事的讨论得以传播的管道。

跨领域地看，这是冷战时期"宣传战"的工业化升级——以前国家花几十亿养机构、买媒介；现在任何一个商业利益用 LLM + 数据中介 + 定向广告，花六位数就能复刻一场"民意"。他说"情报机构其实落后于广告商"——这句话值得当作本世纪基础设施政治的注脚。

四、一个意料之外的教学点：PKI 的失败不是技术问题，是语言学问题

他随口提到：

"PKI 的核心教训是：你一旦告诉用户这是 PKI，它就不会成功。"

这句话应该被写进每一本产品设计教科书。它说明同一个密码学原语（公钥交换），仅仅因为被命名、被暴露、被要求用户理解——就从"可用"变成"不可用"。

同样的现象在很多领域反复出现： - 医学里的 placebo：告诉病人这是安慰剂，疗效立刻降低； - 行为经济学里的 nudge：一旦明说"我们在推你"，它就不再推得动； - AI 对齐里的 Goodhart's law：指标一旦被命名为目标，它就不再是好指标。

所以 Docset 真正难的，不是密码学，是让密码学隐形到用户感觉自己只是"加了个好友"。这件事的难度，和 Apple 当年把文件系统从用户面前抹掉是同一个量级的 UX 革命——而且几乎所有安全类产品都在这一步上翻车。

  1. A piece of metal on the air-intake control valve — a kind of lever — broke off and got sucked into the air-intake manifold, went down to the oil pan, and was crushed into cylinder 3 and 6, I think.
