Emil Michael: A lot of this is on us at the Pentagon. We've got a lot of rules, qualification standards, things written 20 years ago that haven't been modernized. We try to kill them when we find them. We also try to create competitive environments.

For example, we created this program called Drone Dominance. It's not you just applying with your drone product one-on-one. We have a competition, we invite companies, we take the top 20, we put you in a fly-off situation, we give you objective metrics, we measure you against other companies — and at the end, the top three get some money. We call them gauntlets, and at the end we have half a billion dollars of orders to give. You get transparency, objective metrics, and a financial order at the end. If I were the entrepreneur, I'd rather compete and know if my product works, rather than knocking on 20 doors at the Pentagon.

需求改革（Requirements Reform）

Jason Miller: What's your advice for founders trying to decide, am I solving a current need or is this a great transformative idea?

Emil Michael: We've done something called requirements reform. Typically the military would write a 300-page RFP designed for a lawyer, a lobbyist, and a prime contractor. Small companies read it and have to figure out what all these things mean — one thing wrong, you get kicked out.

The new way: here's my problem. I need to fly a missile 500 miles in this kind of environment. It's a one- or two-page description. You come back with solutions. That gives entrepreneurs a creative way to answer with different technologies we might not have thought of. And you get feedback right away — turning what used to be a two-year cycle into 90 days.

何时该在华盛顿聘请游说者

Jason Miller: At what point does a company look and say they should hire someone in DC?

Emil Michael: In theory you want it open so small companies aren't spending disproportionate dollars on lobbying. Congress every line item tries to prescribe where the budget goes. But early on it's not that useful. We consolidated the innovation ecosystem — SBIR, DIU, APFIT, Office of Strategic Capital — all in my world now. So whether you're a small company doing an initial thing, a medium company scaling up, a bigger company doing a prototype, or an established company with a product that works, now they're eligible for a big loan that's low cost. So maybe until you get closer to being a program of record, you could hold off hiring a lobbyist.

快速 Yes 与快速 No

Jason Miller: What have been the fast yeses and fast nos?

Emil Michael: One deficit was hypersonic weapons. The primes' cost was $50 million per unit, taking years. We essentially stopped during the last administration. We found a company, Castellan, doing low-cost high-volume ones — that was a fast yes.

From a no standpoint: there are so many drone manufacturers now, that if they're not in the Drone Dominance program and their capabilities are the same as others, it's tough unless they've done something unique.

Drone Dominance 的多轮迭代

Jason Miller: How does someone get into Drone Dominance if they're not already in?

Emil Michael: We'll have multiple rounds. Group 1, 2 small drones, then Group 3 and 4, and counter-drone with different flavors. We're not going to go down to one vendor — it'll be two or three. The unmanned systems arsenal is pretty broad. We just started with the easiest and we're going to keep moving.

外籍创始人与美国国籍

Jason Miller: You yourself were born in Egypt, grew up in New Rochelle, went to Harvard and Stanford. What should non-US-born founders be looking out for?

Emil Michael: If you don't have a US citizenship yet, and what you're building becomes more central to the Department of War needs, it's likely someone's going to need a clearance. Sometimes we take a board member, sometimes we take the GC, but someone has to be able to do this if what you're doing falls over the line into classified programs or classified materials. Generally we haven't seen that challenge just yet.

五家新 Primes 的愿景

Jason Miller: You said you want five new primes to pop up before President Trump's term ends. What should a founder take away?

Emil Michael: A prime brings multiple products and multiple disciplines to the table. They've mastered the selling process and have a range of things that make them a prime. One-product companies are fine, but a prime has enough engineering talent, enough production capacity, that as our needs evolve, they can be bidding on the next thing.

Take Golden Dome for America. We just put out an RFP for space-based interceptors — something in space that could take down a hypersonic missile in the first few minutes of launch. Very complex physics. Should new companies doing space stuff, if they have capabilities and understand space, then stretch to have another product line? Yeah — that's what I consider a prime.

问答：无刷电机的国内化

Mike Stone (Reuters): All the drone manufacturers have a problem with brushless motors. The winding machine costs $300,000. Should the US government get into the brushless motor business as a merchant supplier?

Emil Michael: The Office of Strategic Capital just announced a drone components deal with a company called PDX, developing brushless motors. We'll see another few deals in the coming months for drone components — brushless motors, batteries — done here in the United States. There are some key components in drones that are heavily China-based. Those are the perfect example of things we have to domesticate here.

问答：乌克兰公司如何参与

Evgeny (retired Ukrainian diplomat): How can Ukrainian companies and the Ukrainian defense ecosystem become part of the startup industrial base in the US?

Emil Michael: We've opened the Drone Dominance program to Ukrainian companies who, if they win, would have to domesticate their operations in the US. A few have participated and done well. Some of it's tied up in export controls by President Zelensky. But I'm optimistic — Ukrainian operators have valuable learnings.

五、Ivan（Splash Industries）— 低成本 USV

I'm Ivan, CEO of Splash Industries. At Splash, we develop low-cost USVs for contested logistics and maritime domain awareness purposes.

与其他 USV 公司的差异

There are a thousand other USV companies out there. What separates us from the rest? Ultimately, it comes down to our highly vertically integrated approach. We develop all of the autonomy stack in-house — from the camera systems to the electric actuators to every single circuit board on the boat, and of course the software.

What that means in practice: we're able to deliver a vessel that is 5 to 10 times cheaper than current similarly capable solutions. Our goal from the very beginning was not to build another million-dollar boat, but to build something that can provide affordable mass to the fight. They are faster to build — it takes one of our technicians eight hours to build one of our Typhoon USVs. They're incredibly easy to use — we can train people in a matter of hours.

The Navy already owns and operates a number of our vessels. The Army recently placed their first orders as well.

三次任务演示

I've done probably 12 exercises this year, and I've selected three that stood out most.

Hawaii — autonomous resupply of a warship on the move

We were tasked to deliver cargo to warships off the coast of Honolulu. Traditionally this is done with manned assets — helicopters, larger ships — expensive and in conflict puts warfighters at risk. This was us approaching LHD2 doing an autonomous beach landing. Not remote controlled — controlled from a different location using autonomy. It was the first time a USV has ever done a fully autonomous resupply of a warship while it was on the move (transiting at ~10 knots).

The next day at RIMPAC, we went out on a grueling 170 nautical mile mission to deliver cargo to CVN 71 — Sea State 5, mostly at night. Competitors thought we were crazy — USVs are usually used with chase boats. This was without any chase boat.

Kwajalein — man-portable, aircraft-shippable, medical delivery

Kwajalein is very far away. Our USVs are small enough for a single person to launch. They use internal combustion — we can dump the fuel and ship them in commercial aircraft. Quite literally, you can have an unboxing experience for your USVs. Lightweight enough to hook up to a golf cart (we got in trouble for that).

We trained local participants — people who'd never used a remote control system — in hours, to successfully execute medical supply delivery missions. Missions across the atoll were about 150 miles. Of 44 companies competing, we were the only USV company to complete all missions successfully.

Force-on-force war game — riverine autonomy

Enemy blocked access to a channel with thick steel cables. Normal boats would foul their props — but we have a water jet. We got over the cables and into the enemy outpost. Our precise mission autonomy let us navigate at high speeds in narrow channels — 15 feet narrow. All done using autonomy, sitting 30 miles away, no remote control.

If you want to reach out — email is on screen. Happy to talk about more, including towing a water skier behind our USVs (world's first as well).

六、Eric Bradham（Deep Night）— AI 夜视

I'm Eric Bradham, from Deep Night.

问题：一切都需要能在黑暗中看见

Everything these days needs to see in the dark: drones, unmanned vehicles, dismounted soldiers, technicians and logistics support chains, marine vehicles. Everything needs to see in the dark digitally. The revolution I'll talk about today is AI-based night vision that runs on commercial imagers and commercial processors, giving you night vision surpassing the latest analog tubes — but digitally, at very low cost.

技术能力对比

Standard off-the-shelf COTS CMOS imager at night: image on the left, 1 millilux — no moon, only stars — hard to see your hand in front of your face. Even Army-specialty CMOS gives a "pretty good" view but not clean enough for downstream AI. Apply Deep Night and you see the rocks, the water's edge, across the bay. Our AI recovers true information — no hallucination — by removing sensor-generated noise to reveal signal.

Raw output from a Deep Night camera: you can barely see a fence. Flip on Deep Night: pebbles, sewer grating, obstacles, tennis court, people. Full HD, clean. This is no moon, only stars, with tree canopy. The darkest it gets.

陆军测试与热成像对比

The Army has been testing at Fort Belvoir in C5ISR, the night vision labs. Gen 3 tube (1800 FOM) vs. Deep Night on a COTS CMOS: full HD, readable signs, facial recognition possible.

More cost effective than thermal too. Compared to a 640P thermal imager (drones): thermal gives good target indication; Deep Night gives full HD — you can tell the person is on grass, see a cat, read reflective bands on signs. In production with a drone company in Q4. Early testing by one military program shows 20% better navigation and target accuracy while reducing cost.

未来路线

Coming: color night vision. After people get used to it, they won't want to go back to monochrome. Just awarded an OTA contract for the Dutch program to apply our processing to thermal cameras.

We're funding development of a low-cost, super high performance digital binocular, upgradable to color and thermal, so night vision can be made available to all troops. Prototype in April, then testing. Please come find me in the demo room across the hall.

七、Luther Lowe 介绍 Secretary Duffy

The voice-of-God person encouraged people to come out from the reception area for Secretary Duffy. I highly encourage everybody to check out the Deep Night demo — set up in a private room over here.

It's my pleasure to introduce the conversation between Y Combinator CEO and President Gary Tan and Sean Duffy, the 20th United States Secretary of Transportation, leading the department responsible for America's aviation, highways, railroads, and other transportation systems. Before joining the administration, he represented Wisconsin's 7th congressional district in the U.S. House and served as an Ashland County District Attorney.

八、Fireside：Sean Duffy × Gary Tan

DOT 的范围与空域现代化

Gary Tan: America's transportation system reflects decisions made generations ago. If we get this decade right, what should Americans be able to do that they can't today?

Sean Duffy: At DOT I have pipelines, ports, rail (passenger and freight), roads and bridges, cars, airports, airplanes, airspace, commercial space launch. So NASA is one thing, but Blue, X, or anybody else launching commercially — that's us. It's been on autopilot for a long time.

One of the biggest projects: modernization of the airspace. We need new radar (maybe with new ideas), digital radios, surface awareness systems ("Voice") so you can see the airfield from the tower. Air traffic controllers pass an airplane from one to the next using a literal paper strip — we're going digital. Old copper wires → fiber. Old telecom architecture → new one. The East Coast shut down 10 days ago because a supposedly redundant line had a single point of failure. I got $12.5 billion from Congress to do this infrastructure build.

空域管理与 AI

How we manage the airspace: humans at the command center with six screens and a paper flight chart above them, trying to assess data and make decisions on weather and flight trajectories. AI and predictive analytics could turn a 2.5-hour ground stop into 45 minutes. If four airplanes are converging on DCA (one runway), we could speed up two and slow one down so all arrive at open windows.

I got some crap for saying I'm turning over air traffic control to AI. This is dumb AI, not smart AI — just going from paper and pencil to digital. Systems are so old it's really hard to rebuild while keeping airplanes flying safely — like changing spark plugs while your car's running.

Pitch: I need really good partners. A lot of my existing partners have contracts for years, sometimes decades, and just don't produce for us. ASI built a smart tool — small company competed with the biggest — and won a big contract with us. We don't care about size. We care about speed and innovation.

效率、燃油与航空公司排班

Gary Tan: It sounds like it's a matter of will — get things 30-50% faster by better coordination.

Sean Duffy: When we're more efficient, we save billions in jet fuel and staffing costs. Carbon emissions substantial too.

Airlines schedule 32 aircraft in a 15-minute window when the airport can handle 15. You're building in delays. I'm giving airlines info: could you spread this out? Not dictating, but asking.

SMART Tool 与现代天空联盟

Gary Tan: Sounds like headway's being made on the Modern Skies Act.

Sean Duffy: SMART is the ASI tool. Airspace was divvied up based on 1950s-60s technology. New tech means radical restructuring. We're starting small — in the DC region — then expanding. By next summer we'll be driving more efficiency. We've asked Congress for $30 billion more with our Modern Skies Coalition. As a fiscal conservative I find myself asking for money all the time, but there's great ROI.

We'll replace every tower in America over the next 300 years on this plan — not great. And do you even need a tower? Some places could use cameras, sensors, and controllers seeing that in a TRACON or other location. Better vision, better data, better results — but a conversation to have.

无人机与超视距飞行

Gary Tan: Autonomous aircraft and drones are becoming useful for inspection, cargo, national security. How are you thinking about safe drone operation beyond visual line of sight?

Sean Duffy: We're working on beyond visual line of sight. Drones are weapons of war (Russia/Ukraine) but also tools of commerce — pipelines, train tracks, Uber Eats. Innovators move fast, government moves slow. If we don't move at the speed of innovation (with safety as bedrock), we lose. Small innovators go under; big ones go elsewhere.

eVTOLs — Joby, Beta, Archer. We have EIP with eight test zones. Certification data will help us certify vehicles. There's a pilot for now — at some point they can be fully autonomous. Same with autonomous vehicles: we're moving quickly. If we import someone else's autonomous vehicles, the data goes elsewhere.

自主性与安全的黄金分割

Gary Tan: Autonomy could reduce injury by up to 90% (e.g., Waymo). When is it ready?

Sean Duffy: Goldilocks philosophy — too fast, no safety bedrock, people get hurt and innovation gets shut down. Too slow, innovation leaves or dies. Continuous analysis, safety systems in place, long runway for innovators. Same conversation across autonomy and AI generally. Safety is bedrock, but zero tolerance for risk means chain up your innovation and send it elsewhere. Not a dichotomy — both.

造船与海事

Gary Tan: How are you working to build a stronger maritime industrial base?

Sean Duffy: It's a national security issue that America doesn't really build ships anymore commercially. We were the greatest shipbuilders in the world through WWII — and gave it up. Middle East shows shipping's importance. Vibrant shipbuilding feeds military ship capability.

The rest of the world subsidized their shipbuilding and stole it from us. I'm a free-enterprise guy, but if you want to build ships you can't beat subsidized competitors on the free-enterprise game alone. Rocket companies get really excited about shipbuilding — there must be some crossover.

Small modular reactors (SMRs) on ships. We sent that to industry, three ports willing to accept SMRs. Multi-use — data centers, ships, the moon (NASA).

观众问答

Kush (current YC batch, unmanned airplanes for pipeline inspection, aiming at cargo aircraft): What about regulation for Part 23 aircraft over 1000 pounds for autonomous cargo?

Sean Duffy: Flying in Alaska is very dangerous, poor roads — that's the first place we go with autonomous supply flights. We have great companies working on autonomous aviation. We drive safety, but we're all in on the technical side. Different political conversations have to be had.

Dennis Willie (Astroscale): What can we expect from the DOT's FY28 budget for in-space logistics?

Sean Duffy: Commerce has in-space; we have Earth-to-space (launch licenses). We need a robust industry — SpaceX is unbelievable, Blue is rebuilding fast after their launch pad issue. President signed an EO telling us to build more launch capacity. We did an RFI: where should we go? We're investing in infrastructure at a new spaceport. Wallops is getting full, the Cape is expanding. All you wonderful billionaires used to buy horses; now you're all buying rocket companies. Very cool space. Need more competition, more players. Our commercial space office is trying to hire another 70 people — talent goes to SpaceX or Blue, but industry can't succeed unless we do our part too.

Theo (Arley Industries): What government incentives can improve openness for more sensing/airspace companies?

Sean Duffy: Case-by-case analysis. Drones at 400 ft in cities — how to manage four companies in the same airspace. eVTOLs layering in. Supersonic flight over land coming. We need the tools to effectively manage — and to move quicker with industry.

结束语与人才招募

If you or people you know want to serve, we're open at DOT and FAA. Might not pay as well, but you could be an SGE or an employee. Elon and DOGE made it OK for people to say, "Maybe I would give back too." We need the brightest minds helping.

九、Dr. Jason Cornelius（Perseus Defense）— 便宜如子弹的导弹

My name is Dr. Jason Cornelius, and today I'm talking about making missiles as cheap as bullets.

Mark III 拦截器

This is our Mark III interceptor — a two-foot long rocket meant to shoot down Group 1 and Group 2 UAS. We build these for about $2,500 each, and we just tested it three weeks ago at Yuma Proving Ground with C-IATO 401, NORTHCOM and NORAD.

We joined YC summer 25. April 2026 — testing at Fort Hood with 1st Cav and US Army DEVCOM (Mark II, a three-foot, not very maneuverable missile). Feedback from end users: more compact, more agile. Four months later, clean-sheet Mark III design demonstrated three weeks ago at Yuma. The team: eight full-timers built a fully active guidance interceptor missile — including Chief Happiness Officer Ariel.

反 UAS 的可负担性问题

Counter UAS lacks affordability and range. We use Coyotes, Patriots, AIM-9Xs to shoot down $3,000–$4,000 drones. Not great. Perseus is dropping the cost curve — our cost per range is about 1/5 of existing solutions.

We're not only building very low cost, we're doing it very quickly — four months from new design to range. Half an hour from a pile of parts to a fully assembled missile. Five technicians × 40 hours/week = about 1,500 interceptor missiles per month.

弹药深度问题

The entire rest of the US builds about 1,000 interceptor missiles per month. Our near-term goal is to match the rest of the United States. Our missiles aren't as exquisite as a Raytheon Coyote or Patriot, but they're built for the low-cost attritable drone mission. Bullish on 1,000/month soon, longer term 10,000/month.

Based in Austin, 18,000 sq ft manufacturing. Group 1 and 2 counter UAS, $5,000 per shot — an order of magnitude cheaper than any other interceptor.

与传统航空异同

We asked: how are missiles built today and how can we build them differently and cheaper? Aerospace is done to 10^9 redundancy. If we're 30x cheaper than a Coyote, it's OK to shoot two. Lower-cost components, additive manufacturing, in-house flight computer.

测试与模块化发射器

April 2026 Golden Shield at Fort Hood; two weeks ago at Yuma with IATO 401. Working with Army Applications Laboratory on TRL-5 → TRL-6/7. Modular missile launchers: eight-shot inside a Pelican case, about 100 lbs, two people can carry it. Discussions with USV, UGV, and UAV providers.

First startup to build an actively guided missile. Within five meters of the drone at several hundred meters range for $2,500. Aiming for direct hit-to-kill (no warhead) — usable domestically for nuclear facilities, airports, the Capitol, the US-Mexico border. Only one endo-atmospheric missile does direct hit-to-kill reliably today: Patriot. We'll try to do it for $5,000 per shot.

十、Dante Weisbord（Albacore）— 无人潜艇

I'm Dante Weisbord, co-founder and CEO of Albacore. We make drone submarines.

背景与愿景

We started in January 2025 looking at how America was starting to mass-produce unmanned aircraft and unmanned surface vessels at low cost. Undersea assets have historically been extremely expensive, used for brief intelligence gathering. Given today's challenges, we need undersea assets that can perform the same types of missions as unmanned aircraft and USVs — attritable systems, mass-produced, capable of kinetic missions, delivering cost-asymmetric threat undersea.

CONOPS

If you can make ocean-wide low-cost vehicles, you can perform portions of the role that manned submarines and very exquisite underwater vehicles (tens of millions of dollars, size of garbage trucks) currently do — intelligence gathering, mine detection, survey, commercial applications, long-range precision strikes.

现状问题

Today's underwater vehicles are limited: really expensive systems that are big and can traverse oceans, or smaller "fire-and-forget" vehicles that last a day or two. Peer competition requires vehicles that last weeks and cross oceans. Low-cost medium-capability systems complementing large exquisite assets.

二战设计的现代重生

Rather than battery-powered systems (batteries don't store much energy, and pushing through water is energy-intensive), we brought back conventional WWII submarine design in an autonomous form factor: surface, use onboard fuel and generators to recharge batteries, then continue transit underwater. 10x the distance in a small envelope.

Deployed in the ocean multiple times, demonstrated to many stakeholders. Contracts in multiple countries, working across three continents — US Navy, international Coast Guard, special ops customers.

与总统的合影与市场机会

Us and the president at Senator McCormick's defense tech conference. Talking with the president about the Strait of Hormuz and many other geographies where unmanned systems matter. Similar to Drone Dominance ramping US production of unmanned aircraft, we anticipate similar things happening in the undersea environment.

Goal for next year: 75 drone submarine systems — probably making us one of the three largest manufacturers in the world. This year: 10 delivered to initial customers.

十一、Russ（Nine Mothers）— 反自杀无人机

I'm Russ from Nine Mothers. We're in the X26/P26 batch. We do affordable autonomous defense against suicide drones (Group 1).

威胁描述

In Ukraine and Russia, small quadcopters — $300–$500 each — kill vehicles and people. Can be entirely RF-denied (fly with fiber, untracked), carry small-to-large payloads, up to 100 mph.

No real cheap defense. Same kind of problem as IEDs in Iraq/Afghanistan — how do you protect everything? Million-dollar systems that work are cool; low six figures is more viable.

演示与产品

One of my co-founders is driving a robot with our system on top. A 20-inch tall robot, low six figures, with a human in the loop, autonomously defeats drones going fast. Publicly we say ~30 m/s (~65 mph) for about a year, but we can do faster. Shotgun on a robot: track and defeat drones day or night. Multiple weather conditions. Also on-the-move, but haven't announced that.

Sub-50 lbs excluding the tracked vehicle. Also a man-portable version.

客户与生产

Air Force is newest. Also DEVCOM, JSOC, SOCOM, Marine Corps Warfighting Lab, DIU, Army Ammunition Labs. Delivering units now.

We own the entire stack — ammunition, gun, software, sources. When things don't go as planned, we have full control. Under-promise, over-deliver.

Other public project: Santo 2 for 20th Engineering, an autonomous breaching project with Forterra. AUSA — come find us. Controlling existing weapon systems using our control algorithms; different munitions added for extended range.

Need more DoD contacts.

十二、Ryan（Metalware）— 嵌入式系统网络安全

My name is Ryan. I'm co-founder and CEO of Metalware, a cybersecurity company in the Bay Area. This is about defending the embedded stack — Department of War platforms including munitions, UAVs, and more.

网络作为首战场

Cyber is the first warfighting domain. Think of Venezuela — taking out equipment and power grids so warfighters can operate safely. On the contrary, Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon show adversaries pre-positioning in our infrastructure to disrupt US mobilization.

AI capabilities in cyber are progressing very quickly. Anthropic announced Mithos in spring, finding vulnerabilities in millions/billions of devices. What's changed recently: these capabilities are commoditizing. Anthropic published a report saying Mithos-level capabilities are now available open source with similar performance — adversaries are only a couple months behind US frontier capabilities.

嵌入式系统的独特挑战

Currently DoW (Air Force, Army, etc.) lack the tools — using bench rigs and checklists rather than best tools. Firmware and embedded systems run components/sensors/controllers on munitions, aircraft, UAVs. Reasons this is harder: lack of updates, legacy code bases, lack of access, hardware-in-the-loop dependency.

A munition/drone/aircraft has hundreds of small embedded computers performing mission-critical functions. Today's DoW cyber requirements for platform-IT embedded systems are typically RMF and ATO — standards adapted toward hardware but very different technical domain. No login pages for an aircraft; a lot of standards don't apply.

Metalware 起源与差异化

Started in the offensive security community building capabilities for the US IC. Now automating those tactics/techniques/procedures to scale for defenders across armed services — increase cyber resiliency before adversaries attack.

Why not use frontier models directly? First, adversaries use them — we need something better. Second, AI models aren't inherently trained on embedded systems code. Third, weapon system testing happens in air-gap high-side environments — how do you access AI there? That's what we help customers do.

Automated platform, easy to use, reduces labor/expertise required. Working with US IC, beginning with Air Force and AFRL, defense primes, and commercial critical infrastructure (OT/ICS).

Email: ryan@metalware.com.

十三、Fireside：Comptroller Undersecretary Hurst × [interviewer]

引言

Undersecretary Hurst, thank you for joining us today — especially on the last day of the fiscal year.

加速技术进入战场的最重要抓手

Interviewer: From your role as Comptroller, what's the single most important thing we can do to get technology into the hands of our warfighters faster?

Hurst: The biggest piece is the defense budget itself — that's where we create markets. In the FY27 request: $54 billion for drone dominance, $60 billion for space, $24 billion for counter UAS. These are markets not locked up — no single dominant provider — so new entrants can step in.

Acquisition reform: moving from Program Manager to Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE). A PM has a narrow task, resources against it — startup with a better idea disrupts his plan. A PAE can move money between capabilities and create opportunities.

Funding flexibility: right now as comptroller I can move less than 1% of the defense budget between appropriations. Two-year advance planning. In the last two years — ISR reconnaissance-strike, Ukraine, frontier AI — we need to move faster.

两类机会

Interviewer: What advice for founders looking at these funded programs?

Hurst: Two types:

  1. Growth opportunities — trends where funding lines keep getting bigger, markets fresh, opportunity to get in.
  2. Value investment — 50,000 suppliers support the F-35 alone. Small/medium businesses — opportunities to get into the supply chain, do things more efficiently.

从"用户喜欢"到"资金到位"

Interviewer: What about founders whose users love the product but who don't have access to budget?

Hurst: Users liking the product is necessary but not sufficient — program offices and PAEs have the power to make you successful. Look at where their gaps are and figure out where your product fits. You have to fit into the cycle — as subcontractor, taking on part of a program, helping shape future requirements. Not as simple as coming in with a good idea.

与 PAE/PM 互动的问题

Interviewer: Simple questions a founder can ask a PAE?

Hurst: Hire somebody who knows how it works. Then find PMs/PAEs who are exceptional and want to court you. Personality shopping — find someone who wants to make change, not fixated on compliance. They can open lots of opportunities across the department.

从 demo 到量产订单

Interviewer: A drone interceptor startup with an amazing demo, customer wants to buy more — what needs to happen?

Hurst: Either adhere to existing requirements or shape requirements as they come out. Two pathways: chase existing requirements (reliable but slow, needs dedication and relationships) or create a great product not aligned to a requirement and come through DIU or APFIT, hoping to survive the transition. Sometimes timing aligns with department needs — autonomous vessels for demining, low-cost interceptors — but that's betting on geopolitics.

支付结构灵活性

Interviewer: Hardware companies often need to hire people or stand up facilities before delivering. Can the department get flexible on payment structures?

Hurst: Anything legal under the FAR can be negotiated with the contracting officer. Make your needs clear. Office of Strategic Capital — low-interest loans. IBAS or DPA dollars. $113 billion in FY27 request for industrial-base support. Ask your program managers.

让承包生产线可预期

Interviewer: What can the department do to give more dependable demand signals?

Hurst: Multi-year procurement contracts — steady signals not just to the prime but to the whole supply chain (tier 4/5 suppliers). Also encourage founders to make products dual-use so you can insulate from government-shutdown flex and showcase manufacturing prowess. We don't have a defense industrial base problem — we have an industrial base problem.

生产能力的证明

Interviewer: What evidence signals a younger company is ready for larger production?

Hurst: Show that you can make stuff. Startups are sometimes "paper deep." Hire people with manufacturing experience.

90 天内成为可信供应商

Interviewer: For founders with commercially proven tech but no Pentagon relationships — 90-day plan?

Hurst: Personal relationships. Reach out to program offices with overlap. Talk to people at Comptroller, R&E, A&S. Develop your reputation, come up with solutions that solve program manager/PAE problems, be creative about fitting into existing programs.

问答

Marcus Weisgerber (WSJ): Status of omnibus reprogramming?

Hurst: Submitted in July. Going back and forth with Congress. Good use of General Transfer Authority this year.

Jane Lee (chair, Senate Defense Modernization Caucus Alliance): New task force on waste/fraud/abuse — how do you build trust with Congress?

Hurst: Secretary Feinberg announced the FAST team. Learned lessons from year one. Sitting under Comptroller because of budget authority. Also building a tool showing obligations and expenditures in near-real time to share with Congress — putting ourselves in a glass house to build trust for more funding flexibility.

On CR (Continuing Resolution): CR hurts. Everyone gets stingy. Ability to start new programs is hindered. The longer the CR, the more it slows technological adaptation.

十四、Grant Demery（OneBrief）— 军事规划的 AI 革命

Good morning. My name is Grant Demery, CEO of OneBrief. Last time I talked to a YC audience was at my own demo day in summer '21 — five years ago.

两部分：产品演示与国防软件观察

Part 1: What we do for the department and why. Live demo of AI creating military plans — from "how do we defend Taiwan" down to "what do we do tomorrow in Ukraine" — validated in a live planet-scale physics-based war game, generating after-action reviews that lead to superhuman decisions.

背景：从 Ebola 到 ISIS 到创业

Pre-OneBrief I was an Army officer. During the Ebola epidemic I was a second lieutenant in the 101st, working out of the Liberian Ministry of Health. Attached to the J-5 in that joint task force — operational planning. Saw large-scale operational plans early.

Two conclusions: (1) planning drives almost every major military decision — fixing planning isn't about fixing planning, it's about fixing decisions; (2) the status quo is nowhere near the frontier of what's possible.

Later, similar experiences with counter-ISIS task forces out of Baghdad. Concluded: this is broad, matters across substantially all military headquarters worldwide. Got out of the Army to try and fix it.

Core OneBrief — 参谋部速度革命

Purpose: serve every military headquarters from receipt of mission to issuance of order.

Sync matrix (militarized Gantt chart — who does what and when). Change on the sync matrix, everything that depends on it changes — automatically updates slides, maps, orders, command relationships. Same for maps.

系统整合与主权

A really important trend: a couple years ago, integrating software applications across the department was hard — lots of stovepipes. Not fixed, but hell of a lot better. We integrate with a wide variety — from new startups to government-owned systems like NGA. Maven Smart System integration shown. Simple drag-and-drop, operational users can do it without an engineer. Instead of disconnected systems, all part of one system.

审批流程与 AI 生成计划

Warning order routing across a joint task force — J3, chief of staff, commander need to approve. Add a comment (categorized as critical) — comment resolution matrix is created for you. Routed, distributed in-app, exported. Huge time savings.

Everything a human can do is fully operable with AI: optimizing sync matrix, placing things on a map, drawing concept sketches, building slides, optimizing orders. UIs converging to interact directly with the LLM.

模拟：错误信号的关键

To get truly superhuman (like software engineering) requires an error signal with fast feedback. Missing in military ops — only way to get there is simulation. Full planet-scale physics-based sim, modeling terrain, individual vehicles, missile trajectories, radar cross-sections, terrain effects. Running at 300× real time. Scalable to hundreds of thousands of entities. Extensible — most military ops end up with a variable no simulation would have thought of (e.g., commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz).

Loop: AI-generated plan → set up war game → let AIs play → after-action review → improve everything about your plan. Envision a world where US and allies find every possible military brilliance every time (do Inchon landings instead of Pusan, discover it right away). Planning D-Day takes seconds to minutes. Every military option going to the president is perfect risk-adjusted. When we talk about decision dominance, that's what we mean.

国防软件三观察

1. Progress in the last year is very different from before. Discontinuity. AI got good, and some reforms really worked. Watched defense-tech startups go from 0 to $12M ARR in one year. Watched a friend go 1 → 50 ARR this year. Program to watch: Army NGC2 (Next Generation Command and Control). Fast/easy vendor swap, seven major exercises in one year, operational commander in charge, efficient contracting command, forced on-site integrations ("thou shalt integrate"), strict penalties for non-performance. Best example to learn from — Congress/senior leaders should do a detailed AAR.

2. AI changed the game dramatically. Transforming our own company into a gen-tech: measured a 45× increase in feature delivery rate from January to present. Insane. Each time you unblock something, you earn the right to find the next blocker. E.g., delivering 180,000-line PRs eventually breaks the DevSecOps pipeline. Frontier task length appears to double every <4 months.

3. Better to have a reasonably good guess on a very important question than a precise answer to an unimportant one. Central question of defense software: how much combat power do we get from various levels of human-to-superhuman C2? Is it a 10% force increase or a 10× force increase? I think it's closer to 10×. Government should independently evaluate; every defense-software person should form an inside view.

十五、Mattia（Hoparo）— 有争议环境下的火箭货运

Good morning. My name is Mattia, one of the co-founders and CEO of Hoparo. We're building rockets that can deliver cargo to contested environments — rocket cargo for contested logistics.

团队背景

Engineer by background; previously founded a satellite propulsion startup, led to orbit on the third-ever rideshare mission with SpaceX (2022). Then scaled production of large-scale loitering munitions for Ukrainians. Co-founder: Marine Corps, based in Okinawa on MV-22 Ospreys, then SpaceX launching 20+ Falcon 9/Heavy, then led the NASA Eclipse lunar lander program at Masten Space.

公司概况

Founded 2024. This morning we announced raising over $11 million in VC funding. Currently delivering on a direct-to-phase-2 SBIR with AFRL. Based in Orange, California — work at the Oklahoma spaceport. Team of 7. Just wrapped up the summer 26 batch.

战场自动化的现实

Warfare has effectively already become autonomous across all domains. Air (drones with RPGs, cruise missiles, ballistic missiles). Same for sea, ground, space. Taiwan scenario: how do you get to one of the most contested environments — adversary 4× closer, tracked by space-domain awareness, potential blockade, barrage of autonomous systems?

Rook 火箭

We're building the world's first cargo delivery rocket: Rook. Launches from a standard 40-foot shipping container — anywhere on earth in minutes. Max speed Mach 7 (hypersonic). Range 450 miles. Okinawa → Taiwan in about 15 minutes. Reenters at hypersonic speed. Lands on unprepared environments (co-founder's Eclipse lunar-lander work — dust, gravel).

Progress during YC: engine built (based on our own tool HopOS), hot-fired, integrated into a half-scale prototype, static-fire of entire system, deployed drones from payload bay. Payloads: drones, interceptors, EW payloads. Vision: a fully autonomous 21st-century D-Day using rocket cargo.

HopOS — 智能层

Not just for engines — many previously manual/laborious tasks done in minutes. Highest-value: user inputs high-level engine specs → get out full 3D geometry, ready to manufacture. Verifiable engines — worked the first time (at Oklahoma spaceport).

DC 支持请求

For TACFI/STRAFI programs with Department of the Air Force — matching funding required. We've submitted our TACFI application; it's a multi-month process. We're ready to move fast, the department is ready — need to make sure stakeholders know they're becoming the bottleneck in getting this to the warfighter.

Lunch break — 20 minutes.

十六、Fireside：Eric Alborg × Olivia Marotta — Built for Defense

Luther Lowe intro: Eric left DIU a handful of months ago and has been working closely with all the YC defense companies over the last four months. He's the author of Built for Defense, a practical guide for helping commercial companies enter the defense market. Previously commercial executive at DIU. Advises founders, investors, and companies. Book copies provided for all attendees; signings at the happy hour.

Olivia Marotta works on partnerships at Y Combinator supporting companies after the batch. Graduated Swarthmore, art history and economics.

这本书是给谁看的

Olivia: Who's it for, and what does the founder walk away knowing?

Eric: For founders who think winning their first contract will be the hardest thing. It's actually not — getting to the second, third, or fourth contract can be quite a bit harder. Depends on the archetype:

  • Pure-play defense (kinetic — missile, drone) → path to market is Department of War, obvious.
  • Dual-use startup — hard to grow two products simultaneously (commercial + DoD are not the same).
  • Commercial-first (like Microsoft selling Office) → think about subcontracting; you might not need a prime contract with DoW.

The mistakes/decisions are different depending on archetype. The book is about the gap between the three archetypes.

从 DIU 到 YC 观察到的创业者

Olivia: What did those founders change your mind about?

Eric: Struck by how much risk they were willing to take — not just startup risk, but literally putting themselves on the front lines in Ukraine or wartime conditions to test products. Incredible breadth of technology: intel analyst tools, wargaming, UAS group 1–5.

The book is really about helping startups optimize for speed — they don't have runway beyond maybe 18 months. If they're not converting on whatever the business model is, they won't make it to the next milestone.

什么在阻挡这些创业者

Olivia: What surprised you most about what's stopping them?

Eric: Access is getting better — heard from Under Secretaries Michael and Hurst today. At DIU, always leaned forward. It's not really that. It's understanding that the market you might be pursuing is not what you think in the beginning. Configuring the go-to-market for defense versus a commercial framework.

DIU 会议室里的观察

Olivia: Two startup founders and an established contractor pitching at the same table — what did you see?

Eric: My job at DIU was diligence. Sitting in rooms where contract decisions were made. Table, 10–20 government folks — active duty, PMs, acquisitions, federal contractors.

  • Startup comes in: tired, casual, exceptional pitch — optimized for the problem-to-solve, engineering-focused. Q&A goes into a black hole.
  • Defense prime: all suits and ties, well-rested. Shake hands — knew people in the room from decades-long relationships. Pitch, great Q&A.

What's the startup getting wrong? Many people in the room, many roles it takes to get to yes. Engineer is a champion (understands the tech). Program manager thinks about fit-to-mission (startups don't discuss mission — huge mistake). Acquisition official is taught to avoid risk at all costs — a two-person startup with $500K looks like a lot of risk. Others just don't understand Silicon Valley language — someone has to interpret.

采购改革的变与不变

Olivia: What's changed?

Eric: Reorganizing the department to be more responsive to founders — good-faith efforts. More money — budget rising, reconciliation adding on. As Under Secretary Hurst said, creating markets for startups.

The thing that hasn't changed: the budget process — annual, arcane, mysterious to founders. Fiscal year 27 starts tomorrow. Likely CR, which does not favor startups; favors incumbents. If we wanted a budget responsive to tech change, it wouldn't be on a year timeframe — quarterly or semi-annual.

国防科技是否是泡沫

Olivia: Elephant in the room — is defense tech a bubble?

Eric: Cash moves quickly. Defense contracts do not move quickly. Founders caught in the middle. Product-market fit looks different in DoW — you fundraise to your first milestone (a demo, a CSO prototype), then the next milestone (transition to a program of record), and eventually 3–5 DoW contracts in production, multi-year — that's when you're thinking about scale, maybe becoming one of the new primes.

周一该做什么不一样

Olivia: What should founders do differently come Monday?

Eric:

  1. Persistence + surface area. Reach out to 20–30 people a day, consistently, until you can say "I've run this to ground." Biggest problem in DoW: people aren't good at saying no. You'll get yes/no through an RFP, but rarely detailed feedback. Getting yes/nos from individuals along the way gives you foundation.
  2. Capital stack awareness. You're in national security. Can't take money from anywhere. Be thoughtful about who's on your cap table — evaluations later will look at that.

十七、Fireside：Senator Tim Sheehy × Vivian Xin

Luther intro: Senator Sheehy represents Montana, serves on Armed Services. Naval Academy grad, former Navy SEAL officer, founded Bridger Aerospace (aerial firefighting).

Vivian Xin: Visiting partner at YC, founder of Juni Learning and Ace Lee. Formerly Google, McKinsey. Stanford CS.

从 SEAL 到创业者到参议员

Vivian: Tell us about your journey.

Sheehy: Bridger Aerospace was our aviation company. More applicable: my defense-tech company. In 2015, defense tech was rare — in the Bay Area they literally laughed at me for starting a defense hardware company. Ascent Vision Technologies (AVT). Invented the MADIS family (L-MADIS, I-MADIS, MADIS, X-MADIS) — first counter-drone program-of-record system. Two guys in a barn → 300 employees → exit to a strategic in 2020.

I'm the only person on Capitol Hill who has founded and scaled a defense company from scratch. Top priority: reform defense acquisition — specification, requirements, buying, fielding. The military hasn't had an innovation problem so much as an innovation adoption problem. Labs, AFWERX, SOFWERX, DIU, on-ramps everywhere — innovate, then sit in a box unused. Focus on fast-tracking to front line.

第一份政府订单与经验教训

Vivian: How did you get your first government purchase order?

Sheehy: Made a lot of mistakes. Never went to the Hill as a founder. Him and Jared Isaacman joked they should have. How we got first customer: our initial business was Bridger — fighting wildfire from the air with an IR sensor. Realized that Yarnell Mountain Fire — 19 hotshots burned alive — happened because the team leader made the right decision with wrong information (no situational awareness we had in Afghanistan). Applied that to defense — Marine Corps LAD community took a leap on us. From back-of-napkin to fielded in combat in eight months.

双用产品的建议

Vivian: Advice on being pushed toward dual-use?

Sheehy: Focus is key. Try to do everything, do nothing well. Start with the customer and mission and work backward. If it's a consumer product, make a consumer product. If it's defense, make it for your customer. DoW is now a real customer.

采购改革与国防工业基础

Vivian: What changes could Congress make to make prototype-to-scale easier?

Sheehy: I don't want us to have a defense industrial base. I want us to have an industrial base that the Defense Department partakes in. Ford made most of our airplanes in WWII. GM. Best telecom company for consumers should also make the best military phones. Bifurcating excellence gives us the worst in both fields.

Won't have to build a separate industrial base from nothing when the big one comes if we don't bifurcate. Ukraine builds more drones in a day than China does — underground, hidden factories all over. Auto industry is the only manufacturing left with real parallel commercial/defense capacity.

多年拨款与供应链弹性

Vivian: How can Congress work with smaller suppliers to scale production?

Sheehy: Multi-year appropriations. Companies can invest behind them. Build a factory with 5 years of certainty, not with one PO. Never had this amount of private capital available for defense infrastructure — Andreessen, Kleiner, 8VC. If we're not a good customer, money follows yield elsewhere (see DJI crushing the drone bubble in 2017).

Downstream supply chain — microchips, thermal cameras, magnets, batteries — the great UGV/USV/counter-UAS on top doesn't matter if the components are stuck in China. Ukraine will save our bacon on this — pace of innovation there is incredible.

We had JIDO (during GWOT for IEDs) — stood up with authority, funding, responsibility. Real-time iteration, saved lives. Then we got rid of it because "why would you keep an aberration?" — bureaucracy eager to return to sclerotic ways. Big announcement from Sec. Hegseth today about a similar effort protected in statute.

退伍军人转型为创始人

Vivian: Advice for those in the military wanting to start companies?

Sheehy: Purpose, mission, brotherhood — hard to recreate outside. Bring your junior-leader lessons; recognize blind spots. Don't jump into your first thing forever; you'll find it's usually not the right thing. Skill Bridge and internship programs are great. Eventually you have to burn your ships — walk away from a paycheck, step into the darkness. Lives in your hands — employees, family, warfighters using your equipment. Every screw screwed in, every line of code written, has to be ready for combat.

十八、Aaron Dell — 全栈反无人机生态

James: We are entering the space section — after this we've got the NASA administrator.

We are Aaron Dell. We build the whole ecosystem — plug-and-play for shooting down fiber-optic drones up to Garand 5s and jet-powered threats. Actively deployed in combat, confirmed shootdowns, all combat veterans.

问题

Patriots are great, expensive, can't build enough. Existing systems: $50K–$80K shot at a $50K drone with Jetsons — asymmetric. Primes sell hardware; training doesn't come with it; kit sits in crates while threats evolve.

产品栈

  • Airgloss interceptor platform (desert/cold-weather variants). Fully autonomous. Months of training → three mouse clicks: launch, pursuit, intercept.
  • Holo sight — believed to be the lightest thermal-through-holographic sight in the world (EOTech that spots people in the dark).
  • Orion headset — originally sensor for interceptors: thermal-fused night vision + rangefinder. Look at a target, laser distance, bearing/heading for a fires order, then watch an Airgloss go in on it. Only thing in the world that lets you shoot AND move as a drone pilot.
  • Training track — updated every two weeks direct from the front line. Flying, engineering, navigation, counter-OS fortifications, interceptor-drone flying.
  • No Chinese components at any stage.

三笔预算，一家供应商

Counter-UAS, soldier sensing, training. Managed services (Raptor). Train-to-equip: plug-and-play capability spun up from scratch.

团队与业绩

  • Pedro (capability lead): shot down so many Shaheds that his unit stopped paying the bonus (out of money).
  • Team collectively shot down more Shaheds than half of NATO combined. More Shaheds and Garand drones than the US Navy did over the recent Iran conflict.
  • Combat-veteran design: wrapped in sniper tape, dropped in a puddle, matte-taped — still works.

Orders going through; actively deployed in Eastern Europe and over the Gulf.

十九、Edward Hinson（Zephyr Fusion）— 轨道核聚变

I'm Edward Hinson, CEO of Zephyr Fusion. We build compact megawatt-scale fusion reactors for orbital applications.

团队

Co-founder and I are lifelong fusion physicists (Oak Ridge and Lawrence Livermore). Engineers from Turion Space, NASA, Proxima Fusion, Commonwealth Fusion, Type 1. Advisors from Relativity, Planet, AFRL, NASA — including space-nuclear experience.

空间能源的现实

Every major space effort is power-starved. About 10 kilowatts is the working ceiling that actually operates commercially. Skylab broke that in the early 70s, essentially stands alone outside government assets. Megawatt power in orbit will be a foundation layer of the space economy — manufacturing, transport propulsion, compute. Gigawatts have been proposed; largest single solar installations still ~150 kW per panel — 10 MW would span the base of the Great Pyramid at Giza.

能量密度

Chemical energy powered the industrial revolution and gets us to orbit, but doesn't pay its own freight beyond that. Nuclear is a million× more energy-dense than a battery. Fusion is another 100× per unit fuel: 1–10 GWh per gram (about a megawatt-day per gram).

为何在轨道上做聚变

Top-line result of decades of fusion research: need lots of volume × field strength. Volume sets total reactor size; ITER = $65B for 500 MW thermal. In space you leverage the natural vacuum — only need to provide high magnetic field. Past 10 years: commercialization of high-temperature superconducting tapes; past 5: price down an order of magnitude.

Zephyr 项目

Initial designs for 1–10 MW installation — fits single launch capacity with room for payload.

Building Baleus — first demo. Fields HTS tape in orbit, levitates the coil via a method we've patented. Launch late 2028.

请求

Fusion should have a lane alongside fission — leverages existing government investment. Common energy conversion, heat rejection, high-power bus work. Fusion advantage: non-hazardous bill of materials on launch pad; higher-energy-density fuel. Strategic: can create sensitive materials otherwise hard to produce.

Zephyr Fusion — founded a year ago, team of 10, initial demonstration late 2028.

二十、Panel：Space — Bram Shork, Skylar Chan, Alex Lissow, Jacob Ossoff × Jacob Reeses

Luther intro: Bram (General Astronautics, robots for microgravity research/manufacturing, Caltech aerospace, ex-SpaceX Starlink laser), Skylar (Gru Space, lunar construction, Berkeley EECS, ex-T-Mobile), Alex (Inflection Space Systems, spacecraft mass manufacturing, Millennium/Rocket Lab/Planet/Interlune), Jacob Ossoff (Orca Aerospace, on-vehicle AI operations, 10+ years Lockheed GNC).

Jacob Reeses (moderator) — recently Chief of Staff to VP JD Vance, previously Senator Hawley's advisor, Stanford Law.

各家在做什么

Bram: General Astronautics — super-intelligent robots for on-orbit and lunar applications. Everything from orbital warehousing to asset resupply to cargo management is a labor problem. 26-year-old robots on ISS. Applying RL and robot control policies to build fully autonomous robots.

Skylar: Gru Space — America's moon-based company. Build the first cities on the moon and Mars in our lifetime. Mission next year: manufacture the world's first product on the moon — a moon brick from moon-dust material. Hawthorne, CA. First to the few unclaimed lunar resources controls the moon.

Alex: Inflection Space Systems — mass-manufacturing spacecraft. Target 10,000 satellites/year by early 2030s. Manufacturing today is structurally high-cost, low-volume. First launch about a year away.

Jacob (Ossoff): Orca Aerospace — super-intelligent spacecraft operators living onboard, fully autonomous, so we don't rely on the fragile ground link. First launch with a major aerospace prime in the next 6 months.

让航天器生产可重复

Reeses: Alex — what has to change?

Alex: Supply chain. Piece parts (microelectronics, screws, adhesives) are almost entirely boutique for space — expensive, subject to bottlenecks and obsolescence. Redesign sub-assemblies whenever a part goes obsolete → new engineering project every time. Solution: only use terrestrial parts from high-volume industries (consumer electronics, drones, cars).

Also, interfaces. Space was a science project — now organic standardization: Ethernet, common voltage levels, mounting patterns. Trend must continue for the industry to scale.

让客户信任在轨 AI 决策

Reeses: Jacob (Ossoff) — how do you build customer trust?

Ossoff: Same as traditional aerospace — climb TRL. Software-in-the-loop → processor-in-the-loop → hardware-in-the-loop. Test on flatsats, then on-orbit tests (launch early March next year). Metrics vs. traditional human-in-the-loop operators — thousands of synthetic and real missions. In our case AI operator has always significantly outperformed human on the ground.

微重力机器人首个可重复客户

Reeses: Bram — who's the first repeatable customer?

Bram: Anyone who pays for astronaut labor. NASA figures ~$135K/hr; private stations 3× that → ~$500K/hr. Not safe or scalable. Manufacturing biologics, metamaterials, and increasingly compute in space. Star Cloud — part of our $30M+ in commercial LOIs.

Government side: Golden Dome, orbital warehousing, orbital logistics. F-35 doesn't get thrown into the ocean — same for satellites. Two days ago Starship launched again — larger launch vehicles make LEO servicing economics work. Repair economics make sense today, will only become more profitable.

从月球基础设施到今日可购买产品

Reeses: Skylar — what can customers buy today?

Skylar: First step: turn lunar resources into construction material. Make a brick on the moon before we can build a moon base, then landing pads, roads, warehouses, barracks. Look around — everything on Earth built with concrete. Instead of bringing all material from Earth to moon (huge problem, unit-economics kicker), use lunar resources locally at scale — not just for us but for NASA and partners. First step: world's first bricks on the moon, next year.

各家最大风险与必须成真的事

Reeses: What has to go right?

Ossoff: Common standards across hardware AND software. Common data-source ingestion so novel software can federate.

Bram: We live in an age of abundant super-intelligence — everyone agrees translation to physical world is "when, not if." American dominance in space requires labor competence in domain — so it's not what has to go right, it's how quickly it can be accelerated.

Alex: Launch — big year with SpaceX going public, potentially winding down rideshare. Optimistic long-term: brilliant people, billions invested in alternative launch. Falcon 9 birthed the new-space sector. When 3–5 more reliable, high-cadence rockets come to market, explosion of growth.

Skylar: On top of launch, the key tech de-risk. Autonomous robotic factory that excavates regolith, processes, compacts, cures, places world's first product on the lunar surface. Approach: critical-path singular demonstration to prove technology possible at low cost.

对 Jared Isaacman 的建议

Reeses: If Jared is listening backstage, what should NASA do?

Ossoff: NASA has the greatest history of ops — great and anomalous. Give training-data access to build operators that learn from prior missions.

Alex: More commercial pathways. Shorten cycle time from science-need identification to launch. Spacecraft often have excess payload capacity — do more with it.

Skylar: Gru laser-focused on the moon-base mission — would love an opportunity to brief the administrator.

Bram: Private capital lets us start today, disjoint from government timelines. Robots ready — cool opportunities on the moon, our robots should be on those rovers.

时代内让人意外的加速

Reeses: What will surprise us over the next few years?

Bram: Humans really suck at exponentials. What's superintelligence if not humanity's greatest exponential? It will be unimaginable.

Skylar: Every tech revolution: humans learning to use resources more intelligently — new set of untapped resources. First time in history we can go to the moon and use its ~38 million km² of free real estate — like Louisiana Purchase 2.0 without buying anything.

Alex: In 10–20 years — thousands of autonomous satellites interacting, lunar infrastructure, refueling, comms. That's what you need to mine the asteroid belt. Physically possible today.

Ossoff: Constellations, mega-constellations, on-orbit warfare. Battlefield shifting from ground (Ukraine) to orbit — most contested area.

问答

Scott Freeman (International Preparedness Associates, NASA NBL astronaut trainer): Human-robot interaction on moon base?

Skylar: Designed for maximum autonomy to reduce astronaut cost. Vision is cities on the moon and Mars, which implies humans — on our roadmap.

二十一、Fireside：NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman × Ashi Dsennayake

Luther intro: Jared — 15th NASA administrator, entrepreneur, pilot, astronaut. Founded Shift4, co-founded Draken International (military aviation training). Commanded Inspiration4 (first all-civilian orbital mission) and Polaris Dawn (first commercial spacewalk).

Ashi Dsennayake — co-founder and CEO of Spacium, fully automated in-orbit refueling stations. Background in orbital mechanics and rocket propulsion.

首个任务与客户

Ashi: For a startup building both civil and defense space capability — how to find first mission and customer?

Jared: Opening disclaimer: NASA is a really terrible buyer; DoW is a great buyer in a lot of regards — just look at budgets. NASA buys a handful of exquisite things but is really good at maturing technology, which should be positive for a lot of folks in the room.

Smart to think through what overlaps both national-security needs and NASA's requirements. Where to put attention: at events like this, listen for what people complain about that doesn't have an owner. Launch (immense demand for more payload mass). Hypergol thrusters (all NASA science-mission payload buses use them; DoW satellites too; immense supply-chain issues).

月球基地机会

Ashi: What about lunar capabilities?

Jared: Excellent place to start. Moon base is akin to how we did things in the 1960s — Mercury before Gemini, many Apollo missions before Eagle. Lots of landers, lots of rovers to execute the science of survival. Should love that. Alternative approach (build the giant glass dome with nuclear plant next door → one prime + 100 subs + international partners → canceled after $20B) is what we're avoiding.

Talk to Carlos Galan (moon-base viceroy). Dropped many RFIs. Payload mass and volume available. Highly steer toward robotics — the astronaut bouncing on the moon is very cool but is the last choice. Get robotics dialed in on the lunar surface. It's a steer for surface payload opportunities.

商业服务 vs. 政府角色

Ashi: Which programs should NASA buy commercially, which take a different role?

Jared: Naturally gravitate toward buying commercial services when clearly one customer of many, not propping up the entire industry as sole customer. Launch, observation, communication (and adjacencies) — markets exist. On-orbit refueling/servicing, on-orbit assembly — will be useful services.

Lower TRL, riskier to say "commercial service." Early moonwalking-suits-as-a-service didn't work — NASA was the only foreseeable customer, and NASA also didn't help drive outcome. Course-correcting. Low TRL → probably cost-plus to mature; then fix-firm-price once at high TRL.

在轨加注

Ashi: What would make NASA buy refueling as a service rather than sponsor another demo?

Jared: Not our best customer today — Nancy Grace Roman at L2 has 23 years of fuel because it's station-keeping. DoW will use prop all the time (dogfighting in space); makes sense to refuel and enhance capabilities.

Just as we'd be crazy today to build a new telescope not sized for a New Glenn or Starship fairing, we need to build vehicles that take better advantage of on-orbit servicing. Fission-powered starfleet — sending fission-powered spacecraft to outer solar system and Mars, will need Xenon top-off and chemical augmentation.

标准与接口

Ashi: Is NASA looking for compatible interfaces?

Jared: I suspect DoW will establish standards for space-based refueling — they'll be the bigger up-front user. Meanwhile NASA will help set standards on lunar surface (surface water interfaces, prop transfer interfaces, power interfaces for rovers).

民防共享需求

Ashi: Where do NASA and defense have genuinely shared requirements?

Jared: Standards across infrastructure. Stage-zero launch complexes, prop-transfer lines, launch vehicles, transfer vehicles, storable and cryogenic propellants — a lot of overlap right up until missions diverge. Even then, Chairman JCS said surface of oceans to cislunar space is a warfighting domain. NASA cares about cislunar comms/observation for the moon base; DoW needs space-domain awareness (beneficial to us) — same bus possibly.

商业 LEO 空间站的下一步

Ashi: Role NASA expects to play in commercial LEO stations?

Jared: Value US presence in LEO greatly. There may come a day, but until moon base is operational or we've exhausted what microgravity teaches us, we'll have a presence. Prioritize: no gap. We had a gap with Shuttle → 10-year dependence on Russians — never again. Model dependent on NASA being one customer of many requires other customers to get there — that's why we prioritized Starliner get-well plan, extending missions, crew-rating for Vulcan. Without transportation, model is dead on arrival.

对小型机器人/服务公司的建议

Ashi: What should they build into their plan now?

Jared: Find the human use case — human-in-the-loop. As astronaut who's been up twice, I want reasons for people living and working in space. Drives demand for commercial stations/hotels. Costs come down with demand.

On robotics — LEO, MEO, GEO, lunar surface — demand will exist. National security demand, on-orbit assembly demand, ISRU manufacturing demand, lunar surface operations must be robotically driven.

工业反馈塑造 NASA

Ashi: How is industry feedback shaping which infrastructure NASA provides vs. buys?

Jared: Extremely informative. Ignition Day in February formalized the president's national space policy — dropped ~two dozen RFIs, several RFPs. Won't build multi-billion-dollar bespoke comm-relay satellites for the moon — platinum age for on-orbit comms. Next Habitable Worlds Observatory sized for reliable 10-years-out fairing (Starship, enhanced New Glenn).

Days of externally imposed "everybody's good idea forced by a congress member" are over — those are what you do when you don't have a space race. We have a real one now.

Artemis III 关键路径

Ashi: Critical path for Artemis III?

Jared: Runs through the landers. Nothing else was a slam dunk. Every step designed for dream-state — "let's fly around the moon on Artemis II, wait three years, then land." Nobody plays golf well when they play every three years.

Suits designed to spec that meant the astronaut would have had a stroke inside — running a marathon every day. Course-correcting: get to the moon, learn, roll improvements. $2B "transformer robot" rover — people would be jazzed just seeing an Apollo-style rover.

Standardized to get back into an evolutionary rhythm. We'll launch in '27. Memo to 55,000 workforce (knew it'd leak): "Six months ago we didn't have an Artemis III — no hardware, no astronauts training. Now astronauts are training, hardware converging. 90 days behind schedule on a mission that didn't exist six months ago — with lots of opportunity to improve." 2028: still protect for up to two shots on the surface.

从供应商找到新供应商

Ashi: What did being a commercial customer and operating in space teach you about spotting new suppliers?

Jared: Perspective from space reinforces why we have to do it — what an adventure. Return to the moon, moon base, fission-powered spacecraft, Enceladus/Europa, astronauts on Mars in our lifetime.

Applied to procurement: appreciate all the development work — three years before Polaris Dawn launched, watching a suit go from IVA to vacuum-qualified — many parties coming together. That's what we're doing at NASA. Acquisition reform where it makes sense — low TRL / high TRL / customer-of-many. Embed NASA talent across the supply chain to drive outcomes.

二十二、Adrian Peterson（Array Labs）— 卫星雷达

I'm Adrian Peterson from Array Labs — space-based radar systems.

空间的战略→战术转变

Space traditionally a strategic asset — periodic imagery for IC. Quality metric: highest-resolution image. Very large, exquisite, capable systems. That's shifting or augmenting as space becomes tactically relevant — higher frequency, higher operation cadence to support real-time. Not every couple hours or days — within seconds. Multi-mission, all-domain, real-time.

Tailwinds: cheaper launch, mature space infrastructure, low-cost satellite buses, high-speed comms networks. Still missing a radar option to support these missions.

为何雷达

Need to see through clouds, operate at night, in all resilient conditions — hard with optical. Current radar options expensive, exquisite, not manufacturable enough.

Array is building the first scalable, economic, multi-mission radar system — imagery, moving-object detection and tracking (maritime domain awareness, air support, etc.). 12 contracts to date with Space Force, Air Force, DARPA — air/maritime awareness, ground imaging.

性能

Traditional systems: 15 m or 3 m resolution. Lower-cost, higher-power approach delivers much greater coverage — single collection pass, wide-area with 4- and 16-sat clusters. AMTI/GMTI/OMTI performance.

二十三、Fireside：Congressman Pat Ryan × Luther Lowe

Luther: Great to have the People's House represented.

为什么关注国防现代化

Luther: Of all the things you could focus on, why defense modernization?

Pat Ryan: Former Army intelligence officer, West Point. Deployed in Iraq/Afghanistan. Co-founded a services-implementation firm for Palantir. Scarring D-SIGS-A battles to get commercial tech to warfighters — we've come a long way, but far to go.

Co-founded the bipartisan Defense Modernization Caucus with Rob Whitman (Virginia) — House and Senate now — Dems, Republicans, authorizers, appropriators.

两党共识与担忧

Luther: Where's bipartisan agreement, and where is it not?

Pat Ryan: Everybody aligned — administration, Congress, American people. This admin coming in aggressively (right focus, urgency, breaking things where not working) should be championed. Two concerns:

  1. Is it happening? Love the briefings/memos/media, but are founders and mission-owners feeling it? Bureaucratic middle continues to kill us.
  2. Trust concerns. Reports that "the best company isn't necessarily getting a contract — is it political, who-you-know?" Are people coming on cap tables who shouldn't be? That's unprecedented and potentially illegal. Not partisan — it's American.

信号与噪声

Luther: How do you separate signal from noise?

Pat Ryan: KPIs: What percentage of the budget actually goes to disruptive, low-cost, commercial, innovative companies? Currently ~1% to venture-backed non-traditional. Old, expensive over-engineered stuff in base budget; new disruptive stuff in reconciliation land — that's not happening.

Five primes = crazy. Not saying kill them — but need actual competition. And hearing directly from you, off the record — what's a pain point, how might we fix it. Example: this year we got into the base NDAA language letting a PAE take up to 10% of RDT&E money and move it to production.

从两边看的意外

Luther: Being on both sides, what's surprised you?

Pat Ryan: We've made changes, given new authorities, created OTA framework — but we keep coming back to culture and mindset. Would welcome ideas on how to affect it. People often come in front of Congress for not-good reasons, upping risk aversion. What could we do to highlight people doing the right things, taking risks that succeeded?

测试场地

Luther: A large fraction of Texas defense-tech startups all test at one guy's ranch.

Pat Ryan: Bandwidth constraint. West Point looking to expand as a proving/testing grounds (Buckner) — cadets testing stuff in summer training with real-time feedback. Old Air National Guard base in my district used for almost nothing — pushing for drone/counter-UAS testing. Central New York has a decade-long effort around Syracuse — took 10 years and going, need to speed up.

理想的最终状态

Luther: End-state vision for a founder navigating procurement?

Pat Ryan: Single point of information entry and delivery — far from, but getting better. Less innovation theater, more actual people who move stuff. DIU good example. But the biggest thing is multi-year path to revenue for great companies — map out "if you hit your metrics, next step is X to Y to scale."

问答

Comrade (attendee): Modeling and simulation labs / partnerships to reduce risk and marry up technologies at various TRLs?

Pat Ryan: Absolutely right. Don't leverage existing investments enough. Would love specific proposals — model-and-sim to me is an area I know less about.

二十四、Jay（Relling）— 制造业机器人

My name is Jay, I run Relling. The American manufacturing ecosystem needs a billion more robots.

问题

US manufacturing can't keep up with demand. Army needed 100,000 motors by last October; we can only do 36,000. Stockpiles and production can't keep up.

The bottleneck isn't the primes — it's one abstraction under the primes. Mom-and-pop shops in Texas, Illinois, Indiana building small fasteners that bottleneck all production.

传统自动化的失败

Traditional automation wasn't built for defense — built for automotive. Millions per machine, 18–24 month ramp-up, and any part change means re-engineering from day zero.

Small mom-and-pop defense shops: Boeing demanding 30,000–50,000 parts/month; the shop has been building 5,000. How do we transition them from 5,000 to 50,000?

解决方案：部署层

The underlying infrastructure exists — Amazon-buyable cameras, vision systems, robotic arms. The problem isn't the raw materials; it's taking a robotic arm and actually deploying it into a factory. Relling is the deployment layer. We bring up massive robots to produce U-joints, high-tension ball bearings, springs, aircraft landing gear, pneumatic systems.

Flexible re-tooling — modify a production line at the speed of software (e.g., going from 737 ball bearings to C-5).

案例：Anthony

Anthony's grandfather started his shop; pneumatic systems for aircraft. Underperforming by 5× vs. customer demand (Northrop/Lockheed/Boeing). Traditionally: take on $10M debt, 18–24 months, hope math closes in 4–5–7 years.

With Relling, $150K to reduce the deburring bottleneck (previously manual — CNC runs overnight, technician deburrs by hand). Anthony now makes 5× more parts. Supports 29 platforms across 6 classes. Not one-off — one of a million manufacturers who can't keep up.

We want to talk to more shops under the primes.

二十五、Johnny（Proven Metal）— PCB 供应链

My name is Johnny, my company is called Proven Metal.

PCB — 关键瓶颈

PCB = printed circuit board — the single most critical bottleneck across aerospace, defense, and robotics. Existing American supply chain is really bad.

市场背景

US in 2000: 30% of world's circuit boards. Today: 4%. Weird: US manufacturers say "not enough demand, dramatically underutilized"; hardware customers say "too much demand, not enough supply."

Break down lead time — most isn't manufacturing; it's quoting, design review, sourcing components, kitting. Automate these and we cut lead times in half.

网络与垂直整合

Partner with existing manufacturers, automate around them. Network of manufacturers with different price/capability/turnaround. Route orders through the network efficiently; increase utilization of idle American capacity.

As we scale the routing layer, we identify where manufacturing itself needs vertical integration (some fab and assembly nodes). Biggest problem in manufacturing isn't the manufacturing — it's the effective deployment of capital. Scaling the routing layer aggregates demand density and reveals where vertical integration makes most sense.

This is how you build the biggest electronics manufacturing company in the US. Ask: if you're building hardware, build your circuit boards with Proven Metal and fix the domestic supply chain.

二十六、Steven（Graypoint Industries）— 隐藏敌人的无人机蜂群

I'm Steven, co-founder of Graypoint Industries. We build drone swarms that hunt hidden enemies — operators, jammers, command nodes, everything that drives modern drone warfare and comms. $30M+ LOIs from Ukrainian military units; Phase 2 R&D contract in Canada.

问题：透明化不可见的敌人

Modern battlefield: autonomous systems controlled by humans we can't see — under camouflage, hidden from cameras, hard for radar. We deploy $200 interceptor drones only to have the enemy operator launch the next one immediately. But most nodes have to transmit — that's the fatal weakness Legion exploits.

Legion — 蜂群工作方式

Low-cost autonomous drones that passively listen across the spectrum and geolocate targets in real time. Fly a drone or key a radio — we find them. Each aircraft takes a bearing; swarm crosses bearings, geolocates, pushes to TAK/Lattice/etc. All on the edge — emits nothing sensor-detectable; mesh designed to be hard to detect. Find enemies in contested territory; they can't find us.

Targets: drone operators (control uplink), interference units/GPS jammers, comms equipment (enemy handheld radios), air defense/counter-battery radars — integrating with SEAD tactics.

使用方式

No EW specialist needed — any soldier designates an area, launches as few as two aircraft, gets live tracks. Swarm makes decisions autonomously based on real-time sensor data. Persistent surveillance — aircraft rotate in and out to recharge. Classify and store signals with onboard AI.

三点差异化

  1. Target the signal, not the airframe. Cheapest way to take a drone team out of the fight.
  2. Passive. Works when GPS is jammed and links degraded — in fact detects the jammers.
  3. Leaderless swarm. Lose an aircraft, swarm heals. No master node to neutralize. Real-time on edge.

Hound — 效应器

Second product: Hound — mount an RF sensor on any small drone, autonomously fly toward emitting targets. Operator authorizes, Hound flies to signal, hands off to camera for final approach. Want to saturate the field — drones, UGVs, static entrenchers, existing infrastructure — thousands of small inexpensive sensors. Full map of the electromagnetic spectrum.

应用场景

Rogue drone operators at airports and transport hubs, counter-narcotics/trafficking for borders, contraband drones over prisons, protect power plants/data centers/critical infrastructure.

状态与团队

TRL 6 demonstrated to Canadian Armed Forces. Deploying to Ukraine in coming months; TRL 8 by end of year. Field data improves classification. Team: Canadian infantry, General Dynamics, Bosch Quantum Sensing. Ship products in defense; radios/airframes/autonomy in-house.

Live demo: right now in the room a drone operator is holding a controller — we're live tracking the unknown signal. Come find us at the booth.

二十七、Sourth（64）— 调查智能基础设施

My name is Sourth, co-founder and CEO of 64 — building the intelligence infrastructure for a world where AI agents make critical decisions on people and entities.

调查代理

Core tech: investigation agents — research agents that work like your best analyst. Combines open-source intel, dark web, clear web, cross-referenced sources, claims sourced and confidence-scored. In a domain where you cannot afford to be wrong.

Applications:

  • Supply chain due diligence — contractors, UBO, insider networks.
  • DPRK screening — catching bad actors infiltrating corporations.
  • Defensive personal — what info about your people could adversaries exploit from public sources.

Analysts take weeks; agents take minutes. Cross-industry: hospice network to defense supplier — entities and individuals share footprints.

案例：临终关怀欺诈

Monterey Park, LA County — 7 people charged from 3 hospices, ~$3.2M over 8 years. Enrolling non-dying patients, rotating them between hospices every 6 months to avoid Medicare review triggers.

Ran investigation with our agents. All public for years: 2016 head nurse from prosecuted fraud network; 2017 billing complaints for visits that never happened; 2021–22 directors suing each other; 2024 attention; 2026 prosecutions.
