item.title: [Bits + Bips] Can THORChain Stay Neutral After the $388M Bitget Hack?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：ThorChain 不是"去中心化过头"，而是"去中心化的可证伪性"被自己亲手推翻

大多数评论者把这次事件读成"去中心化 vs. 中心化"的老掉牙争论，但真正的关键点在 Michael Perklin 那句极短的话里："没有主动签署的选择，却有主动关闭机器的选择。"

这句话把 ThorChain 推入了一个哲学困境——它一旦证明过自己能停机（May exit 事件），就永远失去了"我停不下来"这个抗辩权。这在密码学里叫"承诺方案"（commitment scheme）：你一旦对世界公开过某种能力，就无法再声称你没有。ThorChain 的问题不是它做了或没做什么，而是它在过去用一次停机，为未来所有"不停机"都盖上了自愿的印章。

换句话说：每一个曾经声称过 kill switch 的去中心化协议，都在为自己未来的每一次"不作为"预先签下了法律意义上的自愿声明。 这是一个反身性陷阱——透明度本身把"技术不能"转化成了"选择不为"。

二、跨领域连接：这不是加密行业问题，是"点破客"（Point Break）式的道德结构问题

Austin 半开玩笑地引用《惊爆点》，其实无意中触到了本质。这部 1991 年的电影讲的是抢银行的冲浪者以"体制反叛"包装犯罪的浪漫化叙事。今天的加密安全事故正是同一个心理结构的重演：用"意识形态纯度"（decentralization）为财务损失做美学辩护。

更深的跨领域连接——这和中世纪的"教会庇护权"（sanctuary rights）如出一辙。中世纪欧洲，罪犯只要跑进教堂就能获得神圣豁免，因为教会声称自己是"另一种主权"。这个制度最终因为被系统性滥用（尤其被有组织犯罪利用）而在 16-17 世纪被各国废除。ThorChain 现在扮演的正是"数字教堂"——但历史已经演算过一次这个博弈的终局：当庇护结构被证明可以被少数群体系统性利用，社会最终会摧毁这个庇护结构本身，而不是修补它。

再补一个更冷的连接：保险精算学里有一个概念叫"道德风险的可观测性"（observability of moral hazard）。你能观测到的坏行为越多，保险产品就越贵——最终贵到不可持续。ThorChain 每一笔链上可追溯的洗币，都在为整个 DeFi 板块的"隐性风险溢价"计价。你以为你在看 388M 的损失，其实市场在悄悄把整个 permissionless swap 赛道的估值 discount 上调。

三、被所有人忽略的一层：量子威胁与本次事件的隐秘同构

Chris 在结尾抛出量子威胁看似跑题，其实是这场讨论最尖锐的一根刺，只是没人接住。

注意这个不对称结构： - BitGet 攻击：坏人伪造交易数据，让好人的授权系统自己签署了坏交易 - 量子攻击（Harvest Now, Decrypt Later）：坏人今天收集加密数据，等未来算力成熟后用你自己发布过的公钥破解你

这两者在结构上是同一件事——都是"利用防御方自己主动暴露过的东西反过来攻击防御方"。BitGet 暴露的是授权流程，ThorChain 暴露的是停机能力，公钥密码学暴露的是数学上的可预知性。

加密行业真正的系统性弱点，不是安全预算不够，而是它比任何其他行业都更依赖"透明性"作为信任基础——而透明性正在被 AI + 量子武器化。 这才是 Chris 那句"我们已经看到了 harvest now, decrypt later"背后没说完的话：加密行业正在为自己"一切公开可验证"的建筑美学，支付一笔我们还没开始计价的费用。

一个真正让人不安的推论：未来 5 年内，"选择性透明"（selective transparency，如 ZK 系）会从加密的技术分支跃升为整个行业的默认生存策略——不是因为隐私更好，而是因为完全透明已经成了不可承受的安全债务。ThorChain 事件之所以重要，是因为它可能是"完全透明公链"这一叙事最后的高光时刻之一。

📝 转录文本

开场与频道迁移提示

If you've enjoyed Bits and Bips these last few years, be sure to subscribe to its dedicated channels. All Bits and Bips content has now moved to the Bits and Bips channel and no longer plays on Unchained. Search Bits plus sign Bips wherever you listen and subscribe. We'll see you there.

一、BitGet 被黑事件概述

BitGet got hacked. On September 24th, attackers took roughly $388 million from BitGet, largely the contents of the hot wallets — not by stealing their private keys, but by spoofing transaction data. So BitGet's own approval process signed off on the withdrawals.

The hack reopened some of the neutrality debate around crypto after ThorChain refused to block the hacker's addresses while stolen ETH kept swapping into Bitcoin through the protocol.

So, one: the loss is about $388 million. No private keys were accessed, according to Gracie Chen, CEO of BitGet. And the attacker, quote, "used it to spoof transaction data and triggered our own authorization process to move funds out." She says it's, quote, "consistent with techniques used by DPRK-linked hacker groups." And it is currently the largest reported crypto theft of 2026.

BitGet's $464 million user protection fund covers the losses. BTC withdrawals reopened today. ETH is on the 29th, Tether is on the 30th, and everything else is on 10-2.

二、ThorChain 的回应与业内交锋

ThorChain. Gracie said, quote, "decentralization is a design principle, not a shield for facilitating known stolen funds. The industry is watching."

ThorChain responded: "ThorChain is permissionless. It doesn't censor by design."

To which Star of OKEx said: "ThorChain paused its own network after its May exit. Bitcoin cannot be stopped, but ThorChain can. It simply chooses when to do so."

And Michael Perklin said: "There's no active choice to sign. There is an active choice to turn off the machine."

Reminder for those who are not paying attention: 1.2 billion of Bybit's 1.46 billion path also ran through ThorChain.

A middle path was taken by Near with Intents, where of the 50 million hackers tried to route, about 166K got through, but 503K was frozen. And it says Near Intents are "permissionless infrastructure, but not with no boundaries," according to Alex Shevchenko.

三、Chris Perkins：安全是行业的根本瓶颈

So, I have a couple of thoughts here. We'll come back to the ThorChain part because I want to start with the bigger point, Chris. This is something you've been talking about for a while. When we see these attacks happen right now, the framework is either the attacker succeeds and gets away with the funds or they don't. But that just means they failed with regard to effort. And that's kind of the end of the story. That's a pretty favorable landscape for attacks to continue indefinitely because they either win or have very low cost. What do you think needs to change? Because this remains a theme that's really sapping the space.

It's kind of mind blowing where you have a new technology and people think that the rule of law, like laws just go out the window. It's like it doesn't matter because we have this new technology. It's crazy. I would argue that security is the one thing that is holding us back from — in this industry. I'll continue to argue it.

I really enjoyed the Near post. I retweeted it because they said, look, we moved as quickly as we could. We took the actions that we could because we know how detrimental it is to the system. This is like human nature 101. If you don't have security, guys, you've got nothing. Trust me, you can't have anything. There's no applications of anything else. So we got to solve for it. It's insane.

Look, I welcome — please, I'm begging you with tears in my eyes — if you have solutions, bring them forth. The only thing I could think of is to increase the surface area of the defenders and the counter attackers. Went back to the Constitution. Christian, Carlo and I published it. By the way, Crypto Dad's got a book coming out. I'm going to plug it because he talks about this throughout his book. There you go, Chris.

But the point is, we just don't have the surface area or the sophistication. The great thing about things on-chain is we know where those assets are going. We're starting to see some actors perhaps not doing the right thing, e.g. ThorChain — we'll address that here in a second. But you can trace these things, and if you can trace them, then you can hack them back.

And I'm very hopeful that the president — he put forth an EO that talked about leveraging the skills of the private sector. It was actually embedded in CLARITY. We'll see how that comes out with the sausage making. I'm going to be in Europe this week. I'll see Patrick Witt. Very excited to hear what he has to say about it. I'll report back next week. But we need to solve security or we've got nothing. Rules of law apply. Governance needs to get serious about it and they need to hold people accountable who allow the law to be broken.

Last thing I'll say about decentralization: either you're decentralized or you're not. If you're decentralized, you can't stop something. It's out there. The code is working. You just can't touch it. If you can stop it and you don't, maybe you're not decentralized. My two cents. Austin, back to you.

四、Austin Campbell：ThorChain 陷入自证困境

Yeah, I think — so to pick up on your last thread before I get to some of the other points — this is where I think the ThorChain folks have now got themselves in a serious pickle. You showed that you have the capability to stop your chain when you choose to do so, and you chose not to do so here. That is very different than infrastructure that has no off switch, right?

If you got exploited yourself and there was no way to fix it and it just happened, okay, you know what, I buy your claim of decentralization then. Because the point at which you really would use it is when you yourself are being harmed. And if you don't, that's pretty good evidence you can't.

However, ThorChain did. They transparently did. They stopped the chain when there was an exploit. They've done it. They showed they have the capability. And here they voluntarily chose to launder sanctioned funds for the North Koreans. There are consequences for that.

So, you know, to me, this is actually a much cleaner case for people at the DOJ than something like Tornado Cash, right? Where it was never turned off. This one's clearly — you have elective control over the network and you're choosing when to use it and choosing when not to use it. That's an obvious case, I think.

五、抢劫案 vs. 逃跑司机：法律责任的类比

Sorry, go ahead.

No, I was thinking about this. And again, I don't know every detail, in fact, and circumstance, but let's just do an analogy. If there are a bunch of bad guys that roll into a bank and they rob it and they take a bunch of money out of the vaults and they run off into a car and the getaway driver is there to take them away into the land of safety, usually the guy or the lady who's driving that getaway car is culpable as well. They get in trouble. Is that not the case here?

I don't know — and again, I don't know all the detailed facts and circumstances — but even if you don't rob the bank, but you're driving the getaway car, usually there's some liability there.

And there are some layers to it too, right? There's like knowing involvement and then there's gross negligence, right? If you're the guy at the rental car place and these folks roll up in like the dead-president's masks with guns, and they're like, "hey, we want to rent a car," and you rent it to them, you probably also have a problem. On the other hand, if they pretended to be relatively normal customers and you had no way to know, you probably don't.

So the other point of "well, we process all transactions" is — that is not the standard, to be very clear. Like you said, the law just doesn't go out the window. You can't just la la la la la la about these things.

So one way or another, I think there's going to be a reckoning coming for the people who are — call it the "DINOs," right, where you're claiming decentralization without actually having it. That's going to be a problem.

六、博弈论视角：没有惩罚，就没有威慑

Number two here, Chris, to your privateer's point: until we start inflicting consequences on the people doing this, they're going to continue doing it. This is just a classic game theory principle. If anybody is familiar with this, if you could defect in a game with no consequences to yourself for greater rewards, you will just do that over and over and over and over. And the way you stop that from happening is by punishing people for defecting.

You know, I was recently on stage at the Philadelphia Fed and I said this same thing, which is: to cause this to stop, we need to start allowing people to inflict consequences on the hackers. And there's two ways to do that.

We can do that through allowing companies to counter-hack them, which we are now working on. I believe it was on August 12th, President Trump signed a national security presidential memorandum about expanding capabilities to combat transnational cyber-enabled crime. And it lets participating companies run operations against them. Like we've talked about this — but you need to be able to counter-hack them and disrupt them.

The other, and call it more extreme version of this, is kinetic warfare against these people, right? If you knew every time I hack a crypto exchange there's a 5% chance a drone with a bomb on it comes through my window and ends me, that greatly changes whether you're going to be willing to hack a crypto exchange or not. And so consequences matter.

I think, given the persistence of the adversaries and their structure, this is not three dudes in a basement somewhere. These are nation-state actors or organizations of hundreds to thousands of people. We need to start inflicting consequences.

七、《惊爆点》梗与市场感知

Okay, can I just say: respect for the Point Break reference for the old people that were listening — with the president's mask and robbing banks. I caught that. Just wanted to say it's a great movie. Great movie. If you haven't watched Point Break, it is actually genuinely worth a watch.

But now, Ram, as a markets observer, you're an investor, you're trying to assess risk in this space. How does this change your perception of crypto if we don't fix anything?

It's 2026. It's embarrassing. Imagine going back to 2021. We said five years from now, would we have these issues? And here we are. What if we have these issues two years from now or four years from now or five years from now? Probability that probably is going to be there because of more social engineering, especially these AI-related capabilities which can impersonate humans really well. It's going to drive more adoption to ETFs away from the on-chain ecosystem.

八、中介化的反讽：去中心化理想被自身伤害

Yeah, it's more than that, right? We see it at my current firm. It's really sad, actually. And I don't think enough people are angry. People should really get angry about the way that our industry is getting abused. And I don't think they're angry enough, because a lot of people enter into our space because of the ideals — the ideals of holding on and controlling their own keys and holding their own assets and believing in decentralization in a world without intermediaries. And I totally get that.

But what the security situation is forcing — it's forcing intermediation, to Ram's point. It's forcing — and I don't mean to talk against my own book — but it's forcing folks to trust a big institution to safeguard assets. And look, I've said this all along, intermediaries do offer value. And that's the thing that we do. We provide safety and soundness. Maybe we can do it a little bit more robustly. We've got professionals doing it.

But what gets me angry is that it's really taking away choice for people. I mean, look at the Coldcard hack. You know, these are like OGs who did everything they thought was right. And it's getting very, very dangerous to self-custody. And I know so many people are in this space because that's what they want. That's what they believe in.

So I would like to see — you know, I thought the Near post, Illia and crew, well done. And I'd like to see more people taking that type of proactive action. And I'd like to see people get more angry and really take steps to fix the situation. Otherwise, we're going to be stuck in the land of intermediaries forever without that choice.

Yeah, I mean, if we idealistically built a decentralized system to prevent people from being abused by centralized actors, and the main outcome of that is people having all their money stolen by centralized actors — I do not think we achieved what we were going for.

九、社会契约与金融史的重复课

Yeah, it's like getting back to like core political theory — like social contract, you know. I'm going to use a government to provide me security and I'm going to hand over some of my rights, or I'm going to hand over some of my rights to an intermediary and I'm going to trust them. It forces this sort of social contract.

I think, you know, we've talked on this show before about how crypto is relearning some of the lessons of financial history. This is why centralized intermediaries and regulations were created in the first place. If the core feature of your system is that whoever is the most morally bankrupt and steals the most money becomes the richest, people are not going to use that system to transact. It just becomes something that's pointless.

And Chris, I think you're right. Actually, it should be a combination of being angry and also being disappointed at a lot of the current actors in this space for not having worked harder on this problem already. You know, ThorChain's a great example. If your response to this hack is to just throw your hands up and be like, "whatever, we're gonna collect some fees" — quite frankly, you should be blacklisted from this industry by everybody. Every single crypto exchange should blacklist a wallet that interacts with ThorChain ever, if that's going to be their response. Because that exact attitude will destroy this space over time.

Yeah, like it reminds me of my days in Iraq. Back in the day, every house was allowed to have three AKs, and that was fair because they needed it for security. Is that really the world that we want to go back to? It's not working. We got to fix it. We need more of a grassroots effort to stop it.

十、公链 vs. 半私有链：BIS 论点的隐忧

I would also say: if your goal is for public blockchain infrastructure to win, you cannot keep making the case for semi-private blockchain infrastructure, right? Because we're not seeing these sorts of hacks on the networks that have very strict in-and-out controls. Like Connexus at JP Morgan is not having this happen. We haven't seen it with Canton. We haven't seen it with all of the internal chains. You're making the BIS's argument for them if you won't control this stuff. And to me, I really think that's a second-order effect that the industry needs to grapple with.

Gracie calling out ThorChain — I think, obviously from the personal position of BitGet, I get that. But Star piling on, I think, was correct, right? Like this is the industry starting to grow up and be like, "no, you really do need to do better here." Because, Ram, to go back to the point you were making, which I think you were right about, kind of makes it hard for you to think this space is investable if this is going to be the security posture, right?

Yeah, it comes under confidence. Markets come under confidence.

Yeah. How much money would you guys leave at State Street if they were constantly letting your securities be stolen?

十一、量子威胁：地平线上的下一场风暴

Yeah, and then I think — I told you guys I've been spending a lot of time on quantum. Yes. Quantum's coming and AI is accelerating it. And we're already seeing — what are the bad guys doing? Harvesting now, decrypt later. And, you know, this is — we really got to get our act together, because that's real and it's scary.

Good news is: I think that crypto is going to actually lead us out of this challenge. The $500 trillion in post-quantum cryptography — that's about right now, $500 trillion in assets are being secured by public key encryption. That could be undermined. I do think that crypto will actually lead us out of that, because if only there was a concentration of cryptographers in an industry, probably know what they're doing.

But I feel like AI was the first real tool that the bad guys got. The good guys got it too. I think in the long term, we'll be fine, better off. But I think quantum is also lurking on the horizon. Now, I don't know if the bad guys are going to get it out of the gate — it'll probably stay controlled. But that's the problem: it's been state-controlled actors that have been ravaging our startups. So it could get worse in the future.

十二、节目结尾与赞助信息

If you like this segment, please like, subscribe, and tune in every Monday at 4:30 PM Eastern time. I'm Austin Campbell, the host of Bits and Bips, along with my friends, Ram Aluwalia and Chris Perkins, and our slate of exceptional guests. Every week, we're going to discuss macro, crypto, and the collision of worlds, covering topics that move markets and shape the financial landscape.

One more thing. We've got a listener survey open. It takes just a few minutes, it's anonymous, and it changes what we make next. Use the QR code on screen or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. The link is in the show notes.

Sponsor — 1inch Aqua:

$540 million. That's how much concentrated liquidity sat idle in a given week in the first half of this year. About 30% of the DeFi TVL, if you're wondering. That's according to Dune Research commissioned by 1inch.

But there's a solution. 1inch Aqua is the new shared liquidity platform. It lets LPs back multiple positions with the same token balance and keep their tokens in their wallet till a swap comes. Why does that help? Because LPs don't have to split their tokens across positions. They can cover more market conditions and pairs with their full balance. That means more activity across deeper liquidity.

See how it works at oneinch.com/aqua. Remember that providing liquidity carries risk and fees aren't guaranteed.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：ThorChain 不是"去中心化过头"，而是"去中心化的可证伪性"被自己亲手推翻
大多数评论者把这次事件读成"去中心化 vs. 中心化"的老掉牙争论，但真正的关键点在 Michael Perklin 那句极短的话里：**"没有主动签署的选择，却有主动关闭机器的选择。"**
这句话把 ThorChain 推入了一个哲学困境——**它一旦证明过自己能停机（May exit 事件），就永远失去了"我停不下来"这个抗辩权**。这在密码学里叫"承诺方案"（commitment scheme）：你一旦对世界公开过某种能力，就无法再声称你没有。ThorChain 的问题不是它做了或没做什么，而是它**在过去用一次停机，为未来所有"不停机"都盖上了自愿的印章**。
换句话说：**每一个曾经声称过 kill switch 的去中心化协议，都在为自己未来的每一次"不作为"预先签下了法律意义上的自愿声明。** 这是一个反身性陷阱——透明度本身把"技术不能"转化成了"选择不为"。
## 二、跨领域连接：这不是加密行业问题，是"点破客"（Point Break）式的道德结构问

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的信号：不是"增长"在说话，而是"倍数"在沉默

大多数人看到"标普四年涨90%"就本能地喊泡沫。但这份 presentation 里藏着一个几乎被主持人一带而过、却极具颠覆性的观察：股价涨了20%，估值倍数反而跌了20%。也就是说，这一轮涨幅完全由 earnings 撑起来，而不是由"叙事溢价"撑起来。

这与2000年、2021年是根本反向的两种物理定律。2000年是"倍数扩张 + 增长扩张"（双击估值），本轮却是"倍数收缩 + 增长扩张"（估值在冷却、基本面在加速）。这意味着市场其实一直在"半信半疑"地为AI定价——这恰恰是最健康的一种繁荣：怀疑越多，泡沫越少。真正危险的信号会是有一天 P/E 冲到 40，那时才该逃。

二、被彻底忽视的隐性经济学：数据中心正在补贴普通家庭的电费

这是全场最出人意料的一段：美国研究显示，数据中心容量每增加10%，居民电价反而下降40个基点。为什么？因为电网是一种"共享固定成本"——杆、线、变电站的成本是摊薄的。一个稳定、24/7、大体量的"客户"接入，等于把每千瓦时的分母做大。

这个逻辑值得跨领域联想：它其实是"Costco 会员模型"套用到能源基础设施上——大客户不是掠夺者，而是共同成本的稀释器。同样的原理可以解释：为什么高铁开通反而降低了周边货运价格；为什么亚马逊的物流反而压低了美国邮政的边际成本。"AI 抢电、抢水"的舆论叙事，可能是这个周期里被误导得最深的一件事。

三、真正的"贝叶斯信号"藏在一个几乎没人报的数字里：Carta tender 参与率只有 58%

主流媒体喜欢报"员工套现"，但这份数据反过来讲了一个隐藏的故事——42%的员工在有机会卖股时选择了不卖。这个数字比任何分析师评级都值钱，因为它是最接近内部信息的"用真金白银投票"。

跨域比较：在公开市场，学界公认最强的一类α信号是"insider buying"（内部人买入）。私募市场里，"tender 拒绝参与"就是它的镜像形态——员工放弃的是流动性溢价，赌的是延迟满足的复利。当58%的私募员工在做和Zuck、Musk一样的选择（拒绝短期市场纪律），你其实是在观察一个关于"耐心资本重新定价"的宏观现象。

四、一个几乎无人指出的悖论：AI 让"屏幕时间"这个指标本身死亡

Facebook、Instagram、TikTok 全靠"日均使用时长"定义消费者规模。但主持人无意间说出一句极重的话：deep research 任务在后台跑的时候，你可能正在开车、正在做饭。AI 时代最好的产品可能是"你几乎不打开的产品"——它在你不在场时替你工作。

这在跨领域意义上非常重大：整个数字广告的估值框架（CPM、DAU、engagement）建立在"人类注意力可被中介"这一前提上。当 agent 成为消费的中介人，广告业的估值锚点会从"眼球时间"迁移到"agent 决策权重"。Meta 与 Google 在此周期的分野，本质上不是"谁做得好 AI"，而是"谁的核心资产在 agent 世界里还有意义"。搜索广告可能会活下来（意图明确、直接可变现），而信息流广告则可能面对哲学层面的挑战——因为 agent 不会被"闲逛"。

五、被埋没的最反常识的一句话："the factory is the product"

Elon 多年前的这句话被 Alex 随口引用了一下，但它其实是整个 presentation 的暗线。AI 投资的正统叙事是"软件吞噬世界"，可这一轮的实质是"物理世界正在反向吞噬软件"：$90 trillion 的基础设施缺口、football field 尺度的工厂、SpaceX 100 亿投资路易斯安那——AI 让"原子经济"重新变性感。

一个跨领域的意外连接：这轮浪潮里最好的创业者，很多都来自 Tesla / SpaceX 体系。他们带来的不是"如何做产品"的知识，而是"如何管理物理复杂性"的直觉——供应链、资本调度、产能预测、工程进度。这个技能集在过去二十年被硅谷系统性地贬低（"我们不搞制造"），而现在成了最稀缺的α。这意味着未来10年最贵的招聘岗位，可能不是ML研究员，而是"能把工厂投产提前六个月的运营天才"。

📝 转录文本

AI, Infrastructure, and the Next Investment Cycle

a16z Podcast — 25 Key Slides from the State of Markets Presentation

Cold Open

"Eight of the top 10 valued companies in the world are US tech companies."

"Since ChatGPT came out almost 4 years ago, the market's up 90%, which is 17% annualized. The natural instinct is: well, that's got to come down. We're definitely in a hot period."

"This puts us in a new age of atoms. Global infrastructure investment needs are estimated at $90 trillion through 2040. This goes way beyond AI and data centers. It includes power, water, roads, transit."

"Live deployments at S&P 500 companies — that's at 69%. Now, if you go to the ultimate barometer, which is a metric tracked over time, that's actually only at 2%. AI is generating major revenue and savings. On the other hand, adoption is still extremely early."

"Today's opportunity is so much around taking these capabilities and harnessing them to build reliable services."

"That's all great, but is it a bubble? Um… um… um…"

Introduction

Welcome back to the a16z podcast. I'm David George. I'm here with my colleagues Sarah Wang, Alex Emerman, and Santiago Rodriguez.

Today we are walking through 25 key slides from our latest state of markets presentation: the earnings behind the market's rise, the scale of the AI buildout, the evidence of growing adoption, and what this cycle means for hardware, software, and the next generation of private companies. We'll explain what the charts show and discuss what we're seeing inside businesses along the way, so you can follow along whether you're watching or listening.

David: So, Sarah, Alex, Santi, thanks for joining me.

All: Of course.

David: The day this podcast goes live, we will be releasing our state of markets presentation. This is a now yearly tradition from our growth team where we synthesize the biggest trends in tech, AI, infra, and markets. Today we're just picking out a subset of interesting slides and having a discussion about them. So I would direct you to look at the whole version, which is filled with a lot of nuggets. The areas that we're going to discuss today are: macro — where we'll talk about capex, data centers, accelerating demand at a high level — and then on-the-ground takeaways, where we will discuss models, apps, and some vertical deep dives.

Macro Setup

Technology is driving an economy-wide investment boom, with rising earnings supporting market gains and AI demand pushing infrastructure spending far beyond earlier forecasts. Hyperscalers are investing all of their near-term operating cash flow to build out this capacity for demand that continues to outstrip supply in almost every case that we see. They are channeling this investment into chips, power, cooling, construction, skilled labor, and much more. This expansion coincides with a broader need to modernize physical infrastructure, creating opportunities across industries and potentially lowering shared costs for businesses and households.

So with that, let's jump in.

Slide 1 — Tech Is the Everything Cycle

David: First slide: tech is the everything cycle. Some of this may be a little bit obvious, but the numbers are somewhat striking at this point. High-tech equipment, software, and R&D now account for roughly 55% of US capital spending, which is just a staggering number. Tech is driving the investment cycle obviously across all areas of the economy — from software and models to power, construction, and industrial capacity. Tech is almost 40% of the aggregate value of the whole stock market in the US, and eight of the top 10 valued companies in the world are US tech companies.

So this is a broad story. You're seeing it in capex — this is heavily covered in the data center buildout. It's obviously heavily covered in the amount of capital that's been going into the model companies — together raising I think over $350 billion at this point. And just to put it into very deep historical context, because this is probably the analogy that we've seen the most of: this buildout just surpassed railroads as a percentage of GDP.

So, exciting times, massive buildout. We all happen to think that if you fast forward five to seven, maybe 10 years from now, we'll be looking at these numbers and they'll probably be 20x higher cumulatively.

Santi: Yeah, this does feel like the next chapter of Marc's software is eating the world. Over the last 15 years, software has transformed all these industries, but only a small fraction of the population could build it. None of us could. But today, look at us — we all have like a handful of automations running every night. So if you think about the software demand, that means a lot more compute, chips, power, construction. So it's no surprise to see the majority of investment now covered in tech.

Slide 2 — Is It a Bubble?

David: One of the questions that we get all the time from various audiences is: okay, that's all great, but is it a bubble? So the market has reached new highs, and at the same time that it has reached new highs, the trading multiples of the market are actually down. Stocks are up about 20% while multiples are down about 20%. What that means is the performance is driven by fundamental earnings, not by increased multiples. The S&P 500 earnings multiple is below 20 times.

So, if you just start with that — these are, in most cases, very high-quality businesses. It's nothing like the dot-com boom in that way, where some of the highest market cap companies in the world had their massive stock runups based on increases in their trading multiples and would trade in many cases for like a 100 times PE. That's not what's happening here. In contrast, some of the memory companies — which again are very cyclical — are trading, you know, for call it six times, seven times forward earnings. So very, very different.

Santi: And I think there's an important double click here where — since ChatGPT came out almost four years ago, the market's up 90%, which is 17% annualized. And I think anytime there's been 17% annualized growth for four years, the natural instinct is: well, that's got to come down, right? We're definitely in a hot period. But when you compare that to, as you said, the market trading for below 20 times earnings, growing 15% — this definitely feels a little different than maybe the 2021 period that was recent, or the 2000 period when multiples and growth were not really going together.

Slide 3 — Hyperscaler Capex Scale

David: So I mentioned the scale of the capex buildout in the context of the railroads. And if you fast forward to today, the software index is actually back to where it started the year, but it's really bifurcated into some companies that are deemed AI losers and some companies that are deemed winners. And the public market sometimes simplifies things a bit too much — but to your point, the AI winners are not just the ones that can improve their cost structures. They're the ones that are actually accelerating and capturing some of this net-new dollars up for grabs. If you're not really capturing, then you're probably not riding the wave.

David: Yep.

Slide 19 — Stripe's SaaS Renaissance

Sarah: Yeah. On the flip side, we wanted to showcase some private-company operating data that gives us a view of what customers are actually doing. There's a little bit of a narrative violation in Stripe's SaaS customer data, which actually shows growth accelerating into 2026 across both young and mature businesses.

Santi: Stripe calls it the renaissance.

Sarah: Oh, the renaissance. I actually quite like the renaissance.

Santi: I like renaissance. Yeah, it's very good. It's very good.

Private Markets: Staying Private for Longer

Slide 20 — Six Companies, $2.4 Trillion

Santi: If we talk — we've been talking about public markets a bit; Sarah talked about private market SaaS acceleration. We get a lot of questions around companies staying private for longer. So if you actually look at the top six companies today — Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, Revolut — by last-round valuation, they add up to about $2.4 trillion. This is more than the combined market cap of IPOs we've seen in the last 10 years excluding SpaceX, which adds up to $1.7 trillion.

So just the amount of activity that happens within our market — again, six companies, $2.4 trillion — it's almost as big as the Russell 2000, which is a big index in the public markets where there's hundreds of public managers that spend most of their time in. So it's increasingly exciting to just spend time in these late-stage champions that can keep investing in growth more so than maybe maximize short-term profit.

But David, you can talk a little bit about how we advise companies on the IPO — and when to stay private versus public.

David: Yeah, look, I mean, the IPO — especially for founder-led companies, one of the things that we've talked about and that I've written about is that the founder is the asset class at this point. So the bet that we make — and part of the reason that it's been a benefit for some of these companies to remain private — is they can many times take bigger swings in the private markets that have longer-duration paybacks.

Zuck and Elon are kind of obvious exceptions to the rule in the public markets. But the way you see it manifest in the numbers in companies like Databricks or Stripe is massive, massive new bets in new product areas. You can see revenue acceleration that happens as a result. You can do that in the public markets, but it's going to catch greater scrutiny. Obviously, Meta's stock price at the nadir got below $100 a share, when people were very, very skeptical about their investments in AR/VR.

For us, the way we talk about it with our founders is: just the IPO is another financing event. And what do you get out of being a public company, relative to what do you get out of being a private company? But clearly you can reach big scale in the private markets.

Santi: And there's some other companies that already talked about running themselves like they were a public company — with high focus on efficiency, and just basically every metric being tracked. There's also some companies that benefit from maybe public disclosing of financials and earning customer trust, both at the enterprise level and on a consumer level. I mean, Navan went public and we've seen a reacceleration just on the basis of some of the larger enterprises actually trusting them more because they're a public business.

David: Yeah. And then of course there are examples where capital needs over time could be very, very large. The capital pools in the private markets are very large and can serve the needs of many of these companies. But at some point, the capital needs may even get too big for the private markets — that's the public markets.

Slide 21 — Secondaries and Tender Offers

Santi: In the private markets, one of the things that we spend a lot of time in too is secondaries. There's two dynamics at play. One is: we see an increasing amount of companies holding tenders for their employees. So if they choose to stay private, allowing employees to get liquidity outside of the public markets.

And an interesting data point shown here is — participation in tenders tracked by Carta has only been 58%. So this is employees choosing not to take liquidity because they have so much conviction in the performance of their business. It's the opposite of — I think sometimes there's a narrative of like "employees cashing out" — and what we're seeing is actually employees choosing not to cash out because they believe in their company so much.

David: Imagine SF home prices if that was 100%.

Santi: Exactly.

David: It'd be hard. Exactly. Yeah. The tender offers that happen — we're obviously participating in these and leading these pretty frequently. So we think they're a good thing. They do serve two purposes.

One: for employees and prospective employees, it is sometimes hard to compete with the liquidity appeal of public-markets RSUs that hit your account on a net-tax basis every quarter. So it is a weapon of competition for the private markets that want to compete for employees, or retain their employees, with the public-market companies.

The other side of it is: we're advocates of sort of more-frequent resetting of your valuation. That keeps your private stock price fresh for a number of reasons. One, it's easier to talk about that with employees and prospective employees. But two, in the event that you want to do M&A like many of our companies have done, you have fresh currency that you can use.

Santi: Yeah, no, maybe just the other dynamic. I think people talk about the "secondary discount" quite a bit, because that's a dynamic that we've seen over the last five years. Where maybe coming out of 2021 and '22, '23, '24, the median discount to the last-round price in secondary markets was meaningful, because there was maybe like a round that was priced too high and it was out of date. But actually what you're seeing today is: when there are transactions in secondary markets, the discount to the last-round price is basically zero. Which just speaks to these valuations at which companies have raised that are fresh, and there's always net-new investors willing to pay that same price — which wasn't the case for the last couple of years.

David: Yeah, great point.

Everything Is AI

Slide 22 — AI = 86% of VC Deal Activity

David: So this is a fun slide that says everything is AI, computer. AI-related companies account for 86% of US VC deal activity in this 2026 snapshot, up from 65% in 2025. Obviously AI has become the dominant destination for venture dollars.

Santi: Yeah. But beneath that AI label, the opportunity has broadened a lot, right? So enterprise apps, consumer apps, but also services, semiconductors, power, defense. A lot of the attention goes to OpenAI, SpaceX AI, and Anthropic — but beyond that, our opportunity set has never been deeper and broader.

Slide 23 — Areas of Excitement

David: Last, we thought it would be fun just to talk about some of the areas that we're very excited about right now.

Consumer agents. Obviously we touched on some of the consumer work that will now be done by agents. You could call it long-running agents, you can call it autonomous agents, heavy-use consumer. If you take the perspective that you could have consumer agents do all the tasks that you wouldn't want to do, to give you things that you otherwise wouldn't have spent time or money on — it's very appealing. And I think that the distribution of this could happen pretty quickly.

Robotics. Robotics is an area where we're spending a lot of time and attention. We happen to think that it could be even larger than LLMs — but probably 3 to 5 years earlier. So we think over the next 5 years this is going to be a massive area of investment and excitement.

Autonomy. Autonomy is here. Self-driving works. It's a very exciting time. If you just take a step back and talk about the auto industry and transportation industry — this is one of the biggest industries in the world that we probably don't talk about as much, because we spend so much time talking about AI right now. But if you look at miles traveled by Uber and Lyft, or in Ubers and Lyfts, it represents about 1% of miles traveled in the US. I think with full networks of autonomous driving cars that are 14 times safer than human drivers, we expect that to expand by at least an order of magnitude in the coming years. Plus, there's 17 million new cars sold per year in the US, and I think over the next 10 years those will all be autonomous.

AI × Bio. This is a super exciting area. Obviously, the folks in the labs are talking about this. But new drug discovery, solving some of the most debilitating illnesses or diseases in the world, I think is a promise that we all are very hopeful for — that we'll see a lot of progress over the next 10 years.

Personal health. This is another one that I'm very excited about, for myself as a "healthmaxer." There's not been a great place or avenue to take all of the information about yourself, put it into somewhere, and get very hyper-personalized advice.

Enterprise diffusion beyond coding. And then lastly, diffusion into the enterprise beyond coding. This is one that, Sarah, you were talking about — we're so early in actual diffusion of the technology into the enterprise that I think it's going to be super, super exciting.

American dynamism. And then lastly, there's another area that is not inside the AI bucket, which is what we call American dynamism — the retooling of the entire American dynamism stack. We've been large investors in this area for a while. It's still just a small fraction — less than 5% of overall dollars spent in the military is sort of newer vendors like Anduril, Saronic, Castellan — and we expect that to grow dramatically as needs change.

Closing

So many areas of excitement. Obviously, we've been very active in this AI space, and we're optimistic about the effect that it's going to have on the overall economy. The buildout is massive, but we think it's going to be massively productivity-enhancing in the US.

So — it's a blast to hang out with you guys. Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的信号：不是"增长"在说话，而是"倍数"在沉默
大多数人看到"标普四年涨90%"就本能地喊泡沫。但这份 presentation 里藏着一个几乎被主持人一带而过、却极具颠覆性的观察：**股价涨了20%，估值倍数反而跌了20%**。也就是说，这一轮涨幅**完全由 earnings 撑起来**，而不是由"叙事溢价"撑起来。
这与2000年、2021年是根本反向的两种物理定律。2000年是"倍数扩张 + 增长扩张"（双击估值），本轮却是"倍数收缩 + 增长扩张"（估值在冷却、基本面在加速）。**这意味着市场其实一直在"半信半疑"地为AI定价**——这恰恰是最健康的一种繁荣：怀疑越多，泡沫越少。真正危险的信号会是有一天 P/E 冲到 40，那时才该逃。
## 二、被彻底忽视的隐性经济学：数据中心正在**补贴**普通家庭的电费
这是全场最出人意料的一段：美国研究显示，数据中心容量每增加10%，居民电价反而**下降40个基点**。为什么？因为电网是一种"共享固定成本"——杆、线、变电站的成本是摊薄的。一个稳定、24/7、大体量的"客户"接入，等于把每千瓦时的分母做大。

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] 毒品毒駕零容忍！邁阿密市長給台灣人的啟發：沒治安，談什麼拚經濟？Steven Meiner【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：他把「治安」当作最高级的经济基础设施

大多数人以为的因果链是：经济发展 → 城市繁荣 → 治安改善。 Meiner 悄悄把这条链条反向重排：治安 → 资本流入 → 财政盈余 → 更好的治安。

他不是在"平衡"治安和经济，而是把治安当成最底层的资产类别——一种城市的"无风险利率"。他对商会说的那句"我还没为商业做任何事，但我会是最亲商的市长，因为你们需要的是安全"，其实是在宣告一种资本定价逻辑：当一个城市能保证物权、人身与秩序的确定性，它就能以低"折现率"收割全球高净值人群。

Ken Griffin 移出芝加哥的公开理由不是税，而是犯罪——这条数据点被大部分评论者忽略了。税率是终点线上的博弈；治安是入场券。Miami Beach 卖的不是阳光和沙滩（那是佛州每个城市都有），而是"你的孩子夜里可以在街上走"这份底层信用。

二、跨领域连接：Broken Windows Theory × Capital Flows

Meiner 的策略本质上是把 1980 年代 James Wilson 和 George Kelling 提出的"破窗理论"扩容到跨州资本迁徙的宏观层面。

  • 微观版：一扇破窗不修，社区秩序信号崩溃，犯罪加剧。
  • 宏观版：一次未被起诉的重犯（"turnstyle"回旋门），资本对该司法辖区的信心崩溃，HNW 逃离加剧。

有趣的是，他还把治安的"边际收益"数字化了——度假税创纪录、酒店房价领先第二名 150 美元——这是把"秩序"折算成 P&L 的操作。城市治理正在被证券化：一个市长本质是在管理一支"城市 ETF"，居民和资本是流动性提供者，警察和许可制度是风险控制模块。

而他作为前 SEC 执法律师 17 年的背景，让这个类比不再是比喻——他真的用监管者的思路在为一座城市做信息披露和合规套利。

三、藏在最深处的一条线索：大屠杀记忆如何编码成城市规划

访谈里最容易被略过、但最具解释力的一段是他说自己"祖辈死于大屠杀"。

大多数听众会把这当作情感段落一笑而过。但如果你追踪他所有政策选择的共同底层结构，会发现——

他真正害怕的不是犯罪，而是"政府对人民失灵"的那一瞬间。

  • 增加警力 = 政府履行唯一不可外包的功能
  • 反对安全注射屋 = 政府不能给"缓慢的自毁"背书
  • 反对财富税 = 政府不能靠没收创造正当性
  • 精简许可 = 政府不能用摩擦惩罚生产者
  • 免费水上出租 = 政府应补贴流动性，而不是补贴消费

这套体系不是右翼保守主义模板，而是一种"创伤后的极简政府观"：政府要极其强大地履行极少数职能（人身安全），并在其他所有领域退出。犹太历史记忆里"我们相信过政府，然后被清算"的教训，被转译成了 21 世纪一座迈阿密海滩城市的施政哲学。

四、一个隐藏的战略双层结构

Miami Beach 表面在做"金融科技中心"转型，但仔细看它的现金流： - 旅游税 & 酒店税（老经济）→ 支付警力和基础设施 - 警力和秩序（护城河）→ 吸引对冲基金和 HNW（新经济） - 新经济人口→ 拉高房价，但不直接贡献市政营收（无州所得税）

这是一种"用旧经济的现金流补贴新经济的入场成本"的两层套娃结构。他反复强调酒店房价创纪录，其实是在提醒选民：别忘了游客还在为你们的低税生活买单。这层机制一旦松动（比如春假失控赶走游客），整个金融中心叙事的财政基础就会塌方。

五、一个"啊哈"预测

如果我的分析成立，Meiner 未来两年最大的政治风险不是税收、不是移民、不是华尔街回流—— 而是教育。

他自己都承认："如果学校跟不上，资本流入会被卡住。"

因为他建立的是一座为 CEO 迁徙服务的城市，而 CEO 不迁徙孩子的学校。当 Ken Griffin 已经在公开谈论"需要建新学校"时，这其实是资本对城市投的第一张不信任票的前兆——不是财政的，而是再生产的。

一座城市是否成功，最终不看它吸引了多少亿万富翁，而看亿万富翁是否愿意让他们的孙子在这里长大。Miami Beach 目前赢在"迁入"，下一场胜负在"扎根"。

📝 转录文本

毒品毒駕零容忍！邁阿密市長給台灣人的啟發：Steven Meiner 專訪

頻道：邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain

開場精華剪輯

Take action. Be the solution. Just be the mayor, guys. What are you waiting for? Why are you sitting at home doing nothing? Complaining.

I'm known as the law and order mayor. I have ancestors who were murdered during the Holocaust.

This is going to be the next finance hub of America. We're doing it right.

The wealth tax in California is having an impact and you're seeing a lot of high-net-worth individuals moving here from California because of that. Capital is flowing into Miami Beach and South Florida in a big way. Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Ken Griffin, they're all moving here.

—— What is the number one challenge you have right now? Attracting capital.

We don't create wealth in government. It's entrepreneurs. It's people. It's small businesses.

—— We don't want these big businesses to come. We don't want the super wealthy to come because they're just going to drive up living costs.

The disparity is becoming pretty extreme. That being said, to me, I don't look at it as we need to punish or tax more of the wealthy. That's not the answer to the issues.

Increase police visibility, enhance presence to make people feel safe and feel comfortable going out and enjoying our beautiful city.

—— I'm from Vancouver. One of the biggest issues in Vancouver, BC is the drug use problem. How do you approach that problem? What is your view on safe injection sites?

I am not in favor of that.

一、來賓介紹

We're very pleased to be joined by Stephen Miner, the 39th mayor of Miami Beach. We're going to be talking about the future of business, not just in Miami, but across America. Why are businesses flocking to Miami? What makes Miami unique and what can other cities do to replicate this success?

Co-hosting with me is Bonnie. Thank you for joining us.

Mayor Miner: Sure. Great to be here, Bonnie and David. Thank you.

二、Mamdani 是佛州最好的地產經紀？

David: Mayor Miner, I'd like to start by talking about why people think Mayor Mamdani in New York is the best real estate agent Florida could ever ask for. Does the data actually prove that or just were people just saying whatever they want?

Miner: Yeah, it's actually I think predated Mayor Mamdani, but yes, there's a lot of things that we're doing here in Miami Beach and in South Florida and Miami to entice businesses to move here, to have capital flow here.

For example, we're easing regulations. We're lowering taxes. We are providing a very... I'm known as the law and order mayor because we're cleaning up our city, making sure crime is going down, which it is. Our homeless population — we're getting people the help they need, but we're also not allowing people to sleep on the street. So we're doing a lot of things that make it very friendly for businesses and residents to move here, and we're doing it right.

三、法治與預算：如何兼顧？

David: Okay. Law and order. How are you doing that without blowing up the city's budget deficit? You've got to hire more police, pay them overtime, right? How are you balancing law and order versus out of control spending?

Miner: Right. So yes, the police is a big portion of our budget, but that's always been the case. Really, it's allowing our police to enforce the law.

For example, we used to have a problem during the month of March called spring break, but it wasn't college kids who were causing problems. And we made sure we gave the tools to our police to enforce the law. I reached out to the governor, asked him for state resources, which didn't cost us anything. So that was a huge help and we cleaned it up. The last three years has been a tremendous success.

Also, when you have success and you provide the safety, our resort taxes the last two months broke records. Our hotel room rate is actually the highest in the country right now and second place is over $150 behind us. That brings in revenue to the city. So when you offer that safety and a business-friendly environment, it actually helps us because we're bringing in more money to our city.

為何治安是核心議題？

Bonnie: Why is that important to you that law and order is in place?

Miner: Well, to me that was the number one issue. When I ran first for commissioner — there's seven of us, six commissioners and the mayor which I am — that was always my platform: increase police visibility, enhance presence to make people feel safe and feel comfortable going out and enjoying our beautiful city.

And also making sure cases were being prosecuted. We had a situation before that repeat offenders were not being prosecuted. It was basically a turnstyle. So I made sure that, in fairness, people who are repeating multiple crimes need to be held accountable. So we're doing that and it's having an impact. It's having a real impact on our streets.

Our residents tell me that all the time. Our visitors tell me that all the time. And of course, it's also good for business. And you're seeing that happen in real time where capital is flowing into Miami Beach and South Florida in a big way.

四、Ken Griffin 為何搬到邁阿密？

David: Ken Griffin from Citadel is doubling down on his Chicago to Miami move, especially following his feud with Mayor Mamdani of New York. Have you had conversations with Mr. Griffin on this issue?

Miner: So I spoke to him recently. I don't usually repeat conversations that I have with people, but he said this publicly many times. So I asked him straight out, less than two weeks ago:

"Is it really because of the crime in Chicago that you moved to Miami?"

He goes: "Absolutely. That is absolutely the reason. And here in Miami and Miami Beach, we have a level of safety."

And the other thing we talked about, and I'm very big of this: we can't take it for granted. Things can change. I used to live in New York. I used to live in Manhattan. Things were very safe when I lived there. And it's changed. It's changed a lot.

David: It's not because of the tax rate. [laughter]

Miner: Well, I didn't move because of the tax rate, but certainly you're seeing that the wealth tax in California is having an impact and you're seeing a lot of high-net-worth individuals moving here from California because of that. So we are the beneficiaries of all that.

You see Mark Zuckerberg moving down here. You see Jeff Bezos is here. They're all moving here, if not full-time, having a significant presence. Now, Ken Griffin from Citadel is saying that he's going to even move more of his base down to Miami where it could not be better for us right now. Everything is coming aligned.

五、貧富差距怎麼解？

David: What is your approach to solving the so-called income wealth gap? Different mayors and different jurisdictions have different worldviews on this. I look around Miami, there's super rich people, the ultra wealthy come here for a reason. But there's also those who are less fortunate. How do you close that gap without hurting businesses, without scaring away businesses?

Miner: Yeah, it's actually the issue of our time as a country. I was recently talking with some senators including Senator Scott and it's a hot button issue. It's an important issue and it's an issue that we need to solve to some extent because the disparity is becoming pretty extreme.

That being said, to me, I don't look at it as we need to punish or tax more of the wealthy. That's not the answer to the issues. Creating more jobs is actually a good thing, and that's when you have a Ken Griffin or other businesses that are migrating here — that's going to create more jobs and help everyone, including people coming out of college and getting their first jobs.

So that's what I am looking to do and create that environment that they can do that, and it's happening.

六、歡迎哪類企業？水上計程車政策

Bonnie: It's like this "I'm open for business" type of attitude, but what type of businesses do you prefer?

Miner: So we're seeing a little bit of everything. We're definitely seeing tech here — we're at a Consensus, at a crypto conference. We're seeing finance, certainly a lot of hedge funds moving down here and private equity firms. We're seeing some Class A office space opening up. There's actually a proposal for new development that would add a lot of high-quality Class A office space. We'll see if it has to go through the process for approvals. So we're trying to accommodate that level.

免費水上計程車

The other thing is, for example, I've worked several years — we recently launched a free water taxi. It leaves from Miami Beach to Miami. And I actually stopped by on the Miami side today and it's packed. These taxis are packed.

That's something that we're trying to offer people so that they can be able to move quickly between their jobs, their homes. And I'm actually working extensively to try to expand that water taxi significantly to be not just a Miami Beach–Miami thing, but an entire Miami-Dade County thing to help people get to their jobs, get to their kids' ball game, go see a Heat game or a Marlins game. I think that adds a lot of value. And the fact that it's free can really help people.

David: I'd love to see a drone taxi service, too. One day.

Miner: Maybe one day. Maybe one day.

七、預算赤字：加稅絕非答案

David: Going back to the budget issue, the Miami-Dade County is recording a budget deficit of about $400 million, right? Is higher taxes the answer?

Miner: No.

David: What is then?

Miner: So I'll give you an example. We actually lowered our millage rate. Millage rate is the property tax in Miami Beach. We only control about 30% of the tax because there's county and the school board, but the 30% portion that we control, we actually lowered that millage rate — the property tax rate — for the first time in 10 years. We refunded money to our homesteaded property owners — first time in 20 years we did that.

So we're actually giving money back, and that's with all the police resources and the high quality. I mean, you're in Miami Beach right now. You see the cleanliness. So we're offering those services, but we also tightened our belt. We said whatever is not necessary for our residents and businesses, we're going to tighten our belt. And everything else, we're not only going to keep steady, we're going to enhance — and we're doing that. And while returning money, raising taxes to me is never the answer.

八、市長的背景：律師、SEC、家族辦公室

Bonnie: Mayor, what is your background? Is it business? Why are you so familiar with all these numbers?

Miner: So I am an attorney. I have a business background because I worked for a couple of big firms in New York representing businesses, Fortune 500 companies. I was an SEC enforcement attorney for 17 years, and the last two years working for Farcus Group, which is a family office that is focused on renewable energy, solar, and electric vehicle charging. I'm involved actually with a fund relating to Israeli agriculture.

So my whole career, even as an attorney, has been focused on business. I feel very comfortable in that space, and I've been glad I've been able to utilize those experiences as mayor of Miami Beach.

為何離開紐約？

Bonnie: Why'd you move from New York?

Miner: I love the weather. I love the weather. I really, I have to say it. When I was a kid, my parents, we would come here twice a year to visit Miami Beach. Partly because it's magnificent. It's beautiful. You have the beaches. But also I'm Jewish. I keep kosher. So there's kosher restaurants. There's synagogues here. It was a very... And then when I got married, we did the same thing. We would visit here a couple times a year.

And every time I left, I had a sense of dread. I have nothing bad to say about New York. I loved growing up there. I lived in Manhattan. But to me, Miami Beach was always that very special paradise.

And it's great to see the metamorphosis — that Miami Beach was sort of this touristy great place to live, and now it's becoming a global capital on so many fronts: in tech and finance and also health and wellness. We are now known as one of the elite. We just had several high-level events and competitions during that month of March. Same places that we had this chaos and people jumping on police cars and shooting several years ago — we now had high-level competitions and asset management conferences. To see the change is spectacular.

九、對財經系學生的話：為何選邁阿密？

David: When I was graduating university, I studied finance in Canada. The recruiters were coming all over from Toronto and New York, Bay Street and Wall Street. Now, if you had to go speak to college students today and convince them to move to Miami Beach for finance in particular, what would your pitch be? Instead of going to New York, Chicago, Toronto, Singapore, Hong Kong — why should they move to Miami?

Miner: The pitch would be: we're at the stage — and it's only going to keep increasing — that this is going to be the next finance hub of America.

That's a heavy statement. Wall Street is always going to be Wall Street. But you're seeing the migration of every major asset manager moving here. And what's also key to me is that all the major players — the CEOs or the founders of their companies — are all planting roots here. So it's going to be a natural migration that they're going to open offices here if they haven't already.

And then you're seeing the high level quality of life. Taxes are much lower. So what we're seeing is: in certain places like New York and California where they're raising taxes, at least in Miami Beach — and I think for most of South Florida and Florida in general — we are actually focused on lowering taxes.

十、政治人物 vs. 民選官員

Bonnie: Should we have more politicians that are good with numbers, businesses, law? Should we have that?

Miner: I think it's important. I can't be in someone's mind — another elected official — and I always refer to myself as an elected official as opposed to a politician. You can... to me there's a distinction, and so I always call myself that.

But I think there's a certain cache maybe to be a populist and talk about just "tax the rich." But in my studies and my business experience, but also in studying business and history — that doesn't work. It doesn't work. It doesn't help job creation. People vote with their feet. Just because you tax them in one place, they're going to just move. And you're seeing that happen, and we're the beneficiaries for it right now.

用 AI 精簡許可流程

We're also trying to ease regulations. For example, I called a special commission meeting — that's when we sit together as a body and vote. I called the special commission meeting to streamline our permitting process because we've got businesses who want to move here. We want to make sure it's easy for them to move here.

So we're trying to incorporate AI and get these things — right now it could take weeks if not months depending on the complexity — we want to do it within a matter of hours instead of days and weeks.

十一、平凡員工也能受益嗎？

David: Well, businesses, hedge funds, corporate entities, tech companies — they want to move here to Miami. But what about the average employee and salary man? Why should they move to Miami? What business incentives and job incentives are you providing to the average day worker?

Miner: Yeah. So in Miami Beach, we're actually offering incentives to the employer. There is an incentive program if people bring a certain amount of high-paying jobs. And it's not that high paying — it's actually just about 125% above the mean salary in Miami-Dade County or the state of Florida, depending on the metric. And you really only have to bring like 10 jobs. So we're offering the incentives to the employer.

住房負擔

As far as housing, there's still pockets. It's becoming very expensive, certainly, and certainly the ultra wealthy homes have literally doubled and tripled, but there's still pockets of affordable housing. We've actually tried to put an affordable housing and workforce housing stock available. We opened up recently one in Collins Park.

The state actually did that with Live Local — offering developers extra height and density if they put in 40% workforce housing. So it's tough to keep up. It's a nationwide problem, but we're certainly trying to keep up here in South Florida.

十二、Trump 的住房建設命令能落地嗎？

David: On that issue, the Trump administration issued an executive order in March removing regulatory barriers to affordable home construction. The objective here is to reduce bureaucracy and zoning bureaucracy to incentivize builders to build housing supply like you talked about. How can that be applied to the state and city level in Miami's case?

Miner: To me, anything that removes bureaucracy — obviously keeping safety, and I'm sure the executive order contemplates that — but anything that can remove the bureaucracy, I'm all for. I'm a big believer that government has a strong role, but that strong role is really providing the incentives and the platform for private businesses to flourish.

David: Can you give us some examples? Surely developers are probably approaching you and your office to say, "Hey, Citadel is moving, XYZ tech company's moving. We need houses now. We need apartment buildings. We need complexes. Can we get zoning to expedite?" Have you had these conversations? What do they sound like?

Miner: We do. Really there's two sets. There's within our zoning laws — but generally, Miami Beach is very valuable land. We're a seven-mile island. We're kind of mostly built up. So you really have a situation where when they're redeveloping, it's often not going to be affordable housing.

What we're seeing though is under the Live Local Act from the state, you are seeing some developers coming in trying to take advantage of that. That is actually not something that comes to a commission vote. Those are done administratively — that's by state law. So you're going to see some product come online that's going to be affordable housing, and I think that's going to benefit a lot of people.

十三、最大挑戰：教育系統

Bonnie: What is the number one challenge you have right now attracting capital?

Miner: I think it's keeping up with the educational system — the universities certainly, but also really starting with first grade. Because the schools have waiting lists. The top tier schools — public schools actually have lost some students because a lot of students have gone to private schools and charter schools, but the high-end sort of the "have have."

So I think we really need to keep up with that. I've heard Ken Griffin and others talk about the need to create new schooling. But that to me — if we don't get that done, that could impede the capital flowing in.

David: That's the long-term vision. What about short term? What could impede it right now?

Miner: Right now, I think we are in a sweet spot in Miami Beach and in South Florida. I actually don't see... I only see growing momentum. It's taking off. It's exponential at this point.

Obviously everything is an unknown. I've been meeting — interestingly — not just nationally, I've had capital and also residents from foreign countries who've met with me saying they're looking to move their base of operations here. And sometimes they ask me the same question you just asked me: "Is there anything — are we safe here? Is this the place?" And I'm like, right now this is the safest bet in my opinion in the world: Miami Beach and South Florida. But nothing is forever. You're seeing other parts of our country, other parts of the world that unfortunately when political leaders make decisions could have severe consequences — for the negative or the positive. Right now in South Florida, we're big-time positive.

十四、回應反對聲音：企業進來會不會讓小人物更苦？

David: Now, we're talking about the benefits of businesses coming to a city. But there's a lot of people out there — not just in Miami, but New York and other places — who would probably say: "We don't want these big businesses to come. We don't want the super wealthy to come because they're just going to drive up living costs on a very small piece of property and land like Miami Beach that's already built up. Our living costs are going to go up. Why should we care? Why should you welcome the businesses and hurt the little guys?" How would you respond to that?

Miner: I did hear that actually, shortly after I got reelected as mayor this past November. I put out a social media post — and they ended up having a billboard on Times Square from me saying "We are open for business in Miami Beach." And there were people who had that reaction like, "Why are you trying to bring these businesses down here? We're busy enough. We have enough traffic down here."

To me, the businesses creates jobs. So that is an incentive. And I'm always looking at everything from a lens of safety and law and order. And right now things are really good. But things can change too. To me, when you have good businesses, you have good jobs — that helps everyone and it creates a safety net. And that's one of the reasons I think why you're seeing Miami Beach becoming one of the safest cities in America.

免費交通 vs. 免費雜貨？

Bonnie: Okay. So let's say things get more expensive — I'm not saying they will, but let's say they do. Groceries go up, rent goes up, etc. Would you do anything in the New York playbook? Would you make the metro and buses free, for example? Are you going to go that route?

Miner: Well, for example, the water taxi — that was my initiative. I worked on it for 5 years before launch, and I had a lot of pushback. It's free, and I continue to have pushback because I'm looking to expand this and I keep hearing, "Well, you're going to have to charge this, you're going to have to charge that." And I've been resisting that. I think it needs to be free for people to want to utilize it.

So our residents are utilizing it. Our tourists are utilizing it. I mean, maybe if you charge a dollar, it wouldn't make a difference. But if you start charging $5, $10, people are not going to use it.

So yes, there are certain things. Free grocery stores? No. I don't think you're going to see that under my leadership in Miami Beach. No, you're definitely not going to see that. But I think free transportation, especially because in comparison to other means of transportation, it's really cheap. And I think it's something that we can utilize and help people.

十五、下一步大計劃：基礎設施與交通

Bonnie: What else would you want to work on? Like, what is the next big plan you have in mind?

Miner: So infrastructure — it doesn't sound exciting, but we're a 110-year-old city and some of our pipes are 78 years old. So we're working on that. We've actually completed several world-class parks recently, which our residents and tourists can enjoy.

But transportation is a biggie because traffic — we've become so popular and it's not just Miami Beach, it's really all over South Florida. Traffic is pretty severe. So the transportation mobility is certainly high on the list.

But I am very focused on the business and the capital flow here because I do believe the job creation and the job growth is essential for Miami Beach. And like you said, our moment is now. It's happening and we need to capitalize on it.

十六、溫哥華來的問題：毒品怎麼管？

David: Let me present to you a problem a little bit farther from Miami. I just want to see how you approach it. I'm from Vancouver. One of the biggest issues in Vancouver, BC is the drug use problem. No doubt you've heard about it. How do you approach that problem? Walk us through A to Z.

Miner: Well —

David: And obviously I'm not saying it's happening in Miami, but let's say you're mayor of a city that has this problem.

Miner: Sure. I've actually read up on this a bit. One is to try to stop the flow of illegal drugs into our country. You're never going to eradicate it completely. Certainly, I would never condone drug use to begin with — it is illegal. But unfortunately what happens is some of these drugs are laced and create a compounding effect and they're just lethal. So certainly if somebody's going to use drugs, you just don't want them to have an overdose from it.

I think partly it's also enforcing our laws. For example, when I became mayor, I wouldn't say we had a major drug problem, but we had pockets in our city where there were drug dealers. I'd hear it from our residents. That was something that I worked closely with our police department to make sure that we were able to arrest those drug dealers, move them off our street, and make sure they're prosecuted — because often that was happening too, they weren't prosecuted. So we're making sure all that's done.

I also brought an initiative that we're going to be rolling out fairly soon to have canine dogs because they can sniff out the drugs. It's very hard — you have to have undercover officers try to buy, but the canines can actually just smell the drugs. So it's very important to move the drug dealers. If you don't give them an avenue to make their income and their livelihood, then you're going to get them off the streets.

安全注射屋：明確反對

David: One more question. What is your view on safe injection sites? If the government supplies some drug — doesn't matter what it is — then you eradicate the need for illegal dealing.

Miner: I am not in favor of that. I am not in favor of that.

David: Are you? Personal opinion, but that is happening in Canada.

Miner: Yeah, I am not in favor of that. Unfortunately, there's always going to be some level of illegal drug use. People are going to have the need. We're all human beings. That being said, I look at it as not a healthy recreation. It is not good for someone. And we shouldn't as a government be promoting it and utilizing it.

I think the better source is to try to help people who have that addiction and try to wean them off of it. And certainly if somebody is selling it, then they're committing an illegal act and they should be prosecuted for selling it. The user is a little different — I think there you're trying to get them the help they need so they don't continue to become addicted to something that is harmful to their health.

十七、對亞洲企業家的邀請

Bonnie: For someone in Asia watching that owns businesses, should they move to Miami Beach?

Miner: Come on down! [laughter]

Bonnie: Should they?

Miner: I obviously — I'm mayor of Miami Beach, so you could say that I'm biased, but I'll tell you: when I have people coming here... I was in Israel recently for a mayor's conference. It was actually mostly non-Jewish mayors from 13 different countries around the world. And I'll tell you, there's something special about Miami Beach.

Every time we'd meet either residents there or diplomats or elected officials, people would go around the room, and when I would introduce myself — Miami Beach — the whole room would smile. There's a recognition that something special is happening here.

It's a very safe city. Literally, every group considers it to be a safe haven because we take it very seriously if someone commits a hate crime here, which is very rare. But also the capital flow, the income that's happening here, the paradise, we're right next to the beach. You literally have everything that you want here. People are happy. People are enjoying life and making money doing it.

十八、稅收哲學：政府是納稅人的信託人

Bonnie: Is tax something you focus on?

Miner: Yes. So in Miami Beach, there's state taxes, there's county taxes, and then there's Miami Beach. We control, as I mentioned, a portion of the millage — the property tax rate. We want to make sure that we're being efficient with our residents' funds. It's their money.

And like I said, I was very proud that we were able to return money — first time in 20 years — lowered the tax rate for the first time in 10 years. I was very proud of that. I think that shows you the direction that we're heading.

Somebody actually called me — it was $500 that we returned. Somebody said to me, "Does it really matter?" For some people it does matter — $500. But either way, I said, "You know what? Yes, it does matter, but we're also making a statement." We're making a statement here that it's your money and we're the trustees of it. We're going to utilize it to the best we can, but then we're going to return it to you if we have a surplus.

Because we are looking to lower regulations, make it easier for people to live their life, to open a business, and also to enjoy the wealth that they're creating. We don't create wealth in government. It's entrepreneurs. It's people. It's small businesses. And we have incentive programs for small businesses. It's very important to us. We're not just looking for the big player. We're looking for the mom-and-pop store as well. And we're seeing that thrive in Miami Beach.

十九、教育：全美警訊，邁阿密如何應對？

David: You mentioned education earlier. Let me just give you a few statistics. This is from 2025.

American schools got a big fat F on the report card this week. Reading proficiency for eighth graders hit the lowest level in the 32 years that the federal government has been tracking. US high school seniors are performing at the worst levels in decades. 45% score below basic in math. 22% are proficient in math. And only 35% are proficient in reading.

I know this is a nationwide statistic. Bringing it to the city level, what can Miami do to make education good for the public sector?

Miner: Yeah, fortunately our schools here — we have a lot of private schools, public schools — we're actually doing pretty well, better than the national average.

But we also in Miami Beach, even though the school board (which is a county entity) runs the public schools here, we actually spend several million dollars a year in after-school programs in STEAM Plus. We're offering programs in science and technology and engineering because we feel it's so important. It's an incentive for families to move to Miami Beach or stay in Miami Beach when they're looking at other options.

Also, we are offering Pre-K. We are the only city in the entire state of Florida that supplements VPK, which is something the state of Florida offers. We actually offer a stipend as well for Pre-K students, which is so valuable. The studies all show that is an integral age for higher education.

Our schools are doing well. If you look at our schooling and what our students are doing after they leave high school and going on to college, we are definitely educating our kids. And it's something we have to continue doing because that's the future of our country.

AI 如何改變教育與政府？

Bonnie: How is AI changing the education system?

Miner: That's a good question. I think it's changing everything. I see my kids utilizing it, although they are very careful. The schools tell the students that they check it. They have programs that check their work to make sure they're not utilizing AI. That being said, it's still a great resource for education.

I mean, everyone uses it. I've started using it a lot more. I do check my work though to make sure — because I want to create my own content and not have to rely. But AI is changing the world. It's only going to continue.

Just on ourselves, I brought legislation last year that we should incorporate AI in every level of our government. I actually was meeting with — I hope he doesn't mind me saying — Jack Hidary, used to be with Google and Eric Schmidt. He's actually offered to spearhead and help out incorporating AI into our government, because that's his expertise. It's something we can utilize — like I said with the permitting, I want it done in hours.

二十、最引以為傲的政績會是什麼？

David: My final question to you before I pass it back to Bonnie: if in the future when you leave office you'll look back at your time and people will ask you, what is your proudest accomplishment as mayor of Miami Beach — what would that answer be?

Miner: That I created the environment for people to enjoy their quality of life and for businesses to grow here.

And to me, the first step was the safety. I remember I spoke with the Chamber of Commerce shortly after I was elected and I was already putting in all these different law and order initiatives, and I said, "I will be the most friendly business elected official you will ever meet." And they looked at me like... because I hadn't done anything yet specifically for business. I said: "Because you need the safety. If people don't feel safe and don't see the safety, they're not going to want to live here. They're not going to want to invest here."

I think that has created the environment that people are excited to be here. They're spending money. Our hotels — as I said, our hotel room rates through the roof. We're breaking records on resort taxes. Businesses and capital is flowing in here. And pretty much I think everyone's happy with that. Even though the house has come up — but think about it, people own homes, their house in the last four or five years has doubled or something like that. So pretty much everyone's excited about that.

二十一、大屠殺記憶與治安執念

Bonnie: I love what you're doing, but what I like to do is understanding why people do what they do. What is that personal story that is so important to you that you keep on emphasizing safety?

Miner: It's interesting. I grew up, I guess, when a level where my parents — we'd walk down the street and we'd see a police officer, they would say, "Can you please go over to the officer and say thank you?"

I guess it was always a recognition to me — and I'm a big student of history — that unfortunately governments can turn on a people. I have ancestors who were murdered during the Holocaust. So I know that you need a good government and a good police force to keep people safe.

And that's what happened. I'm going to turn 55 next month. If you told me 10 years ago that I'd be the mayor of Miami Beach, I would have looked at you like, "What?" It was not on my radar. But literally, it started that in my little neighborhood in Miami Beach, I wanted to see more police and I wanted more lighting so people would feel more comfortable. And I just tried to do it without running for office and I couldn't get it done. And that led me down this path that I ended up saying, "You know what? I'm going to run for office."

And that was the first thing I did — make sure there was more police out, which you're seeing if you drive around Miami Beach and you walk around Miami Beach. And in many parts of our areas, I brought initiatives to have better lighting so people could feel safer at night to be able to walk their dog, to walk their kids in a stroller, or to go to a business and enjoy a dinner.

二十二、結尾：別抱怨，就去當市長

Bonnie: I love that. Don't complain. Just be the mayor. Like, run for—

Miner: Yeah. Take action.

Bonnie: Be the solution. Just be the mayor, guys. What are you waiting for? Why are you sitting at home doing nothing? Complaining. Anyway, thank you so much, Mayor Miner. It was an honor to meet you. Appreciate it.

## 一、最反直觉的观察：他把「治安」当作最高级的经济基础设施
大多数人以为的因果链是：**经济发展 → 城市繁荣 → 治安改善**。 Meiner 悄悄把这条链条**反向重排**：**治安 → 资本流入 → 财政盈余 → 更好的治安**。
他不是在"平衡"治安和经济，而是把治安当成**最底层的资产类别**——一种城市的"无风险利率"。他对商会说的那句"我还没为商业做任何事，但我会是最亲商的市长，因为你们需要的是安全"，其实是在宣告一种**资本定价逻辑**：当一个城市能保证物权、人身与秩序的确定性，它就能以低"折现率"收割全球高净值人群。
Ken Griffin 移出芝加哥的公开理由不是税，而是犯罪——这条数据点被大部分评论者忽略了。**税率是终点线上的博弈；治安是入场券**。Miami Beach 卖的不是阳光和沙滩（那是佛州每个城市都有），而是"你的孩子夜里可以在街上走"这份底层信用。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、消费者信心的"精神分裂"：现状109.3 vs 未来63.6，藏着一场"预期泡沫"

真正让我震撼的不是12年新低这个数字，而是"当下感受"和"未来预期"之间前所未有的鸿沟——这是一种典型的"预期泡沫"结构。当人们对现状的评价还算可以（109.3只是2016年水平），但对未来的看法却跌破2015年低点时，说明痛苦并非来自现实，而是来自对现实的想象。

历史上，这种"感知—现实"错位只有两种收敛方式：要么现实追上悲观（衰退到来），要么悲观追上现实（情绪反转拉动一波"松了口气"行情）。而判断走哪一条路，行为数据比调查数据更诚实——视频里那个被一带而过的旅游意愿数据（5年稳定在40%-45%）其实是全片最值钱的一张图：嘴上说着看衰，脚上却继续买机票。这在行为经济学里叫"stated preference vs revealed preference gap"，通常预示着调查数据被过度解读。

二、Williams讲话和DOTS智能体是同一件事：都是"永远在线的预期管理器"

一个反直觉的连接：美联储和OpenAI，正在向同一种形态进化——"always-on 预期管理系统"。

Williams在市场恐慌拐点公开讲话，本质上是把美联储从"周期性政策制定者"改造成"实时情绪调节器"，跟随市场、微调预期、避免任何一次意外波动累积成危机。而OpenAI推出的DOTS——"每个员工的分身，24/7在线"——是把这套逻辑搬进企业内部：不再是员工工作8小时后交付结果，而是知识工作变成一条永不停歇的预期与执行流。

跨领域看，这两件事都是"离散决策"向"连续调节"的范式转移——就像模拟信号取代数字开关，或者从"周月度补货"进化到"实时供应链"。当决策周期从"月"压缩到"分钟"，波动率的性质就变了：不是消失，而是被吸收进底层结构。这也解释了一个悖论——为什么MOVE指数（106）远未破顶，但每一次小波动却比过去感觉更剧烈：因为噪音被高频消化了，剩下的都是真正的信号。

三、AI产业正在走完"从coding到agents"的S曲线——但这条曲线的坡度，是被API价格下降"偷偷推动"的

视频里有一句话极其关键但很容易被忽略："Agent真正落地的前提，不是模型更强，而是每个token承载的intelligence上升到一定阈值。"

这是一个隐藏的"AI摩尔定律"。真正推动智能体爆发的不是GPT升级，而是"单位智能成本"跌破了某条临界线——就像1990年代宽带带宽跌破临界线后，YouTube才成为可能；就像2000年后GPU算力/美元跌破临界线，深度学习才能启动。

更值得关注的是他提到的一个跨领域类比：OpenAI Marketplace = 智能体的App Store。但我想推得更远一步：这不是App Store 2.0，而是一次"通行费经济"的复兴。想想历史上大运河、丝绸之路、苏伊士运河——凡是流量必经的窄口，都会孵化出最赚钱的收租者。AI agent的窄口在哪里？在于"任务被谁翻译成执行链"这一环。谁掌控了这个翻译层，谁就是数字时代的君士坦丁堡。所以OpenAI这次发布会真正的"王炸"不是DOTS，而是那个只有30家公司参与、看起来还很初级的Marketplace雏形——它是在圈地，圈的是未来所有智能体路过时必须缴纳的税。

四、一个额外的意外观察

视频用"模糊正确"这个词描述持仓判断，其实这就是贝叶斯思维的口语化版本——不追求精确底部，只承认"当前处于低位区间"这一后验概率。但更妙的是，同样的思维方式如果用在消费者信心指数上：不用问"是不是衰退前夜"，只需承认"当前身处高度悲观区间"，那么组合最优解就变成——在情绪最悲观时增加实体经济Beta（消费股）、在债券波动最高时降低久期风险，与视频结论恰好相反。这两种"模糊正确"是否兼容？留给读者的一个思考题。

虽然海文我是一直强调说我们不给市场指引、不给市场指引，那其实在上一次9月份的联储会议里边他聊得非常的明确——其实从他上任到现在为止，6月份的联储会议、7月份的联储会议、8月份的 Jackson Hole 会议，一直在给市场信号。他已经说，他说的非常的明确，其实我一直在给你们信号。所以他不是不给市场指引，只是市场没有接收到他给指引的那种渠道或者说话术而已。所以他是一直给指引的。

所以接下去我们就看还会不会有更多的美联储成员出来去调节市场这个预期。当然接下去我们还会看到 CPI 数据，那 CPI 数据包括 PPI 数据也会影响到十月份到底是加还是不加。但我个人还是倾向于十月份是不会加。主要另外一点还是十月份会有中期选举，没有必要在中期选举之前一定要去进行加息，真的没有必要。如果真的有那么急切性的话，9月份应该直接加50个基点，而不是等到10月份再去进行25个基点这个加息，急切性是不在那边。
